note: Akananuru 296's friend turns the hero away because he bathed in the great Vaigai with the dark girl (பெருநீர் வையை அவளொடு ஆடி) and the talk is like Koodal's clamour; Paripadal 10.19-23 lists chaste wives and courtesans (பதிவத மாதர், பரத்தையர்) going together to the Vaigai at Koodal.
teaches: Since the festival put wives and courtesans in the same flood openly, the friend's charge in Akananuru 296 cannot be the bathing itself, a licensed public pleasure, but the companion he chose, so the akam poem turns a shared civic rite into private evidence.

note: Akananuru 195: the mother of the eloped girl, after picturing the other mother preparing her house for the couple, asks the diviner whether the youth will bring the girl first to her house or take her to his own (எம்மனை முந்துறத் தருமோ? தன்மனை உய்க்குமோ?). Thinaimalai 90 asks the same question in nearly the same words.
teaches: The venba keeps the Akananuru mother's question almost word for word while dropping the rival mother's preparations and her own years of nursing, which shows that by the later anthology the question to the diviner had become a fixed turn of the eloped girl's mother that could stand without its reasons.

note: Kuruntokai 32 says appearing in the street on the palm-stem horse is blame (பழியே) for the man; Kalittokai 58 has the man say riding it will fix the blame on the girl (நீ படு பழியே).
teaches: On a defensible reading the two disagree about whom the madal shames, the rider or the woman, which shows the threat worked as leverage precisely because the disgrace could be made to fall on her household.

note: Kar Narpathu 12's friend takes the dark clouds rising on the right (ஏரும் வலம்) every day as a sign beyond doubt of his coming; Ainkurunuru 469's cloud rises on the right (வலன்ஏர்ப்பு) to bring him.
teaches: Kar Narpathu treats the rightward rising cloud as evidence to be read, Ainkurunuru as an escort that brings the man and an occasion to go out and watch, so the omen of the right side could serve the friend both as proof and as a reason to act.

note: Purananuru 25 asks whether Chezhiyan's spear stopped short of further ruin when he saw the widows beating their breasts and cutting their hair; in Patitruppattu 26 the poet himself says நோகோ யானே, I grieve, at the enemy land the Chera's warriors ravaged, whose people blame the season.
teaches: Held together, the two show that pity for the conquered had a place inside victory praise in two forms, as the king's hoped-for restraint in the Pandya poem and as the poet's own grief in the Chera one, and in neither as blame of the king.

note: Both name the bewildering evening (மருண்மாலை, மருள்மாலை). Kural 1222: the woman asks the sad-eyed evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 27: the friend calls the darkening rainy evening the sign the man set for his return.
teaches: The same evening the Kural's woman mourns as a fellow sufferer abandoned like herself is presented by the friend as the very token of his return, which shows that the evening's meaning in love poetry depends on who is speaking and whether she still trusts him.

note: 205 says the bard does not want even the three kings' gifts if given without regard (பெட்பின்றி); Kural 1057 says the heart rejoices on seeing those who give without scorn.
teaches: The Kural states the receiver's joy at a gift given without contempt; 205 turns it into a condition of acceptance, so the manner of giving decided whether a bard would take the gift at all, not only how he felt about it.

note: Kalittokai 95 has the husband say he only watched a quail fight (குறும்பூழ் போர்), and the wife turns each kind of quail fight into a figure for his affairs; in Paripadal 18.12-14 the man says he looked at the peacock and at a quail dazed with revelry, and the woman looked at him as a stranger.
teaches: In the Kalittokai the man's watching of birds is an alibi that the wife exposes, while in the Paripadal his gaze at birds is a lover's thought of her that he can explain away, so the pair shows the same excuse of bird-watching used once for a lie caught and once for a sulk mended on the god's hill.

note: In Akananuru 388 the young hunter asks the girls on the millet platform whether a tusker wounded by his arrow has passed by their field; in Thinaimozhi 8 the friend answers that no bleeding tusker came this way.
teaches: The long poem gives the pretext question and the short one gives only the reply, which a reader can only read as a reply because the question is a fixed form; together they show the wounded-elephant question as a standard opening the girls know how to parry.

note: Kural 1102 has the man say that this jewelled girl is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes; Natrinai 247's friend tells the man that for the girl's pallor there is no medicine other than him.
teaches: Read together, the cure that is also the cause belongs to both lovers, and the Natrinai shows the claim used as pressure: what the man says of her in delight, the friend turns back on him as an argument that only marriage can treat the girl's sickness.

note: Kural 1112: the man scolds his heart for reeling at flowers, thinking her eyes resemble what many can see. Kalittokai 45: the friend asks whether he ruined the girl's eyes because they resembled the flowers of his hill's springs (மலர் ஏய்க்கும்). On one reading the claims are incompatible: the Kural's lover refuses the likeness as beneath her, Kalittokai's friend holds him to it as the motive of harm.
teaches: The flower comparison that the Kural's lover rejects to honour the girl is used by the friend against the man as an accusation, so the same convention of beauty can be denied as praise or pressed as a charge, depending on whether the lover or the friend wields it.

note: Kural 1207: she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns; Kuruntokai 243: she resolves not to think of the shore lord so that her eyes may sleep.
teaches: The poem tries the remedy the couplet says is impossible, a vow not to remember, and the very need to vow it confirms the couplet: remembering keeps her awake and forgetting cannot be chosen, only resolved.

note: In Kuruntokai the stag frisking with its sweet mate in the cool rain seems to taunt the waiting woman; in Ainkurunuru the hero shows his wife the beasts joined in delight, like us.
teaches: The paired beasts of the rainy scrub are one image read two ways: before the return they reproach the absent man through the woman's grief, after it they mirror the couple's reunion, so the image takes its sense from whether the speaker is still waiting.

note: Kural 1308: what use is suffering where there is no lover who knows you suffer; Kuruntokai 93: what is sulking worth when love is gone; do not speak against him, he is mother and father to us.
teaches: The Kural gives the reasoning that sulking needs a lover who will notice; the Kuruntokai wife draws the conclusion in her own case and adds the reason she cannot quarrel, her total dependence on him, so the maxim is shown ending in silence rather than in oodal.

note: Kuruntokai 187: he is harder than stone, yet her heart, never calling him hard, melts; Kural 1291: she asks her heart why it is not hers when his heart stays with him.
teaches: Kapilar gives the image and the Kural the argument of one complaint: the man's heart keeps to itself like stone while hers goes over to him, and together they show the heroine's quarrel is with her own heart's softness more than with his hardness.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 151-154 shows Siva only as one of three lords who come to see Murugan, with Uma, three unwinking eyes and the three forts destroyed; Paripadal 5.22-47 tells how that same god's union with Uma led to Murugan's birth.
teaches: The guide poem gives the kinship only as epithets (son of the god of the banyan, line 256) and shows Siva as a visiting lord, while the Paripadal narrates the birth in full, so the pair shows the story was known to both but told only where a poem chose to narrate rather than to direct a pilgrim.

note: Kar Narpathu 25: the flowers have opened; at the thought that the signs he set have come and he has not, the pallor has thickened on her. Thinaimalai 100: the rains appear in all quarters, his chariot does not, pallor appears and tears appear.
teaches: Kar Narpathu's friend reports the pallor from outside as a result of a broken sign, while the Thinaimalai woman lays it out as one sequence of appearings that begins with his false word, so the same symptom is shown first as a diagnosis and then as an accusation.

note: 241 asks whether the velan can know the hill man's bond; 249 blesses the velan because he does not know the hill man.
teaches: The decade's first poem raises the diviner's ignorance as a doubt and its ninth turns it into a blessing, so across the sequence the friend comes to see his ignorance as the secret's safety and not only as the rite's failure.

note: Both refuse the husband by pointing to the body of a nursing mother: Ainkurunuru 65 says her son-bearing body would spoil his chest; in Natrinai 380 the friend lists the ghee, smoke, milk and birth-smell that make them no match for the man of the courtesans' street.
teaches: Natrinai 380 itemises the household marks that Ainkurunuru 65 leaves as one sarcastic phrase, showing that 'it would spoil your chest' means the labour of the home set against the adorned women of the street.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Kuruntokai 256: before he could say he would return when the work was done, her weeping eyes blocked his chariot.
teaches: The couplet gives the woman's spoken refusal of the promise of a quick return; the poem shows that refusal made without words, before the promise is spoken, and records that it worked: the chariot stopped.

note: Natrinai 284 has the man's body as an old rope pulled at both ends by two tuskers, heart against reason; Kural 1163 has the woman's life as a carrying pole with love and shame hung at its two ends, in a body that cannot bear them.
teaches: Set side by side, the two show one figure, a load-bearing cord or pole strained between two claims, serving both the man's conflict of love against duty and the woman's of love against shame, so the tradition pictured a lover's divided mind as a physical strain whatever the second claim was.

note: Kural 1154: if the man who said 'do not fear' leaves, is the fault in those who trusted his word; Kalittokai 132: the friend asks the man whether the woman's pallor and lost beauty are not the fruit of his 'do not fear' (அஞ்சல் ஓம்பு) and 'trust me' (தெளி) at their secret meetings.
teaches: The couplet's question of who bears the fault is answered in the poem by the friend, who reads each reassurance as the direct cause of a named loss, so the Kural's moral question has a speech situation behind it in which the promise is handed back to the man as a debt.

note: The idyll's herd girl buys food with buttermilk (அளை) but will not take gold for ghee; in Kalittokai 110 the herd girl rebukes a man who thinks one easy to buy buttermilk from is easy for butter too.
teaches: The Kalittokai girl's retort turns on a real price difference that the idyll records, buttermilk as cheap daily barter and ghee as a good kept for livestock, so her wordplay about being 'easy' depends on the herding economy the guide poem describes.

note: Akananuru 80: the friend tells the shore lord that they guard their father's drying fish from birds in the punnai grove and asks him to come there by day. Thinaimalai 51: we watch and sell the fish in the grove.
teaches: The same chore that in Natrinai 45 marks the girls as beneath the suitor is in Akananuru 80 the cover for a daytime meeting, so the venba's bare picture of fish-watching could be either a rebuff or an invitation, which is why its sense stays open.

note: Paripadal 13 orders the elements sky, wind, fire, water by how many of the five each is known through; Tirumanthiram 385 tells the same chain as emergence, space, air, then a doubtful கான், water, the five together.
teaches: Because the Paripadal's count puts fire between wind and water, it supports reading the Tirumanthiram's obscure கான் as fire, and shows the creation chain the later Saiva text tells already present in an early Tamil hymn as a theory of how each element is known.

note: In Kar Narpathu 8 the kaayaa opens buds as if dipped in the eye's collyrium (கண்ணிய லஞ்சனங் தோய்ந்தபோற் காயாவும்) and so announces his return; in Mullaippattu 93 the kaayaa blooms collyrium (காயா வஞ்சன மலர) on the road his chariot is driving.
teaches: The collyrium-dark kaayaa is a promise in Kar Narpathu, pointed to by the friend while the man is away, and in the idyll it is scenery the returning chariot passes, so the same flower serves as proof of the return in the short poem and as the return itself in the long one.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 101-102 gives one of the six faces to smiling with Valli, the hill-dwellers' daughter, after its opening epithet for the chaste wife; Paripadal 9.81 names the god as lord of the bond of love along the path of the bond of karpu (கற்பு இணை நெறியூடு அற்பு இணைக் கிழமை).
teaches: The guide poem lists the two marriages separately, one as an epithet and one as a face's work, while the Paripadal joins them in one phrase after teaching the order of love, so the pair shows the two consorts being read as the two branches of akam, karpu and the love of free choice, united in one god.

note: Akananuru 74: the heroine could hold firm on her friend's comfort if the hard-mouthed small flute (வல்வாய் சிறுகுழல்) of the unlettered herdsmen did not torment her in the evening. Ainthinai Aimpathu 7 calls the same small flute fine (சீர்சால் சிறுகுழல்) and its player glad, yet it strikes her like a spear.
teaches: One heroine blames the flute's harsh mouth and the other concedes its sweetness, so together they show the evening flute's pain moving from the instrument to the hearer, which is why the venba needs the simile of the spear.

note: Purananuru 243's old man remembers garlanding a doll of packed sand and leaping into deep water as the untaught youth he has lost; Ainkurunuru 124 shows a girl with a sand doll punishing the sea that took it.
teaches: The same shore games of sand dolls and leaps into water are, in the puram elegy, the innocence age mourns, and in the akam barb, the proof that a man has taken up with a child, so the scene of youth carries nostalgia or contempt according to who recalls it and for what end.

note: Paripadal 2.20-23 says the god is younger to those who call him younger and elder to those who call him elder; Paripadal 4.69-73 says he bears a different name in each place, sits in the folded hands of his devotees and is the servant (ஏவலாளன்) of each of them.
teaches: The rule that the god takes the place each believer gives him begins in Paripadal 2 as a way out of a dispute over rank, and in Paripadal 4 it is extended to names, places and finally to service, so the pair shows accommodation growing from a theological truce into the god's subordinating himself to every worshipper.

note: Kural 1263: she lives on, longing for the return of the man who went desiring victory with his resolve as his only companion. Kar Narpathu 7: the friend says he went to give to seekers and crush foes, and the rain will bring him back.
teaches: The couplet's woman treats his heroic aim as the rival that left her behind, while the friend names the same aim, giving and conquest, as a reason to trust he will return in the rains: one motive is a grievance in the Kural and a guarantee in the venba.

note: Natrinai 250: the man tells the bard how, coming near to hug his toddling son, his wife took it otherwise and shied away. Kainnilai 39: the wife says he comes bringing the garlanded son, pointing to him, to torment her. On the man's telling the son is a real tenderness she misreads; on hers it is a tactic.
teaches: Read together the two poems give both sides of the same approach through the child, the husband insisting his affection was misjudged and the wife calling it harassment, so neither poem's account can be taken as the plain fact of the scene.

note: In Kuruntokai 7 onlookers see anklets still on the eloping girl's soft feet; in Akananuru 321 the foster mother says the girl took off her pebble-filled anklets for fear her mother would hear, before crossing the bamboo hills.
teaches: Together they show the anklet as the sign of an unwed girl read from two sides: at home its sound must be silenced for her to escape, while on the road strangers recognise from it, still on her feet, that the pair are lovers in flight rather than a married couple.

note: Akananuru 222 tells how Aathimanthi, after the Kaveri seized Aattan Atthi, searched in bewilderment until Maruthi showed her the lover and entered the sea. Kuruntokai 31 is the woman's own voice at the stage where she finds him nowhere.
teaches: Together the two poems order the story: Kuruntokai 31 stands in the middle of the search, 'nowhere do I see him', and the Akananuru supplies the end that the short poem never reaches, so the legend outlived the poet's own lament.

note: Akananuru 144's man imagines his wife saying he does not even remember her hair bare of mullai (கதுப்பும் உள்ளார்); Ainkurunuru 484's man says himself that they have stayed long, forgetting her (நீடினம் நேரிழை மறந்தே).
teaches: The charge of forgetting that the longer poem puts in the waiting wife's mouth, the short poem has the husband confess unprompted, so the return poems treat the man's own guilt over the delay as the counterpart of her reproach and the hurried drive as his answer to it.

note: Kar Narpathu 11: the kodal putting out clusters like snakes' raised heads announces his swift return; 119: the kodal has gone from ladle to snake's hood to finger, bangle and parasol and has withered.
teaches: Kar Narpathu stops the kodal at its snake-hood stage, where it is a promise, while 119 follows the same flower to its withering, so together they turn the glory lily into a clock whose hood marks the hope and whose wilting marks the broken word.

note: In both the wife recalls that he promised not to leave (பிரியலென், அஞ்சல்) and then left; Ainkurunuru 18 ends on her weeping eyes and the question, Kural 1154 asks whether those who believed his assuring words are at fault.
teaches: The Sangam wife quotes his broken promise as an accusation, while Valluvar's wife turns it into a question of blame for having believed, so the couplet adds to the older scene a moral reckoning about trust that the poem leaves unasked.

note: Both are by Kopperunchozhan: in Kuruntokai 129 he tells his comrade, 'friend of poets', that a girl's brow has bound him like a new-caught elephant; in Purananuru 216, fasting to death, he tells doubters his poet-friend, whom he has never seen, will surely come.
teaches: Read together, the king's two voices turn on the same bond of male friendship: in the love poem the comrade is the one he confides his captivity to, in the death poem the friend's coming is the proof of his worth, so the paangan of akam convention is, for this poet, a role he filled with a real friendship of poets.

note: Natrinai 259: the friendship made with the hill lord in the millet field, chasing parrots and bathing in the falls by the vengai slope, now looks hard to keep because the millet heads have ripened dry. Ainthinai Aimpathu 11: the few days in the vengai grove of the millet field have gone, sweet because no one gave orders.
teaches: Natrinai gives the crop's ripening as the reason the meetings end and Ainthinai names what made them possible, the absence of anyone to command the girls, so together they show the secret love as lent by the harvest calendar and taken back by it.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai places Murugan at the veri ground and under the fresh-flowered kadamba; the idyll compares the terrified girls holding hands to the ring of women possessed by Neduvel dancing round a kadamba trunk.
teaches: The possession dance that Thirumurugatruppadai describes as worship is used by Kapilar as the image for the girls at the very moment the love begins, so the god-seizure the mother wrongly suspects in the opening lines comes back as a simile for what really happened.

note: Kar Narpathu 18: the forest, dull like the body of a poor man, has put forth beauty like a rich man's mind. Ainthinai Aimpathu 8: the valli, dull like the body of the parted, has grown lovely like the body of the united.
teaches: Both measure the revived plant by a human state, but Kar Narpathu uses poverty and wealth, the motive of his journey, and Ainthinai uses parting and union, its outcome, so the same simile can point either to why he left or to what she awaits.

note: Both call the wife who bore a son the lamp of the house in a mullai poem: Akananuru 184 குடிக்குவிளக்கு ஆகிய புதல்வற் பயந்த, Ainkurunuru 405 மனைக்குவிளக்காயினள் ... புதல்வன் தாயே.
teaches: Read together they show the lamp of the house was a fixed title of the mullai wife won by bearing a son: Akananuru grounds it in godlike chastity and fame, while Ainkurunuru turns the title back into a seen flame, the red light of a bowl lamp.

note: Kovur Kizhar stands between two Chola kings at war and tells them that whichever loses, their own house loses; the friend says she holds two great fears like the worthy who stand between two great kings bent on war.
teaches: Purananuru 45 shows from inside the position the idyll's simile names, the mediator who can win nothing for either side: so the friend's double fear, for the father's honour and for the girl's life, is modelled on the puram envoy's predicament, and the akam go-between borrows the role of the poet who speaks between kings.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, who did not examine, pronounces his own death.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literal: no enemy or court condemns the king, he passes the sentence on himself the moment his error is shown, and he was easily approached, so only the failure to examine undoes him.

iraicchi.act: the tusker strips the yaa tree's soft branches to ease his mate's hunger
iraicchi.sense: the man who sees such care on his road will remember his own wife and return to cherish her

ullurai.tenor: the man who comes to the guarded house by night

pairs.situation: he slips into the father's guarded house at the guards' lapse
the signs of danger that should warn him

pairs.scene: மெல்லமெல்லப் பிறக்கே பெயர்ந்து தன் கல் அளைப் பள்ளி வதியும்
pairs.situation: he should turn back from night visits and rest in a home of his own by marrying her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a boar of the hill's own millet field in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

ullurai.tenor: the man who lets her go for fear of the watch kept on her

pairs.situation: the watch and talk that frighten him off
he lets go of her, who is left behind
she is left shaken, her beauty gone with him

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the millet field she herself guards and the elephant of her own hill, things she knows (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the girl who will go with the man

pairs.situation: she is bound to the man as the lily to running water
the heat of the forest road will not wither her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a water lily, a thing of the watered land, in a paalai poem, which has no land of its own (porul 1.2), so she does not leave the poem's land (porul 7.27)

ullurai.tenor: the man the friend calls good, and the woman whose eyes he spoils

pairs.situation: the small white, harmless-seeming bird is the man the friend calls good
the neythal it tears is her flower-like eyes, now pallid

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the gull and the neythal of her own shore, things she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the male red dog hunts for his pregnant mate who craves food
iraicchi.sense: the male providing for his mate is what the man has gone out to do, and seeing it he finds her nature, not the errand, has travelled with him

note: Kural 1179 says her eyes do not sleep when he fails to come nor when he comes; in Kuruntokai 301 he does not come, and the bell of a chariot that is not there rings in her ear at midnight while her eyes give up sleep.
teaches: The poem shows how the couplet's 'when he does not come' still keeps the eyes open: the ear makes his chariot out of the night, so absence is lived as an arrival that never quite happens.

note: Both turn on the same line, முருகென மொழியும் ஆயின்: 245 asks whether naming Murugu is a kindness to the girl's afflicter, 247 whether Murugu is the hill man's name.
teaches: The decade gives the one conditional two opposite ironies: in 245 the wrong name shields the man by hiding him, in 247 it names him by accident, so the misdiagnosis is shown as both the secret's cover and its leak.

note: Puram 209 compares the bard to birds that fly to a fruit tree in a mountain cleft and turn back with nothing when it is bare; the guide uses the bird and fruit tree as the image of certain success.
teaches: The bird-and-fruit-tree simile carried the bard's risk as well as his hope, since in Puram 209 the tree can be bare, so the guide poem's use of it is a claim that this patron is never the empty tree, and its first-person testimony is offered to meet exactly that doubt.

note: Kural 1007 likens the wealth of a man who gives nothing to the needy to a beautiful woman growing old alone; the courtesan in Akananuru 276 likens her own beauty, if she fails to win the man, to the wealth of one who hoarded and never gave to those who asked.
teaches: The two verses run the same comparison in opposite directions, beauty as vehicle for hoarded wealth in the Kural and hoarded wealth as vehicle for beauty in the poem, which shows the pairing was a shared idea in which each term could explain the other.

note: The guide here calls the bard he directs முதுவாய் இரவல (line 40); in Thirumurugatruppadai line 284 the god's attendants announce the devotee to Murugan in the same words, முதுவாய் இரவலன்.
teaches: The same title for a seasoned suppliant names a bard seeking a chief in one guide poem and a devotee seeking the god in another, so the devotional guide poem approached Murugan through the bard's petition at a patron's gate and kept even its form of address.

note: In Purananuru 337 a girl courted by kings is hard to see, like the cold spring of Paari's Parambu, shut in the house while her brothers fight the suitors; in Natrinai 253 the girl, guarded like Paari's hill, is hard to reach for her secret lover.
teaches: The pair shows Parambu as the standard image of the guarded marriageable girl in both akam and puram, and sets two kinds of suitor against the same closed house: kings who would take her by war and a lover who must now stop coming by night.

note: 261 likens the house to a கழிகலம் மகடூஉ with shorn head; in 280 the wife foresees becoming one of the கழிகல மகளிர் with shaven head.
teaches: In 261 the shorn widow is only an image for a ruined house; in 280 the wife speaks it of herself as her own future, so the pair shows the same stock figure moving from ornament to fate depending on who speaks.

note: Kural 1188: people say she has paled, no one says he left her. Kuruntokai 87: the god destroys the false, my lover is not false, yet my brow has paled.
teaches: Read together they show why the blame lands on her body: in the Kuruntokai the woman herself clears him before the avenging god, so the only visible sign of the wrong is her pallor, which is exactly the one-sided verdict the Kural's woman complains of.

note: In Kuruntokai 21 the woman refuses to believe the konrai's sign of the rains because he does not lie; in Natrinai 86 the friend calls the men righteous because they came back before the season they had named.
teaches: The Kuruntokai woman's faith that he keeps his word is a wager, and the Natrinai shows the wager won, with the kept promise named as அறவர், virtue, so truthfulness about the season is what the akam poets count as a husband's righteousness.

note: Purananuru 62 describes a field where both kings fell, the umbrellas shook, the famous drums were lost and no one was left to claim the field (களங்கொளற்கு உரியோர் இன்றி); Kalavazhi 37 has the kings' corpses pour out blood that carries off the drums and the elephants, and the field belongs to the lord of the watered land.
teaches: The same lost drums and dead kings make a kalavazhi only because one king survives to own the field; Purananuru 62 shows the case where nobody does, and the poet must turn the praise to the heavenly guests, which marks the victor as the genre's precondition.

note: In Kural 1260 the woman says those whose hearts melt like fat in fire cannot say they will join and then hold out in a sulk; in Natrinai 217 the wife says that though the man is very sweet she will brood and sulk, since making him feel it drives off her loneliness.
teaches: The Kural woman doubts that a loving heart can keep a sulk, while the Natrinai wife resolves to keep one precisely because she loves him and wants the long loneliness to end, so the two disagree on whether the sulk is weakness overcome or a strategy of love.

note: Purananuru 123 makes chariot-giving Malaiyan's mark, chariots given sober outnumbering the raindrops on Mullur; Natrinai 100 names him only as தேர் வண் மலையன் and borrows his musicians' drum to measure a frightened husband's trembling.
teaches: The akam poet can name Malaiyan by the epithet the puram poems established and rely on his fame being known, and turns it to mockery: the drum of a great giver's festivals throbs for a man afraid of his wife, so puram glory serves akam as a scale for comic smallness.

note: Kural 1155 says if he leaves, union becomes hard (நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு); in 51 the man tells his heart that wealth is joined only by parting, and chooses to stay.
teaches: The same word புணர்வு carries both sides of one exchange: the Kural's woman counts what parting costs union, and the Sangam man counts what union costs wealth.

note: In 13 the man tells the woman that if she came the stones would blacken her lotus soles, the beasts' cries would startle her and the hot wind would wither her; in 20 the woman takes the same objections (her feet, no water, no shade, the heat) and denies that any of them weighs against going with him.
teaches: Held together the two poems stage both sides of one dispute: the man argues from her body's frailty, the woman from her life's shortness and the deer pair that cross together, so the paalaikkali treats the wife's right to share the road as a question it argues, not a given.

note: In both the woman says her lover gave her sickness and pallor: Kuruntokai 13 says plainly he gave the sickness and pallor fills her eyes; Kural 1183 says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange.
teaches: The Kural turns Kapilar's single complaint of a gift into an exchange with two sides, naming what was taken (சாயல், நாண்) as well as what was given, so the pair show the 'he gave me pallor' formula growing into an account of loss.

note: Natrinai's hero, back from his work, blesses the cloud whose night rain fell on the town where he lay embraced with his wife; Ainkurunuru's says the rains mingled with the scrub and she embraced him.
teaches: Natrinai turns the coincidence of rain and embrace into thanks owed to the cloud, while Ainkurunuru sets the two side by side without comment, so together they show the returning hero crediting the season with the reunion it once threatened.

note: Purananuru 281 has women guard a wounded warrior from ghouls with neem, music, mustard seed and incense; Natrinai 349's man likens himself, ever behind the fisher girl, to the ghoul that hovers by men gravely wounded on the battlefield.
teaches: Read with the warding rite, the lover's simile casts him as the very presence a household drives from its wounded with neem and smoke, so his self-portrait as tireless follower carries his knowledge that he is the unwanted one at her door.

note: Kural 55: the wife who rises worshipping her husband, not a god, commands rain. Kalittokai 39: the girl, embraced by the man who saved her from the flood, could bring rain at need (line 6), and because hill women rise worshipping their husbands (கேள்வர்த் தொழுது எழலால்) the hunters' arrows do not miss.
teaches: The Kural's claim appears in the friend's disclosure as a belief the hill folk already hold, extended from rain to the whole hill economy and staked on a single premarital embrace, so the maxim on the wife's power was a shared folk conviction that the friend could use to argue the girl was already a faithful wife.

note: Kural 1261: the woman's fingers are worn from marking the days since he left; Kuruntokai 358: the friend speaks to the woman who scores lines and clings to the wall, and points to the mullai buds as the season he promised.
teaches: The couplet gives the counting of days only as the woman's wasting, while the poem lets the friend answer it with a sign outside the wall, the season's buds, so the count the Kural leaves open is closed by the promised season and becomes ground for comfort.

note: Kural 1248 calls the heart a fool for following the man who left while lamenting his lack of grace; Kalittokai 123 asks the simple heart (மட நெஞ்சே) that went to him at night whether it saw, embraced or knew him, and pities it for tossing like the backwater tide.
teaches: The poem shows what the couplet's 'you go after him' looks like as an event, the heart's nightly journey met by three questions it cannot answer, so the Kural's rebuke of the foolish heart is the end of a scene in which the heart keeps coming back empty.

note: Kuruntokai 127: because the man's one bard proved a liar, every bard looks like a thief to the women he left. Kainnilai 47: the wife calls the bard a liar (பொய்ப் பாண) and bars him from her house.
teaches: Kuruntokai 127 states the general effect of one lying go-between and Kainnilai 47 shows its consequence in a single house, the door shut to the bard himself, so the pair shows distrust of the messenger hardening into exclusion.

note: Paripadal 11.122-123 has onlookers call a girl a striking goddess (தாக்கு அணங்கு) whose eyes are Kaaman's army (காமன் படை); Kural 1082 has the man say that her returning his look is a striking goddess come with an army (தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண் டன்ன).
teaches: The rare compound and the army come together in both, so the Kural's lover is speaking a festival idiom: what the Paripadal's crowd shouts as a warning to all who see the girl, the Kural turns into one man's private experience of a single returned glance.

note: Nedunjeliyan vows that if he fails, poets with Mangudi Maruthan at their head may cease to sing his land; the idyll, by Mangudi Maruthanar, ends with chiefs with Maran at their head praising him in assembly.
teaches: The vow names the poet whose song was at stake, and the idyll is that poet's song, ending in a praise-assembly built on the same 'X at the head' formula, so the pair shows the poet answering the king's vow in kind while closing, as kaanchi, on the bound of the king's good time.

note: Kural 1182: the woman says pallor rides over her body (மேனிமேல் ஊரும் பசப்பு), claiming it is his gift. Kainnilai 27: at the rainy evening, thinking of his coming, pallor spreads over her body (ஊர்தரு மேனி பசப்பு).
teaches: The couplet says only that pallor rides her body by his right; the Kainnilai fragment gives it an hour and a cause, the rain-season evening and the thought of his coming, so expectation, not only absence, is what sets the pallor moving.

note: Both liken the thundering rain to the drums of kings (வேந்தர் ... முரசின்). Kuruntokai 380: the friend says their lover is in a far country, not before them; how shall they bear it? Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 23: the friend says he who went will come, and the rain will be greater tomorrow.
teaches: One image, the sky beating like a king's drum, serves the friend once as proof that he is coming and once as a measure of how far away he still is, which shows that in the rains the friend's comfort is a choice of reading, not a fact the season settles.

note: Kural 1151 (the friend or the woman to the man): if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Kuruntokai 135: the friend tells the woman he himself said men are women's life, so he will hold back.
teaches: The couplet states as a threat what the Kuruntokai friend leaves the man to infer from his own words: if men are the women's life, then his going kills her and any promise of a quick return is addressed to the dead, which is why the friend can be sure he will stay.

note: Natrinai 282's friend, the hero within hearing, describes the slipping bangles, faded brow and the old diviner misreading the illness; Ainkurunuru 194's friend tells the hero directly that the mother has suspected a wrong cause (கொன் ஒன்று கடுத்தனள்).
teaches: Set beside Natrinai's full scene of pebbles and diviner, the Ainkurunuru friend's two words show the misread illness was familiar enough to be invoked in a half-line, and that in both its use is the same: to press the man to marry before a wrong cure exposes the girl.

note: In Kural 1157 the slipping bangles proclaim that the lord of the shore has left; in Kainnilai 7 they slip at the mere telling of the hill lord's friendship.
teaches: The Kural gives the bangles as a sign without a scene, and Kainnilai supplies the scene that explains them: a monkey that snatches the fruit and bolts, so the bangles fall because the 'friendship' was a theft and the leaving was already in it.

note: Akananuru 355 says in spring lovers stay in the cool grove of dropping pollen and forget their rich homes (தண்பொழில் அல்கிக் காதலர் செழுமனை மறக்கும்); Ainkurunuru 345 says our fragrant cool grove (நம் மணங்கமழ் தண்பொழில்) is in bloom.
teaches: Akananuru 355 supplies the custom that the four-line poem leaves out: the flowering grove is where lovers spend spring together, so 'our grove blooms' is an empty place set for two, not a pleasant view.

note: In Akananuru 28 the friend warns that if the girl will not scare the parrots her mother will send others to guard the millet and the lover will be out of reach. In Natrinai 147 the parrots have taken the millet, the mother questions her, her denial gives her away, and her going to the field is over.
teaches: The two friends' speeches are the before and after of one plot: the warning of Akananuru 28 comes true in Natrinai 147, and the second poem shows how, through the girl's own guilty denial rather than through the parrots.

note: Kuruntokai's heroine herself refuses to believe the forest's konrai that says the rains have come, because he does not lie; Ainkurunuru's friend calls the same konrai deceived.
teaches: Read together, the two show that discrediting the konrai's sign was the shared way to keep the man's promise unbroken, whether the heroine did it out of trust in his word or the friend did it to stop her weeping.

note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding women by confinement is, since their own steadfastness is the best guard; in Natrinai 68 the friend says shutting young girls in the house is neither right nor good for the household.
teaches: Both reject confinement, but the Kural does so for the wife because her virtue makes it needless, while the Natrinai girls reject it for the unmarried daughter because it blocks a love headed for marriage, so the same verdict rests on opposite views of what the woman's will is for.

note: Kural 211 says duty seeks no return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain; Patitruppattu 43 likens the king's giving to rain that breaks a drought and floods the river banks.
teaches: Both take rain as the model of giving, but the Kural uses it to show giving without return, while the Chera poet uses drought-breaking rain to show giving measured by need and graded by receiver, so the same image yields a rule of disinterest in one and a rule of fit in the other.

note: The Kural commands making wealth as the sharpest weapon; the hero leaving for wealth that is hard to earn counts what the going costs the girl he leaves.
teaches: The Kural's bare imperative to make wealth is weighed here against a girl's quoted plea not to stay long, showing that the duty the maxim states without condition was, in akam, always paid for by someone left behind.

note: Both start from the same premise, that youth passes and does not return; Naladiyar 11 concludes that the wise renounce desire from childhood; Natrinai 314 uses it to condemn the man who left an embrace for wealth.
teaches: The same commonplace of fleeting youth served opposite ends: for the akam woman it is a reason to spend youth in love now, for the didactic poet a reason to give love up, so the ascetic use of the maxim takes over an argument love poetry had already made.

note: Both open on the same refrain to the mother and point to the lover's mount: in the neythal decade the shore lord's chariot is the medicine for the girl's sickness, in the kurinji decade the hill lord's horses have tufted heads like the town's Brahmin boy.
teaches: The two disclosure decades present the lover's mount to the mother as evidence in opposite tones, the neythal friend solemnly as a cure and the kurinji friend comically through a homely likeness, so the same act of disclosure could be made by gravity or by disarming laughter.

note: In both the friend (on Parimelazhagar's reading of the Kural) speaks to the man who is about to leave, to hold him back.
teaches: The couplet holds the man back with a threat that she will not live, while the Sangam friend holds him back with the girl's worth, a daughter begged from the god, so the pair shows two arguments for the same refusal: her death against her value.

note: Kalittokai 33: in spring the silk-cotton flowers like fire and the pungu sheds blossom like puffed rice (எரி உரு உறழ இலவம், பொரி உரு உறழப் புன்கு), and the heroine feels the season mock the lonely. Thinaimalai 64 gives the murukku as scattered fire and the pungu as scattered puffed rice.
teaches: The pungu as puffed rice is fixed across both poems while the fire moves from silk-cotton to murukku, and the same paired images serve the heroine's complaint in Kalittokai and the friend's rebuke of open grieving in the venba, so the spring catalogue was a shared stock that either speaker could turn.

note: Akananuru 59: the friend tells the wasting heroine that on the road the man took a tusker bends a tall yaa tree to feed its young mate, and the poem ends on 'the road he went'. Kuruntokai 37 gives the same tusker easing its mate's hunger on the yaa and the same close, 'the road he went'.
teaches: The long poem spends its lines on her lost beauty, a Mal simile and his forgetting before reaching the tusker and the road, so Kuruntokai 37 shows the consolation reduced to its working parts: a promise of his love, the creature's care as proof, and the road.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is an envoy of the burning evening and a weapon that kills. Ezhupathu 22: herdsmen blow konrai flutes, the herd goes in, evening comes as she watches, and the sky thunders and draws its bow.
teaches: The Kural makes the herdsman's flute the evening's envoy and weapon, and Ezhupathu 22, which names no pain at all, gives the same evening a second weapon, the rainbow drawn as a bow, so the reader of the Kural sees that the evening's arming was a scene the venba poets could show without comment.

note: Kural 467 says to think and then resolve, and that to think after resolving is a lapse; Patitruppattu 72 says the king's foes, from the greatness of their enmity and their folly, resolve without deliberating (சூழாது துணிதல்), unlike the wise who know his nature, and meet him as the doom-fire.
teaches: The Kural gives the rule as prudence in any task, while the Chera poem applies it to war and shows its breach as ruin, setting the wise counsellors who know the king against the foes who resolve unthinking, so deliberation becomes the line between the king's servants and his victims.

note: 12 says the girl will give her shoulders only to the man who swam the flood and set her on the bank; 14 says no one but the man who drove off the elephant shall touch her friend's shoulders. Both use the same 'except him, no one' formula.
teaches: The same exclusive formula is fitted to two different rescues, flood and elephant, which shows that the rescue is an interchangeable warrant and that what the friend really presents to the household is the girl's choice, already made.

note: Ainkurunuru 111 says she cannot live parted because she cannot do hard penance (அருந்தவம் முயறல் ஆற்றாதேமே); Kuruntokai 344 says those who see their lovers return must have done penance (நோற்றோர் மன்ற).
teaches: In one poem penance is the endurance a woman would need to survive separation, in the other the merit that earns the lover's return, so Sangam akam uses tapas both as a power to bear absence and as the price of its ending.

note: Kuruntokai 37's tusker strips yaa branches to ease his mate's hunger, left for the heroine to read as the hero's love; Paripadal 10.42-52 has a tusker turn back to embrace his terrified mate and says outright சிறந்தார் நடுக்கம் சிறந்தார் களையல்.
teaches: The Paripadal poet spells out in one line the sense that Kuruntokai 37 leaves implied, which shows that the caring elephant pair was read by the poets themselves as an image of the lover who removes the beloved's distress.

iraicchi.act: after feeding, the boar stays with its mate on the rock slope
iraicchi.sense: the boar keeps its mate's company, while the man stays away from the woman whose only cure is his coming

iraicchi.act: the stag rests with his doe through the day and stays with her into the evening
iraicchi.sense: as the stag stays by his doe at the evening hour, the man has come back to stay with his wife

ullurai.tenor: the husband and his succession of women

pairs.situation: he takes a new woman
he leaves her for another before the day is out
he comes back to the fine house only after his rounds

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the bee of her own town's fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the gossiping town and the man's kept-off visits

pairs.situation: the town's loud talk about the lovers

pairs.scene: நெடுந் தேர் இன் ஒலி கேட்டலோ அரிதே
pairs.situation: the gossip keeps him from coming openly

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the bees of the shore punnai, a thing of the neythal poem's own grove (porul 7.27)

note: Purananuru 150: Nalli, unnamed, roasts fat in his forest for a starving poet and gives him his own chain. Kuruntokai 210: the friend prices the meal owed to the crow that called a guest in the ghee of the herds of Nalli's forest.
teaches: Holding the two together shows why Nalli's forest is the measure in the love poem: he was remembered as the host who fed a stranger in the woods unasked, so the friend, repaying a bird for bringing a guest, reaches for the most famous hospitality she knows and still calls it too little.

note: In Akananuru 54 the returning man sees the milch herd hurrying home at dusk to the calves with the cowherds behind and wants to reach his wife and son; in Kuruntokai 344 the waiting woman sees the cows with dripping udders leave the herd for the village at dusk and says only the fortunate see their lovers return.
teaches: The same dusk image of cows hurrying home to their calves is the man's cue to return when he speaks and the woman's reproach when she speaks, so the herd's homing is a fixed sign of the duty to come home that each side reads against the other.

note: Kuruntokai 183: the wife wonders whether he will see the stag parted from its doe; Akananuru 34: the hero, seeing a stag feed and guard its doe, bids his chariot hurry home.
teaches: The pair shows the stag and doe of the scrub working from both ends of a separation: the waiting wife hopes he will see a parted pair and feel her loss, while the returning hero is moved by a pair together, so the same creatures carry absence for her and return for him.

note: In Akananuru 99 the man leading the eloped girl through the waste likens the opening kongu buds to women's jewelled breasts and points to paathiri petals on the path; in Ainkurunuru 361 the girl wears a paathiri garland by the summer stream and her breasts and shoulders strike him harder than her eyes.
teaches: Akananuru 99 makes the waste's flowers stand for her body to coax her onward, while 361 has her wearing those same flowers and her body outdoing them, so the eloping man's praise moves from comparing the land to her to letting her eclipse it.

note: Both have the wife alone at evening hearing the cowherds' flutes; Kural 1228 calls the flute the messenger of evening and a killing weapon, Natrinai 69 sets the flutes and cow bells among the evening's signs and says that if such an evening came where he is, he could not stay at his work.
teaches: The couplet makes the evening's music a weapon only against her, while the Natrinai wife imagines it falling on him too and so excuses his absence by supposing his land has no such evenings, turning the same lament into a defence of his love.

note: Kural 51 defines the wife by the home's excellence and living within her husband's means; verse 42 opens with knowing the house's ways in proportion to income.
teaches: Both works put income first in defining a wife, and the verse spells out what the couplet's 'excellence of the home' includes: kin kept content, guests and worship.

note: 37 treats Death as the overpowering thing no plea escapes; 39 calls dying easy beside the hard work of character.
teaches: Within one chapter the work views death from two sides, as the terror that drives penance and as the easy thing beside lasting virtue, and the pair shows death's weight depends on what it is measured against.

note: Paripadal 5 opens by hailing the spear that cut down Sur; in Kalittokai 93 one of the husband's 'goddesses' sang of the red-speared slayer of Sur with him on the hill through the rains.
teaches: The pair shows the Murugan hymn in two settings: in the Paripadal it is temple praise, while the Kalittokai places the same theme in a lovers' pastime on the hill in the rainy season, so devotional song at Murugan's hill was also an occasion for courtship that the wife can use as evidence.

note: Kural 1213: my life lasts because I see in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; Kalittokai 128: the woman tells of a dream in which she quarrelled with the man and he bowed at her feet, and says her life held at the brink hoping he would come awake too.
teaches: The poem shows the mechanism the couplet only asserts: the dream keeps her alive by letting her act out the quarrel and his submission and by feeding the hope of a real coming, so the Kural's 'my life lasts' rests on both satisfaction and expectation.

note: Both are the moment the man announces departure: in Kural 1151 she answers with a sharp demand, tell me if you are not going; in Natrinai 308 she can neither ask nor stop him and only presses against his chest.
teaches: The Kural gives the woman a defiant sentence to stop the journey, while Natrinai shows wordless grief doing what the sentence could not, since it is her silence that melts his resolve.

note: Both are the man struck by the girl's look and both find a doe in it: Kural 1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe; Natrinai 101 says the shore hamlet was sweet to live in before he saw her deer-like look.
teaches: The couplet says what the look contains, the doe beside Death; the Natrinai man shows what Death in it did, measuring the wound as the loss of his home's sweetness from the day he saw her.

note: In Kalittokai 107 the bull tosses the herder's mullai chaplet into the girl's hair by chance; in 115 she herself tied his chaplet in her hair and it fell before her mother; in both the kin then resolve to give her to him (அடை சூழ்ந்தார்).
teaches: The same outcome from accident in one poem and from the girl's own act in the other shows that among the herders the man's flowers in a girl's hair bind her however they got there: the kin read the first as a god's sign and the second as a fact to be ratified, and both end in betrothal.

note: Both put a drought-starved animal couple on the man's road for wealth: in Akananuru 91 the friend cites the elephant shrinking beside his hungry mate to assure the wife of his love; in Natrinai 103 the man himself sees the male wild dog grieving for his starving mate.
teaches: The image the friend offers the wife as reassurance is the one the man meets as self-reproach on the road, so the pair shows the same iraicchi working from both ends of the separation, comfort at home and conscience in the waste.

note: In Akananuru 43 the man who stays calls those who leave their companion for wealth fools (மடமையோர்); in Kuruntokai 20 the woman left behind grants the leavers the name of the wise (உரவோர்) and claims folly (மடவம்) for those who stay.
teaches: The paalai debate is fought over the same pair of words, wise and foolish: the staying man pins folly on the leavers, while the abandoned woman lets them keep wisdom and takes folly as the side of love, so who names whom foolish depends on who was left.

note: Akananuru 380: the shore lord, wooing, showed the girls a crab carrying a naaval fruit to its mate in its burrow and said 'this is a fine way'. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 68: the friend tells the shore lord of the crab with its mate on the dune, and that her friend has paled.
teaches: In the Akananuru the hero himself offers the crab that cares for its mate as a sign of how he will behave, and in the venba the friend returns the same crab to him as a reproach while the girl pales, so the pair shows a courting pledge turned into the evidence against the man who gave it.

note: In Akananuru 134 the returning hero hushes his chariot so the stag and doe in union are not parted; in Ainkurunuru 414, now home, he bids his wife look at birds and beasts frisking in pairs.
teaches: On the road the hero shields the beasts' union as a sign of the one he is hurrying to, and once home he shows the paired creatures to his wife as a shared sight, so the mullai beasts move from his private token to the couple's common pleasure.

note: Thinaimalai 18 fears that the harvested millet ends the bond; in Akananuru 132 the millet ears are already cut and the friend tells the man to take the girl away.
teaches: Thinaimalai 18 stops at the fear that the stubble field ends the meetings, and Akananuru 132 shows what the friend does with that fear, turning it into a demand to take the girl away, so the harvest is the point at which kalavu must become marriage or flight.

note: Ainkurunuru 36 says that if he forgets them, they too could forget and be content, were it not that her eyes go pale; Kural 1207 has the woman say she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns.
teaches: The Sangam speaker claims forgetting is in her power and lays the failure on her paling eyes, while the Kural woman denies she can forget at all, so the older poem places love's hold in the body against the will and the couplet moves it into the mind itself.

note: Akananuru 35's road is held by bowmen of வில் ஏர் வாழ்க்கை, 'the life whose plough is the bow', and their cairns; Ainthinai Ezhupathu 33's road by வில்லுழுது உண்பார், 'those who eat by ploughing with the bow', among the cairns.
teaches: Held together they show the bow-as-plough figure for the wasteland robbers passing intact from the Sangam anthology into the later venba, while its use shifts from a mother's fear for a daughter on the road to a wife's reproach that the man can see the road's dangers but not her.

note: Natrinai 69: if the evening came like this in the land where he went for work, he could not hold to his resolve. Ainthinai Aimpathu 3: is there not this rain in the land where our man went?
teaches: The pair shows a single argument of the waiting wife, that the season must reach him too and would bring him home, carried from evening in the long poem to the rain in the venba, where its failure becomes the sharper doubt whether the rain is in his land at all.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 67-77 marks the god's dwelling on the hill west of Koodal by the bees that sleep in the lotus and hum round the pool flowers opening like eyes; Paripadal 17.37-38 says that when the swingers leap together on festival day the bees that suck the pool flowers' pollen cannot reach them.
teaches: The guide poem gives the hill west of Koodal at rest, its pool bees the sign of the god's ordinary dwelling, and the hymn uses the same pool bees to measure the festival, when the crowd drives them off, so the pair shows the same place on its common day and on its feast day.

note: Both address a ragged bard with a small lute; Purananuru 138 sums up the road he has already crossed in three lines (cattle paths, deer hills, fish fords), and the idyll lays out the road still ahead land by land.
teaches: The guide poem's landscape sequence appears in the short poem as a compressed formula for the journey behind the bard; the idyll turns it round into the journey before him and expands each land into a settlement with its own meal.

note: Natrinai 32's friend ends with the saying that the great take a friend after inquiry and do not inquire after befriending, and that once accepted it is hard to undo; Kural 791 says nothing brings ruin like befriending without inquiry, since there is no leaving once the bond is formed.
teaches: The Kural's rule and its reason, inquire first because a formed bond cannot be left, already serve in the Natrinai as a proverb a friend applies to a girl choosing a lover, so the ethics of friendship framed the irrevocability of a love match before Valluvar set them apart in his book on polity.

note: Both end on the same words, உற்ற சூளே, an oath sworn at the broad ford of 'our town'; in Kuruntokai 53 the friend says it was sworn holding the girl's forearm with the hill goddesses as witness and now afflicts them, in Ainkurunuru 31 the other woman says it was sworn before the bathing companions and asks whether he will call it no debt.
teaches: The witness decides what a broken ford-oath costs: sworn before goddesses it turns into a danger that falls on the women, sworn before human bathers it shrinks to a debt the man can simply disown, so the courtesan's oath is the weaker for lacking a god.

note: The idyll's sea keeps its level because what the clouds take and what the rivers bring balance; the Kural says the vast sea itself would lose its nature if the cloud took and did not give back.
teaches: The sea's unchanging fullness was a stock figure of plenty in the city poem, and the Kural takes the same sea to show that the fullness depends on the return, which, read back into the market, makes Madurai's inexhaustible plenty the effect of continual exchange rather than a fixed store.

note: In both the wife refuses the straying husband's chest: in Ainkurunuru 42 the friend reports it to him as if it were joy-drunk folly; in Kural 1311 the wife herself refuses it because all women feast on it with their eyes.
teaches: The refusal of the chest was a recognised act of the sulking wife before Valluvar; the Sangam friend presents it with mock surprise to shame the man, while the Kural gives the wife her own reason, so the couplet supplies the motive that the older poem leaves to irony.

note: Perunthalai Sathanar says the wealthy who gave nothing to the needy are not remembered, while those who set up fame are; in the idyll the patron counts the enthroned rich whose names died with them as more than river sand and decides that his days shall pass with fame.
teaches: The argument a bard uses in Purananuru 165 to shame and urge patrons appears in the idyll as the patron's own reasoning, so the guide poem shows the bards' doctrine of fame taken in by the giver as his motive for giving.

note: In 262 the friend says the girl has chosen to drink elephant-footprint water with him in a far country; in 274 the man says the cruel forest will be sweet if he goes holding her.
teaches: The claim that the beloved's company sweetens the desert is made for the girl by the friend and by the man for himself, so the elopement rests on a premise both lovers hold, voiced by different speakers.

note: Ainthinai Aimpathu 42: the heroine begs the crab not to blur the tracks of his chariot so she can gaze at the path he took. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 64: she tells the stork that it knows the path by which he went.
teaches: In both venbas the path of the departed shore lord is known only to the shore's creatures, the crab who can erase it and the stork who has seen it, so the pair shows the neythal heroine's knowledge of his leaving lodged entirely in what the animals of the beach can keep or destroy.

note: Both set a hill creature that has handled ripe fruit against snares; in Kuruntokai the hunter sets nets on every tree after the fruit is already touched, in Kainnilai the monkey tastes the fruit and is caught.
teaches: The same fruit-and-snare economy of the hill serves two speakers opposite ways: the friend uses the late snares to tell the man the girl is now guarded too late, while the girl uses the caught monkey to say she herself is the one bound by the sweetness she tasted.

note: Kural 25 names Indra, lord of the wide heaven, as witness enough to the strength of one who has quenched the five senses; Paripadal 19.50-52 records visitors at the Parankunram painted hall explaining a picture: Indra as the cat, Ahalya, Gautama who had gone out, and her form turned to stone in his anger.
teaches: On the reading that Indra is witness through his own fall, the Kural's single name assumes a story that the Paripadal shows painted on a Madurai temple wall and told aloud to anyone who asked, so the couplet's allusion was not learned lore but a tale ordinary pilgrims were taught from pictures.

note: Kural 1221: you are not evening but வேலை, the time that eats the life of the once-wed. Thinaimalai 96: the dark like Maayon's colour and the milk-white moonlight are like a spear (வேல்) to those without a partner.
teaches: The Kural's pun on வேலை (hour, and the sense that kills) is made literal in the venba as a spear, and it moves from the evening to the moonlit night, showing a later poet turning the couplet's wordplay into a simile.

note: In Kalittokai 85 the mother shares out her milk in mockery to the 'other mothers' who wept after trusting the father's deceiving oath (மாயச் சூள்); in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 44 a woman says she believed his words long ago, not knowing them for a false oath (பொய்ச்சூள்).
teaches: Read together, the false oath is the wound the wife shares with her rivals: Kalittokai's mother pities the other women it deceived, and the venba's speaker finds herself among them, so the oath binds all the man's women in one injury.

note: Ainkurunuru 98 has the friend tell the lover that the girl's parents guard her more strictly than she guards herself; Kural 57 asks what use guarding a woman by confinement is, since the guard of her own steadfastness is the best.
teaches: The Kural's rule ranks a woman's own guard above confinement, but the Sangam friend relies on the confinement exactly because in courtship the girl's own guard has already given way, so the household's watch the couplet finds useless is what turns a lover into a husband.

note: Ainkurunuru 65: the wife tells the lord not to embrace her body that has borne a son, since it would spoil his chest. Thinaimalai 152: do not embrace me; our son's wet mouth would wipe off the marks of breasts, jewels and leaf-paint on your chest, and my milk would spoil your garland.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru's mother refuses the embrace by pretending to protect his chest from her post-partum body; the Thinaimalai keeps that pretext and names what is on the chest, another woman's marks, so the pairing shows the old formula of 'spoiling' was an accusation waiting to be made explicit.

note: Both open with the same words, உள்ளார் கொல்லோ தோழி: in Kuruntokai 16 the woman pictures the kalli waste he crossed, a lizard calling its mate with a sound like thieves testing arrows; in Natrinai 241 she pictures her own surroundings, the reed flowering in the north wind and the dewy midnight.
teaches: Read together, the formula question can be answered from either end of the separation, the dangers of his road or the season at her door, so 'do they not think of us' is a frame into which the poet sets whichever world the woman imagines, and the choice of world is the poem's real statement.

note: In Kuruntokai 214 the hill girl has been given a great leaf skirt and garland and the whole town is thrown into uproar; in Natrinai 359 the friend, holding the man's gift of leaves, fears the mother if they wear it and hurting him if they return it.
teaches: Read together, the leaf skirt shows itself as a public sign of courtship: the Natrinai gives the friend's dilemma before it is worn, and the Kuruntokai gives what follows the wearing, the town's uproar, which is just what the friend feared.

note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the idyll says that in the land of Thiraiyan's just sceptre robbers are absent and thunder, snakes and beasts do no harm.
teaches: The idyll extends the Kural's claim that a just ruler's land is blessed by nature from rain and crops to the dangers of the road, so for a travelling bard the just sceptre is proved by a safe journey rather than a good harvest.

note: 194 declares இன்னாது அம்ம, இவ் வுலகம், this world is harsh, and blames its maker; 192 says we do not in disgust call life bitter (இன்னாது என்றலும் இலமே). Read as judgments of the world, they are incompatible.
teaches: One anthology holds both the verdict that the world is bitter and the refusal to pass that verdict, using the same word இன்னாது, so the reader sees that Purananuru ethics offered two stances to grief, protest and equanimity, rather than one doctrine.

note: Kural 118 likens the worthy man's impartiality to a balance that levels itself before it weighs; thirattu 7 has poets weigh the world against Koodal with the balance of their learning (புலக் கோலால் தூக்க).
teaches: Read beside the Kural's just balance, the fragment's praise borrows the authority of an impartial weighing, so the poets present their verdict on Koodal as fairness, the ornament of the worthy, rather than as a court singer's flattery.

note: Both are the separated woman at evening in a pastoral scene: in Kural 1228 the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon; in Natrinai 109 she stands alone like a cow tied by the head in a dripping shed.
teaches: The pastoral evening gives the Kural woman a sound that attacks her and the Natrinai woman a posture she shares, so the mullai hour wounds in one from outside and in the other makes her one of its own tethered creatures.

note: Kural 1154: if he who said 'fear not' leaves, is there any fault in those who trusted his assuring word? Natrinai 224: what can I say now to those who assured me 'we will not part' and set off for the waste?
teaches: The Kural poses as a moral question who is at fault when an assurance is broken; the Natrinai woman, using the same verb of assuring (தெளித்த), cannot even ask it aloud and lets the budding kuravu and the koel's 'stay joined' do the accusing, so the broken word is judged by the season instead of by her.

note: Kural 224 says being begged from is painful until one sees the asker's glad face; Patitruppattu 57 says the king fears the distress of suppliants more than the sulking eyes of the women of his house (ஒண்நுதல் மகளிர் துனித்த கண்ணினும் இரவலர் புன்கண் அஞ்சும்).
teaches: The couplet names the giver's discomfort in general, and the poem measures it against the strongest private disturbance of akam, a wife's sulk, so the giver's pain is ranked above domestic love.

note: Both name Pulli's Venkatam: in 61 the friend says the man would not stay even for Venkatam with its festivals; in 83 the man says her virtues followed him past Venkatam regardless of distance.
teaches: Pulli's Venkatam served akam poets as the fixed far edge of the wealth journey, and they turned it both ways: a prize too small to hold the man, and a distance too short to stop the woman's pull.

iraicchi.act: the decoy hunter, in pity of the shivering heron, takes up his stakes and lets it be
iraicchi.sense: even a hunter spares a creature shivering in the cold, so the man should not leave his shivering wife in it

ullurai.tenor: the ooran and the young women of other houses he spoils

pairs.situation: the man cuts short the bloom of the women he takes
the women are of other houses, not his own
they are young girls just coming into growth

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a field crab and a yard creeper of the marutham town, without leaving the poem's land (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the stag feeds with its doe and stays in the forest with her
iraicchi.sense: the beasts keep to their mates, which is exactly what the man was proposing to give up

iraicchi.act: the heron lays its eggs and nests in the thaazhai on his shore
iraicchi.sense: the lord of a shore where even the heron settles to breed has yet to make a home with the girl, and the shut door says he must now do it

iraicchi.act: the waves ceaselessly play about the tree's branch
iraicchi.sense: the sea never leaves off embracing the tree on his shore, yet the man himself is rarely there to embrace

iraicchi.act: the water-hen calls openly to its mate in the field pond
iraicchi.sense: the bird calls its mate in the open, while the man comes to her only by stealth at night; he should claim her openly

note: Akananuru 66: seeing the son run to him, the man cries 'நெடுந்தேர் தாங்குமதி, வலவ!' and climbs down. Ainthinai Aimpathu 28: the son stands yearning, the man sees him and drives the chariot on without a look.
teaches: Set side by side the two chariots mark the test of a straying husband as whether he stops for his child, and 28 makes the wife's hardening a verdict on his failing that test rather than on his other women.

note: Purananuru 34 quotes dharma that there is expiation for many crimes but none for those who kill a benefit; Kalittokai 149's friend says ingratitude to helpers will not spare a man, however good his sword.
teaches: The rule the puram poet uses to praise a king's gifts to bards is turned in the akam poem against a lover, which shows the ethic of gratitude ran across both halves of Sangam poetry and could bind a man's private love as tightly as a patron's duty.

note: Naladiyar 398: the girl answers the friend who asks whether she can walk tomorrow behind her man through the hard forest: one who gets a great horse learns to ride it at once. Aimpathu 37: the mother asks whether the girl who faltered at play can keep pace behind her lover on the stony path. The mother doubts the feet that the girl says love will make able.
teaches: The same question, can her feet go with him, gets opposite answers: the mother measures the girl by her weakness at childhood play, the girl by the man she has gained, so across the two books the pair stages the quarrel of the elopement between the generation that remembers and the one that goes.

note: Akananuru 86 recalls a wedding of matrons pouring water with petals and paddy and the bride curled in her new cloth (கோடிக் கலிங்கத்து ஒடுங்கினள்); Kalittokai 69 compares the swan pair to a brahmin circling the fire with his shy bride shrunk in her cloth (கலிங்கத்துள் ஒடுங்கிய).
teaches: The shy bride in her new cloth is a shared formula, but the rite around her differs: the Akananuru wedding has matrons, water and paddy and no fire, while the Kalittokai sets her beside a Veda-reciting priest circling the fire, so the two anthologies record two wedding rites in Tamil country.

note: Both are, on Parimelazhagar's reading of the Kural, the friend trying to stop the man's departure: Kural 1151 tells him to promise a quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 269 sets before him his son climbing down his chest and his wife's eyes on his face.
teaches: The pair shows two opposite tactics for one thurai, the Kural's friend making the woman's death the stake and the Natrinai's friend making the man's own pleasures at home the stake, so the couplet's threat is one option among the friend's arguments, not the only one.

note: Both have the man say that his strength has been broken by a young girl: the Kural by her bright forehead alone, though foes in battle feared him; Kuruntokai 119 by the likeness of a hatchling snake felling a wild elephant.
teaches: Kuruntokai 119 supplies the image behind the Kural's paradox of the mighty man undone by a forehead: the elephant brought down by a hatchling snake, a picture of poison not strength, which explains why the couplet's warrior has no defence.

note: Purananuru 101: Avvai tells her heart that Athiyaman's gift, late or soon, is as sure as the food an elephant holds between its tusks. Natrinai 381 (also Avvaiyar): the rain has settled in like Neduman Anji's seat from which he keeps giving chariots.
teaches: The same poet who in puram counts on Anji's giving as something that never fails makes that unfailing giving the image of a rain a waiting woman cannot bear, so the patron's plenty is a blessing to the bard and a torment to the lover depending on who receives it.

note: Both have the wife's side describe the rival by her dress: in Natrinai 170 the girl in a leaf skirt who comes alone to the festival is a danger the wives must rise against, while in Ainkurunuru 127 the garland across budding breasts marks her as a child of no account.
teaches: On a defensible reading the two friends make incompatible claims about what a young rival's youth means, a strength that may overwhelm the household or a weakness that makes her laughable, showing that the wife's party had no settled verdict on the young courtesan and chose the one their moment needed.

note: Kalittokai 124: the white waves ring the white dune like the blue garment worn by the milk-white elder brother of the god who measured the world. Thinaimalai 58: the dark sea and the white sand lie together like Mayavan and his elder brother.
teaches: Both neythal poets read the shore's dark and white through the two divine brothers, but Kalittokai puts both colours on the one white brother in his blue cloth, while the venba splits them between the two brothers, so the sea and the sand become kin rather than body and garment.

note: 216 says the friend, known by hearing alone and never met for many years, will come; Kural 785 says neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed, feeling alone gives the claim (கிழமை) of friendship.
teaches: The Kural's rule and the king's wager share the technical word கிழமை, so the couplet's claim that friendship needs no meeting has a famous royal case behind it, one staked on a seat kept for a man never seen.

note: Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so whoever gets it should at once do what lasts; in Kuruntokai 350 the friend calls the wealth for which the man left நிலையாப் பொருள், wealth that does not stay, and regrets they did not stop him.
teaches: The ethicist's premise that wealth does not stay becomes in akam an argument against the journey itself: the Kural spends unstable wealth on lasting good, while the friend counts the lasting thing given up as the woman's company, so the same premise judges the pursuit of wealth from the household's side.

note: Kural 37 tells us to see the way of aram in the difference between the one who bears the palanquin and the one who rides in it; Paripadal 19.10-13 likens the festival riders on horses and in chariots, in fine ornament and cloth, to those who have done much aram and set out for the world of the excellent to take its fruit.
teaches: Both picture the fruit of aram as riding in finery, but the Paripadal puts that ride in the passage to the next world and uses it only as a simile for festival-goers, while the Kural reads it in this world's ranks, so the pair shows the Kural's hard claim taking a shared image of heavenly reward and pressing it into a judgement on living people.

note: Natrinai 151: even if the girl's forehead pales and her shoulders grow thin, may the hill lord not come by night. Ainthinai Aimpathu 17: because he comes without fail, the girl, afraid for him, loses her bloom and wastes away.
teaches: Natrinai offers her wasting as the lesser harm to be borne so that he stays away at night, but Ainthinai shows the night visits themselves causing the wasting through fear, so neither his coming nor his staying away spares her and only marriage can.

note: Purananuru 55.1-4 gives the mountain bow strung with a snake (பாம்புஞாண்) and the three forts burned with one arrow as the blue-throated god's feat, an emblem to measure the Pandya by; Paripadal Thirattu 1.80-82 says the serpent became the string of the Himalaya bow when the bull-rider destroyed the three cities and that it was they who gave him that ancient fame.
teaches: The same snake-strung bow is Shiva's glory in a court poem and the serpent's own merit in a shrine hymn, so the pair shows that a fixed myth could be re-credited to whichever power a cult served, the bowstring becoming the hero once it had a temple.

note: In Kuruntokai 285 the waiting woman asks where he can be, who crossed sky-high hills where a lone kite sits on the nyemai top; in Ainkurunuru 321 the man on such hills hears the hen kite call from the omai and says her nature never leaves him.
teaches: The same bare tree and kite are imagined by the woman and actually met by the man, and the pair answers her question from the other end of the road: where she fears he has forgotten her, the same scene brings her back to him.

note: Kural 1246 tells the heart its anger is false, since it cannot stay angry on seeing the man who ends quarrels by union; Kalittokai 122 has the woman, chided for sulking, say she knows he keeps other women, yet when he tends her a little her shameless heart melts and is calmed.
teaches: The kali poem supplies the setting the couplet leaves out, a friend mocking her sulks as causeless, so the Kural's confession that the heart's anger is false turns out to answer that reproach: she knows his fault fully, and her heart still gives way.

note: Both poems by Kapilar have toddy made by ripe jackfruit in a long rock pool (பாறை நெடுஞ்சுனை, விளைந்த தேறல்) drunk unknowingly by a creature: a monkey that cannot climb and sleeps, a peacock that staggers like a rope-dancer.
teaches: The same poet uses one formula for two jobs: in Akananuru 2 the drunk monkey is an argument that the lover can easily find the joy he plans, while in the idyll the drunk peacock only praises the plenty of the lover's land, which shows that in Kapilar the image's force depends on where it stands in the speech, not on the image itself.

note: Aimpathu 6: the bee humming at the jasmine is sweet to those who have someone to lean on, but the dark evening comes and saws at us who have no one. Ezhupathu 17: the evening comes like killers upon those with no one to embrace them.
