teaches: Aimpathu 6 states both halves of the rule, sweet to the partnered and cutting to the lone, while Ezhupathu 17 states only the second, so together they show that the evening's cruelty was located in the hearer's state, not in the hour, and the later poem could leave the happy half unsaid.

note: In Akananuru 98 the girl fears that if Murugan, the tall Vel smelling of veri, should actually relieve her at the mother's rite, her lover will hear that her pain was something else; Paripadal 19.89-94 says maidens will not reach young men's arms, nor wives their husbands' grace, unless they eat the leftover of the god's elephant at his hill.
teaches: The akam girl's dread makes sense only if Murugan really does rule a girl's union, and the Paripadal states that power openly as a festival rite that maidens and wives perform, so together they show that the akam irony about the veri rite rests on a public belief in the god as the giver of husbands, not on disbelief in him.

note: Kalittokai 138's madal rider sings that grief and the palmyra horse are what she gave (படரும் பனை ஈன்ற மாவும் நல்கியவை); in Kural 1135 the man says the girl gave him the madal and evening's anguish.
teaches: Both men list the madal among the woman's gifts, so the convention made the beloved the author of the lover's public shame; the kali poem adds the outcome the couplet leaves open, her coming in grace, which shows the gift was meant to be returned.

note: Natrinai 250: the man came near his son practising walking with his little chariot in the street (தேர் நடைபயிற்றும்) and his wife shied away saying 'who are you?'; Kalittokai 81: the son practises walking with his chariot in the yard (கால் வல் தேர் கையின் இயக்க, நடை பயிற்றா) while husband and wife argue over him.
teaches: The Natrinai gives the husband's side in one recoil, while the Kalittokai stages the whole quarrel around the same toddling child, so together they show the son with his toy chariot as the standing occasion for the husband's return in marutham, and the wife's refusal as a scene both anthologies expected.

note: Both have the man in secret love say the girl keeps his eyes from sleep at night: Ainkurunuru 172 likens his wakefulness to the never-resting waves of Thondi; Kural 1136 has him, sleepless at midnight, think of riding the palmyra horse.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 172 stops at the sleepless night and gives it the image of the restless sea, while the Kural shows where that night leads, to the threat of the madal, so the pair marks sleeplessness as the stage of love just before shame is given up.

note: Kural 1171: the woman asks why her eyes weep, when it was they who showed him to her and brought on the sickness; Kuruntokai 241: she bears her desire, while her eyes, which saw the hill man, weep out of their own intimacy.
teaches: The couplet blames the eyes as the cause that now complains, while the poem excuses them as loyal intimates of the man, so the same weeping eyes can be charged as culprits or honoured as the part of her that keeps faith with what it saw.

note: Both have the wife charging the husband with bathing in the new flood with other women; Ainkurunuru 64 rests on the many who saw it, Akananuru 266 says the talk is loud as a feast and then that this is no grief to her compared with the oath he swore before Murugan.
teaches: The long poem moves the offence the short one names: in Ainkurunuru 64 the wound is that many saw, while Akananuru 266 dismisses the gossip and fixes on his broken oath, so publicity was the first charge but perjury the deeper one.

note: Kural 1213's woman says she lives because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; in Ainkurunuru 234 the friend tells the lover that the girl sees his chest in dreams and not awake, and that is why she pales.
teaches: The same split between dream and waking presence is the woman's own comfort in the Kural and the friend's evidence of harm in the Sangam poem, so the couplet's consolation is shown to be what an onlooker reads as wasting, and the dream becomes a lever for marriage rather than a way to live.

note: Kural 1222: the woman tells the evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner is as hard-eyed as hers. Kuruntokai 46 asks whether the sad evening (புன்கண் மாலை) is absent in the land where he has gone.
teaches: Both women make the evening's sorrow a test of the absent man: the couplet asks whether the evening's partner is as hard as hers, the poem asks whether he has any evening at all, and its sparrows settling with their young supply what the couplet leaves out, that evening is when every creature with a home returns to it.

note: Naladiyar 11: knowing grey hair will come, the wise renounce in childhood, while those who delight in fleeting youth rise later on a staff. Thinaimalai 85: because youth cannot be brought back, the man should stay with his wife rather than chase wealth. On a plain reading the same fact counsels withdrawal in one and staying for love in the other.
teaches: From the one premise that youth does not return, the Naladiyar argues for leaving pleasure early and the paalai friend for keeping it while it lasts, so the impermanence of youth was an argument that served the householder's love as readily as the renouncer's flight.

note: Both turn on the woman's own inability to forget (மறப்பறியேன்; மறவா நம்மே); the Kural asks what would become of her if she forgot, Ainkurunuru 319 asks whether he has forgotten her.
teaches: The Kural keeps the question inside her (remembering burns, forgetting would kill), while the Sangam poem turns the same constancy outward into a charge against him, so read together they show the two directions the claim 'I do not forget' could be pointed.

note: Both use the formula of the salt carts that proclaim their rate (கொள்ளை சாற்றி, கொடுநுக ஒழுகை); in Akananuru 159 raiding bowmen cook meat at the cold hearths the salt carters left, on the road the lover crossed.
teaches: The same stock road scene serves opposite ends: in the love poem the salt-carters' track is where raiders lurk and the woman fears for her man, while in the guide poem it is a road made safe for travellers by day under the patron, so the formula's meaning is set by whose land the road runs through.

note: Kural 1102 says the jewelled woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes; in Kalittokai 60 the man tells the friend his only medicine is to see the girl's face, and there is no other.
teaches: The Kural states the paradox as the man's private discovery after union; in the Kalittokai it is relayed by the friend as a plea before union, so the same conceit serves as an argument that obliges the girl to grant the cure.

note: Kural 782: the friendship (கேண்மை) of the wise waxes like the crescent moon, that of fools wanes. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 4: the friendship of the worthy (சான்றவர் கேண்மை) stands firm and grows into strength, so the mountain lord's will too.
teaches: The venba lifts the Kural's maxim about friendship with the worthy into a girl's mouth as her proof that her lover will not fail, which shows the ethics books' rule of friendship being used, within the akam frame, to judge a lover's character before marriage.

note: In 426 the man has given up the king's war; in 429 he says he would go to it if the woman puts away her pallor.
teaches: Within one decade the poet sets a flat refusal of royal service beside a conditional consent to it whose condition, her pallor gone, is undone by the going itself, so 429 reads as a refusal phrased as a promise.

note: In Akananuru 388 the girl would ask the mother's velan whether his god goes hunting on a deer's track with a bloody arrow; in Natrinai 173 the friend asks whether saying that the hill lord caused the sickness would wrong Murugan.
teaches: Both turn the veri rite's diagnosis against itself by slipping the real cause, the hill man, into a question about the god, which shows that disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிலை) had a recognised form: a mock-pious question put within the lover's hearing.

note: 396 praises Ezhiniyathan of Vattaru, whose land has the toddy-drinking Kosar; Akananuru 216 names Athan Ezhini, lord of Selli, among whose people the young Kosar make garlands, and compares the parathai's pain to the elephant his spear pierced.
teaches: If the two Ezhinis are one chief (both are named with the Kosar), akam remembers him by a war wound inflicted on an elephant, used as a courtesan's image of suffering, while puram remembers him as feeder of the kinless, showing how a patron's two reputations were divided between the genres.

note: In Kuruntokai 14 the man wishes that once he wins the girl the town would know it and many in the street would call him the good woman's husband. In Natrinai 159 the friend asks him to let his chariot lodge in the fishing hamlet so that it wakes in uproar.
teaches: Both treat the town's knowing as the way to marriage, but from opposite sides: the man in Kuruntokai 14 wishes for it after winning her, while the friend in Natrinai 159 demands it now as the means of winning her, using the hamlet's noise as pressure.

note: Kural 1151, in Parimelazhagar's reading the friend's words: if you are not leaving tell me, your quick return tell those who will be alive. Natrinai 43: the friend tells the departing man his going is joy to him and ruin to her.
teaches: Both friends answer an announced departure by saying she will not survive it, but the poem adds the grounds the couplet leaves out: the man once said 'fear not', so his leaving is a broken pledge of protection, which explains why the couplet treats talk of a quick return as worthless.

note: In 7 onlookers on the road ask who the pitiable bowman and his anklet-wearing girl are, setting out into the wilds; in 390 onlookers tell the man, mate of the young she-elephant, to stop for the night because of the frontier guards' drum.
teaches: The onlookers of udanpokku move from pity to protection: in 7 they only wonder at the couple, in 390 they name the danger of the road at nightfall and halt them, so the kandor are not only witnesses of the elopement but its guardians on the way.

note: In Ainkurunuru 49 the bard-woman pours a few fish and gets much paddy; in Akananuru 126 the bard's daughter in Evvi's Kaviri land will not even take old red paddy for her brothers' vaalai fish and is given pearls.
teaches: The barter of the bard's women was a stock picture of the bard family getting more than it gives; the Akananuru uses it as praise of a patron's wealth, while the Ainkurunuru turns the same profit into an accusation, since the bard who gets much for little also gets much for his lies.

note: In Akananuru 22 the girl laughs inwardly that the velan's rite was wasted when her lover, the true cure, came by night; in Ainkurunuru 101 the friend tells the mother outright that the coming chariot is the cure.
teaches: Held together, the two show the same diagnosis moving from the girl's secret mockery of the mother's remedy to the friend's open correction of it, which is the step the disclosure to the mother exists to take.

note: Purananuru 233 is a bard's cry at the dawn news of Evvi's wounds, wishing it false; Akananuru 115 recalls the battle where Evvi fell and, on our reading, the bards breaking off and laying down the curved necks of their harps in worship.
teaches: The puram poem gives the bards' words at Evvi's fall and the akam poem their gesture, so together they show that his death was mourned with a known bardic rite that a love poet could cite as an image for seed pods on a road.

note: Verse 37 holds up the farmer who ploughs, sows and waters as the model of provision; verse 42 shows the ploughman who toils without seed as the fool.
teaches: The farmer's image cuts both ways in the fragment: what matters is not the labour, which both farmers do, but whether the seed of austerity was sown.

note: Naladiyar 363 calls a wife who does not enter the kitchen at dawn a disease and one who does not serve what she cooked a demon; Kuruntokai 167 shows a young wife, smoke in her kohl eyes, cooking and serving with delight at her husband's praise. On the Naladiyar's reading the act is a duty enforced by threat; on the poem's it is the wife's own joy.
teaches: The same kitchen duty that the ethics book defines by the horror of its failure is shown in the Sangam poem as freely chosen pleasure, so the pair shows the domestic norm seen from the husband's fear and from the wife's satisfaction.

note: 32 is the man's first sight of the girl guarding the drying fish; 44 has the friend name the grove of that same task as the girl's place.
teaches: Read together the two verses show the fish-drying watch doing for the neythal girl what the millet watch does in kurinji: it is where the man first sees her and, later, the daytime meeting place the friend appoints.

note: Akananuru 321's foster mother wonders whether the girl will rest with her companion in a small hamlet (சீறூர்) or walk on into the night; Ainkurunuru 382 is told from the hamlet where they rested at nightfall (எல்லிடை அசைந்த ... சீறூர்).
teaches: What the foster mother can only imagine is answered from the hamlet itself, where strange women who have daughters feel her pain, so the grief of an elopement was pictured as reaching every house with a girl along the road.

ullurai.tenor: the man who risks death on the night path and the girl who would not outlive him

pairs.situation: the man may meet death coming by the dangerous night path
the girl would not survive him
she would end her own life

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses monkeys of the hill slope in a kurinji poem, not leaving its land (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the male monkey that has got a jackfruit calls its mate to share it
iraicchi.sense: the hill lord, who has the means, should likewise call her to him openly, now that the field where they met is closed to her

iraicchi.act: the tusker breaks the omai tree to relieve the hunger of his young mate in the drought
iraicchi.sense: even the elephant in the waterless land feeds and stays by its mate, so the man who leaves his wife is harder than the beast

iraicchi.act: the stork carries small fish in its cheek and gives itself wholly to its young
iraicchi.sense: a bird that keeps faith with its own brood has seen the road of a man who did not keep faith with his

iraicchi.act: the gull takes fright at a harmless white thing, mistaking it for a net
iraicchi.sense: her earlier fear of the man was a fear of a snare that was never there, and his word has now shown it harmless

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant sleeps beside its mate in the thin shade of the burning forest rather than leaving her
iraicchi.sense: even the beasts of the road he means to cross keep to their mates in the heat, so the man should not leave her to cross it

iraicchi.act: the female monkey stays and plays with her male on the boulder of the hunters' yard
iraicchi.sense: the beasts of his own hill keep to their mates, so the lord should never leave the girl and let her eyes grow pale

ullurai.tenor: the hero who keeps away

pairs.situation: he takes a harmless thing for a danger
he has fled from their union and stays away

ullurai.speaker_fit: the girl uses an elephant of her own hill, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

note: Kural 1221 tells the hour it is not evening but the time that eats the lives of the wedded; Kalittokai 119, after a long catalogue of dusk, says those who call it evening are deluded, not knowing it is the hour that unwraps women's lives.
teaches: The couplet compresses into one address the argument the kali poem builds through fifteen lines of homing birds, closing flowers and lit fires, so the Kural's 'not evening but a killing hour' is a summary of an established neythal rebuttal rather than a fresh conceit.

note: Purananuru 19 (lines 8 to 9) likens arrows lodged in a wounded elephant to a flock of sparrows settled on a hill (குன்றத்து இறுத்த குரீஇஇனம் போல); Kalavazhi Narpathu 8 says elephants hidden by arrows look like countless hills with flocks of sparrows (எண்ணருங் குன்றிற் குரீஇயினம்).
teaches: The near-identical image shows a stock battle simile passing from a Pandya victory poem to a Chola one, and the frames show it carries no fixed feeling: in Purananuru 19 it leads into mothers weeping for sons and Death fleeing in shame, while in Poigaiyar it is pure spectacle of the victor's field.

note: Purananuru 361's patron gives golden lotuses to bards and garlands to the singing women and needs no one to tell him the world does not last; the idyll's king crowns the bard with a golden lotus and garlands the viraliyar after weighing the unlasting world (line 466).
teaches: Placed together, the golden lotus for the bard and the garland for the singing woman appear as a fixed pair of gifts tied to one stated motive, the patron's knowledge that the world does not last, which lets the Purananuru king face Death and makes the idyll's king hurry the gift.

note: Kural 1171 says the eyes showed him and so she came to see an unending sickness; Kuruntokai 305 opens with the bright fire of love that the eyes brought and follows it to a sickness no one can stop.
teaches: The couplet blames the eyes and stops at 'unending'; the poem carries the same sickness to its end in the dunghill cocks' fight that only death stops, so 'unending' is shown to mean ending only in death.

note: Ainkurunuru 90: the other woman says the husband has the bee's nature, and his son's mother wrongly sulks with her. Kuruntokai 8: the other woman says the man boasts in her house but at home moves like a mirror image to whatever his son's mother wants.
teaches: Both courtesans name the wife only as his son's mother, but one says he roves like a bee and the other that he obeys his wife like a puppet, so together they show the other woman claiming no hold on him at all: he belongs to every flower and, at home, to the mother of his son.

note: Kalittokai 133: justice (முறை) is taking life without favour (கண்ணோடாது உயிர் வௌவல்); Kural 541: justice is to examine, show favour to no one (கண்ணோடாது) and act after weighing.
teaches: Both define justice with the same word கண்ணோடாது, but the love poem gives its harshest form, taking life, in a list meant to shame a lover, so the definition of முறை as unbending punishment was common coin a friend could quote, and the Kural's procedural version tempers a stock definition centred on the death sentence.

note: In Natrinai 200 the friend, with the bard listening, has the potter cry through the town that women should guard against this bard's lie-wrapped crooked words; in Thinaimozhi 34 the bard is found standing in the other women's street for his own gain.
teaches: Read together the two show the bard's double standing in marutham: the man's envoy at the wife's door is, to the town and the wife, a known agent of his affairs elsewhere, and the venba adds that he profits from it.

note: Akananuru 355: in spring bees hum on the budding branches like the strings of a paalai lute touched by a master, the season in which the heroine fears her man's going. Thinaimozhi 16: bees hum the paalai melody as the man leads the girl away.
teaches: The same sound of bees playing the paalai mode marks the spring of a parting in the Akananuru and the spring of an elopement in the venba, so the image does not carry a fixed mood but takes its grief or its promise from the uri it serves.

note: Kuruntokai 73 says the Kosar killed Nannan's fragrant mango tree and drove him from his land; the preface of the fourth ten says Narmudi Cheral beheaded Nannan of Peruvaayil and felled his gold-bearing vakai.
teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree on which tree was Nannan's guardian and who destroyed him, so either the name Nannan covers more than one chief or felling his guarded tree was a victory several conquerors claimed, and neither poem alone shows that the deed was told of more than one enemy.

note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife asks why his eyes are red after bathing in the first-rain flood with fine women. Kalittokai 98: the husband says he was delayed bathing in the new flood of the Vaigai, and the wife turns the flood, point by point, into the woman he bathed with.
teaches: The Kalittokai shows the flood-bath as the husband's ready alibi and the wife unpicking it at length, while the Ainkurunuru wife grants the bath in a word and reads his red eyes as the trace of the women in it, so the pair shows the new flood as the standard excuse of the marutham husband and its marks on his body as the wife's standard proof.

note: Weighing the condition of the unlasting world, the king gives before the bard has finished asking; the couplet says wealth does not stay, so when you have it do at once what lasts.
teaches: The idyll turns the couplet's 'at once' into a patron's habit with its motive stated, wealth that will not stay given for fame that will, so the maxim had a heroic model in the bard's patron before it became a rule of the ethics book.

note: Akananuru 59: on the road for wealth an elephant bends a yaa tree so its young mate can eat, yet the man forgets her; Kuruntokai 255: on that road the elephant strips the yaa tree to feed its whole hungry herd, and the men went to fulfil their duty.
teaches: The same road-sign is turned two ways by the friend: feeding one mate in Akananuru 59 shames the man who forgets his wife, while feeding the whole herd in Kuruntokai 255 matches the man's duty to his household, so the friend can use the elephant to reproach the journey or to justify it.

note: In Kuruntokai 229 onlookers see destiny (பால்) at work in two who fought as children and are now joined; in 366 the friend invokes the same destiny before any outcome to refuse to judge the man.
teaches: Destiny serves after the fact as the onlookers' explanation and before the fact as the friend's argument for consent, so the pair shows the akam idea of பால் doing persuasive work, not only describing what happened.

note: Kural 1130: he lives joyfully in her heart, while the town says he is unloving and lives apart; Kuruntokai 289: she grieves for him out in the rain, and the clamouring town grieves for her more.
teaches: In both the woman's thought goes out to the absent man while the town's goes to her plight, but the town's verdict differs, blame in the Kural and pity in the poem, so the town's talk in akam is not fixed as hostile gossip and can be her chorus.

note: Kural 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that does not cut down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமை). Thinaimalai 134 uses both words (கிழமை, பழமை) as two alternative reasons why she, the humble one, received the man's grace when the many women he took did not.
teaches: The Kural states as a definition that old intimacy survives the liberties a friend takes, while the wife applies the same two terms to a husband who has taken many women and cannot decide whether his return came from enduring character or from reckoning the use of old ties, so the pair shows the friendship ethic carried into marriage and the doubt it leaves when the one taking liberties is the stronger party.

note: Purananuru 56.1-8 gives four gods four banners: the bull, the palm (பனைக்கொடி) of the conch-white one with the plough, the bird of the sapphire-dark one, the peacock; Paripadal 4.37-41 gives the dark god the bird, the palm, the plough and the elephant, and says there is no banner that is not his. On the plain reading the palm banner belongs to a different god in one poem and to Mal in the other.
teaches: The puram poet needs four separate gods so that the king can match each in one excellence, while the devotional poet folds the elder brother's palm and plough into Mal's own emblems, so the pair shows how a hymn's claim of sole lordship rearranged the very iconography the court poets used as a fixed set.

note: The materialist's awareness arising from the elements like intoxication from mixed ingredients appears in the Neelakesi's materialist as well.
teaches: Buddhist and Jain polemic both put the liquor simile in the materialist's mouth, which suggests it was the standard Tamil way to state his theory of mind.

note: The Kural's woman says the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only once she has seen him to her eyes' fill; 498 says her shoulders have regained their beauty because he came.
teaches: The Kural states as the woman's own condition that only his presence cures the pallor, and 498 shows that condition met and observed from outside, item by item on her body, so the couplet's claim is confirmed as the accepted course of the return.

note: Kalittokai 11 closes its argument that the man will return with the omens at home: the lizard chirps on the good side and her lovely eye throbs on the left (உண் கண்ணும் ஆடுமால், இடனே). Thinaimalai 80 ends on the same left-eye omen, with the same closing word இடம்.
teaches: Kalittokai 11 reaches the throbbing left eye only after a long proof from the man's own words, while the venba rests the promise of return on the omen alone, which shows the left-eye sign was a recognised closing proof that could carry a whole short poem.

note: Ainthinai 14 has the friend say the man came 'like those who ask after a beast' (மாவினவு வார்போல) with something else to ask; Thinaimalai 9 has the man himself call his asking after a beast deceit.
teaches: The ruse is seen through from both sides, the friend naming it as a likeness and the hero confessing it as a trick, which shows the beast question as a convention both parties knew and played along with rather than a deception that worked.

note: Kural 872: take on the enmity of ploughmen whose plough is the bow rather than of those whose plough is the word. Thinaimozhi 17: the woman fears for her man passing the hamlets of those who live by ploughing with the bow, while her shoulders slacken because he left without grace.
teaches: The Kural ranks the bow-ploughmen as the lesser enemy, and the venba agrees in its own way: the bowmen are only a feared danger on his road, while the wound she actually bears, slackened shoulders, comes from his word, the promise and grace he withheld.

note: Kar Narpathu 12 has the friend say that his coming is certain, shown beyond doubt by the dark clouds that rise every day; in Kuruntokai 314 the full rain cloud flashes lightning at evening and the heroine says he still does not come. On this reading the sign the friend calls certain has failed.
teaches: Set beside the Kar Narpathu's confident friend, the poem shows the other side of the season-sign: the cloud that is offered as proof of return becomes, when he does not come, the measure of his broken word.

note: Purananuru 38 says bards think of Killivalavan's land even in the gods' golden grove, because there no one with means gives and no one in want asks (உடையோர் ஈதலும் இல்லோர் இரத்தலும்); thirattu 12 says Koodal honours givers and rejoices at receivers, so who would go to the gods' world (புத்தேள் உலகு)?
teaches: Purananuru 38 supplies the reason the fragment leaves unsaid, that heaven is poorer for lacking the exchange of giving and asking, so the Paripadal's preference for Koodal over heaven rests on an older argument first made for a king's land and here transferred to a city and its god's hill.

note: Kural 813 says friends who weigh their gains are no better than thieves; Thirikadugam counts the one who clings by fortune and watches for profit as not to be befriended.
teaches: The Kural shames the calculating friend by comparison; the verse adds when he shows himself, at the turn of fortune, which is also when the liar and the hollow man show themselves.

note: Naladiyar 16 says the fleeting pleasures of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling its garland, are not found among the wise; Natrinai 126 says no wealth surpasses youth and that love must be taken in youth because wealth cannot buy it later.
teaches: Both start from the shortness of youth and draw opposite duties from it: the Naladiyar to refuse youth's pleasure, the Natrinai hero to refuse wealth for its sake, so the same premise of impermanence served the akam poets as an argument for love and the didactic poets as one against it.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my home and feast the evening; Kuruntokai 250: the man tells his charioteer to drive the swift horses before evening comes, for her distress.
teaches: The couplet names evening as the feast the returning man looks to; the poem shows why it is a deadline as well as a reward: evening is the hour the stag is with its mate and the hour she suffers most alone, so he must beat it.

note: Purananuru 158 lists Ori of Kolli and Malaiyan who rode Kaari side by side among the seven great givers; Natrinai 320 remembers the street where Ori was killed and Kaari entered as a byword for a stricken town.
teaches: The bards' canon of seven generous patrons hides that two of them were enemies, one killing the other, and the love poem shows that killing had become a proverb for a town in panic.

note: Kural 1157: the bangles slipping past her wrist announce that the lord of the shore has left; Kalittokai 127: the friend tells the lord of the shore that her bangles slip (இறை வளை நெகிழ்ந்த) and asks him to give grace as the wave shelters the adumbu creeper.
teaches: The couplet has the bangles accuse the man to the woman herself; the poem has the friend carry the same evidence to the man's face and pair it with a remedy, so the slipping bangle moves from private proof of desertion to an argument for his return.

note: Akananuru 180: while the girls play at sand houses, a man drives up, hangs a kuvalai wreath down her braid unasked, gazes and leaves, and the town starts talking; Kalittokai 111: a herder offers to build the girl's play-house, tie a garland in her hair and paint her breasts, and she refuses each, saying a girl who takes a stranger's flowers is a great fool (ஏதிலார் தந்த பூக் கொள்வாய்).
teaches: The herd girl's refusal states the rule the shore poem leaves unsaid, that a stranger's flowers in a girl's hair are a claim on her; that rule is why the silent wreath of Akananuru 180 sets the town talking, and why the herd girl answers the same offer by asking her friend to tell her parents.

note: Kural 1293: heart, do you follow him as you please because the ruined have no friends? Natrinai 56: has my heart stayed with him to return together, or has it seen my lost beauty and left me as a stranger?
teaches: The couplet gives only the bitter answer, that the heart deserts her as fair-weather friends desert the ruined; the poem holds that answer beside a kinder one, that the heart is loyally waiting with him, so the Kural's accusation is shown to be one horn of a doubt the woman cannot settle.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone, her shoulders lose their old beauty and her bangles slip; Kuruntokai 239: her bangles have slipped and her shoulders wasted, so is there shame left to give up?
teaches: The couplet lists the slipping bangles as a sign of grief, while the poem draws from the same sign a conclusion: since the body has already told, modesty has nothing left to hide, so the wasting licenses the woman to speak out.

note: Akananuru 296 says the man's bathing in the great Vaiyai with the dark girl has become gossip in Koodal (அலர்ஆ கின்று, அது பலர்வாய்ப் பட்டே); thirattu 2.51-56 shows a woman wearing a garland from the flood openly, for the land to know (நாடு அறியப் பூ மாலை அப்பி), and the town's gossip following (ஊர்த்து அலர்).
teaches: The fragment shows how the gossip the Akananuru friend throws at the man was made: a love token worn in plain sight at the river festival, chosen by the woman as display, so the akam reproach of public shame rests on a festival custom in which the other woman wanted to be seen.

note: In Natrinai 166 the husband himself tells his wife that their son has learnt to play and asks why he should part from her.
teaches: Natrinai gives the husband's own voice answering the friend's argument of Ainkurunuru 424, so the son as a reason to stay worked from both sides of the speech situation: urged on the man by the friend, and taken up by him unprompted.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world endures because there are people who will not eat even nectar alone and who strive for others, not for themselves; Patitruppattu 38 says the king has no wish to enjoy sweet things alone and lives for others.
teaches: The Purananuru gives an unnamed class of people on whom the world rests, and the Chera praise gives the same refusal to eat alone to one named king, which shows the court poet drawing on a general moral picture to make the patron its single instance.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of living at home and guarding one's goods is for feeding guests; Kalittokai 8 ends that living in one's own house, protected by the king and tending guests, is itself wealth.
teaches: The friend turns the Kural's account of what wealth is for into an argument against the wealth journey: if a household already feeds its guests, it already has what wealth exists to buy.

note: Both are the friend forbidding the night visit by a path where elephants go; Akananuru 318 adds 'மன்றல் வேண்டினும் பெறுகுவை', you may have the wedding if you want it.
teaches: The four-line verse stops at the prohibition, and the long poem shows what the prohibition is for: shutting the night road is the friend's way of pressing for marriage, which Thinaimozhi 1 leaves unsaid.

note: Purananuru 22 praises the king under whose umbrella the unarmed sleep safe (வாள் மருங்கு இலோர் காப்பு உறங்க) because he himself does not sleep (நீ துஞ்சாய் மாறே); Mullaippattu sets armed women, old guards, hour-keepers, Yavanas and Mlecchas round the king's own bed at midnight.
teaches: The praise of a wakeful king who lets others sleep safely has a reverse side that only the idyll shows: the king's own sleep needs a whole household of armed and foreign watchers, so royal protection of the realm's sleep rests on others guarding his.

note: Kural 745 praises a fort that is hard to take, holds stored food and is easy for those inside to hold; 44 tells a besieged king that sitting secure behind shut gates and a long wall is shameful while his elephants starve and his people cry for milk and water. On the reading that both judge the king who holds out in a fort, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural values the fort as a means of holding out, while Kovur Kizhar sees the same holding out from inside, through starving beasts and infants, and calls it neither aram nor maram, so the pair shows the fort's strength and its moral cost as two views of one siege.

note: The idyll's அந்தணர் are marked by Veda, rite and high conduct, and only in passing by a loving heart; the Kural says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous because they are kind to every creature.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the Kural keeping the idyll's name but moving its definition from the Veda and the rite to the one trait the idyll mentions last, kindness, so the couplet reads as a deliberate redefinition of a status the court poem took for granted.

note: Kural 1311 has the woman refuse her man's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Natrinai 174 the wife, told she should be well now that he is back and never leaves her side, says he gave his chest to another woman and an embrace is worth nothing without love.
teaches: The Kural grounds the refusal in shared possession; the poem grounds it in absent love even when he is wholly present, so the pair separates two grievances the oodal chapters run together: that he is shared, and that he is there without love.

note: Akananuru 61 tells the heroine not to suffer looking at the tall wall where the days are marked (நாள்இழை நெடுஞ்சுவர்), and pictures Pulli's men trading white elephant tusks for toddy; Patitruppattu 68 has the king's warriors hoping to trade white tusks (வெண்கோடு) for toddy while women at home draw the days on the painted wall.
teaches: The tusk bartered for toddy and the days scored on a wall were a stock pair of the far campaign and the waiting house: the akam poet splits them between the land the hero crosses and the heroine's room, while Kapilar keeps both inside one king's war, so the cost of conquest is counted at home.

note: Paripadal 2.16-17 names one age of creation after the boar form (கேழல் திகழ்வரக் கோலமொடு பெயரிய ஊழி); Paripadal 3.21-24 tells the deed itself, the god as a boar ploughing up the great earth with his tusk when fire, death and the sun gathered in the sea at the age's end.
teaches: Read together, the two hymns show the boar descent known in Sangam Vaishnava worship both as a label for a cosmic age and as a narrated rescue of the earth from the flood, so the avatar was already a deed that also served to count time.

note: Kural 1187: she lay in his embrace and turned aside, and at once pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up; in 399 pallor is moss on the village well that parts where he touches and spreads where he lets go.
teaches: The couplet's instant hyperbole is given a mechanism by the poem: pallor is a surface like well-moss that closes the moment the hand lifts, so the Kural's 'at that very moment' is not exaggeration but what anyone at a village well has seen.

note: Both men, on the burning road, see the girl in sleep; Ainkurunuru 324 says he will surely see her (காண்குவென் மன்ற), while Akananuru 39 calls the dream false (வாய்அல் கனவின்) because it left his hand empty.
teaches: The short poem gives only the traveller's confidence in the dream, and the long one tells how it ends on waking, so together they show the road-dream as both his comfort and his torment, and explain why the returned man of Akananuru 39 can answer her charge of forgetting with it.

iraicchi.act: the bat leaves the old tree where it rested by day, leaving it lonely, and flies off to the jackfruit slope
iraicchi.sense: as the bat abandons its day-tree at evening, so he left her, and she is the tree left lonely

note: The two poems close on nearly the same words to the hill lord about the eyes of the woman he loves: in 264 they have yielded pallor, in 266 tears (பனி), after the friend owns their great modesty.
teaches: Read in order, the decade escalates the friend's case for marriage from pallor to weeping by changing one word, while the boar beside it changes from mating with its sow to fighting a tiger.

note: Kural 7 says only those who reach the feet of the one without comparison (தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான்) are freed from the mind's care; Paripadal 1.53-68 finds no likeness for the god (நின்னோர் அனையை) and ends with hearts made secure (ஏமுறு நெஞ்சத்தேம்) worshipping the shade of his feet.
teaches: The couplet's two terms, the incomparable one and refuge at his feet, appear in the hymn as a sequence: the singer first tries and fails to find a simile, and only then turns to the feet, so the Kural's maxim reads as the summary of a hymn's movement.

note: In both a woman left behind speaks of a man who crossed the hills where the silk-cotton blooms: Akananuru 185 compares the leafless ilavam in flower to the lamps of a great festival (பெருவிழா விளக்கம் போல), Ainkurunuru 320 compares its falling flowers to embers struck by thunder (உருமுப்படு கனலின்).
teaches: The same flowering tree on the paalai road is a festival of lamps in one woman's mouth and a thunderbolt's embers in the other's, so the silk-cotton was not a fixed sign of danger but a vehicle that swung with the charge each woman laid against her man, his iron will in one and the endless sickness he gave in the other.

note: Kural 226 says relieving the destroying hunger of the destitute is where one with wealth should store it; the verse says that if one gives, one should give food.
teaches: The couplet says where wealth is best stored and the verse which gift is best, so together food given to the hungry is both the best gift and the safest store.

note: In Akananuru 98 the velan sings the god's great name (செல்வன் பெரும்பெயர் ஏத்தி) at the veri ground; in Ainkurunuru 244 the girl says the veri is useless unless the velan sings the hill of her man.
teaches: Akananuru 98 shows what the diviner's song praises in the rite, the god's name, and Ainkurunuru 244 asks for the same song turned to the man's hill, so the girl imagines the only working cure as the rite itself with her lover in the god's place.

note: Kural 18 says that if the sky dries, festival and worship cease even for the gods; Paripadal 6.1-13 shows the rain that has come ending in incense, flowers, oblation and fire (புகை, பூ, அவி ஆராதனை, அழல்) at the river's arrival.
teaches: The Kural argues from absence that worship hangs on rain, and the Paripadal shows the positive side as one continuous scene from sea to cloud to river to offering, adding what the couplet leaves out: the same flood that feeds the rite also brings lovers together, so festival here means love as much as worship.

note: Kar Narpathu 5: he left fearing the words of those who scorn. Akananuru 111: the friend says he will come back, ashamed of the mocking words of hostile men (ஏஎச்சொல் நாணி).
teaches: Taken together, other men's contempt both sends the hero away for wealth and, in the friend's argument, drives him home again, so shame works on him at both ends of the journey.

note: The two poems share the refrain துறைகேழ் ஊரன் கொடுமை ... யாமே ... என் தடமென் தோளே; in 11 she calls him good and the shoulders contradict her, in 12 she lets him keep his cruelty and lets the shoulders lose.
teaches: Read in order, the shared refrain moves the wife from denial, where her body overrules her words, to surrender, where she grants him the cruelty and her body the defeat, so the decade builds a progression out of near-identical lines.

note: Saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning; saying 46 denies the name of learning to what is learnt without submission.
teaches: Across two tens, the book first puts reverence for teachers above learning and then makes it the condition of learning, so reverence moves from the greater good to the thing without which learning does not exist.

note: Both mothers weep each time they see what the girl left (காண்தொறும்): Ainkurunuru the doll and the parrot she reared, Natrinai the courtyard, the playmates and the nochchi.
teaches: Ainkurunuru stops at the doubled grief of looking, while Natrinai turns from the same sight to declare the girl faultless, so the scene of the left belongings could lead either to bare lament or to the mother's acquittal of her daughter.

note: Akananuru 74: the heroine says she could hold firm on the friend's repeated comfort (he will see the doe with the stag in the rain-fresh scrub, think of you and come today, இன்றே வருவர்) if only the herdsmen's harsh little flute did not torment her at evening. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 25: the friend points to the buck leaping with his doe and says he will come right now (இன்னே வருவர்).
teaches: The Thinaimozhi verse gives the friend's argument by itself, and the Akananuru heroine quotes that same argument and tells us where it breaks, at evening with the flute, so the four-line comfort is shown as one turn of a longer exchange in which it does not fully hold.

note: Both praise a wife as chaste like the northern star: here the Brahmin wife who cooks for the bards, in Purananuru 122 Kari's wife, the one thing he keeps while all else goes to Brahmins and bards.
teaches: In both poems the star-chaste wife stands at the centre of a house that gives to Brahmins and bards, but in the chief's poem she is what is kept back from giving and in the idyll she is the one who gives, so the simile marked the giving household from either side.

note: In 370 the husband recalls his wife in the lying-in room, smeared with ghee and mustard, newly called 'old woman' after bearing a son, and finds her shy smile the sweetest thing; in 380 the friend says the wife's ghee-soiled clothes, milk-wet breasts and smell of new birth make her no match for the jewelled women he visits.
teaches: The same marks of motherhood are the husband's proof of tenderness in one poem and the wife's side's proof of his desertion in the other, which shows that the marutham quarrel is fought over what a mother's body means, and that the husband's memory in 370 is an answer to exactly the charge 380 makes.

note: Thinaimozhi 2 says the guarding of the millet fields has ended and asks whether his coming will now be hard; Thinaimalai 5 says the millet has ripened like the fruit of past deeds and that this parts them.
teaches: Thinaimozhi gives the harvest as a fact of the field, and Thinaimalai frames the same harvest as the ripening of deeds into their fruit, which turns the end of the meetings from a farming date into something like fate, and so adds weight to the push for marriage.

note: Yavanas make the lamp-figures that light the queen's inner chambers in Nedunalvadai; in Mullaippattu fierce armed Yavanas guard the king's tent.
teaches: Read together, the idylls place Yavanas at both ends of a royal household, as craftsmen inside the women's palace and as bodyguards in the war camp, so the king trusted these foreigners with the light of his queen's rooms and with his own person.

note: In Akananuru 133 the man once asked the woman whether she could come with him, then crossed alone the forest where the twisted-horned stag keeps his young doe; in Kalittokai 20 the woman asks to go and the man refuses, saying the forest is too hot, while she points to the stag and doe that go together.
teaches: The two poems give opposite men, one who invites idly and one who forbids, while the deer pair on the road answers both: whoever speaks, the creatures of the waste show the journey can be shared, so the stag and doe work as the paalai poets' standing proof against the lone journey.

note: Kalittokai 67's three refrains say 'I would say I will sulk' (புலப்பேன் யான் என்பேன்மன்) and the heart says it will join him; Kural 1284 has the woman go to sulk and her heart go to unite (ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்மன் ... கூடற்கண் சென்றது).
teaches: The Kural's couplet is one turn of a song the Kalittokai performs three times with three different marks on the man's body, and the Kalittokai names the heart's act outright as treason (அறைபோகு), showing that the couplet's quiet split between woman and heart was heard as betrayal from within.

note: 71 line 25 has the king weigh the strong and the simple (உரவரும் மடவரும் அறிவுதெரிந்(து) எண்ணி) before he shows grace; 73 line 1 has the strong and the simple reckon the king (உரவோர் எண்ணினும் மடவோர் எண்ணினும்) and find no one to compare him to.
teaches: The decade turns the same pair round: first the king judges the wise and the foolish to decide whom to spare, then the wise and the foolish judge him and find no measure, so judgement runs both ways between the king and those he rules.

note: Both use the elephant pair shrinking together in hunger on the scorched hill; in Akananuru 91 the friend uses it after he has gone to comfort the woman, in Ainkurunuru 305 before he goes to shame the man out of going.
teaches: The same image of the starving pair that will not part is turned on the man as reproach before the journey and on the woman as reassurance after it, so in the convention one karu image carries opposite arguments depending on whether the departure is still preventable.

note: In both, the friend tells the waiting woman that the konrai bloomed foolishly, taking an unseasonal shower for the rains (Natrinai: கார் என்று அயர்ந்த ... மடவ; Ainkurunuru: காரென மயங்கிய பேதையம் கொன்றை).
teaches: Natrinai answers a question about the promised date by blaming both the mindless cloud and the flowers, while Ainkurunuru answers tears by blaming only the konrai and then vouching for the man, so the 'foolish flower' was a stock rebuttal the friend could aim at the calendar or at grief.

note: In Purananuru 144 bards see a woman weeping over Pekan's neglect and rebuke him; in 475 the heroine says the bard wept over her wasting more than his master.
teaches: Puram shows the bard's pity for the neglected woman turned into a public rebuke of his patron, and akam shows the woman herself noticing that pity and setting it against her lord's coldness, so the bard's tears were a recognised charge against the man in both genres.

note: Both say the world stands because of a certain kind of person: 182 names those who strive for others, Kural 996 those of courtesy (பண்புடையார்), without whom it would sink into the earth.
teaches: The Kural compresses into a two-line rule what the Pandya prince builds as a list of concrete refusals, so the reader of the Kural can see which deeds (not eating alone, dying for honour, refusing blame-tainted gain) its abstract பண்பு was taken to mean.

note: Kural 1315: the man says they will not part in this birth, and her eyes fill with tears. Kuruntokai 49: the woman asks that even when this life turns into the next he be her husband.
teaches: The couplet's joke rests on a wish it never states, that the bond reach past this birth; Kuruntokai 49 is that wish in the woman's own mouth, so the pair shows why 'in this birth' wounds her: she had asked for the next one too.

note: Kalittokai 98 has the husband excuse his absence by the Vaiyai's new flood (வையை வரு புனல் ஆடத் தவிர்ந்தேன்); Paripadal thirattu 2.36-39 has the rival excuse the lover's garland in her hair by the same flood (தானே புறன் தந்து வேய்தந்தது ... அறிந்து புனல் புணர்த்தது).
teaches: Held together, the two show that the festival flood was the stock excuse of the whole triangle: the man pleads it to his wife, and the other woman pleads it to the wife too, so the wife's scorn in the Kalittokai answers an alibi that every party in the Vaiyai festival could use.

note: In Kural 1081 the man cannot tell whether she is an anangu, a peahen or a woman; in Kuruntokai 337 he is sure she is an anangu (அணங்கென) and adds that she herself does not know it.
teaches: The couplet's bewilderment is about what she is; the poem moves it to the gap between her power and her ignorance of it, the one-sided love of kaikkilai, so the pair shows the anangu figure turning from a lover's confusion into an observation about a girl not yet aware of herself.

note: Kural 1255: the dignity of not going after one who has turned away is unknown to those sick with love. Kuruntokai 219: her restraint has gone far and her mind urges her to go to him, but she holds back for fear he will ask 'who are you?'
teaches: The couplet says the lovesick cannot know the pride of not following; the Kuruntokai heroine, lovesick, still stays, held back not by pride but by fear of being met as a stranger, so the poem shows a restraint that survives the loss of honour and the couplet's claim is too absolute.

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; Patitruppattu 54 wishes that the giving king not go to the high world (உயர்நிலை உலகத்துச் செல்லாது) but stay long on the earth.
teaches: The couplet sets heaven aside as irrelevant to the worth of giving, while the bard treats the giver's heaven as a loss to those who live on his gifts and wishes it postponed, so the same detachment of giving from heaven appears once as an ethic and once as the suppliants' self-interest.

note: Both open on the earth a boar has ploughed: in 269 a wild reed rises there like a crop and the friend fears the lord will stay away; in 270 the hunters reap the first crop from it and the lord comes of himself.
teaches: The decade ends by answering the friend's fear on the same boar-tilled ground, where the field that bore only a wild reed now yields a harvest and his return, so the image tracks whether the love will bear fruit.

note: In Kural 1081 the man, first seeing her, cannot tell if she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; in Kalittokai 56 he asks if she is a craftsman's doll, a woman assembled from all women's best parts, or Death in a form it chose.
teaches: Both stage the first sight as a failure to classify the woman, but the Kalittokai adds Death and a girl too young to know her effect, so the Kural's bewilderment turns into a complaint that her beauty is a public danger no one has announced.

note: Both mothers lament a daughter gone with a man through the bowmen's wasteland; Akananuru 35 prays to the god that the stranger may adorn her and lull her on his chest, while Ainthinai Ezhupathu 30 can only wonder whether the girl pines or walks on behind him with reddened feet.
teaches: Together they give the mother's lament two stages, first not knowing whether the girl regrets her going and then accepting it and praying for the man's care, so the venba catches the moment the Akananuru poem has already passed.

note: In Paripadal 11.80 unmarried girls bathe under the brahmins' fire rite praying 'may the wide land not be scorched'; Kural 55 says it rains at the word of the wife who does not worship a god but worships her husband. On the plain reading these name incompatible sources of the rain women can bring: public worship by maidens, or a wife's devotion that sets worship of a god aside.
teaches: Held together, the pair shows two rival accounts of women's power over the rain, the festival rite of the unmarried at the river and the wife's domestic devotion, and the Kural's தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் reads as a choice of the second over the first.

note: Both have the woman's foolish heart following the man who has left (Ainkurunuru: பேதை நெஞ்சம் பின்செல; Kural: பின்செல்வாய் பேதைஎன் நெஞ்சு).
teaches: With the same words the couplet blames her own heart for going after an unkind man, while the Sangam wife lets the heart go and blames the man as harder than stone, so the following heart was an image that could lay the fault on either lover.

note: Kural 1137 praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not mount the palmyra horse; in Natrinai 94 the woman herself says that speaking out desire suits a man while womanhood makes her hold it in, and asks what kind of man he is not to know.
teaches: The Kural's praise of the woman's silence becomes in the Natrinai a grievance spoken by the woman under that rule, aimed at the man who is free to speak and does not, so the restraint the couplet admires is shown from inside as a constraint she resents.

note: The Kural's man says the bond between him and the girl is like that of body and life; the Ainkurunuru hero speaks of their faultless bond as lives mingled into one (உயிர்கலந்து ஒன்றிய).
teaches: The Kural states the life-bond as a lover's private claim, while the Ainkurunuru hero, past a parting, finds it acted out by the scrub's mating beasts and makes the couple the measure of them, so the general likeness gains a witness in the season of return.

note: Paripadal 11.37-38 asks who notices the days run down (நாள் குறைபடுதல் காணுநர் யாரே) as the flood wanes like the moon; Kural 334 says the day is a saw cutting life, for those who can perceive it (உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்).
teaches: Both turn on the same observation, that daily loss goes unseen, but the Paripadal draws from it a request to the river to slow down and keep its plenty, while the Kural draws a warning to the perceptive; the image of unnoticed waning could serve plenty as well as renunciation.

note: Akananuru 5's colophon has the man give up the journey (செலவழுங்கியது) at the sight of her tearful face before he sets out; in Ainkurunuru 330 he has already crossed the scorching forest (வந்தனம் ஆயினும்) when he calls off the journey (ஒழிகஇனிச் செலவே) thinking of her weeping eyes.
teaches: The pair shows that giving up the journey is not tied to a moment: the tears seen at the doorstep in Akananuru 5 and the tears only imagined halfway in Ainkurunuru 330 do the same work, so in this situation her grief, present or pictured, is what overrules the errand, not the danger of the road.

note: Kural 559 says if the king bends justice the sky withholds its rain; Patitruppattu 24 ends that even if the rain-cloud forgets its season the king's wealth will keep its yield.
teaches: The Kural binds the land's rain to the king's justice, but the praise poem claims the just king's plenty survives even a failed monsoon, so court praise pushed royal power past the cosmic dependence the ethical maxim keeps.

note: Natrinai 0 builds the discus-bearer's body from the cosmos: earth his feet, sea his garment, sky his body, the quarters his hands, moon and sun his eyes; Tirumanthiram 2774 gives Shiva the same map, space his body, the eight directions his hands, the three lights his three eyes, as he dances.
teaches: The body made of sky, quarters and heavenly lights is a frame older than either sect: the Sangam invocation fills it for the discus-bearer as a fact the Veda reports, and Tirumular fills it for Shiva and sets it dancing with a third eye of fire, so the image passed between gods while its parts stayed fixed.

note: Natrinai 210 defines the wealth of the worthy as gentleness that fears the distress of those who depend on one; in Natrinai 214 the man leaves his wife, whose bangles slip from grief, to win wealth because fame, pleasure and giving need it.
teaches: By 210's definition the departing man of 214 is pursuing the wrong wealth, since the distress of a dependant is exactly what true wealth fears to cause, so the anthology holds the akam parting for wealth and a moral critique of it side by side.

note: In both the woman tells her friend, before the man leaves, that she cannot survive his going: Kural 1155 asks her to stop it since union will be impossible once he goes, and Kalittokai 24 says her life has already gone with him.
teaches: The kali adds how she knows and why she yields: she learned of the journey from his sleep-talk and gives up her life to save his name from blame, so the couplet's plea to prevent the departure is shown coming from a woman who has already lost the chance to plead.

note: In Akananuru 253 gossip is louder than the cheering at Kudal when the green-jewelled Pandiyan drove out the Kongar; in Kuruntokai 393 gossip is louder than the Kongar's shout when the green-jewelled Pandiyan's general Athikan fell at Vaakai.
teaches: The Pandiyan's wars with the Kongar gave akam poets their yardstick for gossip from both outcomes, his victory cheer at Kudal and the enemy's cry over his fallen general, so the measure was the loudest noise of a known war whichever side made it.

note: Purananuru 230: while Ezhini lived, the herds rested in the forest unguarded and safe; Kuruntokai 80: the courtesan tells the wife to guard her husband like the great herds at Ezhini's war front.
teaches: The courtesan's taunt rests on Ezhini's puram fame as the protector of herds, so she casts herself as the cattle-raider and the husband as plunder that only a war-chief's watch could keep, using the heroic guard to mock a household one.

note: Tirumanthiram 7 declares the Lord elder to the three (மூவர்க்கும் மூத்தவன்) and father to the one who calls him father; Paripadal 2.20-23 makes Thirumal younger to those who call him younger than the conch-white brother and elder to those who call him elder.
teaches: Both poets let the god become the kin-name the worshipper uses, but only the Paripadal applies the rule to seniority itself, so where Tirumular fixes his Lord as eldest the earlier hymn shows rank among gods as a matter of the believer's tradition.

note: Both men say the bangled girl has given them suffering, with the verb of a gift (துயரம் நல்கி; தந்தாள் ... துயர்); in the Kural the gift is the palmyra horse and the evening's pain, in Ainkurunuru 195 a grief that will not pass and lost sleep.
teaches: Read together they show the stages of the same plea to the friend: the Ainkurunuru man stops at sleeplessness, and the couplet shows where his complaint goes next if no one answers it, to the threat of riding the palmyra horse.

iraicchi.act: the male dove that lives in the house calls for its mate
iraicchi.sense: a bird that stays at home calls its mate, while the man means to leave his; she will hear in it the call he will not make

iraicchi.act: the stag holds his young doe close and rests with her in the shade
iraicchi.sense: the man will stay and keep his wife as the stag keeps his doe, even in the season that invites travel

iraicchi.act: the tusker strips the yaa tree to ease the hunger of its weary herd
iraicchi.sense: the men who saw it on the road will remember the household they went out to provide for, and come back to it

iraicchi.act: the she-elephant, sleepless with fear, cries through the clefts for her bull seized by a python
iraicchi.sense: the man who crossed that land has heard a mate grieving for its lost partner, and will remember the one he left

note: Kuruntokai 236: the friend tells the shore lord to go if he must, but first give back the beauty he consumed (நீ உண்டவென் னலனே). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 63: the heroine would accost him herself and say 'give back the colour' (வண்ணந்தா).
teaches: The demand to give back consumed beauty belongs to the friend in Kuruntokai, but the venba puts it in the heroine's own mouth and doubts that only looking at him would suffice, so the pair shows the reproach moving from the go-between to the injured woman herself.

note: Kural 211: duty seeks no return, and the world makes none to the rain. Natrinai 194: the friend asks what return (கைம்மாறு) they can make to the elephant and the parrot.
teaches: The friend applies the Kural's word for repayment to beasts who helped without meaning to, the parrot that raided the millet and so kept the girls in the field, so her mock gratitude turns the rule of unrepayable benefit into a teasing way of announcing that the meetings are over.

note: Purananuru 56 makes the Pandya equal (ஒத்தீயே) to each of four gods in one quality; Paripadal 1.53-57 says no one can be found of whom to say the god is like them, so he is like only himself (நின்னோர் அனையை); both describe the bird-bannered god's body with the same formula, மண்ணுறு மணி (Pura 56.5, Pari 1.62).
teaches: The pairing shows a limit to the பூவைநிலை way of praising a king by the gods: the likeness runs one way only, since a king can be measured by a god but the hymn finds nothing by which to measure the god.

note: Kural 1330 says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is the embrace that follows; Paripadal 9.12-22 ranks love, equal union and karpu, and places the courtesan, the reproach and the சுணங்கறை inside karpu, with their fruit in the sulk (ஊடல்).
teaches: The Kural gives the sulk's worth as a man's two-line saying, while the Paripadal builds it into a ranked theory addressed to Vedic scholars and then uses it to excuse a god's wives, so the pair shows oodal already held as doctrine of Tamil porul, citable to outsiders and to the gods.

note: In Kuruntokai 66 the friend says the konrai is foolish to bloom for a stray rain before the promised season; in Natrinai 99 the friend, answering the woman's own question, says the cloud itself forgot itself and the pidavam, konrai and kodal bloomed because they are foolish.
teaches: The Natrinai takes the Kuruntokai's single foolish tree and widens the folly to the sky and to three flowers, and places it as the answer to the woman's doubt, so the consolation grows from a remark about one tree into a whole season declared mistaken.

note: Both returning men, speaking to the charioteer, picture the wife with the same words, the freckle-waisted woman who deceives their son (புதல்வற் பொய்க்கும், திதலை அல்குல்); Akananuru 54 fills it with her promising the moon milk for a gold tali, Natrinai 161 with her pointing out strangers to the boy.
teaches: The shared phrase shows that soothing the son with a fiction was a fixed mullai picture of the home a returning man imagines, and the two fillings show where the poet's freedom lay: in choosing the fiction, a coaxed moon or a stranger passed off as the father.

note: In Akananuru 98 the girl tells her friend that the mother does not know her ache is eased only on the hill lord's chest, while the velan's rite goes on; in Kuruntokai 362 the friend puts that same claim to the velan as a question: will his chest eat the offering?
teaches: The pair shows the step from private knowledge to disclosure: what the girl can only say to her friend in the long poem, the friend turns into a riddle spoken at the rite itself, so the mockery of the diviner is the means by which the secret reaches the mother.

note: Kural 1269: for those who long for the day of the far one's return, one day passes like seven. Thinaimalai 101: since the man of the decorated chariot went, only the days on which he does not come keep coming.
teaches: The couplet stretches each day of waiting while the venba empties the calendar of the one day she waits for, so together they show waiting as both a lengthening of days and an endless supply of the wrong ones.

note: Natrinai 80 has the man, kept away, say there is no medicine but the broad-shouldered girl for his sickness; Ainkurunuru 99 has him say the broad-shouldered girl has become the medicine for it.
teaches: The one formula of the girl as the only medicine marks the two ends of courtship, a remedy denied while the friend keeps him off in Natrinai 80 and a remedy received in Ainkurunuru 99, so the tense of the line tells where in the affair the man stands.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend calls the season, with peacocks and konrai, the medicine for the heroine's wasting pallor. Ainthinai Aimpathu 2: with the peacock calling and the rain cloud low, every sight of the sky turns the heroine's shoulders yellow. On a plain reading the same season cures the pallor and causes it.
teaches: Set side by side the friend's argument and the heroine's experience disagree about the same sky, which shows that the season-as-proof consolation works only from outside, while to the waiting woman the season itself is the illness.

note: Both close with the same line, ஒண்டொடி யூடுநிலை. In 23 the friend shows the season to reassure; in 38, by the colophon, she concedes that he has lied.
teaches: One closing question about sulking serves first to dismiss the heroine's grievance (the season has come, so he will) and then to grant it (the season has come and he has not), so the series uses a formula line whose force is fixed only by the lines before it.

note: Kar Narpathu 14: the friend is sure he will come quickly, since the cool rain cloud laughs softly as the jasmine shows its bright teeth. Ainthinai Aimpathu 9: he will come; the jasmine has opened its buds, having heard the secret of the new rain.
teaches: In both the friend's proof is the budding jasmine, but one reads it as the season's laughter and the other as the season's whispered secret already received, so the same flower serves as a public sign in one and as private knowledge in the other.

note: In the idyll the forest men who have broken a hard stronghold (அருங்குறும் பெறிந்த) set aside their spoil as guest-tribute for their lord; in Akananuru 349 Nannan pours out unasked to weary bards the great wealth taken from broken strongholds (அருங்குறும்பு எறிந்த).
teaches: Read together the two poems show a chain of wealth: the spoil of forts taken by the hill people goes to Nannan as tribute and goes out again from him to the bards, so the patron's generosity praised in love poetry rests on his people's raids.

note: Purananuru 71: Boothappandiyan vows that if he does not rout the allied kings he may be parted from his wide-eyed wife. Kuruntokai 36: the lover swore a vanjinam that he would not leave her.
teaches: Separation from the beloved is the penalty the king stakes on his battle vow and the very thing the lover's vow forswears, so the akam vow borrows the puram form and the friend's trust in it rests on the warrior's honour that a vanjinam is never broken.

note: Akananuru 369's foster mother fears the girl had her anklets removed without honour in a poor stranger's hut (சிலம்புடன் கழீஇ); Ainkurunuru 399 concedes the anklet-removal to the youth's house but claims the wedding for the girl's own.
teaches: The anklet-removal that Akananuru dreads as a rite done without the family is in Ainkurunuru granted to the other house on condition of a proper wedding at home, so the girl's people could accept the lost rite once the honour of the wedding was kept.

note: Both are about restraint that can no longer keep love hidden: Kural 1254's woman says she used to think herself restrained but her love now breaks out in public; Natrinai 15's friend tells the man they have let go even their long modesty and the town may gossip.
teaches: The Kural records the loss of restraint as an inner confession, while Natrinai 15 makes the same loss a threat spoken to the man, likened to a mother forced to give her child to a demon, so the collapse of naanam also served as a lever to force marriage.

note: Kar Narpathu 38: even in this cool season, when the bull elephant plays with his mate, he has not come; why sulk? Thinaimalai 102: the deer everywhere play with their does, and I, not judging his going a harm, have paid my life for it.
teaches: In Kar Narpathu the friend uses the playing pair against the absent man and against the woman's sulk, while in Thinaimalai the woman reads the playing deer against herself, so the same sign of paired beasts can be turned to blame him or to blame her own consent.

note: In Kural 1148 the woman says hoping to quench love with gossip is like quenching fire with ghee; in Kuruntokai 175 she refuses to tell everyone she is not grieving and asks what the gossip matters.
teaches: The Kural's woman answers the town with an argument that talk only feeds love, while the poem's woman refuses the remedy the friend proposes, public denial, so the pair separates two defences against gossip: rebutting its power and declining to perform the concealment that would silence it.

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; 191 says grey hair has not come to the poet because of his good wife, children, servants, king and the worthy men of his town. On the reading that both speak of how to meet old age, one counsels leaving the household and the other credits it.
teaches: The Naladiyar's answer to ageing is renunciation, while Pisirandhaiyar's is a good household and good company, so the pair shows two Tamil remedies for the same fear, one by leaving the world early and one by living well in it.

note: In Akananuru 166 the husband soothes his wife by calling on the Velur god to afflict him if he went to the other woman, and the other woman exposes the lie; in Paripadal 8.65-66 the wife forbids such an oath by Murugan, since the god's true spear would eat him.
teaches: The Akananuru shows the god-oath used lightly as a husband's comfort, the Paripadal shows a wife who takes the same self-curse seriously enough to block it, so together they reveal that the oath was believed to bind the swearer bodily and that a knowing wife could protect a lying husband from it.

note: Kural 1235: the friend says the shoulders, bangles gone and old beauty faded, declare the cruel man's cruelty; Kalittokai 124: the friend tells the man the woman hid her pain even from her, but her pale forehead, wasted shoulders and streaming eyes could not hide it.
teaches: Together they show the body as a witness that overrides the woman's own silence: the poem adds that she tried to keep the pain even from her closest friend, so what the couplet calls the shoulders 'declaring' is a betrayal of her will to conceal, which the friend then turns against the man.

note: Akananuru 53: the woman says the man who loves wealth more than her crossed a waste where a red dog rests with its starving mate in the sweet shade of a lettered hero-stone (எழுத்துடை நடுகல் இன்நிழல்). Aimpathu 35: on the road of the man bent on wealth a ghoul gorged on the fat of the slain sleeps in a hero-stone's wide shade.
teaches: In both the hero-stone's shade is the only rest on the wealth-seeker's road, but Akananuru shelters a hungry pair there and the Aimpathu a sated ghoul alone, so the pair shows the stone's shade turned from a picture of shared hardship into one of the road's appetite for men, which is the woman's fear.

note: Kural 1218: when I sleep he is on my shoulder, when I wake he runs into my heart; Kalittokai 126: the friend says the woman, thinking of him, believes him on her shoulder (தோள் மேலாய்), embraces him as if awake, finds nothing and knows it was a dream.
teaches: The poem tells the couplet's moment from outside and counts its cost: what the Kural's woman offers as a defence of her lover (he never leaves me) the friend reports as the last of three daily delusions ending in grief, so the shoulder-dream is comfort in the first person and harm in the third.

note: Paripadal 9.8-11 says that when the god married the fawn-like girl, the eyes of the daughter of the thousand-eyed one rained like rain in summer at Parankunram; Paripadal 19.5-7 says the wedding with the peacock-like bride at the same hill seems to vie with that of the bride from heaven.
teaches: In song 9 the second marriage is a wound to the first wife, while song 19 turns the same two weddings into a contest of splendour in which the earthly bride matches the heavenly one, so the hill's lore of two marriages could be sung either as a domestic grief or as the claim that Parankunram brings heaven's festival down to earth.

note: Ainkurunuru 241 doubts that the velan can know the girl's bond with the hill man; Natrinai 34 tells Murugu himself that he came to the veri house knowing the sickness was not his seizure (நின் அணங்கு அன்மை அறிந்தும்).
teaches: Ainkurunuru blames the rite's error on the diviner's ignorance, while Natrinai charges the god, who knows the truth, with folly for coming anyway, so the pair shows the friend's protest against veri aimed either at the man who performs it or at the deity who accepts it.

note: Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji calling her words a child's babble he graciously hears; 352 measures the friend's sweetness against a famous bard's new tune for Anji's praise.
teaches: The praise songs for Anji, which Avvai offers modestly as babble, had become in akam a byword for sweetness, showing that puram performances were known to the love poets' audience as celebrated pieces of music.

note: Every poem of the decade says the time has come (தான் வந்தன்றே); 350 says it is the time of which he assured them with sweet words (தேம்படு கிளவி ... தெளிக்கும் பொழுதே).
teaches: Read from 350 back to 341, the unnamed 'it' of the refrain turns out to be his promised date, so each spring sign in the decade is a clause of his oath being checked off, not a description of the season.

note: Kural 17 says even the great sea loses its nature if the cloud withholds rain; Paripadal 8.128-130 prays that the hill's streaming falls and springs last even when the sky dries and the earth cracks (மண் பரிய வானம் வறப்பினும், மன்னுகமா).
teaches: The Kural makes every water, the sea included, depend on rain, and the Paripadal asks that the god's waterfall be exempt from that law, which is what marks the shrine's water as sacred rather than natural.

note: In Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palmyra horse; in Kuruntokai 173 he mounts it with shame killed (நாணட்டு) and says the town will name her fault.
teaches: The Kural counts only what the madal costs the rider, his shame; the poem names what it is for, turning his public shame into her blame on the town's tongue, which is the pressure that makes the threat work on her kin.

note: The figure painted by a god on the western face of Porayan's Kolli measures the girl in both; in the Kuruntokai the friend uses it, in Natrinai 185 the lover.
teaches: The friend uses the Kolli figure to plead that so innocent a girl can bring no harm to the town, while the lover uses the same figure to say she is killing him; the shared image shows the figure stood for a beauty both harmless in itself and dangerous to the one who sees it.

note: Akananuru 6 calls Tittan of Uranthai the great giver who brings the wealth of rain (மாவண் தித்தன்); 80 asks Tittan to witness the hero's victory 'whether he grants or not' (நல்கினும் நல்கான் ஆயினும்).
teaches: The akam poet uses Tittan's fame as a giver as a byword, while 80 makes his grace toward one man uncertain, so the same chief appears as a public giver and as a withholding judge whose favour must be won.

note: Kural 978 says smallness adorns itself with self-admiration; the line says birth in a small house shows in pride.
teaches: The same mark of pride serves the Kural as a sign of small character and the Muthumozhikkanchi as a sign of small birth, which shows the ten tying character to family.

note: Ainkurunuru 81: the other woman says his wife would grieve if she heard him say he desired her. Natrinai 100: the other woman laughs at how the man trembled when she said she would go and tell his wife.
teaches: In both the other woman's hold on the man is the wife's knowledge: the Ainkurunuru voices it as mock pity for the wife, the Natrinai as a threat that sets him shaking, so together they show that the courtesan's power in marutham rests on what the wife may hear.

note: Tirumanthiram 3021 asks where he is and answers that the Lord stands everywhere like rain; Paripadal 4.65-70 names the banyan, the kadamba, the river islet and the trackless hill, where he dwells under a different name in each, and concludes எவ் வயினோயும் நீயே, you are the one in every place.
teaches: Tirumular reaches omnipresence through the image of rain falling on all places alike, while the Sangam poet reaches it by gathering particular shrines with their own local names, so the pair shows the claim 'he is everywhere' first serving to unite many local cults under one god before it became a claim about space.

note: The idyll's warriors trade raided cattle for toddy and drink home brew all day as part of a life of valour; the Kural forbids drink, allowing it only to those who do not wish to be counted by the worthy.
teaches: The Kural's ironic concession names a class of people who do not seek the esteem of the worthy, and the idyll shows that such a class was a whole warrior community whose honour lay in the raid, not in sobriety, so the Kural's ban addresses a scale of values the older poem did not share.

note: Paranar cites Pekan's gift of a cloak to a peacock as proof that his giving looks to others' need and not to merit in the next world; the idyll lists the same gift as Pekan's emblem among the seven.
teaches: In Purananuru 141 the peacock's cloak is evidence in an argument about why a chief gives, while in the idyll it is only the sign by which Pekan is recognised, so a deed that once carried a claim about motive could circulate as a bare token of liberality.

note: In Kalittokai 74 the wife answers the bard who praises the man as not loveless by calling the bard, the trusting women, the man and his chariot all deluded; in Thinaimozhi 38 she stops the bard's praise of the man's goodness by pointing to the loosened hair his garland lay on.
teaches: Both wives reject the bard's praise of the husband, but the Kalittokai argues the case at length while the venba answers with a single visible sign, so the shorter form shows the refusal resting on evidence rather than rebuttal.

note: Kalittokai 35 counts Koodal's seasonal pleasures (bees on the Vaigai's sandbank, the festival, the townsmen savouring poets' new words) as the times the absent man promised to return; thirattu 13 lists the Vaigai flood, the god's hill and spear-eyed women as pleasures among which Koodal's people lose their way daily.
