teaches: The same catalogue of Koodal's pleasures marks the hour of a promised return in the Kalittokai and causes daily indecision in the Paripadal, so the city's festive plenty was a stock that akam used to sharpen absence and city praise used to show abundance.

note: Kalittokai 135's friend tells the shore lord that abandoning the girl would lie as a great fault on his lineage (குடிமைக் கண் பெரியது ஓர் குற்றம்); Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out high like the spot on the moon.
teaches: The couplet's rule that high birth makes a fault more visible is what gives the friend's threat its force: she aims at his lineage rather than his love because a lord's desertion, unlike a commoner's, would be seen by all, so the maxim is already a working argument in akam persuasion.

note: Kural 776 says the hero counts as wasted every day on which he took no noble wound; Patitruppattu 42 says the king's men wear the thumbai only beside men whose bodies already hold arrows and whose chests show the surgeon's needle-scars.
teaches: The Kural keeps the ledger of wounds inside one man's private reckoning, while the Chera poem turns it into a rule of the company, so that scars decide who may stand in the thumbai line and the wound becomes a public credential rather than a personal measure.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the velan's veri ground and the festivals of every town among the places where Murugan is found; the idyll shows the velan and a priestess at work in Madurai's squares, serving pregnant women, with kurinji and kadamba worn in the city.
teaches: The guide poem gives the rite's places and the city poem gives its users, so together they show the hill god's veri carried into the capital and used for women's life crises such as pregnancy, which neither poem states alone.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world endures because some would not eat even Indra's nectar alone; the idyll says the king would not leave true friendship for a lie even if he gained the high world with its nectar.
teaches: The 'even for the gods' nectar' test appears in both, but Purananuru 182 uses it for sharing among anonymous worthies while the idyll uses it for a king's truthfulness to his friends, so the virtues that hold the world together were also demanded of the ruler, and the measure for them was the same.

note: Purananuru 233 names Akuthai as the strong one whose elephants never ran short for those who came for gifts; Kuruntokai 298 recalls the young she-elephants Akuthai's father gave to singing women and likens the lover's long waiting to that gift.
teaches: The puram lament knows the house of Akuthai only as givers of elephants, and the akam friend turns that known generosity into a figure for a lover's patience, so a patron's fame for gifts served akam as a ready image of an act that waits on a return.

note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the sad-eyed evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 330 she asks whether the sorrowful evening (புன்கண் மாலை) and its loneliness exist at all in the land he went to.
teaches: Both make the evening testify against the absent man, but in opposite ways: the couplet makes it a fellow sufferer, the poem imagines a land without it, which would explain why he stays away, so the pair shows the evening serving as companion and as accusation.

iraicchi.act: the hen dove croons to give her mate pleasure
iraicchi.sense: the man, hearing a mate call to her partner, knows his wife waits calling for him, and so hurries home

iraicchi.act: the cows, udders dripping, leave the herd at evening to go home to their calves
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle go home at evening to those who need them, but he stays away for wealth

iraicchi.act: the gull sleeps undisturbed through the roar of the spray
iraicchi.sense: the man who left sleeps as easily, untouched by the uproar his leaving has raised in her

iraicchi.act: the male monkey takes the sweet fruit in its cheek and runs away at once
iraicchi.sense: the hero, like the monkey, took his pleasure and made off, which is why the mere mention of his friendship loosens her bangles

iraicchi.act: the buffalo in rut breaks away and plunges into the cool pond, scattering the men at work
iraicchi.sense: the man, hot with desire, goes heedless after his pleasures and leaves his household in an uproar

iraicchi.act: the crow, fed on the offerings, goes at dusk to crowd in with its own kin
iraicchi.sense: even the crow goes home to its own at evening, while the man stays away in the far land for wealth

ullurai.tenor: the lover and the girl's family who have shut her in

pairs.scene: சிறு பொறி மாட்டிய பெருங் கல் அடாஅர்
pairs.situation: the family's confinement of the girl, set against intruders
the strong lover himself is caught and foiled by it

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the hill farmer's trap and tiger in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

note: Akananuru 29: the returned man tells his wife that only his body stayed in the burning waste for the work, while his foolish heart was with her. Kainnilai 22: the friend asks whether she thinks the heart of the man who crossed the robber forest has parted from her.
teaches: The friend's question in the Kainnilai presumes exactly what the man asserts on his return in the Akananuru, that the body went and the heart stayed, so the pair shows the body-heart split was a shared assurance used by the comforter before and by the man after the journey.

note: Kural 557: as the lack of rain is to the earth, so the king's lack of grace (அளி) is to those who live; Kalittokai 25: as is this world when the sky withholds rain, so is her beauty when his grace (அளி) is withdrawn.
teaches: The kali poet takes the moralist's image of rain and royal grace and applies it to a husband, so the man stands to his wife as a king to his realm and his leaving becomes a failure of rule, not only of love.

note: Kural 1227: this sickness buds in the morning, swells through the day and blossoms in the evening. Kuruntokai 220: in the evening the jasmine opens its small buds like a wild cat smiling, and the man who left for wealth has not come.
teaches: The couplet makes a flower's day the shape of love-sickness; the Kuruntokai poem shows the real flower, the mullai opening its buds at dusk in the season he named, at the moment her grief opens, so the metaphor rests on the evening flowering of the jasmine land.

note: Kalittokai 74 opens with a striped bee that has fed on pond flowers and backwater neythal moving on to the field lotus, and says the man joins one woman at forenoon and seeks another by afternoon; Thinaimozhi 35 likens him openly to the bee that sips fresh flowers and leaves the women only their bodies.
teaches: What the Kalittokai leaves as an opening scene to be matched with the man's day, the four-line venba states as an explicit simile with its result, the emptied body, showing the hidden image of the longer poem made plain in the later form.

note: Verse 2 says the slips of speech of one praising the faultless are no slips; verse 17 says a fault stays a fault even in those who have reached truth and in a god.
teaches: The fragments hold two standards side by side: the poet excuses faults by the worth of what is praised, while the moral verse refuses to let any height excuse a fault, so the apology rests on devotion, not on a rule about faults.

note: Paripadal 4.11-21 tells of பிருங்கலாதன் tormented by his father, the god embracing the son and tearing the father's chest with his claws from the broken pillar (ஒடி தூண்); Thiruppugazh 870 tells of a child chanting நம நாராயணாய, the father asking where his god is, and the lion bursting from the pillar to tear Hiranya's chest.
teaches: In the Sangam hymn the story turns on the god's two acts on two chests, the embrace and the tearing, while Arunagirinathar's version turns on the child's recitation of the name and the father's challenge, so the pair shows the Prahlada story shifting its centre from the god's protecting hand to the power of the uttered name.

note: Kuruntokai's waiting woman says the men went for wealth without regard for youth (இளமை பாரார்); Ainkurunuru's returned hero says youth is sweet if spent together (இனிதுடன் கழிக்கின் இளமை).
teaches: The charge the abandoned woman makes in the rains is answered in the same season by the man come home, who adopts her measure of youth as his own, so the two poems stage the mullai argument over youth and wealth from both sides of the parting.

note: Akananuru 18 says that if the man suffers harm on the night ford even once, her friend will not live after it, and asks him to come by day; Thinaimalai 7 says that if he comes by night the daughter of the hill lord will not live.
teaches: Thinaimalai's flat 'she will not live' is explained by Akananuru 18: her life hangs on his safety on the path, so forbidding the night visit protects her through him, and the long poem's offer of a daytime meeting shows what the short ban leaves for him to infer.

note: Kural 247 says this world is not for those without wealth and the other world not for those without grace; Kuruntokai 174 says that if he leaves for wealth, in this world wealth alone is wealth and grace has no one.
teaches: The heroine grants the Kural's premise about this world in its own words (இவ்வுலகத்து) and drops its consolation: with no other world in view, the couplet's balance of wealth and grace collapses into a world where grace has no owner.

note: Kural 228 asks whether hard-eyed hoarders who keep and lose do not know the joy of giving; the verse ranks those without wealth above those who have it and only guard it.
teaches: The couplet says the hoarder misses a joy; the verse goes further and ranks him below the man who has nothing, so wealth kept unused is shown to be worse than poverty, not merely less than giving.

note: Kural 101 says that help given unasked cannot be repaid by earth and heaven together; in Ainkurunuru 288 the man, knowing the good of the parrots' help, asks his heart what he can do in return.
teaches: The Kural's unrepayable help is a deliberate kindness, while the parrots helped without knowing or meaning it, so the lover's echo of the gratitude maxim stretches it to an unintended benefit and makes the debt even less payable, since the helpers cannot know they are owed.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a village tank full of water; the verse makes the gift of water itself the first of five charities.
teaches: The Kural's tank is a figure for wealth all may draw on; the verse makes it literal and the lowest step of a scale that ends in founding temples and halls.

note: Kural 1325 has a faultless man delight in being kept from his beloved's arms; in Kalittokai 89 the husband says he has done no wrong (தீதோ இலேன்) and the wife calls the claim deceit and expects him to fall at her feet confessing.
teaches: The Kural builds the pleasure of oodal on the man's real innocence, while the Kalittokai shows the same plea of innocence as the stock defence of a straying husband, so the couplet's playful exclusion presupposes a faultlessness that akam wives treat as the thing in dispute.

note: The guide tells the bards to enter Nannan's heavily guarded gate without hesitation; Purananuru 151 tells a kinsman of Nannan of the golden chariot that the poet's people have shunned his hill because of a door shut against singers.
teaches: If both poems speak of one house, the open guarded gate the idyll promises is the standard by which Perunthalai Sathanar shames the kinsman: a lineage's fame for an open door becomes a claim its heirs can fail.

note: Kuruntokai 359: the friend shows the bard the man embracing his son on the bed and the wife embracing his back; Kalittokai 75: when she quarrels, he hugs the son and feigns sleep (புதல்வன் புல்லிப் பொய் துயில் துஞ்சும்).
teaches: Read together, the Kuruntokai's picture of a seemly household and the Kalittokai's account of the husband's tactic show that the son held in sleep was both the sign of reconciliation and the means of forcing it, and the wife in 75 knows it and yields anyway.

note: Ainkurunuru 74: a young woman climbs the marutham tree on the bank and leaps into the water, her hair spreading like a descending peacock. Purananuru 243: an old man recalls how in youth he climbed the low marutham branch at the ford and leapt into the deep pool to the wonder of those on the bank.
teaches: The leap from the riverside marutham was a common game of youth in the field towns, and the two books use it oppositely: the akam poet freezes it as the height of a woman's beauty seen by a lover, while the puram poet, leaning on his staff, makes the same leap the measure of what age has taken.

note: Both have the hill lord of the vengai coming at midnight with spear in hand; Kainnilai 10 is the girl's eager forecast, Akananuru 298 her words when he has come, sweet yet unable to speak her love for fear of the mother.
teaches: Read together the two give the before and after of the night tryst: the quatrain's sleepless certainty that he will come turns, once he is there, into fear of the household and a plea for marriage, so the midnight visit is never the end the girl longs for.

note: Akananuru 214: in the rain-drowned camp the king, set on glory, has no sleep (கண்படை இலனே), and the soldier wonders how his wife fares alone in the rainy evening; Mullaippattu 67: the king, eager for battle, gets no sleep (கண்படை பெறாஅ), and the next lines turn to the wife.
teaches: Akananuru 214 compresses the idyll's two scenes, the sleepless king in the rainy camp and the wife alone at evening, but splits king and husband into two men, which shows that Mullaippattu's joining of them, the wife's husband being the sleepless king himself, is the idyll's choice and not the convention's rule.

note: Kural 1192: the grace a lover shows the one who loves is like rain to those who live by it. Kalittokai 46: the girl longed for his grace like the bird that sings up to the sky for raindrops (துளி நசை ... அளி நசை), yet it was a stormy midnight (கனை பெயல் நடுநாள்) that kept him from the tryst.
teaches: The Kural's image of grace as rain is set in Kalittokai against real rain, which is what stopped the meeting, so the girl craves one rain while the other keeps it from her; the pairing shows the kali poet testing a stock equivalence against the weather of the kurinji night.

note: Kuruntokai 37: the friend tells the heroine that the road he took is a loving one, where the tusker strips the yaa branches to ease his mate's hunger. Aimpathu 32: on his road the tusker pours the little water of a rock pool over his heat-worn mate's head.
teaches: Kuruntokai 37 states the friend's conclusion itself, that the road is loving (அன்பின), while the Aimpathu gives only the tusker's act and leaves the inference to the heroine, so the pair shows the same comfort working first as a stated argument and then as an image she must read.

note: Kural 70 says a son repays his father by making people ask what penance the father did; Kalittokai 86 has the mother wish the son to resemble the father in valour, justice and giving but not in leaving women.
teaches: The Kural assumes the father is the standard the son's goodness reflects back on, while the akam mother makes the son's goodness a correction of the father, so the same likeness that honours a father in the Kural reproaches him in the Kalittokai.

note: Both have winged termites pouring from a red anthill (Purananuru: செம்புற்று ஈயல்; Ainkurunuru: நெடுஞ்செம் புற்றம் ஈயல்); Purananuru makes them the one-day life of kings who defied Vazhuthi.
teaches: The swarm of the first rains meant short-lived ruin in a war poem and food that ends the beasts' hunger in a love poem, and 497's war-loving lord stands between the two, come home from the kind of war in which other men were the termites.

note: Both are Ammuvanar's and end on the same demand, தந்தனை சென்மோ ... நலனே and நலம் தந்து சென்மே; Natrinai 395's colophon says the friend uses it to press the lover to marry.
teaches: The same poet's colophoned use of the formula supplies the occasion that this decade's colophons leave out, so 159's demand for the beauty back can be read as a push to marriage (வரைவு கடாயது) rather than a farewell.

note: Both answer the man with the same self-naming, குறவர் மகளிரேம், we are daughters of the hill folk; 6 adds that their kin would rage, 8 that no wounded tusker came this way.
teaches: The repeated formula works as a fence: in 6 it states the kin's threat outright, and in 8 the same words deflect his hunting pretext, showing that naming the tribe is itself the friend's refusal.

note: Paripadal 10.125-127 likens the flood pouring gold on the fields to the Vazhuthi pouring gold into poets' hands; thirattu 2.95-101 likens Maran bathing in the same flood with the people of Koodal to Indra bathing in the river of the sky.
teaches: Read together, the two Vaiyai songs place the Pandya on both sides of the flood: song 10 makes the river like the king in giving, the fragment makes the king like a god in bathing, so the king stands between the river's bounty below and Indra's heaven above, and the festival praises him through both.

note: Paripadal 8.17-28 has the hill answer back and forth (மாறுமாறு அதிர்ப்ப) with the cloud, the cock, the elephants and the caves, and the bees hum like the lute; Paripadal 17.9-21 sets the bards' lute, flute, drum, dancers and singer side by side with bees, tumbi, falls, creepers and peacock, each answering the other (மாறு எதிர் கோடல்).
teaches: In song 8 the echo contest is among the hill's own things and the lute only a likeness for the bees, while song 17 puts the festival's real musicians into the contest against the hill, so together they show the Parankunram echo becoming a set piece in which worshippers and mountain compete as equals.

note: Akananuru 305: on cold north-wind midnights a single anril on the palm cries in grief, and the heroine asks how she can live while he is away for wealth. Kuruntokai 160: at hushed midnight in the cold north wind the anril cries with its hen from their nest, and he does not come.
teaches: The anril's midnight cry in the north wind is shared, but the Akananuru bird is alone and mirrors her, while the Kuruntokai bird is with its mate and shows what she lacks; together they show that the anril, bird of the unparted, can serve as either likeness or contrast to the waiting woman.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels. Thinaimozhi 49: the man asks whether she was a peacock, a young woman or a goddess of the sea waves, and his heart aches from her eyes.
teaches: The same three-way doubt in both shows the first-sight ஐயம் was a fixed form of kalavu, and the venba adds what the couplet leaves open: a place for the seeing, the njazhal grove, and a goddess native to that place, the one who lives in the waves.

note: In Akananuru 213 the friend assures the heroine that the man will not linger abroad even if he were given the world of the gods with its nectar (அமிழ்தொடு பெறினும்); in the idyll the man himself says he will not leave her even if he were given the city (பட்டினம் பெறினும்).
teaches: The 'even if he were given' formula is in the Akananuru a friend's comfort about a man already gone; Pattinappalai puts it in the man's own mouth before he leaves and spends 217 lines making the offered prize a real city, one it has itself likened to heaven (line 104), so a convention of comfort becomes the frame of a whole idyll.

note: Natrinai 267: crabs of the sand dune with eyes like the nochchi's dark buds (நொச்சி மா அரும்பு அன்ன கண்ண). Kar Narpathu 39: nochchi buds opened like crabs' eyes (அலவன்க ணேய்ப்ப).
teaches: The simile runs in opposite directions: the neythal poem makes its shore crab the subject and borrows the nochchi as image, while the mullai venba makes its nochchi the subject and borrows the crab, so each poet takes the tenor from the poem's own land.

note: Kuruntokai 0 knows Murugan by his lotus-red feet, the spear that split the mountain and the cock banner, and says his guarding keeps the world safe; Thiruppugazh 323 names the same spear that pierced Krauncha, the cock banner and the golden anklet feet, and asks for release from desire.
teaches: The same three marks of Murugan pass from a guarantee of the whole world's safety in the oldest invocation to one devotee's plea for rescue from his own lust, so the iconography stayed fixed while the god's protection moved from the world to the self.

note: Kural 1187: she turned aside a little from his embrace and the pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up. Kar Narpathu 27: if we sulk that he left without a thought for us, pallor spreads over her in bed (பள்ளியுட் பாயும் பசப்பு).
teaches: The couplet's hyperbole, that the least turning away from him in bed brings pallor, becomes in the friend's mouth a practical warning against sulking at an absent man, so the venba shows the Kural's figure used as an argument for bearing up.

note: Ainkurunuru 360: the long burnt road was easy because he drove his chariot thinking of her; Akananuru 9: the returning man's heart outran even his sleepless chariot and has already reached her.
teaches: Read together the two returns show desire working on the journey in two stages: in 360 it shrinks the road the chariot must cover, and in Akananuru 9 it leaves the chariot behind altogether, so the heart arrives before the man does.

note: In Natrinai 34 the friend tells Murugan he knows the sickness is not his affliction; in Natrinai 322 she tells the girl, within the man's hearing, that the velan has called it a spirit's work.
teaches: Together the two show the friend undoing the velan's diagnosis before two different audiences, the god himself and the hidden lover, and only the second can end the rite, by marrying the girl.

note: In Akananuru 91 the elephant that shrinks with its hungry mate in drought lets the friend reassure the heroine after the man has gone; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 31 the elephant sleeping with its mate in the burning forest comes when the man only speaks of going, and her tears answer it.
teaches: The same iraicchi of the elephant pair keeping together in the heat serves to comfort after the parting and to dissuade before it, which shows the image carries the lovers' bond itself and the speaker turns it to whatever the moment needs.

note: Kalavazhi 39 ends on the field where the Chola killed the Vanji king (வஞ்சிக்கோ), his white umbrella torn down and full of flesh; Purananuru 74 is a Chera king's own poem from captivity, held like a chained dog (தொடர்ப்படு ஞமலியின்) and begging water. The two are tied by the tradition that the Chera defeated in Kalavazhi was Kanaikkal Irumporai, the poet of Purananuru 74; neither text in our corpus states it.
teaches: The victor's song counts the Chera's defeat as the end of the matter, but the defeated king's poem says that being taken alive and fed by strangers is worse than the sword, so on that reading the field the Kalavazhi praises produced a fate its own frame cannot see.

note: Both are neythal poems of a girl neglected by the lord of the shore with the sea crow and its 'lovely hen' (காமர் பேடை, காமர் பெடை): in Akananuru 170 the small sea crow rests with its mate while she is alone at midnight, in Natrinai 272 the crow fishes for its pregnant mate while the man is not kind.
teaches: The pair shows the shore crow with its mate measuring the man's neglect in two ways, by companionship in the one and by provision in the other, so the bird's pairing was a flexible yardstick for whatever the girl lacks.

note: In 428 the rains, with the rainbow, halt the chariots and end the king's task; in Akananuru 84 the rains and the rainbow come but the angry king refuses tribute and moves his army on.
teaches: The convention that the rains end a campaign, which 428 takes for granted, is broken in Akananuru 84 by one king's anger, so the rainbow is a promise of return that only the king can keep or cancel.

note: Akananuru 44 has a man bid his charioteer hurry home to his wife because the king's war is finished and the foes have paid tribute; Patitruppattu 81 has the poet ask the king himself, in the rainy season with the siege still on, to yoke his chariot for one day to see his wife, so that the sleepless besieged kings may sleep too (துஞ்சா வேந்தரும் துஞ்சுக).
teaches: In the akam poem the homecoming waits until the war is over, but the court poet asks the king to go home in the middle of the war and gives the besieged enemy's rest as a reason, so the mullai motif of the rainy-season return becomes, in praise poetry, a way of asking for a pause in the fighting.

note: Kural 484 says even the world comes to hand (கைகூடும்) if one weighs the time and acts by the place; the line says gain coming to hand (கையுறல்) for one who does not know the time is false.
teaches: The couplet makes knowing the time enough for even the greatest gain, and the line makes it necessary for any gain, so together they give timing both halves of a condition: without it nothing comes to hand, with it even the world can.

note: Both use the formula of the kin who cut and plough (எறிந்து உழுது, எறிந்தெமர் தாம்உழுத); in Ainthinai Aimpathu 18 it is the field they cleared, in Thinaimalai 24 a sign of their hardness.
teaches: In Ainthinai Aimpathu 18 clearing and ploughing is just the kin's labour whose harvest ends the meetings, but Thinaimalai 24 reads the same labour as a temperament, men who fell fragrance for grain, so the friend can turn the hill family's farming into a reason the girl will not pity the man.

note: Paripadal 11.120-121 has the bathing women ask that for seven births, without growing old, their rich kin last and bear children; in Kuruntokai 49 a wife asks her husband that even when this birth gives way to the next he be her husband and she the one close to his heart.
teaches: What the Kuruntokai wife says privately to one man, the Paripadal's women ask together of the river at a public festival, so the wish to keep the same spouse beyond this birth was a recognised petition of the Thai rite, not only one woman's vow of love.

note: Natrinai 303: the heroine lies sleepless at each cry of the anril joined with its mate in the palmyra of the common ground. Thinaimalai 56: the friend tells the shore lord that the anril calls from the tall palmyras of their front yard.
teaches: Natrinai 303 shows what the anril's cry does to the heroine at midnight, so when the friend in the venba points the hero to the anril in their own yard she is telling him, without saying so, what the girl hears each night he is away.

note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan for the great food he gave at the war of the hundred and the five; Natrinai 113 likens the heroine's sob to the ambal pipe the musicians blow on the hushed field after Udhiyan's loud battle.
teaches: Where the praise poem remembers Udhiyan's war for its feeding of the armies, the love poet remembers its aftermath, the silent field and the mourning pipe, so akam took from the same king's fame the grief that puram praise leaves out.

iraicchi.act: when the herd scatters, the stag does not run with it but stands searching for his young doe
iraicchi.sense: the man too will not rest until he has found his wife again, so the chariot must hurry

iraicchi.act: the female monkey plays openly with her mate (துணையோடு) on the hillside
iraicchi.sense: the beasts may be together in plain sight, while the lovers' meetings set the village whispering, so only marriage will let them be together openly

iraicchi.act: the tusker wards off the bowmen so its mate and calf can drink at the hamlet's trough, and then goes on
iraicchi.sense: the man who crossed that land, seeing a male provide for its own and move on as he did, will think of the wife he left

iraicchi.act: the hen, after barring the nest, pities her drenched mate and calls him in beside her and the chicks
iraicchi.sense: the wife who waited will take back the man who comes home at the rainy evening, and the house will close round him

ullurai.tenor: the town's gossip about the heroine and the lord of the shore

pairs.situation: her clean name is made to reek of scandal
the talk spreads through every street of the village
the stuff of the talk is the town's own catch, not anything she did

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the drying catch of her own shore, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the stag, having drunk, frisks at evening together with its mate
iraicchi.sense: the man who sees the pair together presses to reach his own wife before the evening she spends alone

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 206-217 describes the god as red, in red clothing (செய்யன் சிவந்த ஆடையன்), dancing on every hill with the women's soft shoulders in his arms; Paripadal 19.97-100 tells him his dress and cloak are red, his weapon coral-coloured, his form like fire and his face like the young sun.
teaches: The guide poem's red god is roaming from hill to hill in the kurinji dance, while the hymn addresses the same red figure as the image standing by the kadambu at one shrine, praised by a gathered company, so the pair shows one colour iconography carried from the wandering god of the hill people to the fixed god of a temple.

note: Puram 140 mocks the lord of Nanjil as a simpleton who gave an elephant when asked for a little rice, giving that knows no measure; here Karikalan gives elephants with mates and calves by the measure he knows, and the bard takes by the measure he knows.
teaches: The elephant given to a bard was a stock sign of excessive giving that one poet could tease as folly ignoring measure, while the idyll answers that charge by naming two measures, the giver's and the taker's, so the excess is kept in bounds by the receiver's restraint.

note: The two poems end on the same words, என் மாமைக் கவினே, for the same shore lord: in 144 the beauty has turned pale, in 146 it is surely sweet to him.
teaches: Read together, the decade measures the whole state of the love by one phrase about her complexion, which can stand for neglect or for delight with nothing changed but the verb.

note: Kuruntokai 258: the friend says talk has risen on seeing the beauty, like Azhisi's Arkkadu, of this girl wasting. Natrinai 227: the friend says the man's grace has become talk as loud as the streets of the Cholas' Arkkadu.
teaches: In two speeches of the same kind, a friend telling the man that gossip has risen, the one town Arkkadu stands once for the girl's endangered beauty and once for the noise of the gossip itself, so a famous town was a measure akam poets could set against either side of the alar.

note: Akananuru 14: the wife asks what will become of them by morning if he does not remember even in the evening when the cattle crowd into the common (மன்றுநிறை புகுதரும் மாலையும்). Kainnilai 30: the hour when the cowherds with konrai pipes enter the common (மன்றம் புகுதரும் போழ்து).
teaches: The Akananuru wife names the homecoming to the common as the hour by which a man who remembers would be back, which explains why the Kainnilai poet could mark the waiting by that hour alone: the village's return is the measure of his not returning.

note: Kural 1151 refuses any promise of quick return and asks only whether he is leaving; Ainkurunuru 302 grants that his work for wealth has its own right and argues only that the woman has an equal one.
teaches: Read together they show the friend's dissuasion in two registers, the couplet's flat ultimatum of death and the poem's balanced concession of rights, so the Kural's line is an extreme the Sangam friend reaches only after first admitting the claim of wealth.

note: Kural 1183 has the woman say he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; Ainkurunuru 278 says the lord gave a sickness never forgotten and took the beauty onlookers never tired of.
teaches: Valluvar keeps only the exchange as the woman's own complaint, while the Sangam poem sets it in an image of a bamboo springing back like a rod that has landed a fish, which shows the taking and the man's unharmed recoil that the couplet's bare bargain leaves out.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone her shoulders have lost their fullness and the bangles slip; Kuruntokai 260: the bangled shoulders are filling out again, read with heron and bush as a sign he will return.
teaches: The couplet makes the shoulders a record of his absence; the poem reads them forward as an omen of his return, so the body that registers separation is also consulted to foretell its end.

note: Paripadal 1.1-2 opens with the god's form whose thousand awful hooded heads (ஆயிரம் விரித்த அணங்குடை அருந் தலை) rise over his crown, white as a conch and carrying the plough; Paripadal Thirattu 1.83-85 uses the same words for a separate lord with his host, bowed to before the god is praised.
teaches: One formula line serves in the first song as a form of Mal himself and in this song as an attendant lord with his own retinue and his own deeds, so the anthology shows the serpent both absorbed into the god's body and kept as a distinct object of worship at his shrine.

note: Karunkuzhal Athanar tells Karikalan to his face that his delight in plunder by the light of burning towns makes the good lands of others cease to be; the idyll describes the same king's wasting of enemy fields and halls as glory and then uses it to measure the heat of the desert.
teaches: The same king's ravaging of fertile land could be addressed to him as a praise with a sting (நல்ல இல்ல ஆகுபவால்) or listed without reserve in a long court praise, so the pair shows how much the frame, a short puram address or an akam idyll, decided whether a poet could let the cost of conquest be heard.

note: Kural 247 takes as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; the heart in Kuruntokai 63 states that premise, and the man answers it only by asking whether she can come along.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the poem shows the Kural's blunt premise as a voice inside a lover's head that he can neither refute nor obey, so the maxim's truth is granted and its price is made visible in the separation.

note: Kural 1251 has the woman say desire's axe breaks the door of restraint; Paripadal 20.91-94 has the onlookers say no one can bar men's chests from women and ask whether love stays within its bounds (கட வரை நிற்குமோ காமம்?).
teaches: In the Kural the claim that desire breaks every bound is a woman's confession about her own longing, while in the Paripadal the same claim is turned into an excuse for the husband's straying and urged on the wife, which shows how one maxim about love's force served opposite ends depending on whose desire it named.

note: Kural 586 counsels the king to use spies who go in the guise of renunciants and wanderers; 47 insists that the bard's wandering life, crossing many wastes from patron to patron, harms no one. On the reading that 47 answers a suspicion of the wandering bard, the two disagree about whether such travellers should be trusted.
teaches: The Kural's advice to disguise spies as wanderers is the very reason a real wanderer could fall under suspicion, and 47 gives the wanderer's side, a life of gifts and honour that 'knows no harm to others', so the pair shows the cost the state's craft laid on the travelling poet.

note: Kuruntokai 87's woman meets the belief that the old god of the common destroys the false by saying her lord is not false at all, though her brow pales; Natrinai 358's woman grants that he swore and stays away and goes to make offerings so that the god will not harm him.
teaches: Together they show the belief that the oath-god punishes the perjured lover pressing on the woman in two moves, first denial that he is false and then propitiation on the oath-breaker's behalf, so the one he wronged becomes his protector before the god.

note: Paripadal 1.32-39 says even sages free of delusion find the god hard to know and asks him to accept inadequate praise; Paripadal 3.45-47 asks whether anyone but the god himself could know what is like him (நின்னைப் புரை நினைப்பின் நீ அலது உணர்தியோ).
teaches: The first hymn stops at the limit of the praiser's knowledge, while the third turns that limit into a claim about the god, that he is the only knower of himself, so the pair shows the apology of the Tamil hymn hardening into a doctrine of self-knowledge.

note: Kuruntokai 204: the companion says love is neither a spirit nor a disease but a feast always new; 206: the hero says love brings unbearable grief and warns the wise to keep away.
teaches: Read together, the two poems are the two sides of the companion's rebuke and the hero's answer: the friend outside love calls it a light pleasure, and the man inside it calls it a pain the wise should flee, so the anthology lets each speaker's place decide what love is.

note: Akananuru 146: refusing the bard, the wife asks who the woman will be who now trusts the deceiving philanderer and will weep and pale as she did. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 55: the wife tells the other women directly not to embrace him to love's end or pine for him, but to give up their longing.
teaches: Akananuru 146 only pities the next woman from a distance, while the venba turns to the rivals and counsels them, so together they show the wife's grievance passing into a warning to the women who will suffer as she did.

note: Kural 597 holds up the elephant that plants its feet under a sheaf of arrows (புதையம்பிற் பட்டுப்பா டூன்றுங் களிறு) as the model of a mind that does not give way; Kalavazhi Narpathu 10 shows elephants pierced everywhere by arrows that cannot move and sink wearily where they stand (செல்கலா தொல்கி யுயங்கும்).
teaches: Seen from the battlefield, the Kural's emblem of steadfastness is ambiguous: the same arrow-struck elephant that stands its ground is, for the victor's poet, a beast too spent to move, so the maxim's courage depends on reading stillness as resolve rather than as defeat.

note: Ainkurunuru 200: the lord of the golden chariot has come, her bangles fit again and they can laugh at the pallor. Kainnilai 60: her golden pallor is gone, for here is the chariot of the man who saw the backs of fleeing kings, nearing Koodal.
teaches: Both mark the end of pallor by the chariot's arrival, but the venba arms the returning lover with a victor's epithet and the Pandya's Korkai and Koodal, showing a late akam poem borrowing puram glory to make homecoming a triumph.

note: Patitruppattu 47 says that whenever Kuttuvan slays, the suppliants never cease receiving elephants; in Purananuru 394 a bard given a killing elephant is terrified, sends it back, and is given a bigger one, so he warns other poets away.
teaches: On one reading the war elephant is the crown of royal gifts, and on the other it is a burden a poor bard cannot use or feed, so the pair shows the gift-poem's ideal of the elephant gift and the bard's comic protest against it from inside the same tradition.

note: Akananuru 375: the girl tells her friend her eyes would not weep if she knew the man who crossed the wasteland of killers would return unharmed. Thinaimozhi 15: she asks her friend whether the man who gave up grace for wealth halts on the long waste where the hawk attacks the dove.
teaches: In Akananuru 375 fear for his safety is the whole cause of her tears, but the venba puts that fear in the same sentence as the charge that he abandoned grace, showing that the heroine's worry for him survives her own accusation against him.

note: Both dissuade the man from leaving, in the friend's voice on Parimelazhagar's reading of the couplet: the Kural argues from her survival, 423 from the rain already falling and her filled eyes.
teaches: The two show that the dissuasion of a departure had two set arguments, the season and her life, and the Kural keeps only the harsher second, while the Ainkurunuru friend leans on the order of the seasons that a man who leaves in the rains breaks.

note: 77 likens the Chera's many elephants to the cattle of the Kongar spreading over the gravel upland (கொங்கர் ஆபரந் தன்ன); 78 likens the horses and elephants he had in his own land after razing Tagadur to spreading goats and cattle (ஆபரந் தன்ன யானையோன்).
teaches: The decade moves the herd simile from the enemy's ground to the king's: first the elephants spread like a hostile people's cattle in an army on the march, then like home herds after victory, so one image marks war-strength turning into the settled wealth of peace.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend points to the bloomed konrai that has made the forest lovely as proof that the season of his return has come. Kuruntokai 21: the woman says that even if the konrai forest declares the rains, she will not believe it, since he does not lie.
teaches: The same konrai sign is proof of his return in the friend's mouth and a sign the woman refuses in her own, so the season argument of the mullai poems could be turned around: faith in his word can deny the season rather than read it.

note: Akananuru 214 has a soldier in the rain-soaked camp where the king, eager for glory, does not sleep, asking how his wife bears the evenings alone; Patitruppattu 50 asks how the sleepless king himself passes the camp days away from women's embrace.
teaches: The akam poem treats the king's sleeplessness as the cause of the soldier's separation, while the puram poet lends the king the soldier's own longing to praise his endurance, so the same camp night is a lover's grief in one book and a king's virtue in the other.

note: Paripadal 2.62-65 counts the seizing of the goat in the sacrifice and the fire oblation as the god's own food; Kural 259 says not to take one creature's life and eat it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices. On the plain reading the hymn honours the animal sacrifice that the couplet ranks below abstention.
teaches: The hymn's aside that others will not accept the brahmins' rite (பிறர் உடம்படுவாரா) and the Kural's ranking of not killing over sacrifice show the same quarrel from both sides, so the dispute over animal sacrifice was live within the Tamil tradition itself.

note: Patitruppattu 24 praises the king for walking by the word of the Brahmins who keep the six duties; the preface of the decade says he made the elders of moon-clear tradition his own and finally went to the forest with Nedumbarathayanar leading.
teaches: The preface completes the portrait of 24: the king whose rule followed the learned Brahmins ended by following one of them out of rule into the forest, so the deference the song praises was remembered as leading to renunciation.

note: Kural 120 says true trade for merchants is caring for others' goods as their own; Patitruppattu 59 tells the king that protecting the land, where goods of hill and sea are shared out and the roads stay unblocked in the way of dharma, is his duty.
teaches: The Kural places fair trade in the merchant's conscience, while the Chera poem names the condition it assumes, open roads that the king must keep, so the trader's ethic depends on a ruler's duty the couplet does not mention.

note: In Purananuru 141 a bard resting on the road with his gifts tells a hungry bard that before seeing Pekan they were poorer than he; the idyll's speaker, with horses and elephants, says he and his hungry kin come from Thiraiyan.
teaches: The meeting of a rewarded bard and a hungry one is the whole drama of the short poem but only the opening frame of the idyll, which shows that the long guide poem grew by keeping that encounter and filling the space between it and the patron with the road.

note: Kural 1060 says the one who asks must not be angry; Iniyavai calls it foremost sweet that one who lives by alms does not clamour.
teaches: Both place restraint on the receiver rather than the giver, and the pair shows the ethics group laying a duty on the needy as well as on the rich.

note: Kural 1321 has the woman say that though he has no fault, his grace has the power to bring on a sulk; in Paripadal 12.55-60 the man has eyed another woman's breasts, and when beaten he 'sees no fault' (பிழை ஒன்றும் காணான்) and bows asking to be told it, and the onlookers call him the pure one (தூயவனைக் காண்மின்).
teaches: The couplet takes the faultless lover of the oodal at the woman's word, while the hymn shows a crowd that has watched him look and mocks his innocence as he begs to hear his fault, so together they show that the faultless husband of the sulk was a convention its audience knew to be a pose, and that the Kural's version is the inside view of a scene the festival saw from outside.

note: Kural 1117 asks whether a woman's face has spots as the moon does; Kalittokai 55 has the man make the same correction six times over (not the moon, for it has no stain; not the crescent, for it does not wane), reported by the girl.
teaches: The Kural's single corrected simile is shown in the Kalittokai as a wooing technique that the girl sees through, so the man's praise-by-correction is not only admiration but a calculated approach she names as such.

note: Kuruntokai 313 says the friendship with the lord of the shore is knotted and settled, hard to untie; Kuruntokai 304 says the friendship made with the lord of the shore has brought enmity.
teaches: Held together they show why 304's grief is so sharp: the bond that 313 praises as impossible to untie is the same bond that, once it brings hostility, cannot be undone either.

note: Kural 1147 has the woman say her love-sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water; in Akananuru 273 she says the sickness sprouted between her breasts, grew a trunk, spread branches of gossip and budded with scandal into a tree shading the world.
teaches: The Kural's two-line plant metaphor, gossip feeding the disease, is the seed of Avvaiyar's full tree, which adds the stages of growth and makes the scandal not only food for the love but its flowering.

note: The same poet praises the same king for the battlefield sacrifice: in Purananuru 26 with crowned heads for a hearth, blood for water and bangled arms for ladles; in the idyll with the arm as ladle and the flesh-rice served to the soldiers who did not step back.
teaches: Mangudi Maruthanar's two accounts of the rite show what it was for: the short poem sets it beside the king's Vedic sacrifices as a second, martial sacrifice, while the idyll names who eats it, the soldiers who held their ground, so the horror is also the army's feast and reward.

note: Both look at the reaped millet field: in Natrinai 306 the friend, in the man's hearing, says the girl has been sent home and asks how he will come day after day to the bare stubble; in Ainkurunuru 284 the parrots keep coming to the stubble, unable to part from it.
teaches: Natrinai 306 assumes that the harvest ends the man's reason to come, but Ainkurunuru 284 shows creatures whose love keeps them at the empty field anyway, so the harvest cannot end such a love; it only leaves marriage as the way it can go on.

note: Both concern the woman's indifferent glance in early love: Kural 1099 says looking at each other like strangers is found only in lovers; in Natrinai 75 the rejected man says her glance that does not look has wounded him like a hunter's arrow.
teaches: The look the Kural's observer reads as proof of love is, to the man who receives it, a fatal wound, so the pair shows the same sign read from outside as a disguise and from inside as a refusal.

note: Kuruntokai 49 (Ammuvanar): even when this life changes to the next, may you be my husband and I the one close to your heart. Natrinai 397 (Ammuvanar): I do not fear death, but I fear that in another birth I may forget my lover.
teaches: The same poet gives the hope and the fear of the same belief: in Kuruntokai 49 rebirth is a chance to be joined again, in Natrinai 397 it is the risk of forgetting, so for these women the next birth mattered only as it kept or lost the present love.

note: Kural 719 says those who speak well in a good assembly should not speak in a mean one, even by slip; Pazhamozhi 15 calls fine speech among the unlearned the worst thing for a man and a lapse of conduct.
teaches: Pazhamozhi moves the Kural's rule of assembly into the field of ozhukkam, so speaking to the wrong audience is a fault of character that lowers the speaker, not only a tactical error.

note: Kuruntokai 32: if one can tell morning, day, helpless evening, midnight and dawn apart, love is false. Natrinai 152's lover tells the hours exactly: the sun as it dims gave him loneliness, and the night with the andril's call gave him helplessness.
teaches: On one reading the claims are incompatible: Kuruntokai 32 makes losing track of the hours the proof of true love, while Natrinai 152 gives a lover whose love is real precisely because each hour is known by its own fresh pain, so knowing the clock is no sign of coolness.

note: Purananuru 127 praises Aay, whose bards led away his elephants and whose palace stood bare from giving; Natrinai 167 makes the rattle of the chariots bards won at Aay's feast the sound of a heron's cry on the shore of the man whose bard the friend turns away.
teaches: The pairing shows an akam friend borrowing Aay's puram fame as the measure of a generous patron, so the bard who in puram goes home rich is in akam the go-between sent home empty: one profession seen from the giver's hall and from the wronged wife's door.

note: In Akananuru 7 the foster mother, following her eloped daughter into the waste, cannot catch up and questions a hill girl she meets; in Kuruntokai 44 her legs are worn out, her eyes dimmed from looking, and the others she sees are more than the stars.
teaches: Together they give the search its course: the long poem is its middle, where the nurse still questions each stranger in hope, and the four-line poem is its end, where every face has proved to be someone else's and the looking itself has cost her sight.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 6 names the god only as husband of a bright-browed woman of spotless chastity (மறுவில் கற்பின் வாணுதற் கணவன்); Paripadal 9.8-11 names her as the daughter of the thousand-eyed one and sets the wedding at Parankunram, marked by rain in summer.
teaches: Held together, the guide poem's opening epithet turns out to rest on a wedding story that the Paripadal ties to one hill, which explains why Parankunram, the hill of that marriage, is the first abode the guide poem then visits.

note: Kuruntokai 18 says her love hangs on her small life like a great jackfruit on a small stalk; Kural 1163 says love and shame hang from the two ends of a carrying pole that is her life.
teaches: Both picture love as a weight hanging from life, but the Kural adds shame as a counterweight, so the Sangam image of a stalk about to snap under one load becomes in the couplet a pole balanced between two loads that will snap either way.

iraicchi.act: the stags play everywhere with their does in the rains
iraicchi.sense: even the beasts of the scrub keep their mates by them in this season, while the man who should be with her is away

iraicchi.act: the female dove calls for her mate with a lonely cry from the dead branch
iraicchi.sense: the dove near the hamlet where he rests calls its partner as she, alone, calls for him

iraicchi.act: the wild cow sleeps unafraid on the man's slope
iraicchi.sense: as the creatures of his hill rest secure there, the girl who has no one but him should rest secure in his kindness

iraicchi.act: the boar eats from the guarded millet field and then sleeps unafraid on the rock slope
iraicchi.sense: the beast of his own hill dares the guarded field and rests without fear, yet the man she loves stays away for fear of her father

iraicchi.act: the bees hum through the groves together with the mates they love
iraicchi.sense: even the bees have their partners beside them tonight, while she lies alone without hers

iraicchi.act: the young she-elephant is left bewildered and grieving when the thunder strikes her tusker on the path down the hill
iraicchi.sense: the heroine would be left the same way if the man keeps taking the night path, so he should stop coming by night

ullurai.tenor: the husband who brings the other woman's marks into the wife's house and expects to be received

pairs.situation: what the bard's people bring is poured into the wife's own basket, as he brings the courtesan's marks into her house
the wife pays with the store of past years, as she is expected to repay his visit with the love of their long marriage

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the barter at her own door, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the hill lord courting the heroine

pairs.situation: he slips past the kin who guard her
he takes her favour without the bride price, by flattering words

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the boar that raids her own people's hill fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

note: Akananuru 92 forbids the night and promises the man a day meeting by a cool fall where red glory lilies open; Thinaimalai 29 describes such a place by a forest stream in a glory-lily thicket.
teaches: Akananuru 92 gives the day tryst as the friend's offer in exchange for the dangerous night, and Thinaimalai 29 gives only the place, which shows the daytime meeting ground was a fixed set (stream, glory lilies, low shade) a four-line verse could call up without the bargain around it.

note: In Akananuru 351 the returning man pictures the lizard chirping at her ear as she worships the omen birds; in Natrinai 169 he speaks to the lizard on the long wall and asks whether it will chirp to end her worry.
teaches: Together they show the house lizard as an oracle both ends of the separation rely on: she listens for it at home, and he, on the road, begs it to speak for him.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 71-77 places the god's hill west of Koodal of crowded mansion streets, among wide muddy fields of lotus and bees; Paripadal 19.8-18 fills the whole stretch between the hill and Koodal (குன்றொடு கூடல் இடையெல்லாம்) with a pre-dawn procession of riders, chariots and garlanded heads.
teaches: The guide poem gives the pilgrim the hill's place relative to the city and its quiet fields, and the hymn shows the same stretch on festival day as one continuous human garland, so together they show Parankunram as Madurai's own shrine, whose road from the city was itself part of the festival.

note: Kural 1137 says nothing is worthier than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the madal; Kalittokai 147's woman, maddened in the street, begs Kama's arrows so that the man will come riding the palmyra horse.
teaches: The kali woman keeps the rule the couplet praises, she does not mount the madal, but she gets around it by wishing the madal on him, so the restriction on women survives even in the most extreme akam scene and shapes the form her desire takes.

note: Akananuru 20: the friend recalls chasing birds from her father's drying fish (எந்தை தந்த கொழுமீன் உணங்கல் படுபுள் ஓப்பி) among the shore pastimes now forbidden. Kainnilai 56: while driving the birds from the fish her kin brought (எமர் தந்த ... வன்மீன் கவரும்புள் ஓப்பின்), the shore lord took her beauty.
teaches: The same chore, keeping birds off the family's catch, is innocent play in the Akananuru list and the very hour of the theft in the venba, which explains why the mother's ban in the long poem falls on just those shore tasks.

note: Both turn on the same words, செய்குறி வாரா ரவரென்று: in 25 the friend says that thought thickened the heroine's pallor; in 40 she says the darkening sky has become the medicine for the woman who grieved at it.
teaches: The series states one despairing thought twice, once as the cause of pallor in the friend's confession of her own distress and once as the sickness the sky now cures, so her speeches of despair and of comfort rest on the same premise and differ only in how they read the sky.

note: Natrinai 330: the male buffalo plunges into the pond and rests from the day's labour in the sweet shade of the marutham (இன் நிழல் வதியும்), and the friend blames the courtesans' mean hearts. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the buffalo breaks its clog, eats the crop and then rests in the shade (நிழல்வதியும்).
teaches: The resting buffalo is innocent after labour in Natrinai and guilty after plunder in the venba, and the blame follows suit, falling on the courtesans in one and on the husband in the other, so what the beast did before the shade decides whom the poem accuses.

note: Kural 1216: if there were no waking, the lover met in the dream would not leave. Kuruntokai 147: the hero says the dream, as if it had brought her, rouses him from sweet sleep.
teaches: The Kural's woman blames waking and spares the dream; the Kuruntokai's man blames the dream itself for ending his sleep, so set together they show that the dream meeting was felt as both gift and cheat, and that the blame shifts with which side of it the lover dwells on.

note: In Kural 1188 the woman says people speak of her pallor but none says he left her; in Natrinai 219 the girl says she will not blame him though pallor spreads and she dies, since he and she joined of their own accord.
teaches: The Kural woman complains that blame falls on her skin and not on him, while the Natrinai girl takes the pallor as her own because the union was her own choice, so the pair shows how a self-chosen secret union changes who can be blamed for the suffering.

note: Both mothers wish on the mother who bore the youth the same grief they feel (Natrinai: எம்போல் பெரு விதுப்புறுக; Ainkurunuru: நினைத்தொறும் கலிழும் இடும்பை எய்துக).
teaches: Natrinai ties the wished grief to the sight of the girl's playmates at a festival, Ainkurunuru to every thought of the road, so the curse on the youth's mother was a set move whose point is to make the other mother feel exactly the speaker's own loss.

note: Both open the cold season with white musundai, kodal and cowherds coming in from the rain with wet garlands, and both close the description with the same words, கூதிர்நின் றன்றால் followed by பொழுதே (here போதே, line 72).
teaches: In Akananuru 264 the formula hands the season to a waiting woman who asks whether the men in the king's camp know their own state, so the idyll's cold-season opening, which ends on the same words, reads as that akam season-poem expanded, with its closing camp scene as the answer to her question.

note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife, saying she is not sulking, reads his reddened eyes after the flood-bath as a sign of the women he bathed with. Kural 1313: the husband says that even if he wears a wreath of branch flowers, she grows angry, saying he wore it to show another woman.
teaches: Both turn the husband's body into evidence in a love-quarrel, but the Kural's husband protests that the sign is innocent and the suspicion hers, while the Ainkurunuru sign comes from a bath with women he did take, so together they show that the oodal's reading of marks on the man can be either jealous fancy or plain proof, and the couplet's comedy depends on the scene being the first.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும்). Thinaimalai 60: the hero names the long-eyed girl plucking neythal as the fisherman's daughter who has made him mad (மையல்).
teaches: The couplet's lover reels because he cannot tell what she is, while the venba's lover knows exactly who she is, a fisherman's daughter at the shore, and is mad all the same, so the scene shows the bewilderment surviving the answer to the Kural's question.

note: Kural 613 says the pride of generosity rests on effort; the man of Natrinai 214 leaves saying fame, pleasure and giving do not come to those who sit idle.
teaches: The akam poem shows the Kural's rule as a departing husband's stock reason, quoted by the wife he leaves and then mocked by the thunder, so the maxim that giving needs effort was already common speech, and the poem counts what it costs the one left behind.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute, envoy of the burning evening, is a weapon that kills. Ainthinai Aimpathu 7: at red evening the herdsman's fine little flute, played in joy once the cattle have fed, is to her like a spear thrown.
teaches: The couplet states that the flute is a deadly weapon, and the venba supplies the scene that explains it: the herdsman plays for joy at his own day's return, so the weapon is someone else's homecoming.

note: Purananuru 168 praises Kotran's hill, where hill people sow millet unploughed in the earth a boar has turned and feast on the first new grain; in Ainkurunuru 270 the hunters reap the first crop from the boar-ploughed slope and leave the hill bare.
teaches: The same unploughed tillage and first harvest is plenty and hospitality in the praise of a patron but, for lovers who met at the millet watch, the end of their season and a bare hill, so akam reads the hill's farming calendar as a calendar of meeting.

note: Ainkurunuru 84: the other woman calls his chest a Thai bathing pond that many plunge into. Kural 1311: the wife refuses his chest because all women feast on it with their eyes.
teaches: The Kural wife's complaint that his chest is common property is made, in the Ainkurunuru, by one of the women who share it, who boasts of it rather than complains, so the same image of the common chest serves as reproach from the house and as triumph from outside it.

note: Akananuru 91: even if he won Kuttuvan's Kudanadu, he would not stay there forgetting her beauty. Natrinai 391: who would leave for wealth even to win Nannan's Ezhil hill, and make her eyes weep?
teaches: The friend's comfort had a fixed shape, a famous chief's rich land weighed against the woman's beauty or tears, and the pair shows its two stages: in the Akananuru the man has already gone and will not linger, in the Natrinai the journey is only announced and will not be made at all.

note: In both the friend tells the man who has announced his journey that the woman's bangles will slip; Akananuru 271 wishes his work be capable (வல்வதாக) and asks if there is medicine for her, Ainkurunuru 310 asks whether he is capable (வல்லுவை) of parting.
teaches: Both friends turn வல், the capacity a man needs for his work, into the hardness that parting demands, so the pair shows the dissuasion convention attacking the hero's prized strength itself rather than his reasons for going.

note: In both the friend (for one Kural commentator) tells the man who announces his going that the woman will not survive him: 'tell your quick return to those who will be alive' and 'she will not live a blink without you'.
teaches: The couplet's bare refusal of comfort becomes in the kali an argued case: the friend first sets his two promises against each other and shows that wealth cannot be earned, and only then says the girl will not live, so the Kural's line reads as the last move of a dispute the long poem spells out.

note: 394: Kuttuvan gives a killer elephant, and when the frightened bard returns it gives a bigger one, ashamed the first seemed small; Kural 221: true giving is giving to those who have nothing.
teaches: The Kural defines a gift by the receiver's want, but Kuttuvan's elephants are sized to the giver's honour and are useless to a hungry bard, so the poem shows a royal giving that the Kural's definition would hardly count as ஈகை at all.

note: Both men speak to the heart that stands behind them (பின்நின்று): in 3 it drives him from behind toward wealth (பின்நின்று துரக்கும்), in 19 it plans to stay behind with her (பின்நின்று ஒழியச் சூழ்ந்தனை).
teaches: The heart at the man's back is a fixed paalai figure that can push either way, toward the road or toward home, so in these poems the heart is not one side of the debate but the place where the debate happens.

note: Kuruntokai 66: the friend says the konrai are foolish (மடவ) to take the stray rain for the season and bloom. Thinaimalai 104: the woman says the konrai, blooming at the cloud's word, has killed her (கொன்றாய்).
teaches: On the friend's reading the konrai's early flowering is a harmless mistake that proves nothing, and on the woman's it is a killing, so the same tree judged foolish in the consolation is judged guilty by the one it was meant to console.

note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 5 warns the man off because the kin carry bows, spears and swift arrows; Thinaimalai 28 warns him through the precious trees the kin cut down to plough.
teaches: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 5 states the threat as weapons, and Thinaimalai 28 leaves weapons out and lets the felled sandal and agil show what the brothers would do to an intruder, so the threat can be carried by how a family treats its own hill rather than by its arms.

note: 48 describes the pearl-lit village at nightfall with no hearer; 49 addresses the shore lord with the same pearls dispelling the midnight dark and asks where he will come.
teaches: Read together, the bare description of 48 gains its speech act from 49: the pearl-light that seems praise of the shore's riches is the friend's ground for refusing the night tryst.

note: Akananuru 292: the girl, afraid of the veri rite, blames the hill lord, where a sling stone flung at an elephant scatters vengai blossom and lodges in a jackfruit. Natrinai 51: the girl, facing the veri rite, names the hill lord where a killer tusker broke the young jackfruit among vengai with strewn flowers.
teaches: Two poets give the girl facing the velan the same hill emblem, a blow among vengai blossom that strikes a jackfruit, which shows it was a stock figure for the harm the unmarried lover does and supports reading the broken young jackfruit of Natrinai 51 as a hidden comparison rather than scenery.

note: In Kuruntokai 300 the man says he would not leave her even for the sea-ringed world; in Kuruntokai 288 the woman says even the hurt love brings is sweeter than the world of the gods.
teaches: The man measures his love against earthly rule and the woman against heaven, so the two speakers of kalavu each renounce the highest good of their own sphere, kingship for him, the gods' world for her.

note: 45 tells two quarrelling Cholas that their fight will delight other kings; 58 tells a Chola and a Pandya that if they never break their union the whole earth will be theirs.
teaches: The two poems state one calculation from opposite sides, division gives the gain to outsiders and union takes it from them, so together they show Sangam poets thinking of alliances between crowns in terms of who profits.

note: Both show a bard's hunger by a mushroom growing in a cold kitchen (ஆம்பி) and a starving woman and her children; Perunthalai Saathanar shows it to Kumanan as his present state, the idyll's guide as a past state the patron ended.
teaches: The same kitchen of poverty serves as a petition in the Purananuru poem and as testimony in the guide poem, which shows how the guide form works: the bard's own former misery, once relieved, becomes the credential that sends another bard to the same patron.

note: Akananuru 355 says spring has come of itself (செவ்விவேனில் தானே வந்தன்று) to a woman whose man is about to leave; the Ainkurunuru refrain says the same with தான் வந்தன்றே after he has gone.
teaches: The same formula serves first as the woman's argument against going, the season lovers spend in cool groves, and then as the proof that he went anyway, so 'it came of itself' carries the reproach that the season keeps its time unasked while the man does not.

note: Kazhuvul's Kaamur is a place of blessed vengai fragrance in 365 and the town thrown into turmoil by the fourteen Velir in 135.
teaches: The same chieftain's town gives one poet the image of calm sweetness for the wife's hair and another the image of a besieged, shaken heart, showing that a puram name entered akam with its whole history, peace and siege alike, available for comparison.

note: Kural 90 says a guest withers when the host's face changes; in Natrinai 120 the man brings a guest into the house because his sulking wife will not show an angry face to a guest and he will see her smile.
teaches: The rule of the welcoming face that the Kural lays on the host becomes, in the poem, the husband's lever against the wife's sulk, so the guest is both the object of hospitality and the akam go-between (வாயில்) that ends an oodal.

note: Both strip the suppliant's rag like old pond moss, dress him in new cloth and feed him meat and rice; Purananuru 390 ends by saying that kings with elephants do not even know such feeding.
teaches: The rag, cloth and meal follow a fixed order of the gift rite in both, and holding them together shows the idyll claiming for a crowned king the very hospitality that Purananuru 390 boasts only the lesser chief gives, so the boast was rhetoric and not a rule of rank.

note: Ainthinai Aimpathu 50: the heroine says she rose at what she took for his horses' bells and turned back on hearing it was birds. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 59 tells the same mistake of her in the third person, with the same words புள்ளரவம் கேட்டுப் பெயர்ந்.
teaches: The two venbas share a stock scene, and the second adds what the first leaves out: in the heroine's own telling she turns back from a melting heart, in the onlooker's telling from fear of the hamlet's talk, so the formula carried either the private grief or the public danger of kalavu waiting.

note: Purananuru 62 describes a battle in which both kings die, their drums are abandoned (முரசு ஒழிந்தனவே) and no one is left to claim the field (களங்கொளற்கு உரியோர் இன்றி); Kalavazhi Narpathu 11 describes the abandoned drums (ஒழிமுரசம்) of those whose strength failed, kicked by blinded elephants, on the field Sengan won.
teaches: The abandoned drum is the same sign in both, but whose drum it is decides what it means: when only the loser's drum is dropped it proves a victor and the field becomes his song, and when both drums fall, as in Purananuru 62, the field has no owner and the poet can only ask what the war was for.

note: Purananuru 15 addresses Mudukudumi himself, asking whether his enemies or his completed Vedic sacrifices are more; the idyll measures Nedunjeliyan's feast against one shared with the teachers trained in the sacrifices of Mudukudumi of many halls.
teaches: The sacrifices that Purananuru 15 praises as one king's deeds had become, by Nedunjeliyan's time, an inherited institution with its own line of teachers, and the standard against which a later Pandya's liberality was measured.

note: In both the man praises the woman he has just joined by addressing a creature of the flowers: Kuruntokai 2 asks the bee whether any flower is more fragrant than her hair; Kural 1111 tells the anicham it is soft but she is softer.
teaches: Valluvar keeps the Sangam device of praise through an apostrophe to nature but changes the sense judged, from smell to touch, and drops the witness: the Kuruntokai man asks the bee for evidence, the Kural man simply declares the verdict.

note: Kural 301 says anger is truly restrained only where it could take effect; Patitruppattu 32 marvels that the king, having broken the enemy and taken their land, is not angry even in the country of those who reviled him.
teaches: The Kural's rule names the only test of restraint that counts, and the Chera poem shows a king passing it at the one moment conquest gives his anger full power, which is why the poet calls it a wonder rather than a duty.

note: Kar Narpathu 10: the thunder roars and the herd bull bellows back at it, and the chariot comes so her body will freshen; 117: the thunder rages, the rutting elephant trumpets back and the cobra hides, and her shoulders pale.
teaches: In both the beast answering the thunder marks the height of the rains, and the pair shows that this moment is the hinge of the mullai wait: with the chariot heard it brings her colour back, and without it the same roar is when the pallor sets in.

note: Kural 4 names God as the one without liking or aversion (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்); Paripadal 3.53-58 makes Maal first of the immortals and first also of the asuras who fled from him into the sea, and asks whether there is any 'these are enemies, these friends' for those who know his nature.
teaches: The Kural states the god's freedom from liking and aversion as a bare attribute, while the hymn tests it against the war of gods and demons, where the god plainly took a side, and saves it by making him lord of both, so the pair shows the attribute had to be defended against a mythology of partisan war.

note: Kalittokai 104 likens the pen strewn with gored men to the field where the five archers killed the hundred (நூற்றுவர் மடங்க... ஐவர் அட்ட பொரு களம்); Purananuru 2 praises the Chera who gave food without limit while the hundred fought the five and fell on the field.
teaches: The Bharata war that Purananuru 2 treats as a dated occasion for one king's generosity is already, in Kalittokai, a stock picture of any heap of the fallen, used even for a village bull-catch, so the epic had passed from a remembered event into the common image store of the poets.

note: Kural 1108: sweet to two who desire each other is an embrace that not even a breeze can part. Natrinai 240: even the closest embrace is such that sleep comes between, yet the forest road stands like a mountain.
teaches: The Kural makes the gapless embrace the ideal of union; the Natrinai lover admits that even such an embrace is parted by sleep, and that admission is what lets his heart argue for leaving, so the ideal of perfect closeness becomes, in the man's mouth, a reason that union is already imperfect.

note: In Akananuru 28 the mother would replace the girl at the field if she failed to scare the parrots; in Thinaimozhi 10 the mother bars her from the field because she has learnt of the union.
teaches: The pair shows two routes to the same confinement, neglect of the field-watch and the mother's knowledge, which makes clear that the millet field is the one place the girl is allowed out, and losing it is losing him.

note: The Kural says giving without the misery of saying 'I have nothing' is found only in the well-born; the patron, hailed as the scion of an unfailing line, will not let the bards even finish telling of their journey before he welcomes them.
teaches: One of the senses of the couplet, giving before the asker must speak of his need, is in the idyll a court scene in which the patron cuts short the suppliants' account, and the idyll ties it, as the Kural does, to the giver's lineage.

iraicchi.act: the doe follows the stag across the rocky waste and the pair do not part
iraicchi.sense: if even the deer cross the waste together, the wife should not be left behind by her husband

iraicchi.act: the boar joins its mate
iraicchi.sense: the beast of his hill unites with its own mate, while the man leaves the woman he loves to grow pale, so he should come and marry her

note: Kural 1157: do the bangles slipping from her wrist not already proclaim that the shore lord has left? Kainnilai 55: if the shore lord leaves without embracing her, the bangles will not stay on either hand.
teaches: The venba states as a condition what the couplet packs into a past tense, so it supports reading the Kural's 'has left' as anticipatory: the bangles slip at the mere prospect of the shore lord going.

note: Kural 335 says that, because death stops the tongue unannounced, good deeds must be rushed to; the man of Kuruntokai 267 argues from Death's crooked, daily taking that those who know it do not leave their women to go after work and wealth.
teaches: The same awareness of death leads to opposite conduct: the Kural spends the short life on merit done in haste, the lover on staying with her and refusing the journey, so impermanence by itself does not decide between duty and love.

note: 628 prevents pain by not desiring pleasure. 669 accepts pain for the sake of the pleasure that results. One asks you to stop wanting joy and the other to work for it.
teaches: They may differ in scope, since 628 speaks of how one meets pain and 669 of which tasks to take up, but neither verse says so.

note: Kural 66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute and lute sweet; in Natrinai 212 the bards tune their strings on the road while at home the child's sweet voice asking to be held made the mother anxious each time.
teaches: The child's voice that the Kural ranks above music becomes, while the father is away, a reminder of his absence, so the couplet's household joy assumes the father is present to hear it.

note: Kural 1247: the woman tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both; Kuruntokai 231: neglected by the man in her own town, she says her desire, having killed shame and lost good sense, has gone far like a loosed arrow.
teaches: The couplet presents a choice still open between desire and shame, while the poem shows it already made and past recall, desire having killed shame on its own, so the Kural's dilemma is the moment before the poem's confession.

note: Both say give now because death is certain; the Naladiyar warns that wealth is useless after the funeral drum, 359 promises a fame that outshines the burning ground.
teaches: The same deathbed counsel serves two motives: the Naladiyar argues from the uselessness of hoarded wealth, the Purananuru from the name left behind, so the later book drops the reward the earlier one offered.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the generous man to a fruit tree ripening in the town; Kalittokai 27 likens the riverbank trees flourishing in spring to the wealth of a man who gives without stint and lives by virtue.
teaches: The comparison runs one way in the Kural (wealth like a tree) and the other in the kali (trees like wealth), showing that the moral image had become common enough for a love poet to turn it round and use the giver's wealth to describe the season.

note: Ainkurunuru 142's heroine resolves not to think of the shore lord so that her eyes may sleep; in Kural 1207 the woman says she does not know how to forget and asks what would become of her if she did.
teaches: The Sangam heroine treats not-thinking as a cure she can choose for her sleeplessness, while Valluvar's woman declares forgetting impossible and fatal, so the couplet denies exactly the resolve the older poem lets her voice.

note: Paripadal 11.62-71 praises the Vaigai water-sport of men with gold-garlanded women as an open custom (கரவா வழக்கிற்று); in Akananuru 296 the friend refuses a husband who bathed in the great Vaigai with another woman and says it is already common talk.
teaches: The same Madurai river festival that the devotional song celebrates as a public glory with nothing hidden is, seen from the wife's door, the proof and occasion of a husband's straying, so the openness the Paripadal praises is exactly what feeds the alar of the marutham quarrel.

note: The Naladiyar says the passing joy of youth is not found among the wise; the Ainkurunuru hero says youth spent together is sweet and the union is sweet now.
teaches: Both accept that youth passes, but the Naladiyar draws from that fact a duty to withhold delight, while the Sangam hero draws from it a reason to spend youth in shared pleasure, so the same premise yields opposite counsel in the old love poetry and the later ascetic quatrains.

note: Both have the woman in separation with eyes that cannot sleep; Kuruntokai 5 uses the sleeplessness to ask whether this is love-sickness, Kural 1179 says the eyes do not sleep when he is away nor when he comes.
