teaches: The Sangam woman learns from sleepless eyes that she is in love, while the Kural woman, past that discovery, finds the sleeplessness survives even his return, so the couplet assumes and goes beyond the moment the older poem records.

note: Kural 1151 says: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 129 mocks as a great joke the man who says he will go and that we will live on at home until he returns.
teaches: Both turn the man's promise of return into a question of whether she will survive to see it, but the Natrinai supplies what the couplet leaves out, the midnight thunder she must hear alone, so the Kural's bitter one-liner has behind it a scene in which the waiting itself is the threat.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the season is the medicine for her pallor. Kural 1265: the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading the two disagree about what cures pasalai.
teaches: The friend claims the sign of his return heals the pallor and the Kural's woman holds that only the sight of him will, so the couplet reads as the heroine's answer to the whole method of the Kar Narpathu's friend.

note: Purananuru 233 refuses to believe the dawn news that Evvi, leader of the bards' families, lies with spear wounds in his chest; Kuruntokai 19 compares the man's grieving heart to the flowerless heads of the bards impoverished by Evvi's loss.
teaches: The puram lament gives the moment of the news, and Paranar's simile gives its aftermath, bards going bare-headed without flowers, so the pair show a patron's death becoming a recognised mourning custom that akam could borrow to measure a lover's estrangement.

note: In Akananuru 112 the friend tells the man who has come at night of the bear and the tiger on his path and asks why he does not marry; the idyll ends with the girl weeping over the tiger, bear, elephant, crocodiles and spirits of his night path, told to the mother.
teaches: The dangers of the night path press for marriage from both sides: in Akananuru 112 they are told to the man to make him propose, and in the idyll to the mother to make the family consent, so the same catalogue is used as leverage on whichever party is holding back.

note: Both use the saying 'eating one's own in one's own house': Kural 1107 for the joy of the beloved's embrace, Kuruntokai 83 for jackfruit hanging sweet on the lover's own hill as the mother announces he will come.
teaches: The pair shows the phrase was a common measure of untroubled, owned pleasure; the Kural applies it to union itself, while the Kuruntokai friend lays it on the lover's land at the moment marriage is promised, so the image belongs to the settled household rather than to secret love.

note: Akananuru 376: the courtesan tells the lord to give back her beauty, which was like Kuttuvan's Maranthai, and then go. Natrinai 395: the friend tells the shore lord to give back the girl's beauty, which is like Maanthai on the sea, and go.
teaches: The same formula, beauty likened to a Chera town and demanded back before he leaves, is spoken by a discarded courtesan in the Akananuru and by the friend of an unmarried girl here, so the restitution formula belonged to the speech of any woman wronged by the man, and in the friend's mouth it becomes a demand for marriage.

note: Kuruntokai 148: konrai buds like the gold coins of rich children's anklets bloom with the kurunthu; if you say this is not the rainy season, is it a dream? Thinaimalai 98: the konrai blooms into anklet, golden coin, garland and more; look at it now, you and the others.
teaches: Kuruntokai uses the anklet-coin likeness to make the konrai unanswerable evidence that the season has come, and the venba expands that single likeness into a run of six ornament shapes and calls witnesses, so the flowering becomes a proof displayed to an audience.

note: Paripadal 1.40-51 says you are the moon, the sun, the sky and the earth; Paripadal 4.25-32 says your coolness is in the moon, your heat in the sun, your form and sound in the sky.
teaches: Inside one collection the god is first said to be the moon and the sun and then said to have only lent them his qualities, so the anthology holds both the identity form and the participation form of praise without choosing between them.

note: Natrinai 1's heroine calls her man sweeter the longer one knows him (நீடுதோறு இனியர்) and the bond of the noble lofty; Kural 783 says the companionship of people of character delights the more it is practised, as a book does the more it is studied.
teaches: The heroine uses the Kural's rule about friendship with the noble as the premise of a love argument, reasoning from his character that he cannot leave her, so a maxim about good company served in akam as evidence against a report of parting.

note: Kuruntokai 199: the lover tells his heart his love-sickness will last on into the other world; Kural 1315: he told her they would not part in this birth, and her eyes filled with tears.
teaches: The Kural's joke works only because Paranar's belief was the convention: love was expected to outlast this birth, so a lover who promised only 'this birth' had set a limit the older poem's lover would not accept.

note: Paripadal 1.1-5 addresses Thirumal with Balarama's emblems as one god (ஒரு குழை ஒருவனை); Paripadal 2.20-23 names the conch-white palmyra-banner brother as a second figure and leaves open whether Thirumal is his younger or his elder.
teaches: Read together, the two hymns show that the fusion of the brothers in the first song was a devotional claim made against a known two-brother story, which the second song keeps in view by refusing to settle their order.

note: In both the friend, with the man listening, reads the mother's look at harvest time: in Akananuru 302 the mother keeps the girl home and stares at her body; in Natrinai 206 the father sends her to guard the millet while the mother wishes the wedding vengai would flower and looks at her face.
teaches: Together the two show the ripe millet as the moment when the parents read their daughter either as a field guard or as a bride, and the friend in both turns the mother's silent look into the deadline that should make the listening man ask for marriage.

note: Kuruntokai 184: the hero tells his companions his heart is caught in the net of the fisher girl's eyes; Kural 1084: the man says the artless girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them.
teaches: Both men describe a first sight as the girl's eyes acting on them, but the Kuruntokai draws the weapon from her own people's trade (the fishermen's fine net), showing that the Kural's abstract killing gaze was, in the older poetry, given a landscape and a craft.

note: Kural 1108: an embrace so close not even the wind can part it is sweet to two who desire each other; Kuruntokai 237: the man far away says he cannot count what now stands between their embrace, groves where tigers roar.
teaches: Read together, the measure of separation is the same embrace the couplet praises: where once not even a breeze passed between them, now forests and tigers do, so the poem's distance is felt as a gap inside the embrace.

note: Kural 508: one who trusts an outsider without examining him brings trouble without end. Natrinai 50: the friend failed to guard the girl because she trusted the man without seeing, taking his smallness for greatness.
teaches: The couplet is a rule for a king choosing men; the friend applies the same failure to herself in the household and names its cause, a public reputation (even his enemies admire him) taken in place of examination, so the pair shows the akam go-between bound by the same duty of testing the Kural lays on the king.

note: Kuruntokai 182: the lover asks whether throwing off his great shame (பெருநாண் நீக்கி) and riding the palm horse through the street will win her after the messenger failed; Kural 1132: body and life will mount the palm horse once shame is put aside (நாணினை நீக்கி).
teaches: The Kural states the madal threat as a general law of the unbearable, while the Kuruntokai shows its occasion (a failed go-between) and counts its price in other men's mockery, so the Kural's 'putting shame aside' is a public cost the hero weighs, not a private loss.

note: In Natrinai 144 the girl, with the man overhearing, says her heart frets now that she knows he comes alone by night over the forked paths (கவலை) where the tigress prowls; in Ainkurunuru 362 the same fear of the forked night path (கவலை) and its elephant is put to the man's face.
teaches: The overheard complaint of Natrinai 144 and the open question of 362 make the same plea, stop coming by night, in two registers, and holding them together shows that Ainkurunuru's direct-address decade turns the indirect device of the overhearer into plain speech without changing the situation.

note: Both open on எந்தோள் துறந்த and ask எவன்கொல்: 108 sets the abandoned shoulders against the shoulders he desired, 109 against the many days of his grace.
teaches: Read as a pair, the near-identical poems move the friend's charge from the body he wanted to the time he spent, so the decade builds the case against the lord in two steps, desire then history, before the mother.

note: Kural 1311: the woman refuses the chest of the man she calls a philanderer, because all women feed on him with their eyes. Kainnilai 38: the wife bars him from her house from today because he lives desiring young women's shoulders.
teaches: The couplet's refusal rests on a witty pretext, that other women merely look at him, while the venba's rests on his actual desire for other women, so the pair shows the Kural turning a real grievance of the marutham poems into the fine point of a lovers' quarrel.

note: Both rank modesty above life: Kural 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for it but never shame for life; Natrinai 17's girl says she almost forgot the modesty dearer than life when her mother spoke softly.
teaches: The Kural states the ranking as a firm rule, and the Natrinai girl who holds it nearly breaks it not under threat but under a mother's tenderness, so the poem shows the rule's weak point to be a kindness the maxim does not foresee.

note: The Kural says a guest wilts at a host's changed face; in the idyll the hill people take the troupe in as kin without asking who they are and speak sweet words to end the loneliness of a far country, but only after the troupe says it is the Vel's musicians.
teaches: The idyll confirms the Kural's point that a welcome lies in the manner more than the meal, but it shows the welcome opened by the patron's name rather than owed to any guest, so in the guide poem hospitality is a sign of a king's reach, not the householder's duty the Kural makes it.

note: Akananuru 388: a young hunter with a hound comes to the millet platform asking whether a wounded tusker has passed through their field. Ainthinai Aimpathu 14: he came like those who ask after a beast, but there is something else he means to ask.
teaches: Akananuru stages the hunter's question in full while Ainthinai compresses it into a simile, 'like those who ask after a beast', which shows that the asking-after-game approach was a recognised pretext the girls themselves could name and see through.

note: Both men measure the girl by a divine figure on Kolli: in 185 the figure-like girl has plotted his death; in 192 thinking of her figure-like beauty makes the beast-haunted path safe.
teaches: Read together, the Kolli image proves double-edged: the same god-made beauty is a killing power when the girl or her friend refuses him and a protecting charm when she fears for him, so its force depends on which way her favour runs.

note: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one is sweeter than sleep in the soft arms of the one you love; Paripadal Thirattu 1.33-46 lists the shrine crowd as matched men and women and says the god's town is like the heaven where ripened deeds are enjoyed.
teaches: The couplet sets lovers' joy against Mal's heaven as rivals, but the hymn builds its likeness of heaven out of the paired lovers in the god's own crowd, so the opposition the Kural plays on was not one the temple festival felt.

note: Purananuru 22 praises the Chera on campaign abroad, under whose white umbrella's shade the unarmed sleep safe while he does not sleep; Kalittokai 26 has the woman say her man guards unfailingly those who come weary to his shade, praised by the world, while he lives in a stranger's land.
teaches: The akam woman quotes the very virtue the puram poet praises, shelter given abroad to all who seek it, and asks why it does not reach her, so the pairing shows the cost of the heroic ideal falling on the household the hero leaves.

note: Kuruntokai 25: the only witness of the secret union was a heron watching for fish. Kuruntokai 26: against the lover's possible denial, the friend says even the male monkey of the hill knows that cruel man.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the lack of a human witness to kalavu as a standing fear, answered by pointing to the land's own creatures: the woman doubts that the heron saw anything, while the friend insists that the monkey knows.

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats the leftover (மிச்சில்) needs sowing at all; Kuruntokai 233 praises her father's town where the leftover (மிச்சில்) of rice poured out for the great is shared with all without limit.
teaches: The love poet measures a bride's family by the very household ethic the Kural states, even with its word for the leftover, so the hospitality rule was already a mark of a good marriage before it was a maxim about prosperity.

note: Natrinai 283 and Ainthinai Aimpathu 46 both have the friend ask the shore lord, beside girls decking their sand-houses (with neythal flowers, with pearls), whether it is fitting (தகுமோ, தகுவதோ) that the girl's beauty should waste.
teaches: The friend's reproach has a fixed form, the girls' sand-house play set against the heroine's wasting beauty with the question 'is it fitting?', and Natrinai adds the ground the venba leaves implicit: his word was held truer than the sun, so the wasting is a breach of his truth.

note: In 381 the friend says the girl's wasting and pallor are the only fruit of having laughed with the shore lord; in 401 the girl says that even laughing play with the shore lord has been forbidden.
teaches: Read together the two neythal poems show laughter with the shore lord as the whole of kalavu at its smallest unit: one laugh costs the girl her beauty in 381, and in 401 the household guards against exactly that, so the forbidding is the town's answer to the danger the friend names.

note: Purananuru 12 asks the Pandya Kudumi whether it is dharma to take others' land so that it is painful to them (இன்னா ஆகப் பிறர் மண் கொண்டு) and do sweet things for his admirers; in Kalittokai 62 the girl asks whether forcing on others what pains them because it is sweet to oneself (தமக்கு இனிது என்று, வலிதின் பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்வது) is good.
teaches: The same sweet-for-oneself, painful-for-others test is put to a conquering king and to a forceful lover, and in both the one questioned claims it as virtue (அறன்), so the Sangam poets judged seizure in war and in love by one moral rule.

note: Ainkurunuru 43 calls the husband's bard a bigger liar than the husband, full of oaths; Akananuru 56 shows that bard on the street hurrying to bring new brides to the lord, scared into the wife's own house by a cow, and laughed at.
teaches: The two give the bard's double role in marutham: the Ainkurunuru names the charge (he lies and swears for his master) and the Akananuru shows why the wife can mock him openly, since attacking the go-between lets her shame the husband without naming him.

note: Innaa Narpathu 33 counts as painful the matter of business a drunkard speaks of; the line says a drinker free of lapses is false.
teaches: The Innaa line names the pain of dealing with a drinker's affairs and the Muthumozhikkanchi line gives its cause, the lapse that is certain in him, so one reports the effect and the other the reason no business with him is safe.

note: Ainkurunuru 24 says he takes the beauty (நலங்கொண்டு) of the women he embraced and abandons them; Kural 1183 says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange.
teaches: The Kural turns the friend's accusation of plain taking into an exchange in which pallor is the payment, so the same loss that the Sangam friend calls the act of a kin-destroying creature becomes, in the couplet, the woman's own bitter bookkeeping.

ullurai.tenor: the town's gossip and the girl it frightens

pairs.situation: the loud talk of the town about the secret love
the girl who fears that talk and her mother's hearing of it

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the salt carts and the heron of the backwater, things of the poem's own neythal shore (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the tusker trumpets because the mist hides his mate, who sleeps right beside him
iraicchi.sense: once the girl is shut in the house she will be near yet out of his sight, and the man will cry out like the tusker unless he marries her

ullurai.tenor: the girl, ruined by the man and still turning to him

pairs.situation: she was taken unawares by one who did not care what he cut
she does not yet own the harm done to her

pairs.scene: தெறு கதிர் இன் துயில் பசு வாய் திறக்கும்
pairs.situation: she still opens to the man who scorches her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the neythal flower of her own shore and the paddy harvest she sees (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the hill lord and the girl his secret love has wasted

pairs.situation: the hill lord has broken the innocent girl's health
her beauty fallen away, the change the velan is called to cure

ullurai.speaker_fit: the girl uses the tusker and trees of her own hill, things she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: having fed on the wide sea, the heron flies as if its life would leave it to reach its mate's nest on the palm frond, never ceasing to call its partner
iraicchi.sense: even the heron hurries home at nightfall to the mate it calls, while her man, gone only a short way, does not come

iraicchi.act: the doe, with her fawn beside her, frolics in the newly rained land
iraicchi.sense: a mother and young at play together on his road set before the absent man the home and family he should be back with in this season

iraicchi.act: the bulls stand together with their heifers, ready to go home with the herd
iraicchi.sense: as the bulls keep with their mates, the man means the two of them to go home together

iraicchi.act: the crab keeps with its mate on the dune when the waves draw back
iraicchi.sense: even the crab stays beside its mate, yet he leaves her friend to pale

note: Kalavazhi 36 sings the day the Kaveri lord took Kalumalam (கழுமலங் கொண்டநாள்), the enemy umbrellas overturned like mushrooms; Akananuru 44, a hero hurrying home after his king's war, names the Chola Senni who took Kalumalam and captured Kanaiyan (கணையன் அகப்படக் கழுமலம் தந்த) and likens the heroine to that king's rich town Kudavayil.
teaches: Kalavazhi leaves the loser at Kalumalam unnamed and shows only the carnage, while the akam poet names the captive Kanaiyan and spends the victory as a mark of the Chola's prosperity, so together they show one battle remembered both as a field of dead and as a byword for a well-kept land.

note: In Kural 1183 the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; in Ainkurunuru 55 the friend tells the man that because he desired her beauty and left her, her brow has paled for many to see.
teaches: The Kural keeps the exchange of beauty for pallor as the woman's private complaint, while the Ainkurunuru friend turns the same exchange into public evidence held up to the man, so the pallor that is a lament in the couplet becomes an accusation in the town.

note: Kalittokai 141's rider says she made him, who rides the war horse in battle, ride the madal to the common; in Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal.
teaches: The couplet's before-and-after inventory is spelled out in the kali poem as three lost ranks (warrior, protector, orator), which shows that the manliness the Kural says is lost is a public standing, not only a private virtue.

note: The guide promises the bards rice toddy brewed by fisherfolk and roasted fish until they stagger; the couplet says do not drink, or let only those who do not care for the esteem of the worthy drink.
teaches: The idyll counts drinking to the point of staggering among the best hospitality of the road, given freely by the poorest folk, while the couplet makes drink the mark of one who forfeits esteem, so the ethics book is rejecting a pleasure the oldest praise poetry offered as part of the gift.

note: The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death; the man of Thinaimalai 22 says her two eyes shot him as her brothers shoot beasts.
teaches: The Kural names the killing look in the abstract, and Thinaimalai 22 grounds it in her people's trade, measuring her two eyes against her brothers' single killing arrow, so the deadly glance of the couplet turns out to be a hunter's weapon of the hills.

note: Akananuru 296 makes the husband's bathing in the great Vaigai with a dark girl the gossip of Koodal; Paripadal 6.26-43 shows the whole town, young and old, rich and strong, going down to play in the same river.
teaches: Read against the Paripadal's crowd at the fords, the Akananuru friend's charge cannot be that he bathed in the Vaigai, since everyone did; the scandal lies in whom he bathed with, so the akam reproach depends on a public festival that the akam poem itself never describes.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who rises worshipping her husband commands the rain; Paripadal 20.88-89 has onlookers tell a wronged wife that worthy women praise and bow to their husbands even when the husbands slight them (கேள்வரை ஏத்தி இறைஞ்சுவார்).
teaches: The Kural offers the wife's worship of her husband as a source of power over nature, but the Paripadal shows the same ideal used in a quarrel to silence a wife whose husband has given her bangle away, so the couplet's praise of devotion could serve in practice as counsel to put up with a man's straying.

note: Both are night-tryst poems the lover overhears, and both close on the same formula, a tusker and his mate asleep on the plantain slope (வாழையஞ் சிலம்பிற் றுஞ்சும் / வாழையம் சிலம்பில் துஞ்சும்): in 328 he strokes a mate who has just calved, in 332 he lies down with her after killing a tiger.
teaches: A shared formula takes a different act each time to suit the speech: the calving mate presses toward married life in a poem of fear, the tiger-killing protector confirms the lover in a poem of praise.

note: Ainkurunuru 5: the girls wish that the lover's chariot stand at their front gate. Akananuru 160: the friend tells the girl that his chariot, which used to come by night, has now come by day, loudly, for the whole village to see.
teaches: The Akananuru scene shows what the Ainkurunuru wish means: a chariot that comes by day to the gate, seen by the village, is a suitor's public claim, so the single wish for 'the chariot at our gate' is a request for marriage.

note: Kural 1137 holds that nothing is nobler than a woman who suffers a sea of desire yet does not ride the madal, that is, does not make her love public; in Natrinai 365 the friend proposes that they slip the mother's watch, go to the common in daylight before everyone and ask the way to his town to rebuke him.
teaches: The couplet makes the woman's silence a virtue, but the Natrinai friend uses the threat of breaking it, a daylight public walk being the woman's form of the madal, as a lever on the overhearing hero, so the restraint the Kural praises was also a weapon that worked only while it might be dropped.

note: Akananuru 46: the red-eyed buffalo breaks its tether, raids the pond, scatters the fish and eats the lotus, and the friend says he has brought another woman home. Thinaimalai 147: the red-eyed black-horned buffalo plunges into the field pond and comes back crowned with lilies and kayal fish and carrying frogs.
teaches: The Akananuru states the situation the raiding buffalo stands for, while the Thinaimalai keeps only the image and adds the buffalo coming home dressed in the pond's spoils, which shows the image had become a sign of the straying husband that a later poet could leave unexplained and even play for comedy.

note: Kuruntokai 206 tells the wise to keep from love because the woman is too sweet, her words like ambrosia; Naladiyar 41 tells men to turn from desire because the admired body is a frail bag the crows would tear.
teaches: The same counsel, keep away from love, rests on opposite judgments of the beloved: the Sangam lover flees because she is ambrosia and the pain is love's own, the Jain moralist because she is carrion under skin, so the later ethic keeps the advice and reverses its reason.

note: Innaa Narpathu 29 counts begetting children without understanding (அறிவறியா மக்கட் பெறல்) among painful things; the line calls the getting of children, unqualified, the greatest gain.
teaches: Read plainly, the two works give the same act opposite values, and only the qualifier about the child's understanding, which the Kural supplies, reconciles a supreme gain with a pain.

note: In Akananuru 146 the wife, refusing the bard, says the woman who trusts the deceiving philanderer's word (மாயப் பரத்தன் வாய்மொழி) will lose her beauty; in Ainkurunuru 139 she tells the lord that his bard ruins good women's beauty more than he does.
teaches: The longer poem lays the ruin of beauty on the husband's own lying word, the short one shifts it to the bard who carries that word, so the pair shows the go-between counted as an agent of the harm and not merely its messenger.

note: In Natrinai 386 the great-tempered boar that gorges on the hunters' millet and sleeps unafraid of the tiger frames a man who offers the dread oath and comes to wed; in Ainkurunuru 261 the boar that has grazed the millet and sleeps on the rock slope frames a man the heroine suspects of fearing her father.
teaches: The fearless sleeping boar was a stock frame whose point turns on the man set beside it, matching the bold suitor in Natrinai and shaming the timid one in Ainkurunuru, so the same image can carry praise or an unspoken reproach.

note: 291 defines truthfulness as speech without harm; 200 demands use.
teaches: Harmless idle talk passes the one test and fails the other, so the two chapters set different standards for speech.

note: Akananuru 178's friend rejoices that marriage is settled (வரைவு மலிந்து); Ainkurunuru 258's friend says the household has agreed to give her if he weds, yet her grief has not ceased.
teaches: Against the friend's joy in Akananuru 178, Ainkurunuru 258 shows that the household's consent alone ends nothing for the girl, so the akam sequence separates the family's yes from the man's coming as two steps.

note: Kural 1151's friend refuses comfort with an ultimatum about who will still be alive when he returns; Kuruntokai 363's friend asks whether crossing the waste is sweet when even the bull there stays by its doe.
teaches: The same dissuasion of a man about to leave is made by threat in the couplet and by the example of the road's own creatures in the poem, so the pair shows the friend has two arguments, death of the one left and the shame of being less faithful than a beast.

note: In 189 the lord of the gentle shore has come and her eyes have become good; in 190 the same மெல்லம் புலம்பன் is the one who made her many-petalled eyes weep.
teaches: Placed side by side in the decade with the same name for the man, the two poems make the heroine's eyes a gauge wholly in his hands, healed by his coming and wet by his absence, and the neythal image follows them, dusted with gold in one and cut down in the other.

note: Kural 1224: with the lover absent, evening comes like enemies to a killing ground. Ezhupathu 17: as kodal buds and thunder greet the rains, the little evening comes like killers so that those with no one to embrace them tremble.
teaches: The Kural's image of evening as executioner, spoken by one woman of one absent man, appears in the Ezhupathu tied to the rainy season and widened to a class (those with no one to hold them), which shows the image was a mullai convention of the promised-return season before or beside its use as a private complaint.

note: Purananuru 92 says a son's prattle keeps no tune and makes no sense, yet moves fathers to grace; in Kalittokai 80 the mother hears the son's sweet 'attatta' but the father is away with other women.
teaches: The puram poet's comparison assumes a father present to be moved by the prattle, and the Kalittokai shows the house where he is not, so the grace the prattle should draw from the father falls to the mother and is mixed with pain.

note: Kural 1268 wishes the king victory so that the man may join his wife and keep an evening feast for guests; Natrinai 81 is that moment reached: the king has quelled the enemy and the man hurries home to a wife whose grief was her longing to host guests.
teaches: Held together they show that the soldier's picture of home was a feast for guests, voiced as a wish before victory in the Kural and as a race home after it in the Natrinai, which adds that the wife's sorrow was her inability to host alone, so hospitality is a couple's act that war suspends.

note: 255 says the girl's grace resembles the mountain goddesses (வரையர மகளிர்ப் புரையும்); 256 says she herself is a great அணங்கு.
teaches: Two consecutive poems on the same opening line move from likeness to identity, so the decade itself shows a comparison with the hill goddesses hardening into the claim that the girl is one.

note: Both are the woman's love-sickness at evening in separation: Kural 1227 says the sickness buds at morning, grows through the day and blooms at evening; Natrinai 117 sets her evening on the shore, where the neythal closes and birds go home together while he does not think of her.
teaches: Set beside the shore's evening, where the neythal shuts, the couplet's sickness that blooms at evening reads as the one flower that opens when the others close, and the poem supplies the scene the couplet compresses into a single growth.

note: Kuruntokai 192 and Akananuru 97: the friend says do not grieve (இனையல், ஆழேல்), and the heroine answers that she cannot stop weeping when the koel calls in the flowering mango.
teaches: The same reply to the same comfort shows the spring koel in the mango was a fixed answer in the heroine's mouth: the long Akananuru spends its lines on the dangers of his road, while the Kuruntokai replaces them with the gesture of stroking flowerless hair, so the short form puts the proof in her body rather than in the landscape.

note: Patitruppattu 13 sets enemy farmland ruined by the king beside his own flowering land; Patitruppattu 62 describes a rich farm of cattle, grain heaps and toddy-drinking workers as what the enemy keeps if he bows and pays tribute.
teaches: The second decade shows ruin and plenty as two places; Kapilar makes them two futures of the same enemy land, so the farm scene becomes the terms of surrender rather than a picture of the king's own country.

note: Both use the belief that the crab is killed by its own young: Ainkurunuru 24 names the crab born at its mother's death (தாய்சாப் பிறக்கும்), Sirupanchamoolam 10 lists its own brood as death to the crab (ஞெண்டிற்குத் தன்பார்ப்பு).
teaches: The pairing shows a piece of field lore surviving from the akam landscape into the didactic list: the Sangam friend uses it to charge a man with destroying his own, while the later moralist uses it to say a thing's own offspring or speech is its death, so the same belief turned from accusation of another into warning to oneself.

note: In Akananuru 214 the man in the rain-soaked camp says the war is ours (அமரும் நம்வயினதுவே) while the king does not sleep; in Ainkurunuru 451 the wife says holding out in camp is the king's work (வேந்தனது தொழிலே), not her husband's.
teaches: On the same rainy-season campaign the soldier claims the war as his own duty and the wife assigns it wholly to the king, so the mullai situation is a dispute over where a man's obligation ends, and each side rests on a reading of whose war it is.

note: Purananuru 108: in Pari's Parambu the firebrand a hill woman lights is sandalwood, its smoke reaching the vengai. Natrinai 55: the friend explains the bees on the girl by pointing to a burning sandalwood firebrand.
teaches: The puram poem records that hill households burned sandal as ordinary firewood, which is what makes the friend's lie in Natrinai 55 credible to the mother: the girl could smell of sandal from the hearth, so the trick depends on a fact of hill life the puram poet praises as the land's wealth.

note: Kar Narpathu 19: the returning man sees the maraa blossom white like the plough-bearing god's colour and his heart runs ahead. Thinaimalai 96: the moonlight is like the pale colour of the discus-bearer's elder brother and falls like a spear on the parted.
teaches: Balarama's whiteness is a stock likeness in the Kilkanakku mullai poems, but it serves the hurrying man as the colour of the flowers that call him home and the waiting woman as the colour of a moonlight that wounds her, so the same divine colour signs joy or pain by who sees it.

note: In Kural 1167 the woman swims love's flood without seeing a shore and at midnight is the only one awake; in Kuruntokai 329 she cannot sleep in midnight's thick dark, thinking of the man on the desert road.
teaches: The couplet gives the midnight wakefulness as a bare state; the poem gives it a content, the road he took buried under fallen iluppai flowers, so the pair shows the sleepless mind of separation travelling the absent man's road.

note: Akananuru 153: the foster mother says the girl who grew hot and tired even running after a ball with her friends has gone into the burning summer forest, and asks whether her tender feet can manage it (வல்லுநள் கொல்லோ). Aimpathu 37 asks the same with the same verb (வல்லவோ), recalling her faltering at play by the ford.
teaches: The verb வல் and the evidence from play recur in both, which shows the mother's doubt as a set argument of the form: she judges the girl's strength for the road only by her weakness at games, a measure that the girl's going has already overturned.

note: The idyll's bards wander like birds that search for fruiting trees on a hill the rain has left; the Kural likens the wealth of a man with nayan to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town.
teaches: The patron-as-fruit-tree image is seen from the tree's side in the Kural and from the birds' side in the idyll, and the idyll adds the condition the Kural's town tree removes: the guide poem exists because, for the wandering bard, the fruiting tree is far off and must be pointed out.

note: Akananuru 26: the wife recalls that lately her husband held back from embracing her for fear of spilling the milk meant for their son. Thinaimalai 152: the wife herself refuses his embrace, saying her milk would spoil his garland.
teaches: In the Akananuru it is the husband who fears the milk and the wife who is hurt by his caution; in the Thinaimalai the wife takes up the same fear as her weapon, so together they show the nursing mother's milk standing on either side of the quarrel, as his excuse or as her refusal.

note: In Natrinai 224 the red-eyed dark koel (செங் கண் இருங் குயில்) calls as if saying 'you who are joined, stay joined' before the man leaves; in Ainkurunuru 346 the same koel (செங்கண இருங்குயில்) cries after he has gone and not returned.
teaches: One bird in one spring is a plea against parting while the man is still at home and an announcement of his failure once he is away, so the koel's call has no fixed sense of its own and takes its meaning from the stage of the parting.

note: In Akananuru 117 the foster mother says the girl did not think of the nochchi or her playmates when she left; in Natrinai 184 the mother cannot bear to see the nochchi and the terrace where the girl played.
teaches: The pair shows the same household shrub on both sides of the elopement: forgotten by the daughter who has gone, and unbearable to the mother who stays, so the left-behind play things measure how unequal the parting is.

note: Both have the woman's bangled shoulders lose their beauty when her partner leaves (Kural: துணைநீங்கித் தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்; Ainkurunuru: பிரிந்தெனப் புல்லென்றன என் புரிவளைத் தோளே).
teaches: The couplet describes the wasted shoulders as a fact, while the poem puts them as a helpless question to the absent man's own bard, so the same bodily sign becomes in the older poem a complaint lodged with his side of the household.

note: Kural 1185: look there, my lover goes; look here, the pallor spreads on my body. Thinaimalai 100: the rains appear, the lover's chariot does not, the pallor appears.
teaches: The couplet times the pallor to his leaving and the venba times it to his failure to return, so the two together show pallor at both ends of the absence, first as its shadow and then as its proof.

note: In the idyll a kingfisher strikes a bathing girl's golden earring for a fish and carries it off to a sacrificial pillar; in the Naladiyar quatrain a kingfisher takes the beloved's eyes for carp but does not dive, seeing her brow as a drawn bow.
teaches: The kingfisher's mistake about a woman's ornament or feature was a set conceit: the idyll lets the bird act on its mistake as part of a port scene, while the later love quatrain stops the bird short, turning the same error into praise of the woman's brow.

note: Natrinai 142: returning, the man tells his charioteer of the young woman of mullai-fitting chastity who rejoices when a guest comes even at night. Ainthinai Aimpathu 10: returning, he tells the charioteer to hurry to see her who stands with the bolt of her chastity drawn shut, hand to cheek.
teaches: The same speaker on the same road imagines the wife's chastity as an open door to guests in one poem and as a shut bolt in the other, so the pair shows karpu as both the household's hospitality and its closing against the world while the husband is away.

note: Patitruppattu 13 says that in the king's guarded land Venus does not run to the burning quarter and rain stands where wanted; Patitruppattu 69 says that under the rulers before him the land yielded, the sun's heat softened, Venus stood in its place and the rains answered need.
teaches: The second decade grants the good omens to the reigning king, while Kapilar grants them to the ancestors who were like him, so the same signs serve as proof of a present reign and as the inheritance a king must live up to.

note: Both foster mothers ask யாங்கு வல்லுநள்கொல் தானே of a girl who refused milk held up in a fine vessel at home: Akananuru 105 follows the question with the raiders' road of Ezhini's bowmen, Kuruntokai 356 with the scalding muddy water she must gulp.
teaches: The shared formula of the refused milk and 'how will she manage' is a stock frame of the foster mother's lament, and the two poems show its slot filled differently: the long poem measures the girl's leaving by the road's dangers, the short one by what she must now drink, so the same frame can carry either fear or tenderness.

note: Both kuthirai maram poems name the young rider with one formula: நோக்கினர்ச் செகுக்கும் காளை (302) and எள்ளுநர்ச் செகுக்கும் காளை (303).
teaches: The epithet for the young horseman was a fixed frame with a free slot for his victims, those who look at him or those who mock him, so two poets of the same thurai shared a stock line and varied only whom it threatened.

note: Ainkurunuru 154's woman can only call the town a liar and ask what she can do; in Kuruntokai 34 the friend says the town would not believe their denials (மறுப்பத் தேறலர்) and is silenced only by the sweet news that the lord will marry her.
teaches: Read together they show that in the neythal love story gossip cannot be ended by calling it false, since the town does not believe denials, and the only cure the poets allow is marriage, which turns the lying town into one that rejoices.

ullurai.tenor: the lord and the wives he has gone back to

pairs.situation: he moves in among his wives' household
the wives, closed in grief, open to him again

ullurai.speaker_fit: the other woman, who may use any thing freely (porul 7.29), takes a fish and lily of the marutham pond in a marutham poem

iraicchi.act: the she-elephant, when the tiger attacks her bull, is terrified for him
iraicchi.sense: the woman's fear for the man crossing tiger country by night is the fear even a beast feels for its mate, so it is love, not weakness, and he should end it

iraicchi.act: at evening the stag embraces his doe
iraicchi.sense: even the stag is with his mate at nightfall, which the absent husband is not

ullurai.tenor: the husband who tires of his wife and seeks women elsewhere

pairs.situation: he has tired of what is his own at home
he longs for other women away from the shore

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses a stork of her own shore, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the anril pair hold back their night call, thinking the woman without her partner would suffer
iraicchi.sense: even the birds of his shore spare her at night, while the man who caused her pain stays away

iraicchi.act: the hen swan, missing her mate for a moment, panics, runs to his false likeness and is shamed when he comes
iraicchi.sense: a wife who loses her husband even briefly is as anxious as the bird, so his long desertion is the greater cruelty

note: Kural 791 says nothing is as ruinous as making a friend without inquiry, since the devoted cannot leave once the bond is made; Natrinai 378 ends with the friend (or the heroine) calling her sleepless nights and the neighbours' gossip the measure of the bond made without inquiry (நாடாது இயைந்த நண்பு) with the lord of the shore.
teaches: The akam poem applies the ethics book's rule for choosing friends to a love made at a girl's sand-house, and its suffering shows the second half of the couplet at work, that she cannot leave the bond once made, so the maxim on friendship was available as a verdict on unwise love.

note: Purananuru 133: go and see Ay of the chariots, whose giving is like the rain. Natrinai 237: the rain clouds rise like the elephants Andiran gathered for suppliants.
teaches: The puram poet likens Ay's giving to rain, and the akam poet turns it round and likens the rain clouds to Ay's gift elephants, so the patron's bounty and the monsoon were interchangeable images and the friend can offer the season as a promise as sure as a great giver's word.

note: Akananuru 318: the friend tells the man who comes alone at night by a path made fearful by elephants, snakes and tigers not to come from today, and to blow his horn on reaching home so they know he is safe. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 10: the girl asks her friend to tell the lord of the snake-haunted groves not to come by night, to keep a life safe.
teaches: The long poem spells out what the four lines only hint, that refusing the night meeting is an act of care for the man's life on a dangerous path, and the venba moves the plea into the girl's own wish (குறையொன்று உடையேன்), showing the same refusal felt from inside.

note: In Natrinai 284 the man already away hears heart and reason argue and fears his body will snap like a rope; in Natrinai 298 the man about to go tells his heart it cannot hold both the hills and her shoulders, and he stays.
teaches: Read as a pair, the two poems show the same divided man before and after the journey begins: before it, the heart can still win and the journey is dropped, but once the work is under way reason rules and only the body is left to break.

note: Verse 4 says women's hearts melt for another as fish delight in new floodwater; verse 46 says a divided woman's mind can no more be made one than oil spread on water gathered.
teaches: The fragment moves from women's hearts straying to their being past recall once divided, which completes its case for giving them up.

note: In both the woman has accepted the man's part with her mind, in Kural 1181 by consenting to his absence, in 169 by knowing the truth of his heart, and still the pallor spreads on her.
teaches: The couplet makes her consent the reason she cannot complain of her pallor, and the Ainkurunuru adds that even trust in his heart does not stop it, so pallor in this tradition is a bodily fact beyond the will rather than a charge against the man.

note: Kural 785: shared feeling alone, without meeting or acquaintance, gives the claim of friendship. Ainthinai Aimpathu 23: the bond of those who know needs no bard to plead for the man's grace.
teaches: The wife turns the Kural's rule about friendship into an argument against intercession in marriage: if feeling alone makes the bond, then the presence of a go-between is itself proof that the feeling is gone.

note: Kural 1146 says she saw him on one day only, yet the talk has spread like the serpent seizing the moon; Kuruntokai 320 says they have not even the blame of laughing together one day, yet the town spreads gossip.
teaches: The Kural concedes one meeting behind the talk while the poem denies even that, so the pair shows the gossip of kalavu needing ever less fact, until in 320 it rests on nothing but the town's cruelty.

note: In both the woman tells her friend that the man's departure must be stopped because union after he goes will be hard; Natrinai 79 rehearses the words she might say and asks by what means to stop him.
teaches: The Kural gives the friend a reason to act, while the Natrinai woman supplies the argument she would use, that rejoining after parting makes another parting harder, and then doubts any words will work; the poem shows the couplet's advice as a thing she has already tried in her head.

note: Kural 1044 says poverty brings even the well-born to degrading words; Natrinai 262's man, seeing his wife already wasting, ends on 'hard indeed is the shame of having nothing' (இன்மையது இளிவே).
teaches: The Natrinai shows what Valluvar's shame of poverty weighs against in a man's life: it is the one argument strong enough to set beside a wife's midnight suffering, so the couplet's social fear turns out to be the engine of the paalai parting.

note: Both wives put to the bard a question about the evening of the herding land in the rains (Akananuru: மாலையும் உள்ளார் ஆயின் ... பாண; Ainkurunuru: மாலையும் உடைத்தோ ... பாண).
teaches: Ainkurunuru gives only the wife's accusing question and her name for him, loveless bard, while Akananuru tells it from the bard's side, who could not answer, played and prayed and went toward the man, so the pair shows the question was one the bard had no words for.

note: Both use the felling of the old punnai at Kurukkai in the war of Anni and Thithiyan: in 45 the gossip is louder than the bards' cheers that day; in 145 the foster mother curses her own hand to be cut down like that tree.
teaches: One puram event served the akam poets as a measure of two different things, public noise in one poem and deserved ruin in the other, so the war's fame had become a store of ready comparisons.

note: Kural 754 says wealth rightly gained yields virtue and pleasure, placing wealth below and in service of aram; Natrinai 243's woman says that if parting for wealth in such a season is men's nature, wealth must be dearer than aram itself. On the plain reading men's conduct, as she sees it, contradicts the Kural's ordering.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's ordering of virtue over wealth being turned into an accusation from inside the household: the woman accepts the scale but finds that men's going inverts it, so the ethical rule became a weapon in the akam speaker's mouth.

note: Kural 1133: he once had shame and manliness, and now has the madal. Natrinai 160: shame, decency and good conduct he knew better than his friend, before he saw her.
teaches: The couplet says the virtues were possessed and are now gone; the poem says they are still known, better than the rebuker knows them, and simply no longer govern him, so love takes away their rule, not the knowledge of them.

note: Kainnilai 21: the woman says her heart swims the long way after him (நீந்து). Kainnilai 22: the friend says he will swim back over the old clefts (நீந்திப் பெயர்ந்தவர்) and they will soon see him.
teaches: Read in sequence, the friend answers the woman's image with her own verb turned round, the heart swimming outward becoming the man swimming home, which shows how the friend's comfort in this book works by reversing the heroine's words rather than contradicting them.

note: Kural 1085 has the man at first sight find in her look Death, an eye and a doe; Thinaimalai 8 has the man at the fields find Kaman's arrows, five twice over, in the girl's two eyes.
teaches: Both men read a killing power in the first look, but the Kural names it Death while the field poem gives it to the love god and counts the arrows, which shows the same wound drawn once as mortal danger and once as a wound meant to be healed in union.

note: In Natrinai 213 the man asks the girls which is the small rock-fenced village near the roaring falls, and whether the guarding of the millet is theirs too. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 12 the friend says their guarding of the millet is over and this village by the waterfall is their place.
teaches: The man's question and the friend's answer use the same two markers, the waterfall village and the guarding of the millet, which shows the exchange as a set dialogue of kurinji courtship in which the friend's answer comes only when the guarding has ended.

note: Paripadal 8.112-117 says the eyes, faces, feet, hands, breasts and lips of girls rising from the hill pool cannot be told apart from the lotus and lilies of the water; Paripadal 22.32-34 says onlookers cannot decide whether the women adorn the Vaiyai or the Vaiyai's flood adorns them.
teaches: The hill song confuses women and flowers part by part, while the river song lifts the doubt to the whole, women against river, and refuses to settle which is the ornament, so the pair shows the Paripadal using the undecided likeness as its stock praise of festival bathing and widening it from a catalogue to a single question.

note: The guide scripts the bard's praise of the patron (warrior of warriors, lord of the wealthy, of unceasing giving) as the way to his gifts; Arunagirinathar confesses that praising people as lotus-handed and clouds in giving, to beg from them, wounded his heart, and asks to serve Murugan instead.
teaches: The patron praise that the guide poem teaches as a craft with a sure reward is in the later hymn the very habit the poet repents, so the bard's profession that founded Tamil praise poetry became for the devotional poet the model of misplaced service.

note: Kar Narpathu 10: as thunder roars and the bull bellows back, the swift chariot comes with the sound of a forest stream. Kuruntokai 155: the evening of the season has come, but not the word that his chariot with its ringing bells is on its way.
teaches: The venba lets the sound of the chariot arrive with the season, but the Kuruntokai keeps season and chariot apart and has the heroine wait first for the report of it, which shows the chariot-sound of mullai as a promise the older poem could leave unkept.

note: Purananuru 158 lists Malaiyan who rode Kaari and won great battles among the seven givers; in Natrinai 77 Kapilar likens the relief the girl's look once gave the lover to Malaiyan riding his horse into enemy land, breaking forts and breathing out his weariness.
teaches: The puram poem keeps Malaiyan as a rider and giver in a public roll, while the akam poem takes the same rider at the private moment after the raid, his sigh of relief, so akam used the king's fame for the feeling of a finished deed rather than for the deed.

note: Both use a shore bird that takes something else for a heron's chick: in Ainkurunuru 151 a stork treads a neythal flower going to see it; in Thinaimalai 36 a heron feeds a screwpine bud and shades it with its wings.
teaches: The same mistake of a bird taking a flower for a chick can carry opposite senses: in Ainkurunuru the error bruises the flower, which still gives off scent, like the heroine who stays tender to the man who hurt her, while in Thinaimalai it becomes devoted care held up to shame a man whose visits do not stay.

note: Kural 4 names God as the one without liking or aversion (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்); Paripadal 4.49-55 says the god has harm and grace, cruelty and rightness wherever these are found and none where they are not, and treats the lives of those who praise him and those who do not without exchange, having neither foes nor kin.
teaches: The Kural defines the god by what he lacks, while the hymn shows what that lack allows: he can hold cruelty and grace alike because they answer what is in things rather than his own preference, so freedom from liking and aversion is seen to include, not exclude, the god's harshness.

note: Kural 1143 welcomes the gossip the whole town knows, because it gives as if already got what is not yet got; Kalittokai 76 ends that if the town has done what their kin would do at the wedding, nothing is left to do.
teaches: Both turn alar from shame into a kind of marriage, and together they show the two uses of the same claim: the Kural lover savours the gossip as a foretaste, while the Kalittokai friend uses it as an argument that the wedding is already public and must now follow.

note: Kural 403 calls the unlearned very good if they keep silent before the learned; Pazhamozhi 13 says silence leaves their insight unshown and so gives no ground for thinking themselves good.
teaches: The Kural's ironic praise of the silent unlearned is limited by Pazhamozhi: silence spares them shame but cannot make them one of the good.

note: Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man sees the small mullai buds pointed like the girl's teeth; 116: the friend tells the mullai and its companions that their tooth-white buds have made the girl pale.
teaches: The bud that looks like her teeth is a pleasure on the road home and a wound in the waiting house, so the image's sense depends on whether the man is coming: the same likeness that recalls her smile to him drains her colour while he is away.

note: Kural 1185 is built on the pointing words உவக்காண், இவக்காண்: look there, he goes; look here, the pallor spreads. Natrinai 96 points with இதுவே, உதுவே, அதுவே to the places where she met him, and ends on the pallor.
teaches: Both make pallor out of pointing, but the Kural points across the distance of a departure seen as it happens, while the Natrinai friend walks back through the places of meeting before an overhearing man, so pallor comes in one from the sight of leaving and in the other from memory of place, used to press for marriage.

note: Kural 1311 has the woman refuse her lover's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Paripadal 7.69-75 the woman's fury falls on her lover because he looked at the ornaments of the bathing women (யாறு ஆடு மேனி அணி கண்ட).
teaches: The couplet makes the man's being looked at enough for oodal, the hymn makes his looking the offence, and the song's crowded bathing shows why both could be true at once: in the festival everyone sees and is seen, so the sulk needs no act of straying, only the eyes.

note: Both turn on the girl's hand laid on the man's eyes: in Natrinai 28 the girl recalls how in the secret love he took her hand and pressed it to his eyes, then left her like a thief; in Ainkurunuru 293 the wife covers his eyes from behind in play and he says no one else lives in his heart.
teaches: In Natrinai 28 the hand on his eyes was his gesture of a promise that his leaving made false, while in Ainkurunuru 293 it is her game in the married bed that draws from him the vow of no other, so the pair shows the same touch losing its doubt once the promise of secret love has been kept in marriage.

note: Purananuru 62 asks what winning a war can mean when both kings die, and shows demon women dancing in the blood of the dead; Patitruppattu 35 shows demons dancing in the red field and calls that war the king's unfailing wealth.
teaches: The same picture of demons dancing on the blood-field is proof of glory when a victor lives to be praised and proof of futility when no one is left to take the field, so the image itself carries no verdict and the surviving king supplies it.

note: In 424 the friend warns the man that his son will cry for the breast if he goes; in Akananuru 66 the crying son actually stops the man's chariot on the way to another wedding.
teaches: The friend's threat in Ainkurunuru 424 is the plan of which Akananuru 66 shows the working: the son as the one claim a departing husband cannot argue with was a recognised move, used against a journey for the king's work and against a journey to another woman alike.

note: Both wish the wasteland the girl has crossed with her lover cool with rain or cloud, in the same frame (...ஆகுக ... போகிய சுரனே); Kuruntokai's speaker is the foster mother, Ainkurunuru's the mother.
teaches: Kuruntokai's wish asks only shade, sand and cloud for a frightened road, while Ainkurunuru adds that the girl judged the going to be the path of right, so the same blessing formula could also carry the household's grudging moral consent to the elopement.

note: In Akananuru 378 the deserted girl says she lives only because the peak of his hill, crowned with a waterfall, is in sight (வான்தோய் சிமையம் தோன்றலானே); in Ainkurunuru 209 she says she cannot forget him because his cloud-crowned hill never stops appearing (தோன்றல் அனாது).
teaches: The same visible peak is what keeps the girl alive in the Akananuru and what defeats any demand that she forget in the Ainkurunuru, so together they show the hill working as a bond that neither absence nor counsel can loosen.

note: In Purananuru 145 Paranar asks as his only gift that Pekan ride to the grieving woman tonight; in 480 the bard, unheard, declares that he is no longer the man's bard.
teaches: Puram's bard spends his claim on the patron to win the woman's cause, while the Ainkurunuru bard, his plea having failed, gives up the claim itself, so the pair shows the patron bond as the bard's leverage and its renunciation as his last resort.

note: Akananuru 263's mother says that had she known she would gladly have married the girl to him in her rich house; Ainkurunuru 380's mother says she was only mother in name and the playmates gave her away.
teaches: Read together the two show the mother grieving a lost office as much as a lost daughter: the giving of the bride that 263 wishes she had performed, 380 says was done behind her back by the girl's companions.

note: Here a pleasant word beats a gladly given gift. In 225, relieving hunger is a power above the ascetic's.
teaches: A hungry person's view of 92 might differ, which suggests the ranking in 92 assumes someone who isn't in need.

note: Naladiyar 16: the fleeting joy of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling the garland leaves at the slaughter ground, is not found among the wise. Natrinai 46: pleasure and youth pass like an arrow's shadow, so the man should not leave her for wealth.
teaches: The two start from the same premise, the speed with which youth passes, and draw opposite duties from it: the Naladiyar says renounce its pleasure, the Sangam friend says spend it in love and despise wealth instead, which shows that impermanence was an argument both renouncers and lovers used, and settles nothing by itself.

note: In Kuruntokai 367 the friend tells the girl that her shoulders may regain their beauty now that his hill with its cool boulders (துறுகல்) shows after the rain; in Ainkurunuru 210 the friend tells the mother the girl's sickness may abate if she climbs their boulder (துறுகல்) and looks at his hill.
teaches: The sight of his hill, offered privately as comfort to the girl in the Kuruntokai, becomes in the Ainkurunuru a cure the friend asks the mother to allow, so the pair shows a consolation turned into an open request that names its source.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50: the wife calls it folly that he seeks entry with the son as his backing. Kainnilai 39: he comes with the garlanded son, pointing to him, to trouble her.
teaches: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50 names the son as the man's 'witness' (துணைச்சான்றோன்) and Kainnilai 39 shows the boy dressed in a garland and pointed out, so the pair shows the child being staged as evidence of the marriage the husband has broken.

note: Akananuru 347 measures the town's gossip by the drum of Cheralathan made from the kadamba he cut after driving back the sea; Patitruppattu 44 shows the making of such a drum from the Mohur neem.
teaches: The puram decade shows how a Chera trophy drum was made from a felled guardian tree, and the akam poem shows that drum so well known that a heroine can use its roar to measure the gossip about her, so a war trophy had passed into the household's common speech.

note: Akananuru 260 lists the signs of evening on the neythal shore (the sun dimming, herons crying, the crab slipping into its hole, the waves falling quiet) before the heroine asks what will become of her. Thinaimozhi 48 gives a chariot cutting the sand, crabs scattering and the sun hurrying away as the evening comes.
teaches: The long poem shows that the neythal evening was built as a catalogue of shore signs ending in the heroine's dread, which lets the four-line venba keep only three signs and the bare 'evening will come' and still carry that dread unstated.

note: In Natrinai 43 a starving red dog kills a weary wild cow on the road the man is about to take; in Ainkurunuru 354 the red dog, with its mate, lets the doe with her fawn go on the road he has taken home.
teaches: The same predator of the waste kills on the outbound road and holds back on the homeward one, so the paalai poets set the beast's act to the direction of the journey: cruelty when the man leaves, restraint when he comes back to his wife.

note: Kural 1134 says love's fierce flood carries off the raft (புணை) of shame and manliness; Paripadal 6.80-81 says the husband's chest, like a log in the river, became a raft (புணை) for women skilled at seizing.
teaches: In the Kural the raft is the lover's own virtue swept away by his desire, in the Paripadal the man himself is the raft that others ride, so the same river figure moves from an inner confession to a wife's accusation, and the festival's real floats show where the Kural's metaphor came from.

note: Both have the friend fearing the man's night path, where storms strike down snakes on the hill; Akananuru 182 tells him directly to come by day, Natrinai 114 speaks to the heroine within his hearing and adds the thunder-killed tusker and his grieving mate.
teaches: The pair shows the two routes of the same warning: the direct plea in Akananuru 182, and in Natrinai 114 the overheard speech that lets the friend show him, through the she-elephant, what his death would leave behind without telling him what to do.

ullurai.tenor: the lord who has slipped the bond of his house and takes his pleasure where he likes

pairs.situation: he has broken the tie that held him to her
he feeds openly in the light of day on what is not his to graze
his open daytime roaming is why her pain comes even by day (பகலும்)

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses the buffalo and paddy of her own town's fields, things she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the tusker embraces his young cow and calf and feeds them golden mouthfuls of vengai
iraicchi.sense: the man leading her away from her kin will feed and shelter her on the road as the tusker does his mate

ullurai.tenor: the man who has had the girl's love and is now kept from her

pairs.situation: he has enjoyed her love and is now barred by her guarded house
he lingers near, pleading

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses an elephant of the hill millet field in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

ullurai.tenor: the man about to leave and the woman left behind

pairs.situation: he turns away on another road, for wealth

pairs.scene: புன் தலை மடப் பிடி புலம்பிய குரலே
pairs.situation: she will grieve alone when he goes
his coming had once been gentle and near

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses an elephant pair of the poem's own dry hill country (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the lonely dove on the waste calls to its mate
iraicchi.sense: even a dove in the hot waste calls for its mate, while the man who went that way has left his own

iraicchi.act: the elephant and his mate, deceived by the mirage, run to it together and fall together
iraicchi.sense: even beasts fooled by the waste do not part from their mates, yet the man leaves her

note: Naladiyar 385 has the wife wonder how women who embrace many chests for gain can do so daily; Paripadal 20.48-51 has the wife's companion call the courtesan a bought woman whose womanhood is common to all (பெண்மைப் பொதுமைப் பிணையிலி).
teaches: The Naladiyar's contrast of chaste wife and common woman is a private wondering, while in the Paripadal the same contrast becomes public abuse at the river, worked out as a farmer's claim on a straying ox, which shows the wife's chastity defended as a household's ownership of the husband and not only as her own shame.

note: Both close on the same half-line, மாலை என்மனார் மயங்கியோரே; Kuruntokai 234 says that for the lonely even dawn and day are evening, Kalittokai 119 says that evening is really the hour that undoes women's lives.
teaches: The shared closing formula was a set rebuttal that could be turned two ways: the short poem stretches evening over the whole day, the long one narrows it to a killing hour, so 'those who call it evening are deluded' was a commonplace the poets argued with, not one poet's phrase.

note: Both are the same midnight on the guarded shore: in 303 the woman lies awake while the hamlet sleeps and asks whether he knows; in 319 the man, kept away by the watch, lies awake while even the fish sleep.
teaches: Set side by side, 319 answers the question in 303: he is awake too, and the anthology places the same sleepless midnight on both sides of the guard that separates them.

note: Both measure a woman's beauty by Iruppai of the generous Viraan: in Natrinai 350 the wife says she would let that old beauty perish rather than accept the straying man; in Ainkurunuru 58 the friend says he seems possessed by it yet keeps house for others.
teaches: The same rich town names the wife's beauty both as what the straying husband pretends to be captured by and as what the wife herself is ready to lose rather than take him back, so the marutham quarrel is fought over who holds that beauty as a claim.

note: In Akananuru 244 the bard's report of the wife's words makes the man yoke the horses at once, his work being done; in 479 the man, still kept away by the lands between, asks to hear her words again because they are sweet.
teaches: The same report of the wife's words could be a spur that ends the campaign or a comfort savoured while the man stays on, so the bard's message did different work depending on whether the man's task was finished.

note: Verse 20 lists not stealing, not gambling and not befriending the black-hearted among five abstentions; verse 27 says the friend of outsiders picks up toddy, theft and gambling.
teaches: Verse 20 puts bad company beside theft and gambling as one more abstention; verse 27 shows it as their cause, so the book's ban on bad friends is a ban on the way the other vices are learned.

note: Kalittokai 25 likens the woman's eyes, bangles and brow, bright while he is near and failing when he leaves, to the bond of base men who praise to the face and slander behind; Thinaimozhi 33 likens the man himself, who ate her youth and moved on, to the friendship of the base.
teaches: Both poems borrow the moral figure of the false friend for a husband's desertion, but the Kalittokai sets it on the wife's changing body while the venba sets it squarely on the man, so the same ethical simile can either describe the damage or name the culprit.

note: Purananuru 25 praises Chezhiyan because his spear stopped short when he saw the enemy's widows beat their breasts and cut their hair; Kalavazhi 29 shows the enemy's bereaved kin wailing in all four directions and closes on the Chola's field.
teaches: Both poets put the defeated side's mourners in a victory poem, but one makes the king's restraint before them the glory and the other makes their wailing part of the spectacle of the field, so the pair shows two incompatible uses of the same grief in royal praise.

note: On Mudaliar's reading, 132 says learning lasts as long as its owner lives; 398 says learning gained in one birth protects through seven.
teaches: Shanmuganar's reading, that it lasts through fame, is closer to the Kural's.

note: Naladiyar 370 says fresh floodwater and a courtesan's friendship are alike, both ending when their source ends; Paripadal 6.72-75 has the wife say love's shrinking and swelling is the Vaiyai's flood.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the flood's ebb to condemn bought love and spare the household, but the Paripadal puts the same flood image in the wife's mouth against her own husband, so the didactic contrast of faithful wife and fickle courtesan breaks down once the river festival shows the husband's love rising and falling like the stream.

note: Both carry the thurai of the friend disputing the season of his return: in Kuruntokai 66 the konrai are foolish to take the untimely rain for his season; in Natrinai 274 the rain has come and she asks whether the man who invited the girl along the rain-washed hills has those words now.
teaches: The pair shows two ways to deny the season: Kuruntokai 66 blames the trees and so keeps faith in his promise, while Natrinai 274 sets his own old words against the rain and so doubts him, so the same thurai could comfort or accuse.

note: Both refuse the night visit on the hill path: Kuruntokai 141's girl would tell him she has been sent to drive parrots from the millet and that he should not come in the deep midnight when the tiger waits; Ainkurunuru 282's friend tells him not to come in the dark where tuskers roam.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 282 gives only the refusal, while Kuruntokai 141 adds the alternative the refusal implies, the millet field by day, so the pair shows that the night ban in kurinji is a redirection of the tryst to the guarded field, not a denial of it.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the wife tells the greasy-mouthed bard to go to the street of young women and eat there even if he must dance for it (கூத்தாடி உண்ணினும் உண்). Kainnilai 42: if he is in want, let the bard take the man as his dancer, make him dance and eat even so (ஆட்டுவித்து உண்ணினும் உண்).
teaches: The closing formula is the same, but Kainnilai moves the dancing from the bard to the husband, so the pair shows the later poet sharpening the taunt into a picture of the man as a performer worked by others.

note: The Kural defines a land as one free of severe hunger, endless disease and destructive enemies; the idyll describes a town that has never known hunger, whose granaries grow old unopened and whose children sleep fed on milk.
teaches: What the Kural defines by absences the idyll shows by presences (unopened granaries, toy chariots, nurses, white rice and fowl for a guest), and its phrase தொல்பசி அறியா makes freedom from hunger a property of the town's history, not only of its present.

note: Both are the woman's own words: Kural 1257 says she knows nothing called modesty when the beloved does what love wants; Ainkurunuru 112 tells her modest heart they have forgotten, as they wait to see him come.
teaches: The Kural's general claim that shame vanishes before love is shown in the poem as a single moment, the heroine speaking to the heart that owns modesty just as she gives it up to watch him arrive.

note: Both liken the woman's fragrance to the kaanthal flowers of Nalli's hill slopes.
teaches: Nalli's hill and its kaanthal were a fixed image for a woman's scent, so a patron's country lent its fame to the beloved's body in more than one poet's hands.

note: The Kural's woman says he went away with his resolve as companion (உள்ளம் துணையாக) and she lives only by longing for his return; 496's friend says he has come back to be the companion of her shoulders (தோள் துணையாக).
teaches: The word துணை marks the turn of the plot: the reproach that he chose his resolve as companion over her is answered on his return, when the companionship is given back to her as embrace, so the Kural's complaint is a stage the akam story expects to close.

note: Kural 1156 says that a man who can speak of leaving leaves no hope; Ainkurunuru 221 shows the heroine's beauty fading at the quoted word செல்வல், before any journey begins.
teaches: The couplet judges the announcement as a moral sign of hardness, while the poem shows it working on the body at once, so together they make the spoken intention, not the absence, the first wound of parting in Tamil love poetry.

note: In Kural 1170 the woman says her eyes would not swim in a flood of tears if they could go to him as her heart does; in Ainkurunuru 358 the eyes, which have become a flood however often they are wiped, will not let him stay away long.
teaches: The couplet makes the flood of tears a sign of the eyes' helplessness, bound to the house while the heart travels, whereas the Sangam poem turns that same flood into a power that pulls him back, so the tears are complaint in one and pledge of return in the other.

note: Both use the formula விழுத்தொடை மறவர் வில் இட ... எழுத்துடை நடுகல்; in Akananuru 53 it is the stone on the outbound road the woman says he chose over her, in Ainkurunuru 352 a simile for an elephant on the road he did not call hard on his way back.
teaches: The one formula of the lettered hero-stone serves opposite arguments: in Akananuru 53 the woman reads the deadly road as proof he loves wealth more than her, while 352 makes the same road proof of love because he crossed it home without counting its danger.

note: Ainkurunuru 14 praises the chest of the ford-town lord for its softness that gives cool sleep; Naladiyar 389's wife of the field-town lord looks at the same chest smeared with sandal by other women's breasts.
teaches: The marutham husband's chest is the wife's place of rest in the Sangam poem and the evidence of his other women in the Naladiyar, so the later moralist turns the older image of comfort into the record of its betrayal.

note: Kural 1330: sulking is love's pleasure, and its pleasure is to embrace after it. Ainthinai Aimpathu 30: even while sulking, union with the man's fragrant body is sweet, like the south wind in the cold season.
teaches: The Kural places the embrace after the sulk, while the wife finds it sweet during the sulk itself, so the venba collapses the Kural's sequence and shows desire overriding the quarrel instead of crowning it.

note: In Kural 1313 the man complains that even if he wears a garland she accuses him of wearing it for another woman; in Kalittokai 88 the wife points to his faded garland, the pollen of other women's hair and the nail marks on him.
teaches: The Kural presents the wife's suspicion of a garland as groundless jealousy from the man's side, while the Kalittokai wife reads the same evidence correctly, so the couplet's comic complaint rests on an akam scene in which the garland really was a sign.

note: Kural 84: the goddess of fortune dwells gladly in the house of one who tends good guests with a glad face. Natrinai 142 sets the wife who rejoices at a guest even at night in a woodland of unfailing plenty (பொய்யா யாணர்).
teaches: The poem gives the couplet's householder a face and a hour: the glad host is the waiting wife, her welcome extends even to guests who arrive after dark, and the plenty the Kural promises is already the landscape the returning husband drives through.

note: Natrinai 380: refusing the bard, the friend says they smell of ghee, smoke and new birth, holding the son with milk at the breast, and are no match for the man of the bright-jewelled women's street. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the wife says the son is suckled and she is old, and sends the bard to the street of the budding-breasted women.
teaches: The pair shows that the nursing mother's body is a set argument in refusing the go-between: the friend in Natrinai offers it as humble unfitness, the wife in the venba turns it into scorn by sending the bard to dance for his food, so the same motherhood can be pleaded as modesty or thrown as contempt.

note: 82 lines 12 and 13 praise wealth that does not lessen however much singers take and an army that does not lessen however much foes kill (கொளக்கொளக் குறையா, கொலக்கொலக் குறையா); 90 line 16 makes the same quality the ground of a likeness: like the sea, because taking does not diminish him (கொளக்குறை படாமையின் முந்நர்ண அனையை).
teaches: Read together, the two poems show the poet's own method of comparison: a quality he first states as a bare formula about wealth and army becomes, in the last poem of the decade, the stated reason why the king is like the sea, so the ground of the simile is set out before the simile is made.

note: In Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palm-stem horse; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the tusker-like warrior who threatens the mocked madal is truly without shame (நாண் இலன்).
teaches: The Kural gives the man's own confession that madal means the loss of shame and manliness; the Kalittokai gives the woman's side seeing that loss, and shows it is what persuades her that he will not stop.

note: 402 measures the couple's bed by the sweetness of bards plucking strings; 410 says the bard's lute could not match the joy once the son rode on his father's chest.
teaches: Within one decade the bard's music first serves as the measure of the couple's sweetness and then falls short of the family hour, so the poet ranks the joy of the child above the joy of the couple's union.

note: In 280 the man would give up even half a day of life after a single day's union; in 271 the woman says one day's union has become a disease lasting very many days.
teaches: The same single day of union is priced in opposite currencies: the man offers the rest of his life for it, and the woman, who has had it, pays in many days of wasting, so the two speakers measure the secret love by different costs.

note: Purananuru 281 calls a friend to guard a warrior's wound with lute, mustard, incense and the singing of kaanchi; Malaipadukadam hears among the hill's sounds the song hill women sing as a guard (காப்பு) to soothe the tiger-torn wounds on their husbands' chests.
teaches: The rite of guarding a wound with song, which the Purananuru gives to a hero hurt in the king's war, appears in the idyll as an ordinary household sound of the hill after a hunting injury, so the puram poem's rite drew on a common practice of protection rather than one reserved for battle.

note: Kural 1155 asks the friend to prevent the departure of the man fit for her, since union is hard once he goes; Ainkurunuru 228 asks what becomes of their life if he leaves without having pleaded for favour.
