teaches: The poem supplies the mechanism the couplet leaves out: in secret love the man's suit must pass through the friend, so the heroine's plea that the friend stop his leaving is a plea that she accept his pleading.

note: 376's mother curses the fate that joined and sent the girl as without right (அறனில் பால்); 385's girl calls her mother without right (அறனில் யாய்) for keeping her at home.
teaches: In two adjoining decades by one poet each side of the elopement denies aram to the other, the mother blaming the fate that joined the lovers and the daughter blaming the mother's guard, so the dispute over whether the going was right is staged from both ends.

note: The Kural says victory comes not from the spear but from the sceptre that does not bend; the idyll gives Karikalan both, the spear hot to his enemies and the sceptre cool to his people, and uses them as the measures of the forest's heat and the heroine's coolness.
teaches: The Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear as the source of victory, while the idyll keeps the two as equal faces of one king, each true in its own sphere, so the pair shows the rhyme வேல் and கோல் as an older fixed figure of kingship that the Kural argued with and the akam poet borrowed for love.

note: In Akananuru 4 the returning man has tied his chariot's bell-tongues so as not to startle the paired birds sleeping in the flowering boughs; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 50 the waiting girl takes the noise of birds for his horses' bells.
teaches: Held together, the two poems make the chariot bell the sound by which each lover's attention is measured: the man who has come home to his wife silences it out of care for mated birds, while the girl still in secret love hears it in every bird.

note: The Kural tells friends to read a painful act of an old friend as folly or deep intimacy; the heroine of 167 calls the man who promised grace and gave none an old companion, தொல் கேள்.
teaches: The heroine applies the ethics book's rule of old friendship inside love, and the poem shows its cost: the same rule that keeps a long bond alive lets a broken promise go unanswered, so the wronged side carries the whole duty of forbearance.

note: Both heroines face a lover who swore assurances to the friend and stays apart while her beauty fades; Natrinai 358's heroine goes to pray that the oath's god not harm him, Ainkurunuru 227's asks the friend whether she has released him from it.
teaches: An oath sworn before the friend binds the lover through a god's punishment, so the heroine is caught between wanting it held and fearing what holding it would do to him, and the two poems show the two halves of that bind.

note: Akananuru 208, also Paranar's man speaking to his heart after union, tells of Minjili's war at Paazhi and ends on her hair fragrant as the flowers of Ori's Kolli; Natrinai 265 names Minjili guarding Paaram and Ori's Kolli in its run of comparisons for her hair.
teaches: The longer poem tells the war story behind the names that the short one only lists, so Natrinai 265's Minjili is not a decorative name but the victor of a battle Paranar's audience knew, and the girl is measured against fame won in war.

note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart whom it goes to seek when the lover is inside it; Kuruntokai 228: though he left for a far country, he is near to her heart.
teaches: The same indwelling is used two ways: the couplet makes it a reason to scold the restless heart, while the poem makes it a consolation that cancels the distance, so the lover in the heart can either rebuke longing or quiet it.

note: Kuruntokai 382: the friend says the rain is unseasonable (வம்பு); if this were the true season, would he not come? Thinaimalai 103: to the friend who says the rain is unripe and the season not yet come, the woman says she has already wasted her life in tears.
teaches: Kuruntokai gives the friend's consolation in full and lets it stand, and the Thinaimalai venba shows it being received and failing, so the pair shows the stock argument of the false season from both the side that offers it and the side it does not reach.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai names the common, the public hall and the place with the sacred post (மன்றமும் பொதியிலும் கந்துடை நிலையினும்) among the places where the god is worshipped; the idyll shows such a hall with its post (கந்துடைப் பொதியில்), once lit with lamps and worshipped by many, now a lodging for a wild elephant and its cow.
teaches: The pair shows that the hall with the sacred post was a standing institution of town worship in both poems, and that wasting an enemy country meant emptying exactly these places of worship, so the idyll's picture of conquest is measured against the ordinary religious life the Murugan poem describes.

note: Both set a sleepless woman against a night in which everyone else sleeps: Kural 1168 says the night that lulls all creatures has only her for company; in Natrinai 303 the hamlet has fallen silent and only the paired anril cries.
teaches: The couplet's lonely vigil turns out, in the Natrinai scene, to have one other waker, a bird that has its mate, so her sleeplessness is measured against a pairing she lacks, and her question is whether he lies awake too.

note: Aimpathu 7: after the cattle have fed, the herdsman's glad flute at the red evening is like a spear thrown at her. Ezhupathu 22: the herdsmen's konrai flutes and the herd entering the fold are only watched, with no feeling stated.
teaches: Aimpathu 7 states the wound the herdsman's dusk flute gives, and Ezhupathu 22 relies on it unstated, so read together they show that by these short anthologies the homecoming herd and flute were enough on their own to signal the waiting wife's pain.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one but the thief was there, and only a heron watching for aaral fish, so if he lies she has no recourse. Ainthinai Aimpathu 45: will the herons of the grove let his oath go? On a plain reading one heron is no witness and the other herons are.
teaches: The same bird stands at the secret oath in both, but Kuruntokai's heron, intent on its fish, proves that a kalavu vow has no witness, while the venba's herons are made guarantors, so the pair shows the heroine's two answers to the oathless union: despair, or a trust that invents its witnesses.

note: Both compare a courtesan's love to a river that fails with the rain; the Naladiyar's மாரி அறவே அறுமே and வாரி அறவே அறும் lie close to the Valayapathi's lines 3 and 1.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives only the ending, love cut off when income ends, while the fragment makes வாரி mean both flood and income and adds the rise, so the love is shown swelling with the wealth as precisely as it dries.

iraicchi.act: the tusker bends down tall sugarcane to feed his mate's craving in pregnancy
iraicchi.sense: the man who says he will not leave his own will care for her as the tusker cares for his mate

iraicchi.act: the bat flies at evening to the tree where its fruit is
iraicchi.sense: even the bat goes at dusk to where its food and rest are, yet the man stays away from her

iraicchi.act: the heron dwells with its kin in the marutham tree
iraicchi.sense: as the heron lives among its own flock, the man should bring her to live among his kin in his own town

iraicchi.act: the peacock dances in hope though it does not know that the rain will come
iraicchi.sense: the man keeps the girl in his thoughts and loves on, though no sign of her grace has come

iraicchi.act: the male sea crow searches the backwater pool for fish to feed his hen resting heavy with young
iraicchi.sense: a crow provides for the mate it has made pregnant, while the man of the same shore leaves the girl he has taken neither married nor cared for

ullurai.tenor: the man who sought a pleasure and found a wife

pairs.situation: the man who came for a passing love
the pleasure he sought
he gains the girl, a treasure worth taking home

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a hunter of the hill in a kurinji poem, without leaving its land (porul 7.27)

note: Kural 1151: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 148 ends, after the man has gone for his work, with 'I will not grieve, friend; may his journey prosper'.
teaches: On the same departure for work the two voices take incompatible stands, the couplet refusing all comfort as if the going were a death, the poem blessing the journey; the iraicchi of the tiger hunting for its mate shows how the friend's comfort turns the one stance into the other.

note: Both are Kapilar's: in Akananuru 248 a boar holding a narrow pass to guard its young is spared by a hunter who sees in it his own chief holding the path; in Ainkurunuru 265 a boar rears the young of a sow the tiger killed, beside a man who left his wife and son.
teaches: Kapilar's boar guarding its young is a model of protection that even the hunter honours as heroic, which makes the husband of Ainkurunuru 265 fail a standard that both the beast and the hunter keep.

note: Kural 1147: the sickness of love grows long with the town's gossip for manure and the mother's words for water; Kalittokai 105: the girl asks what joy equals this, that her mother beat her with a stick and the town made gossip linking her to the herder (யாய் என்னைக் கண் உடைக் கோலள் அலைத்ததற்கு... அலர் செய்துவிட்டது இவ் ஊர்).
teaches: The same two forces, the town's talk and the mother's harshness, feed a growing pain in the couplet but are welcomed as joy by the herd girl, because once the bond is public her marriage follows from the bull-catch; whether exposure hurts depends on whether an open road to marriage lies ahead.

note: Both are cold-season war-camp poems that end on the same turn, யாமே ... பாசறையேமே: in Akananuru 24 the man pictures his wife swimming alone through the long cold nights (தமியள் நீந்தி); in Natrinai 341 he pictures her well companioned at play and calls himself the one without company (துணை இலேம் தமியேம்).
teaches: With the frame and the closing words the same, the pair shows that the camp poem could place the loneliness on either side, so whether the wife pines or the soldier envies her company was the poet's choice and not something the convention fixed.

note: In Kural 1188 people say only that she has grown pale and never that he has left; in Ainkurunuru 145 the friend says the shore lord has now taken her pallor away.
teaches: The friend names the man as the one who can remove the pallor, which makes him its cause, so the Sangam poem supplies the very attribution that the couplet's woman complains no one makes.

note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife asks why his eyes are so red after he bathed in the first-rain flood as the shoulder-companion of fine women. Naladiyar 387: the wife complains that the man who embraced other women comes to embrace her too without bathing.
teaches: In the Naladiyar the husband's fault is that he comes to his wife unwashed from other women, while in the Ainkurunuru the bath itself is the scene of his straying and its red eyes the evidence, so the pair shows bathing in the field country as both the cleansing a wife expects after his absence and the occasion of the absence.

note: In both the heroine sends the hill lord word that she has been set to guard the millet against parrots: in Kuruntokai 141 through the friend, with a warning not to come at midnight, in Natrinai 102 through a parrot itself.
teaches: The millet-guard message was a fixed kalavu signal meaning she can be met by day, and Natrinai turns the crop's enemy into its carrier, so the bird she is posted to chase becomes the go-between she bribes with the crop.

note: Both set the king's war against the home feast in the man's mouth: the Kural lets the king win and the man feast at evening with his wife; Ainkurunuru says one more day with the victorious king would be an age.
teaches: The Kural states the two duties as a calm pair of wishes, while the Sangam poem shows the strain inside that balance, since the king's victory is honoured in a line and then a single day of further service is weighed as an aeon.

note: In Kural 1265 the woman wishes to see her husband (கொண்கனை) and says the pallor of her shoulders will then leave; in Ainkurunuru 134 she tells the bard her dark-gold beauty has come back with the chariot of the shore lord (கொண்க).
teaches: Valluvar states as a wish that only the sight of the husband will cure the pallor; the Sangam poem shows the cure already happened, the beauty arriving in his chariot, so the couplet's claim that news is not enough rests on the older scene of the bodily return.

note: 373 wishes on the youth's mother the grief of weeping at every thought (நினைத்தொறும் கலிழும் இடும்பை); 398's speaker says that she herself weeps so at every thought (நினைத்தொறும் கலிழும் என்னினும்) but the town is lonelier still.
teaches: Read together, the curse in 373 turns out to be the speaker's own condition, wished on the other mother, and in 398 the same grief is no longer used against anyone but set beside the town's loss while she blesses the road.

note: Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the unbending sceptre; the bard's song praises both, the sceptre that shades the ploughmen and the spear that burns the chariot warriors.
teaches: The bard gives sceptre and spear equal places by assigning them to different people, subjects and enemies, while the Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear even in war, so the ethical book turns the praise poem's balanced pair into a hierarchy.

note: Kuruntokai 382: the friend says the rain that opened the mullai is untimely, for if this were the season he would have come; 118: the heroine says the forest has kept its season and rejects the friend's 'it is not the season'.
teaches: The Kuruntokai gives the friend's argument from his absence to the season's falseness, and 118 gives the heroine's refusal of it from the forest's evidence, so read together they show the untimely-rain consolation as one move in a dispute the heroine could win.

note: Purananuru 59 tells the Pandya he is like the sun to his foes and like the moon to us (ஞாயிறு அனையை ... திங்கள் அனையை); Paripadal 1.41-45 tells the god he is grace to those who love him and terror to foes, the moon and the burning sun, with no marker of likeness.
teaches: The devotional poet took the king-praise formula of grace to friends and fire to foes and dropped its marker of comparison, so what the court poet offers as a simile becomes in the hymn a statement of identity.

note: Ainkurunuru 77: the other woman asks the husband to bathe with her so that gossip rises in the town, and not to go home. Kuruntokai 80: the courtesan says she will go to bathe at the flooded ford, and if the wife is afraid, let her guard her husband's chest with her kin like Ezhini's herds.
teaches: The Kuruntokai courtesan aims her dare at the wife, while the Ainkurunuru rival speaks to the man and names the gossip itself as her goal, so together they show the flood-bath as a public move in the rivalry, staged to be talked about and to pull him from his house, not a pleasure she hides.

note: 20 answers 'who is your king?' with Neduncheralathan, who went against foes on an island of the sea and cut the kadamba at its root (கடம்புமுதல் தடிந்த); 88 has the kadamba's whole trunk felled and the spear hurled into the dark sea as deeds of the ancestors of the present king.
teaches: In the second ten the felling of the kadamba is what identifies one king to a stranger, and in the ninth it has become an inherited title that makes a later king great by descent, so the pair shows a personal feat hardening into a dynastic emblem.

note: The Sankhya speaker counts twenty-five principles with no maker; Tirumular says the Lord makes the twenty-five within the womb.
teaches: Tirumular keeps the Sankhya count and adds a maker who shapes the twenty-five for each embryo, which is the step the Sankhya account leaves out.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my wife and feast the evening; Kuruntokai 270: his work done, the man lies on her hair and bids the rain pour.
teaches: The couplet's wish is the poem's fulfilled state: the evening feast he pictured while the king's work held him is given its weather and its pillow, and the rain he dreaded on campaign becomes a blessing once he is home.

note: Patitruppattu 23 shows the king feeding the street-singing bards (வயிரிய மாக்கள் ... மறுகுசிறை பாடும்) even in a drought; 29 uses the same line-words for bards tuning lutes and singing at street corners in the enemy's settlements before the army spread.
teaches: The singing bard is the decade's sign of a living land, so 29 measures the enemy's loss by the very figure 23 uses for the king's bounty: the war silences in other lands the music the king pays for at home.

note: Ainkurunuru 403: watching the boy, who bears his grandfather's name, pull his little chariot with tottering steps, the man's heart grows great toward the son as well as the wife. Thinaimalai 139: the wife names the field town only as the town of the father of the boy whose chariot does not run (ஊராத்தேரான் தந்தை). On the reading that 139 speaks during the man's absence, the two claim opposite effects for the same sight.
teaches: In the mullai poem the son's toy chariot binds the father to the house, while the marutham wife uses the same child to name a man who is not there, so the pair shows the son as the household's strongest tie and, when that tie fails, the wife's way of addressing the father without speaking to him.

note: Kural 1222 pities the sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) evening and asks whether its partner is as hard-eyed (வன்கண்ணது) as hers; Natrinai 89 calls the evening sad (புன்கண் மாலை) but makes it the ally of the hard-hearted (வன்கணாளர்) who do not come. On this reading the evening is a fellow victim in one and an accomplice in the other.
teaches: The same two words, புன்கண் and வன்கண், are distributed differently: the Kural gives the evening its own hard partner and so makes it a sister in grief, while the Natrinai joins the evening to her own hard man, so the woman's view of the hour turns on whether she sees it as abandoned or as sent.

note: Kural 1226: the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband had not yet left; in 386 the woman knew evening only as the festival hour of jewelled women and did not know its sorrow wide as the earth.
teaches: The poem fills in what the couplet's woman did know of evening before: the public festival hour of the women's gathering, so the Kural's 'I did not know' is the reversal of a known, shared evening into a private sorrow.

note: Ainkurunuru 95: the black-horned buffalo snaps its rope and grazes the long-eared paddy all morning; its lord gives her pain even by day. Thinaimalai 148: the dark-horned buffalo grazes the great field pond, then lows remembering its calf and comes home wearing paddy straw.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru's straying buffalo is left grazing, as the husband is left away, while the Thinaimalai brings the same animal home and gives the calf as the reason, so the pairing shows the marutham buffalo could carry the wife's hope as well as her complaint: the child that draws the stray back.

note: In both a wife refuses the husband who has been with other women: Kural 1311 says 'I will not come near your chest, philanderer' (நண்ணேன் பரத்தநின் மார்பு); in Paripadal 9.30-40 the wife blesses him ironically and cries 'don't come near' (குறுகல்), while the rival gives him her chest (மார்பு அளிப்பாளை).
teaches: The Kural's refusal is private and the rival only imagined, while the Paripadal stages the same refusal with the rival present and offering the very chest the wife denies, so the pair shows the one gesture of refusing the chest working as a quarrel between two women, not only between wife and husband.

note: Kural 1260 asks whether those whose hearts melt like fat in fire can say 'we will join and then sulk'; Kalittokai 90 ends with the wife asking whether women whose hearts cannot hold restraint (நிறை ஆற்றா நெஞ்சு) can say they will not bear his wrongs.
teaches: The Kalittokai gives the couplet's rhetorical question a full case: a detailed charge of a night visit, his dream defence and his plea, so that the wife's collapse comes after she has proved him guilty, showing that the melting heart of the Kural overrides evidence and not only pride.

note: The Kural says a ruler easy to see and not harsh of speech has his land praised above others; the idyll praises a gate never shut to bards, poets and brahmins, a glad face and freedom from fierce anger, each praised by a named class of people.
teaches: The Kural's abstract reward of praise has a concrete source in the idyll, where the people at the open gate (wise men, warriors, women and suppliants) are the ones who do the praising, so accessibility is rewarded by the very classes it admits.

note: Kural 1229: when evening spreads, the whole town is bewildered and suffers (on the reading that the town shares her pain). Kuruntokai 28: the town sleeps, not knowing her grief.
teaches: On that reading the Kural imagines the town grieving with the lovesick woman, while Kuruntokai 28 has the town sleep through her grief, so whether the community shares a private sorrow is answered both ways in the love poetry.

note: Kural 1145 says love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is craved each time one is drunk; Paripadal 10.63-68 likens lovers who hide their love from gossip to drinkers who hide their drunkenness.
teaches: Both join love and toddy, but the Kural's lover welcomes exposure while the Paripadal's festival lovers hide from it, so the same comparison serves to praise and to fear gossip, and the couplet's bravado reads as one stance among those the poets knew.

note: In Kuruntokai 111 the friend wishes the hill man would come and expose the household that believes the diviner's word about Murugan; in Akananuru 22 the girl, embraced by her lover on the very night of the rite, laughs (நக்கனென்) at the offering wasted on a stranger priest.
teaches: The laugh the friend in Kuruntokai 111 hopes for is the laugh the girl of Akananuru 22 actually has, so together they show the veriyattu rite was framed in akam as a comic error waiting for the lover's arrival to undo it.

note: Two hymns by different poets to different gods, Nallezhuthiyar's to Maal and Kesavanar's to Sevvel, close the same way: the god thought of as mother, worship repeated, and இன்னும் இன்னும் asking for more of it.
teaches: Since the same close serves two poets and both Maal and Murugan, the mother-address and the prayer for more worship belong to a shared Paripadal liturgy, not to one poet's devotion or one god's cult.

note: Kural 888: a house with inner enmity wears itself away like gold rubbed by a file; 45: two Cholas wearing the same aar garland fight, so whichever loses, their own house loses.
teaches: The Kural's file image says the house wears itself down, and 45 supplies the political arithmetic behind it, that between two branches of one house no outcome is a win and the only gain goes to rival dynasties, so the couplet's metaphor gets a concrete case and an outside beneficiary.

note: In Akananuru 91 the friend points to the elephant that shrinks together with its hungry mate on the scorched road as proof that the man still loves; in Kuruntokai 307 the heroine points to a tusker that fells a tree to feed its weary mate as proof that he has forgotten.
teaches: The same iraicchi of the tusker's care on the wasteland serves the friend as comfort and the heroine as reproach, so the device's sense is fixed by who is speaking and what she wants, not by the beast.

note: Acharakkovai 10 makes bathing the removal of impurity on ten occasions; Sivavakkiyar addresses those who bathe daily and whose dirt never goes, asking where the dirt really lies.
teaches: The Siddhar denies the premise the bathing list rests on, that the impurity is where water can reach, whereas the Kural only ranks it below inner purity.

note: Purananuru 3 tells the Pandya that even if the earth shifts his word must not; Kuruntokai 373's friend says that even if the earth shifts and fire and water change places, the lovers' bond suffers no harm from gossip.
teaches: The akam friend borrows the puram formula for a king's unbreakable word and gives it to a secret love, so the pair shows that the lovers' bond was claimed in the language of royal oath, and that a pledge, not a feeling, is what kalavu asks to be trusted.

note: Kural 1225's woman asks what good she has done the morning and what wrong the evening, so morning is the friendly hour; Ainkurunuru 183 ends that even if morning comes there is no one to clear her pain.
teaches: The Kural's separated woman still has a kind hour in the morning, while the Ainkurunuru heroine denies even that, so the pair shows two degrees of the same grief: one that rises and falls with the day, and one that the day's turn no longer touches.

note: In 61 Kapilar comes to the Chera after Pari's death, saying he will not beg or understate but has come for the king's fame for giving; 85 says this later Chera's gifts are more than the villages Kapilan won (கபிலன் பெற்ற ஊரினும் பலவே).
teaches: The seventh ten shows Kapilar arriving at the Chera court without a patron, and the ninth uses the reward he got there as the standard a later king's giving is said to exceed, so one poet's payment became the dynasty's own yardstick for generosity.

note: Akananuru 17's foster mother asks whether her girl's small anklet-filled feet (சிலம்புஆர் சீறுடி) can walk the waterless waste; Ainkurunuru 389's searcher asks whether her anklet feet (அம்சிலம் படியே) kept pace with the youth who walked slowly.
teaches: The anklet foot is the searching woman's measure in both, but Akananuru weighs it against the road's hardship while Ainkurunuru, told the youth went slowly, weighs it against him, so the same worry could move from the danger of the way to the fitness of the match.

note: Both praise the charioteer's wit with the same epithet (Ainkurunuru: மதியுடை வலவ; Kuruntokai: மதியுடை வல்லோய்): Ainkurunuru before the drive, Kuruntokai after it, for cutting a new road and bringing the chariot home today.
teaches: Ainkurunuru asks for the charioteer's skill and Kuruntokai thanks him for having used it, so the two show the charioteer as more than a driver: the returning man credits him with the judgement that ends the wife's suffering.

note: The neythal of Thondi stands for the girl's eyes in both: in 195 the flower cut by reapers tossing in water, in Akananuru 290 the flower whose sapphire beauty has turned to gold.
teaches: The pair shows that Thondi's neythal was a set measure for the beloved's eyes, and that two poets spoiled it in two ways: by tears, the cut flower tossing in water, and by pallor, the blue turned to gold.

note: 333 says wealth is by nature unstaying; 753 calls it the unfailing lamp that drives out darkness wherever one intends.
teaches: The chapter on impermanence and the chapter on acquiring wealth describe the same thing in opposite terms.

note: Kural 1150: the friend says the town raises the very gossip they want, and the lover will grant marriage if asked; Kalittokai 104: the friend tells the girl that her kin have gladly agreed to give her to the herder who leapt on the black bull, trampling on the heads of the town that raised the gossip (அலர் எடுத்த ஊராரை உச்சி மிதித்து).
teaches: The couplet hopes that the town's talk will move the lover to marry; the herders' poem shows a second way gossip ends, through the kin's public consent once the bull is taken, so in the mullai village it is the girl's family the gossip moves, and the wedding then silences the town.

note: Kural 1182 has pallor ride the woman's body proud that 'he gave it'; Kainnilai 1 has her body waste pale as if saying 'the forest lord joined with her'.
teaches: Set in the guarded millet field of the secret love, the Kural's private conceit of pallor naming its giver becomes a public danger, since a body that names the lover undoes the secrecy that kalavu depends on.

note: Paripadal 21.30-38 makes the peacock, thumbi, bees and waterfall into dancer, flute, lute and drum on the god's hill; Paripadal 22.36-44 has real drum, lute, flute and hand drum sounding with bees and thumbi at the Vaiyai ford, the wind as dancer (வளி நடன்), and says they exchange their work (தொழில் மாறு கொள்ளும்).
teaches: On the hill the orchestra is made of creatures only, while at the river the town's instruments and the grove's creatures play together and trade parts, so the two songs, set side by side in one chapter, show the hill as nature performing for its god and the ford as the town and nature performing with each other.

note: Akananuru 199 measures the wealth a man refuses to leave his wife for by the land Narmudi Cheral regained when Nannan fell in the battle at the great ford of the vakai; Patitruppattu 40 praises the same Narmudi Cheral for cutting down Nannan's vakai at the root.
teaches: The love poem adds that the country won from Nannan was one the Chera had lost before (இழந்த நாடு), which the praise poem does not say, and it shows the king's greatest gain already serving akam poets as the very largest wealth a lover could turn down.

note: Kar Narpathu 8: the woodland where the kaayaa opens buds as if dipped in the collyrium of an eye announces the return of the man who went for fame. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 21: with the collyrium-dark kaayaa in bloom, the lover has come.
teaches: The same collyrium-blue kaayaa that in the Kar Narpathu is still only a herald of the man becomes, in the Thinaimozhi verse, the flower already open when he arrives, so the mullai venbas use one stock blossom to mark both the promise and its keeping.

iraicchi.act: the wildcat goes out on the dangerous ground to watch for prey to feed its young
iraicchi.sense: the man too has gone out on the robbers' road to win what his household needs, so his going is provision as well as desertion

ullurai.tenor: the secret love taken from the kin's keeping while they are off guard

pairs.situation: the lovers' meetings, taken while the household sleeps
the hero takes by stealth what the kin keep

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the beasts of the hero's own hill in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: does the heron of the grove not know his cruelty, though it saw him turn graceless? Kainnilai 50: the stork of the grove, which saw his harsh oath, is the one she bids listen.
teaches: The two shore venbas value the same bird witness in opposite ways, reproached for seeing and not knowing once the oath is broken, confided in because it saw while she still hopes the oath can be held, so the witness's worth follows the stage of her trust.

note: Pazhamozhi 14 says fine points of learning spoken before the unlearned turn bad; Nanmanikkadigai says a learned man before the unlearned has no standing.
teaches: Pazhamozhi says the words go bad, Nanmanikkadigai that the man loses standing, so the group counts the damage to both the teaching and the teacher.

note: The idyll gives the victory at Alankanam as its patron's crowning deed (camping fearsomely, killing kings, taking their drums); in Akananuru 209 the friend says the gossip about the heroine is louder than the roar at Alankanam when Chezhiyan beat the seven.
teaches: Held together, the two show the battle the court poet offers as the king's defining glory already serving an akam poet as a proverbial measure of noise for village gossip, so a royal victory entered the common stock of comparison and was expected to be known to every hearer.

note: 339 says death is like sleep and birth is like waking from it, as an image of impermanence. 1216 wishes waking away altogether, for the sake of staying with her lover.
teaches: If the two were read together, her wish would come close to a wish not to be reborn, though nothing in the verse says this.

note: Both warn that the girl may lose the guard of the millet: in Akananuru 28 the friend, with the man nearby, warns that if she does not rise and scare the parrots her mother will send others; in Ainkurunuru 289 the friend says the elders may stop her guarding because her own voice draws the parrots.
teaches: The threat to the field meetings comes in Akananuru 28 from the girl's neglect, which she could mend, and in Ainkurunuru 289 from her very voice, which she cannot, so the second friend can leave the man only one remedy, to marry her.

note: Both reward the crow whose cawing brings a guest (விருந்துவரக் கரைந்த காக்கை; வரக்கரைந் தீமே): Kuruntokai's friend after the man has come, Ainkurunuru's speaker before the girl has.
teaches: Kuruntokai pays the crow afterwards and calls even seven bowls too little, while Ainkurunuru promises meat in a gold bowl in advance, so together they show the crow offering working as a bargain struck with the omen on either side of the homecoming.

note: Kural 1257: the woman says she knows nothing of shame when her beloved does what she longs for. Kalittokai 37: the girl says that, since he could not speak and she might not, she resolved (துணிதந்து) to do one shameless deed (நாண் இன்மை செய்தேன்), staging a fall into his arms.
teaches: The Kural makes the loss of shame something that happens to a woman when the lover acts, while Kapilar's girl chooses the shameless act herself because the man will not, and then praises him for the restraint that sends her home; held together they show that akam allows the heroine to set aside naanam as a tactic when the rules of speech leave both lovers mute.

note: Both tie the slipping bangles to the absence of the lord of the shore (துறைவன்): in the Kural they announce his leaving to the town; in Kuruntokai 117 the friend says let him stay away, smaller bangles can be bought from the sellers.
teaches: The same sign of wasting is grief in the woman's mouth and a weapon in the friend's: Kuruntokai 117 shows the slipping bangle could be turned into mockery meant to shame the man, which the Kural's lament never does.

note: Kural 110: there is escape for every other killing of good, none for one who kills a benefit; in Kuruntokai 225 the friend promises the girl's hair to the man only if he does not forget kindness as an enthroned king does.
teaches: The Kural's absolute rule becomes a condition of marriage in the poem: the friend uses ingratitude, the one unpardonable fault, to define in advance what deserting the girl would be.

note: Akananuru 195's mother says the youth's mother will joyfully paint her walls for the couple's coming; Ainkurunuru 373's mother wishes that same woman grief.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the bereaved mother's view of the other house in its two moods, envy of the joy it awaits and a curse that it should share her grief, so the youth's mother is a fixed counter-figure of this lament.

note: Naladiyar 203: the great never say they will not support those who have come to depend on them (தற்சேர்ந் தவரை), as a branch bears its own fruit. Ainthinai Aimpathu 48: can those who do not hold to the distress of those who have come to depend on them (தற்சேர்ந்தார்) carry great renown?
teaches: The shared word தற்சேர்ந்தார் shows the friend borrowing the maxim of supporting one's dependents and turning it on the lover: the girl in secret love is made a dependent with a kinsman's claim, and his renown is staked on marrying her.

note: The line 'she stood crying till her kohl eyes went red' closes both; in 69 the river flood sweeps away the rival's sand-play at the bathing ford, in 125, a neythal poem, the clear wave snatches her doll.
teaches: The mockery of the rival as a crying child was a stock retort carried across landscapes by changing only the water and the toy, river flood and sand-play for marutham, sea wave and doll for neythal.

note: Kuruntokai 58: the man tells his rebuking friends it would be well if they could hold back his sickness, but it has spread like butter melting on a hot rock. Natrinai 160: he tells his rebuker that he knew good sense, shame and conduct better than him, before he saw her eyes.
teaches: These are two answers to the same rebuke: one grants that the friends' aim is good and says no one can carry it out, the other says the friend's lesson is one he already knew best, so together they show the rebuke fails not for lack of knowledge but because sight of her has overridden it.

note: Kuruntokai 53 says the oath the man swore at the sandy ford with the hill goddesses as witness is what afflicts us, the women (எம்மணங் கினவே); Paripadal 8.66 says the god's spear will devour the man himself if he swears falsely.
teaches: On the plain reading of each, the two poems disagree on whom a broken god-witnessed oath strikes, the deceived women in the Kuruntokai and the perjurer in the Paripadal, so the pair shows two Sangam answers to where the god's punishment falls.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by the right way; Patitruppattu 89 lists the rain in its season, the paired deer, the humming boughs, unfailing fruit and tubers, grazing herds and endless grain, then gives the cause: because your sceptre is straight (நின்கோல் செம்மையின்).
teaches: The couplet states the link between a just sceptre and rain as a rule, while the poem spreads its consequences over a whole countryside of herds, forest creatures and grain, which shows how wide a land's well-being the belief was taken to cover.

note: Akananuru 14: in the evening when good cows with swollen udders ooze sweet milk (தீம்பால் பிலிற்ற) and call to their calves, the wife asks the bard how she will be at dawn if he does not remember them; the bard then sees the chariot coming. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 30: with the herds oozing sweet milk (தீம்பால் பிலிற்ற), the friend asks 'will our man come?'
teaches: The same phrase of cows streaming milk carries the question of his return in both poems, and the long Akananuru supplies the answer the venba leaves open, the chariot on the road, so the milk-heavy herd going home is a fixed cue that the man too must be on his way.

note: Both have onlookers ask of the couple on the road யார்கொல் அளியர் தாமே; Kuruntokai leaves the question open over the rattling waste, Ainkurunuru answers it with the magandril pair.
teaches: The same onlookers' formula could end in fear for the pair (Kuruntokai's dangerous bamboo waste) or in a verdict that they are to be pitied only because they cannot be parted, so அளியர் held both pity and admiration.

note: Kural 906 says men who fear their wife's shoulders are worthless even if they live like gods; in Kuruntokai 8 the other woman mocks the man for doing his son's mother's bidding like a mirror image, and on the akam reading this obedience is the household holding him, which the poem does not condemn.
teaches: Read together they show that the conduct the Kural brands as a man's vice appears in akam only as the other woman's spiteful jibe, so the ethical charge of wife-obedience and the love poem's victory of the wife are the same act seen from opposite sides.

note: On the road, stones stand at the forks bearing the names of undying fame (செல்லா நல்லிசைப் பெயரொடு) of warriors who gave their lives; at court the patron reflects that rich men who did not give died taking their names with them.
teaches: The idyll makes one argument across the road and the court: a name survives on the stone of the man who gave his life or in the fame of the man who gives his wealth, and is lost with the man who gives nothing.

note: Akananuru 242: with the man listening, the friend tells the girl the mother has called the velan, and the man should come and hold her before the goat is killed. Natrinai 47: with the man listening, the friend asks whether she may tell him that the mother's Murugu rite cannot help the girl's pallor.
teaches: In the same overheard situation the Akananuru friend names the cure outright while the Natrinai friend only asks whether she may speak and lets a bereaved elephant show the loss to come, so the pair shows how much directness the overheard speech allowed: the remedy stated, or the danger shown and the remedy left for him to supply.

note: Kural 1090 says liquor delights only one who drinks it while love delights at a look; in Kuruntokai 165 the man, having only seen her hair and grace, says the sight came on his desire like toddy on top of joy.
teaches: The poem accepts the Kural's claim that love works by sight alone but denies the contrast with liquor: for the man who has looked, seeing acts exactly like a second drink, so the couplet's rule holds while its comparison is turned around.

note: Both have the man name the girl's power with the word அணங்கு: in Kural 1081 he cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; in Ainkurunuru 173 her fragrant hair is the அணங்கு and those it seizes lose their sleep.
teaches: The Kural leaves the smitten man's question open, and the Sangam poem answers it not by settling what she is but by the symptom, sleepless nights and a cutting pain, so that in the tradition the afflicting goddess is known by what she does to the one who sees her.

note: Puram 117 says that even when Saturn smokes, comets appear and Venus runs south, the rain never failed in the dry land of the just king; the idyll describes a sun that makes kings tremble, falls that dwindle and clouds that forget the sea, and sets the Kaveri against them.
teaches: Both poems meet the same fear, that signs in the sky foretell drought and blame the king, but Puram 117 denies that the rain fails in a good king's land while the idyll admits the failure and lets the river make it harmless, two different ways of protecting a ruler's name from a bad season.

note: Both use the marutham buffalo as ullurai for the straying husband: in Akananuru 46 it breaks its tether at night, scatters the fish and grazes the lotus; in Natrinai 260 it has grazed the red lilies, tired of the lotus, and sleeps on the sand away from the field.
teaches: Read together, the one creature carries different stages of the husband's straying, the breaking out in Akananuru 46 and the surfeit and sleeping elsewhere in Natrinai 260, so the buffalo ullurai was a fixed vehicle whose actions the poets chose to fit the moment of the quarrel.

note: Kar Narpathu 37: will our man, who took up the king's hard work, not come even in the season of great rains? Akananuru 304: in the king's war camp as the first rains fall, the man fears she will think him unkind, not knowing his pain.
teaches: The friend's confidence rests on the season alone, and the Akananuru shows that season from inside the king's camp, where the man is still held and can only dread her reproach, so the king's work she counts to his credit is the very thing keeping him away.

note: Natrinai 279: the mother asks whether the feet of her jewelled girl, her anklets removed, are weary on the sun-glittering track. Thinaimozhi 20: the mother asks a man on the road whether her daughter can bear to walk the harsh waste with a youth whose bow is like Death.
teaches: Natrinai's mother fears only the road and the girl's tender feet, but the venba's mother fears the companion too, calling him Death-like, which shows the mother's grief can doubt the very youth the girl trusted for protection.

note: Paripadal 7.65-76 has a woman, angry that her lover looked at the bathers, punish him in the river; Paripadal 12.55-74 has the same offence of looking at another woman at the flood and the same sulk, carried through the blow and his fall to her return to his breast, which the poet credits to the Vaiyai's flood (வல்லதால், வையைப் புனல்).
teaches: Song 7 leaves the river quarrel at the lover's punishment, while song 12 carries the same quarrel to its making-up and gives the river the credit, so the two Vaiyai songs show that the oodal episode was told in the hymns in order to praise the flood as the reconciler, the go-between that akam poems give to a friend or a bard.

note: Kural 218 says the discerning do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even without means; the Innaa line counts a man without wealth desiring to be liberal as painful. Not a tension on our reading: the Innaa line names a cost, not a fault.
teaches: The pair shows the pain hidden inside the Kural's praise: giving steadily in want is admirable, and the wish to give without means is also an ache.

note: Purananuru 35 counsels the Chola that rain comes when sought in a land of the just sceptre and warns that if rain fails or yield shrinks the world blames its guardians (காவலர்ப் பழிக்கும்); Patitruppattu 89 tells the Chera that rain pours in season because his sceptre is straight and the land worships him daily.
teaches: The same belief works as praise in one poem and as warning in the other: credit for the rain in the Chera poem implies the blame for drought that the Chola poem spells out, so a king praised for good seasons was held answerable for bad ones.

note: Akananuru 387: on the road, a lizard's small click by the hero-stones makes even lords with elephants halt and turn back. Kainnilai 18: at home, the truthful lizard chirps as if it has seen the traveller's return.
teaches: Held together they show that the lizard's voice was trusted at both ends of the journey with opposite force, as a warning that turns travellers back on the road and as a promise of return to those at home, so the omen's sense depended on which way the hearer faced.

note: Akananuru 99: the man leading the eloping girl bids her admire a forest strewn with murukku buds like the gripping claws of the striped tiger (கோள்உகிர் அன்ன). Aimpathu 31 uses the same simile, murukku buds like a tiger's blood-dyed claws, for the spring that breaks the waiting woman's heart.
teaches: Aimpathu 31 says outright that this season gives joy only to those who are together (எதிருநர்க்கு இன்பம்), and Akananuru 99 is that joy spoken by a man walking beside his girl, so the pair shows one flowering read as delight or as wound according to whether the lovers are together.

note: Kural 1171's woman asks why her eyes weep when it was they who showed him to her; Ainkurunuru 190's woman says the lord of the shore surely is the one who made her eyes weep.
teaches: For the same tears the Kural's woman blames her own eyes for having looked, while the Ainkurunuru woman blames the man with an emphatic மன்ற, so the pair shows the two directions in which the abandoned lover can turn the fault, inward on her own seeing or outward on him.

note: The Kural says household life and its guarding of goods exist to care for guests; the man's oath promises a house of open doors where he and the girl will eat what is left after feeding guests.
teaches: The Kural's rule that the household exists for guests is already in the idyll the language in which a hill man pledges marriage: what he swears to give the girl is not a feeling but a guest-feeding house, so the ethic of virundhu was the content of the promise before it was a maxim.

note: Both are told by the friend to the mother in disclosure: in Akananuru 48 a garlanded hunter with a bow asks the girls which way the beast went; in the idyll the hunter says he has lost a beast that came this way and, when they keep silent, asks whether even speaking with him is a blame.
teaches: Read together, the hunter's question about a lost beast stands out as the conventional opening of the hill meeting reported in அறத்தொடு நிற்றல், and the idyll supplies what the short poem leaves to the mother's wit: the girls' silence out of fear of blame and the man's answer to that fear.

note: In Akananuru 66 the sight of his small son stops a husband on his way to a second wedding; in Natrinai 166 the husband himself names his son's first games as one reason he will not leave.
teaches: Read together, the son is the akam poets' anchor of the husband to the house, named by the man himself in 166 and working against his intent in 66, so in both the wife's fear is answered by the child rather than by her own claim on him.

note: Paranar in Purananuru 348 compares a girl to rich Unur of truthful Thazhumban and pictures suitors' chariots in every shade and elephants tied at every place for her; Paranar in Natrinai 300, with strangers' marriage offers in the colophon, has a chariot set at the gate as her bride-price and likens the lover to Unur's begging elephant at the kitchen.
teaches: Holding the two Paranar poems together shows him using Thazhumban's Unur for the same occasion, a girl besieged by suitors with chariots and elephants: in puram the siege threatens the town, in akam the friend turns it into a goad to make the hidden lover ask for her before others do.

note: Akananuru 265: the woman asks whether the wealth her man went for is as great as the Nandas' treasure hidden at Pataliputra; Kuruntokai 75: the woman wishes the bearer of news of her lover's return to win Pataliputra rich in gold.
teaches: Pataliputra's gold was the akam measure of the greatest wealth, and the two women price it against love from opposite sides: one doubts it outweighs her, the other would give it for word of his coming.

note: In Kuruntokai 69 a widowed female monkey leaps from the ridge to her death and the friend begs the lover not to come at midnight; in Ainkurunuru 274 the male monkey carries his mate up the slope from the roaring tiger while the girl's lover has gone away.
teaches: Read together, the monkey couple names both fears of secret love: in Kuruntokai the girl would not survive losing him to the night path, in Ainkurunuru she is left by a man less faithful than the beast that shields its mate, so the danger lies as much in his leaving as in his coming.

note: Kural 584 says a spy examines everyone, the king's servants and kin first; Thirikadugam names a secret-leaking friend, a woman without regard for honour and a rancorous servant as those called spies.
teaches: The couplet turns the king's surveillance inward on his own circle; the verse shows why from the other side, since those closest, friend, woman and servant, are the ones who leak.

note: Both set peacocks in their finery and the konrai-lovely forest of the rains before a waiting woman; Kar Narpathu's friend names the season the cure (மருந்து) for her pallor.
teaches: Kar Narpathu spells out that the season's beauty is a promise of return and so a cure, while Ainkurunuru only calls his road good for having it, so the decade's bare praise of the road is the same reassurance left unspoken.

note: Kural 1119: the man tells the moon that if it would resemble her face it must not appear for many to see. Kuruntokai 47: the friend tells the long white moon it does no good to those who come at night for secret love.
teaches: Both speakers wish the moon would not shine for others, for opposite reasons: the Kural's lover wants her face kept to himself, the Kuruntokai friend wants the meeting kept from watchers, so the moon's openness, which the couplet turns into a compliment, is in the older poem the danger that ends secret love.

note: Kural 322 ranks sharing food (பகுத்துண்டு) first among all that the authors gathered (தொகுத்தவற்றுள்); Patitruppattu 38 praises the king for the manliness that gathered the sharing of food (பகுத்(து)ஊண் தொகுத்த ஆண்மை) and for living for others.
teaches: The same pair of words, sharing and gathering, ranks a virtue in the Kural's list of teachings and names a king's acquired valour in the Chera poem, so a virtue the Kural places among the vows against killing appears here as a warrior's manhood.

note: Purananuru 20 tells a Chera that those in his shade know no burning but the cooking fire and the sun, no bow but the rainbow and no weapon but the plough; Patitruppattu 28 says the Chera's land knows no heat but the uproar of the great river's flood, even in drought.
teaches: Both Chera poems praise the guarded land by negating violence with a harmless counterpart, and the Patitruppattu adds that the protection holds in drought because the river floods when the hills are dry, so the figure served as a court convention that each poet bent to a new claim.

note: Both describe Kuttuvan's western land by a buffalo that leaves the lotus pond to rest in jackfruit shade; Akananuru 91 says the hero will not stay for it even if he gains it, and the idyll calls even Kuttuvan's Vanji empty.
teaches: The buffalo resting in the jackfruit shade was a set emblem of the Chera land's ease, and both genres used it as the standard of plenty that is outweighed: by the heroine's beauty in the love poem and by a minor chief's giving in the guide poem.

ullurai.tenor: the young man who wants the girl and comes into the village despite its talk

pairs.situation: the young man who desires the girl
the villagers' noise and talk around him
he still comes openly into the village to see her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the hill elephant and hill folk of this kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant plays in accord with his mate when the cool rains come
iraicchi.sense: even the elephant keeps company with its mate in this season, so the man who stays away has broken his word and the grievance is just

note: The queen's dream of the falling umbrella and sceptre is fulfilled in the king's lowered umbrella and slack sceptre at the verdict.
teaches: The omen comes first in the queen's private dream and is fulfilled the same hour in public, so the fall of justice is shown as already decided before Kannaki speaks.

note: Patitruppattu 16 asks whether the queen's bed will escape its loneliness while the king lingers in camp; Patitruppattu 68 shows women in the palace marking the days on the wall while the warriors fast before the fort.
teaches: Two poets of two decades both end a war poem at the women left behind, which shows the waiting house was a set part of Chera praise, and Kapilar extends it from the queen alone to the whole palace and sets the warriors' own longings beside it.

note: Purananuru 278: the old mother, told her son fled, searches the field and rejoices more than at his birth to find him cut to pieces; Kalittokai 106: the herd girls sing that they will bind the bull-gored wounds against their breasts and that the tamer's blood on their curd-spotted shoulders is an ornament.
teaches: Akam takes over the puram pride in wounds taken facing the foe and moves it from the mother to the beloved: the wound that proves in Purananuru 278 that a son died well proves in Kalittokai 106 that a man is fit to be embraced, so the herd girls' desire is built on the warrior ethic.

note: In Natrinai 246 the friend reassures the woman with a lizard chirping on the lucky side, a koel on the house's nochchi and the season's flowers; in Kar Narpathu 12 she calls his coming certain because the dark clouds rise every day on the right.
teaches: The pair shows that the friend's reassurance in the rains rested on reading omens, the right side being lucky in both, and that the rainy season itself was read as one more omen of return, which is why Natrinai 246 can end its certainty as a question.

note: Kuruntokai 1 says the hill of the Red One, who killed the demons till the field ran red, is thick with kanthal clusters the colour of blood (குருதிப் பூவின் குலைக்காந் தட்டே); Paripadal 18.35-36 says the close-packed kanthal of the god's hill are like the hands of men defeated in war and bound.
teaches: Both poets make the kanthal of Murugan's hill a sign of his war, but the Kuruntokai reads it by colour, the blood of the slain, and the Paripadal by shape, the clasped hands of the captured, so the pair shows the flower fixed as the god's war emblem while each poet chose a different basis for it.

note: Kural 1131: for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and no strength but the palmyra horse. Kuruntokai 32: to ride the madal in the street is shame, and to live apart is shame too.
teaches: The same lover's threat is a safeguard in the Kural and a disgrace in the Kuruntokai, which only weighs it as the lesser of two shames, so the madal was argued both as the lover's last strength and as an equal dishonour to living on without her.

note: Both are elopement poems that see the flowering trees of the wasteland as the lamps of a town festival: kongam like Karthigai lamps in Natrinai 202, silk-cotton like a festive town's oil lamps in Akananuru 17.
teaches: The eloping man offers the festival-lit forest to the girl as something homely and beautiful, while the foster mother left behind sees the same lights on a waterless road her girl's little feet must cross, so one image of the paalai road comforts or terrifies according to who speaks.

note: The Kural says that if the sky fails, hunger torments the whole wide world; the idyll says that though the sky fails, the Kaveri does not, and the Chola fields never stop yielding. On the literal reading the claims conflict: the Kural admits no land exempt from failed rain, the idyll names one.
teaches: Read together they show that the Kural's universal law of rain met a regional boast in the poets' own geography, a river delta praised precisely as the place the warning does not reach, although the idyll's own line 6 (மலைத்தலைய) concedes that the river too begins as rain on the hills.

note: In Akananuru 156 the mother, not knowing the cause, weeps and offers toddy and a goat to the god of the ford while the girl's gem-dark skin turns gold; in Ainkurunuru 105 the friend tells the mother that the girl's brow has gone more golden than gold since the lord came.
teaches: The golden pallor that sends the mother to the god in the Akananuru is given its human cause in the Ainkurunuru, so reading them together shows that the friend's disclosure is the answer to the mother's misdirected rite.

note: Natrinai 282 says it would be fine indeed (நன்றுமன்) if the old diviner's word could calm the bond; Ainkurunuru 248 says fine indeed (நன்றால் அம்ம) will be her beauty if his beads find the cause.
teaches: The same mock approval of the diviner is aimed in Natrinai at his cure and in Ainkurunuru at his diagnosis, so the friend's ironic நன்று is shown as a set turn of the veri situation that can be pointed at either half of the rite.

note: Both have the woman's heart following the man who has left; Kural 1248 calls the heart a fool for going after him, Natrinai 107 says the heart that went has the good share and she who stayed has the pain.
teaches: The same split between a heart that follows and a self left behind is judged in opposite ways: Valluvar's woman despises the following heart, the Natrinai woman envies it, because she is the one left to bear the town's gossip.

note: Natrinai 168 and Ainkurunuru 273 share a formula: the young of the dull-headed female monkey feeding on the good hill and the girl called நின் நயந்து உறைவி; in Natrinai 168 the friend uses it to forbid his coming at midnight, in Ainkurunuru 273 to forbid his going away.
teaches: The same formula serves to stop the lover coming and to stop him leaving, which shows the double bind of secret love: the girl's life is staked both on the danger of his night visits and on his absence, and only marriage ends both.

note: Kural 1102: other diseases have other cures, but the sickness this jewelled woman causes she alone cures. Natrinai 384: eloping, the man calls her the one who was the medicine when he suffered after casting off shame.
teaches: The Kural's paradox that the woman is the cure for the sickness she causes becomes in Natrinai 384 the eloping man's reason for taking her across the waste: he now carries his medicine with him, so the couplet's moment of union is extended into the whole journey of udanpokku.

note: In 357 the man sees the season-dressed forest himself and gives up the journey for wealth; in 499 he gives up his hard work because she would grieve if she saw the rain-dressed forest.
teaches: Ainkurunuru gives two reasons for the same turning back, the forest's beauty moving the man himself in the paalai decade and the forest's power to hurt her moving him in the mullai decade, so the season is at once his longing and his sense of her danger.

note: Natrinai 84: the woman reports that he will go (they say) by the hard waste where the mirage lures the deer, and excuses him as one who cannot live a home life unable to relieve beggars. Kainnilai 24: the woman reports that the hard waste where the deer runs after the mirage is, they say, the road of the loveless one.
teaches: The same reported road with the same mirage-chasing deer ends in opposite verdicts on the man, a duty that excuses him in the Natrinai and a want of love that condemns him in the Kainnilai, so the landscape fixed the scene while the poet chose the moral.

note: Both blessings are said by the woman to a thing of nature that governs her sight of the man who has left: the Kural blesses the moon on condition that it not set (படாஅதி வாழி மதி); Ainkurunuru 312 blesses the hill that has already hidden him (மறைத்த குன்றே).
teaches: The Kural's blessing is a bargain for sight, while the Sangam woman blesses the hill after it has hidden him, so her wish can only be for what the hill will do to him on the way, which shows the blessing turning from her own need to his safety.

note: Both have the girl, with no human messenger, beg a creature to go to her man: in Akananuru 170 the crab, since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak; in Natrinai 277 the bee, after she scolds it.
teaches: Together they show the creature-messenger as the last resort of a girl who cannot speak openly, and Natrinai 277 adds the grievance that the creature has its own pleasures to prefer, so the appeal is also a complaint that even the messenger neglects her.

note: Both have the woman of the shore say her bangles registered the lord's leaving (தணந்தமை ... உணர்ந்த வளை; பிரிந்தென நெகிழ்ந்தன); Ainkurunuru 192 adds that they have grown tight again (வீங்கின).
teaches: The Kural treats the bangle only as an early witness of separation, while the Ainkurunuru poem shows it registering his return as well, so the convention is a two-way gauge of the man's presence and not merely a sign of wasting.

note: Kural 1222 asks the dim evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Kuruntokai 310 sees the sky dazed like herself at day's end and then says she may yet live if someone will carry word to him.
teaches: The couplet stops at fellow-feeling with the evening; the poem turns that fellow-feeling into a need for a messenger, so the evening lament is shown as the point where the heroine starts to seek a go-between.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one but the man was there, only a heron watching for fish, on the day he took her; Thinaimalai 37: the tide knew it that day (ஓதநீர் அன்றறியும்), so marry her before the common square.
teaches: Kuruntokai's girl fears that a union witnessed only by a shore creature leaves her helpless if he lies, and Thinaimalai's friend answers that fear: a witness that cannot speak is why the union must be made public in the square.

note: Kural 1168's woman says the night that puts every creature to sleep has only her as companion; Natrinai 348's woman lies sleepless while moon, festival town and paired bees all rejoice, and asks whether the world fights her or she the world.
teaches: The couplet makes the sleepless woman the night's one companion in a sleeping world, while the Natrinai wakes the whole world in celebration around her, so the same sleeplessness becomes either a bond with the dark or a quarrel with everything else.

note: In Akananuru 118 the friend fears gossip if the hero comes by day and fears the tiger still more if he comes alone at midnight, and says the girl has stopped the millet songs. In Natrinai 156 the friend refuses the night tryst and asks him to come by day, since they will guard the millet for many days.
teaches: The two friends weigh the same choice of day or night and decide it by the millet: while the girls still guard the field, as in Natrinai 156, the day offers a safe meeting place, and once the guarding has stopped, as in Akananuru 118, day and night are both closed and only marriage is left.

note: Purananuru 107 answers the poets who praise Pari alone: there is also the rain (மாரியும் உண்டு) that sustains the world; Paripadal 22.8 says the sky poured water like the king's bounty (அவன் வண்மைபோல் வானம் பொழிந்த நீர்), after likening clouds, thunder, drops and lightning to his elephants, drum, arrows and spear.
teaches: Kapilar measures the patron against the rain and lets the rain win, while the Paripadal measures the rain against the king and makes the whole storm a copy of his war and gifts, so held together they show the rain-and-giving comparison run in both directions, with the river hymn making the king the original and nature the likeness.

note: Purananuru 165 opens with those who wished to last in the unlasting world (மன்னா உலகத்து மன்னுதல் குறித்தோர்) and set up their fame; Kalittokai 54 ends with the girl wanting it said she acted from love, which in the unlasting world (மன்னா உலகத்து) is what lasts.
teaches: The akam heroine takes over the puram formula for lasting fame and applies it to a woman's choice of lover, so the Sangam ideal of a name that outlives one could be earned by love as well as by giving.

note: Kar Narpathu 22: the returning man says the plumed, spirited horses are yoked (உளையணிந்து ... கலிமாவும் பூட்டிய). Kainnilai 33: the friend says he will come yoking his fine spirited plumed horses (உளையார் கலிநன் மாப்பூட்டி வருவார்).
teaches: The friend's promise uses nearly the words with which the hero himself reports setting out, so the comfort at home is shown to be an accurate picture of what is happening on the road, and the formula passes between the friend's and the hero's mouths.

note: Kural 66: only those who have not heard their children's prattle (மழலைச்சொல்) call the flute and lute sweet. Ainthinai Aimpathu 25: the son's மழலைவாய் talk eases the pain of longing for the husband.
teaches: The Kural ranks prattle above music as a pleasure; the venba gives it a harder task, standing in for an absent husband's embrace, so the general praise of children is tested in the one place it might fail.

note: Kar Narpathu 26: the thondri blooms over every field like the first-night lamps of Karthigai, and the rain comes as messenger. Kainnilai 26: the blood-red thonri buds are so like fire that a bird shies from them.
teaches: Both friends read the red thonri as flame, but one sees festival lamps and the other a fire that frightens, so the same sign of return can carry welcome or alarm, and the Kainnilai friend lets a trace of fear into her comfort.

note: Both set a wing-worn heron at the ford of Thondi: Kuruntokai 128's பறைதபு நாரை on the eastern sea longs in vain for the ayirai fish of Thondi's harbour, as the man's heart longs for a distant girl; Ainkurunuru 180's பறைதபு முதுகுருகு sits fed on the rich fish the netters bring.
teaches: The flightless heron of Thondi is hopeless longing when it must reach the fish itself and secure dependence when the fishermen bring the fish to it, so the friend's version answers the lover's lament: the helpless are fed only when someone provides, which is what she asks the man to do by marrying.

note: Ainkurunuru 215: at evening the bee hums sweeter than the musicians' flute, and those who leave then will do worse. Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon.
teaches: The Kural makes the evening flute itself the weapon, while the Ainkurunuru keeps the music sweet and turns its sweetness into the measure of the leaver's cruelty, so together they show evening music wounding the parted woman not by harshness but by sweetness heard alone.

note: In Akananuru 20 the friend says mother, on the word of spiteful women, has confined the girl because a chariot circles the great ford day and night; in Ainkurunuru 186 the friend quotes mother herself saying a chariot comes often to this ford, so do not go.
teaches: In the long poem the confinement rests on the town's report, in the short one on the mother's own sight of the chariot, so the friend's warning to the lover can come in two strengths, and the second leaves him no excuse that it is only gossip.

note: Two responses to the same crisis mark the moral range of the Book of Wealth. When honour or distress comes, those like the yak give up life (969), and the base sell theirs for a price, in haste (1080).
teaches: The book ends on the second.

note: Purananuru 373 (Kovur Kizhar, thurai மறக்களவழி) praises the Chola Killivalavan who made the Kongu turn their backs (கொங்கு புறம் பெற்ற) and ends among vultures on the fearful field, asking a gift; Kalavazhi Narpathu 14 names the Kongar as the enemy the lord of the river country killed (கொங்கரை அட்ட களத்து).
teaches: Read together they show that a Chola victory over the Kongu was already sung as a field-of-battle poem in the Purananuru, with the bard asking for his share; Poigaiyar keeps the enemy and the field but lets the stanza end on the field itself, turning a petition into a celebration complete without the bard's request.

note: Kural 1102 says the woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes the man; in Ainkurunuru 59 the friend says she was once the cure for his love-sick heart but can be no cure for the girl now.
teaches: The couplet makes the beloved the only remedy for the man's love-sickness, but the Sangam friend shows a third person who served as that remedy by bringing them together, and who has none for the woman once he strays, so the cure flows only toward the man.

note: Both make pallor the immediate price of the lover's absence: Kural 1187 says it came the moment she turned in his embrace; Natrinai 304 says beauty joins her when he joins and pallor wrecks it when he parts.
teaches: The couplet records the speed of the pallor; the Natrinai woman draws the moral that the same chest is joy and harm at once, like the hand that plays to the asunam and then kills it.

note: Purananuru 184: a king who takes his due like an elephant fed balls of paddy keeps the land rich, but one who grabs is like an elephant loosed in the field. Natrinai 226: kings do not take gold that ruins the land's wealth, yet her lover does not know the measure of the wealth he seeks.
teaches: The counsel that a king must take tribute without ruining its source had become a proverb a wife could quote, and Natrinai 226 turns it on the household: a husband who leaves to make wealth regardless of her life is the elephant loose in the field.

note: In Natrinai 53 the mother herself says the new stream water coming down from the high hill is medicine and sends the girl to drink and bathe in it; in Ainkurunuru 203 the friend tells the mother that the muddy water of his land is sweeter than their honeyed milk.
teaches: The mother who prescribes the water of the far hill without knowing whose hill it is, and the friend who tells her that the water of his land is sweeter than home's milk, together show that in kurinji the lover's water stands for the lover, so the disclosure turns the mother's innocent remedy into a confession.

note: 72 says the king's foes resolve without deliberating (சூழாது துணிதல்) and, from the greatness of their folly, do not know his nature as the wise do; 84 says his foes knew well that he was strong (வலியை ஆதல்நற்(கு) அறிந்தனர் ஆயினும்) and still rose against him, not knowing how to bow.
teaches: The two Chera decades give opposite causes for the same ruin: the eighth ten blames the enemy's ignorance of the king, the ninth blames their refusal to bow although they knew him, which moves the fault from a lack of judgement to pride.

note: Natrinai 11: the friend tells the heroine, wilting since the tryst he set failed (அவர் செய் குறி பிழைப்ப), to drop the resentful thought that he will not come, for his charioteer is driving along the moonlit shore sparing the crabs. Thinaimozhi 41 is that resentful thought spoken: his trysts have turned false (செய்த குறியும்பொய் யாயின).
teaches: Held together the two give the complaint and its answer in one neythal exchange: the venba lets the heroine conclude from the failed tryst that his bond is false, while the older poem shows the friend refusing that inference and offering his gentleness on the road as proof.

note: Kural 957: a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon. Kalittokai 41: if a falsehood appeared in the hill lord's truth it would be like fire appearing in the moon (திங்களுள் தீத் தோன்றியற்று).
teaches: The Kural uses the moon to say a noble man's fault cannot be hidden; the girls use it to say such a fault is impossible, so the same figure that warns the great serves in akam as a pledge of trust sung for the lover to overhear, binding him to live up to it.

note: Ainkurunuru 372 asks whether the girl thinks even of her mother (என்னும் உள்ளினள் கொல்லோ); Akananuru 383 says the girl never thought of the mother who raised her; gossip rises in both.
teaches: What Ainkurunuru leaves as an anxious question Akananuru settles as a charge, so the pair shows the mother's doubt about being remembered hardening, in the longer poem, into reproach.

note: The materialist calls knowledge of former births the delusion of possession or dream; in kaathai 9 Manimekalai, carried off by the deity in sleep, knew her former birth without error.
teaches: The materialist's objection names the very conditions of the heroine's own knowledge, so the epic's story stands as her unspoken answer to him.

note: Kural 471 says to weigh the strength of the deed, oneself, the opponent and allies before acting; verse 57 says the minister acts after measuring his own state, the work, the opponents' state and the order of things.
teaches: The couplet's four-fold weighing is given to the minister and its fourth term changes from allies to the matchless order of things, so prudence moves from counting forces to reading circumstance.

note: Kar Narpathu 1 makes the rainbow the garland on the chest of sea-coloured Mal; Ainthinai Aimpathu 1 gives Mal the cloud's dark body and gives the garland to Shiva as the konrai.
teaches: Both opening verses of the mullai collections divine the storm, but they share it out differently, so the god of the mullai was a ready frame that each poet filled by choosing which part of the sky belongs to which god.

note: Kural 1081: on first sight the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels; Ainkurunuru 363: the man tells the hunters' sister that what she calls freckles (சுணங்கு) his stricken heart calls a goddess (அணங்கு).
teaches: Where the couplet leaves the goddess as one of three guesses about the whole woman, 363 pins the striking power on one small mark she herself thinks a blemish, so the pair shows the anangu is not in her but in the gap between how she sees herself and how he is struck.

iraicchi.act: the male tiger hunts the elephant to relieve the hunger of his mate who has just given birth
iraicchi.sense: the man crossing that land is doing the same for the woman he left, so his going is care for her and she may bear it

ullurai.tenor: the husband who takes the other woman's pleasure without effort and goes home to obey his wife

pairs.situation: the pleasure that falls to him unsought, the other woman herself
he snatches what drops within reach, and gives nothing for it

ullurai.speaker_fit: the other woman is not bound by porul 7.26 to 7.28 and may use the mango and fish of his marutham town freely (porul 7.29)

ullurai.tenor: the girl, afraid of the rumour that the man has left her

pairs.situation: she has come through the dangers of the secret love so far
she now dreads a mere report as though it were the desertion

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a prawn and a screwpine of the shore in a neythal poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the peacocks take a stray cloud's thunder for the season and dance to meet it
iraicchi.sense: the heroine, grieving because she thinks the season of his promise has come and gone unkept, is answering the same false sign

iraicchi.act: the tusker raids the millet, braving the hunter's firebrand, to restore his mate weak after calving
iraicchi.sense: the man who braved the night roads will now provide for her as a husband

iraicchi.act: the stag, just escaped from the tiger, calls its doe with its male voice to come and join it
iraicchi.sense: the youth's call drew the daughter into the same danger, so the mother sees on the road the very call that took her girl

note: In Natrinai 359 the hill lord's gift of a leaf skirt is a danger, since wearing it will alarm the mother; in Ainkurunuru 147 the shore lord gives his country as the price of the leaf skirt.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the leaf skirt moving from a secret courting gift that cannot be worn openly to the token for which a bride price is paid, so the same object marks both ends of secret love.

note: Both men in the war camp turn on the wife's ignorance of their pain: Akananuru 304 says she does not know it (நந்நோய் தன்வயின் அறியாள்), Ainkurunuru 441 wishes she knew it (அவள் அறியினோ நன்றே).
teaches: Akananuru 304 spells out what the wife who does not know will think, that the man is without right or grace, so the bare wish of 441 is revealed as the soldier's answer to an imagined accusation of neglect.

note: In Kural 1249 the woman asks her heart whom it goes seeking, since the lover is within it; in Kuruntokai 340 her heart, where he dwells, can settle on neither side and sways like a kandal with ebb and tide.
teaches: The couplet treats the heart's going out to him as an absurdity to point out; the poem's rooted kandal, bent out by the ebb and back by the flood, makes the same divided heart a rhythm she cannot stop, so the paradox becomes a condition rather than an error.

note: Akananuru 175: the clouds flash more often than the spear Chezhiyan raised after his victory at Alankanam; the time he set for return has come. Natrinai 387: the cloud flashes like swords drawn in Chezhiyan's camp at Alankanam; he will come.
teaches: In both poems the lightning of the promised rains is measured by the weapons of Chezhiyan's victory at Alankanam, spoken once by the waiting woman and once by her friend, so the battle had become a stock sign of the season of return and could serve either as complaint (the time is here) or as comfort (he will come).

note: Kalittokai 1 names three of Shiva's dances (kodukotti, pandarangam, kapalam); Tirumanthiram 2733 lists kodukotti and pandarangam among the dances whose king he is and places them in the nadis and at Tillai.
teaches: The dance names the Tirumanthiram files into a yogic doctrine were already in the oldest love anthology as stage dances with a partner keeping time, so the later mystic list inherited a performance repertoire, not a private vision.

note: Both are a friend's reproach to the hill lord for his absences in courtship, with a tusker's embrace in the same words (இரும்பிணர் ... தழு): in Akananuru 78 he clasps his trembling pregnant mate in his rough trunk, in Ainkurunuru 239 he clasps a rough boulder, taking it for his mate.
teaches: The one image of a tusker's embrace serves the friend two ways, as the care the man owes the girl when the mate is there and as the blind longing of a beast whose mate is gone, so the reproach can shame the lover either by what the beast does for its mate or by what it suffers without her.

note: Kural 774's hero sends his spear away with an elephant and laughs as he pulls one from his own body; 274's warrior hurls his spear at the oncoming elephant and, weaponless, takes the enemy's attack upon his body.
