teaches: The Kural's couplet compresses a set scene that the Purananuru gives at length with dress and enemy horse, which shows that Valluvar's chapter on martial pride was built on stock battle episodes the audience already knew from heroic song.

note: The eloping man in Natrinai 362 vows that if a fight comes he will not fear and will drive it off, but if her kin come he will hide (நுமர் வரின் மறைகுவென்); Pattinathar's antadhi verse 922 gives the hero the same two conditions, hill men he will make food for kites, but if they are her kin he will hide (உமராயின் மறைகுவனே).
teaches: Pattinathar kept not only the eloping lover's boast but its exact limit, courage against strangers and concealment before her family, which shows the devotional kovai inherited the Sangam udanpokku speech as a fixed thurai with its own logic, since striking her kin would undo the marriage the flight is meant to make.

note: 389 describes Venkatam where a captured elephant calf is tied in the common while its mother grieves; Akananuru 83 shows Pulli's young men separating a calf from its wailing mother and tying it at the toddy houses of the Venkatam town.
teaches: The calf-taking scene was a fixed picture of Venkatam shared by both genres, and the pairing shows the akam hero's heart racing past a scene that the puram poet offers as plain proof of the lord's wealth, the same image put to opposite uses of distance and of plenty.

note: Natrinai 200 has the friend warn the town's women against the bard's lie-wrapped crooked words; Ainthinai Aimpathu 21 treats his pleading not as dangerous but as pointless.
teaches: The two refusals name two faults in the go-between, falsehood that endangers others and futility before the wife who already knows, so the refusal of the bard had both a public and a private argument.

note: Kural 1014 asks whether shame (நாணுடைமை) is not an ornament of the worthy; thirattu 6 calls modesty the girl's ancient ornament (நாண் எனும் தொல்லை அணி) at her first union.
teaches: The same figure of shame as an ornament serves the Kural for the moral restraint of the worthy and the Paripadal for a bride's reserve at first union, which shows that naanam named both and that the poets ranked the bride's reserve above her jewels as the Kural ranks restraint above pride.

note: Kural 980: greatness hides another's weakness, smallness tells only faults. Kalittokai 44: the girl hid the man's ungraciousness from her friend, the street and her companions, ashamed that others would blame him, and the friend calls this a nature rare even in a mother.
teaches: The Kural's mark of greatness is shown in the one wronged, a girl hiding her lover's fault, and the friend's report of it becomes a reproach, since the man learns that the greater one in the affair is she; the pair shows the maxim working as leverage in a love quarrel.

note: In Akananuru 22 the girl laughs because during the velan's midnight rite her lover slipped past the guards and his embrace cured her; in Kuruntokai 360 the girl, while the velan misreads her sickness, prays that the lover not come at night.
teaches: The two girls in the same veri situation take opposite views of the lover's night visit, one as the cure that mocks the rite and the other as a danger worse than the rite's misdiagnosis, so the veri scene could be turned either to triumph or to selfless restraint.

note: In Akananuru 266 the wife says the husband's water-play with young women in the evening flood is gossip but that what hurts is his oath by Murugan of Alaivay; in Paripadal 6.88-96 the husband, accused after the water-play, swears by cool Parankunram.
teaches: Both husbands answer a water-play charge with an oath to a Murugan shrine, but the Akananuru wife treats the oath as the worse betrayal while the Paripadal lets the oath pass into a reconciliation brokered by others, so the pair shows the festival hymn softening into play what the akam anthology records as a wound.

note: Natrinai 57: while the herd of wild cows sleeps with their calves, a female monkey creeps up, squeezes the swollen udder and wrings the milk into her young one's hands. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 3: the monkey strokes the udder and the wild cow, glad as with her calf, lets the milk flow.
teaches: Held together they show one scene turned from theft to gift: the older poem's monkey steals while the cows sleep, fitting a friend who warns of the girl's ruin, while the later venba makes the cow consent, fitting a girl who says she cannot part, so the speaker's case decides whether the milk is stolen or given.

note: Both are the friend's comfort that the rain is false: in Kuruntokai 66 the konrai is foolish for taking stray rain for the season 'before the season comes' (பருவம் வாரா அளவை); in Natrinai 316 the cloud itself is foolish for pouring 'before he comes' (வரல் வாரா அளவை).
teaches: Natrinai moves the foolishness from the flowers that believe the rain to the cloud that sends it, so the consolation could discredit the season at either end, the sign or its source.

note: Both compare a woman's hair to the bright ripples (அறல்) of a named river: the Arisil by Killi's Ambar in Natrinai 141, the forest stream north of Vaanan's Sirukudi in Akananuru 117.
teaches: The one simile marks the two ends of the girl's story: in Natrinai 141 the river-dark hair is what keeps the lover from leaving her, and in Akananuru 117 it is the mother's last picture of the daughter who left with him, dressed now by his hands.

note: Both poems are by Kachchippettu Nannakaiyar and both ask about the man who left (துறந்தோர்): in 172 the woman at evening asks whether he is happy being alone; in 180 the friend asks whether he has grown hard in the land he went to.
teaches: Read together, the poet's two questions mark the turn of a long absence: the first still imagines him as lonely as she is, the second fears his heart has changed, so the doubt moves from his comfort to his constancy.

note: Both are the woman's complaint that ends on almost the same closing line (கோடுயர் பிறங்கல் மலை இறந் தோரே; நிலையுயர் பிறங்கல் மலைஇறந் தோரே) after naming her wasted broad shoulders (பணைத்தோள்) and slipping bangles.
teaches: The five-line decade poem is the bare frame of the thirteen-line Akananuru poem, the body's signs followed by the closing formula of the men who crossed the high hills, so the pair shows how a long paalai poem was built by filling the road between those two fixed ends with a scene.

note: 270 explains poverty as too little austerity, which is something people could change. 377 says enjoyment is only as the apportioner apportioned.
teaches: The same fact gets a moral cause and a fatal one.

note: Kalavazhi Narpathu 30 likens the pooled blood of the battlefield, dragging killed elephants, to a flood that rolls boulders down the hill (மலையுருட்டு நீர்போல்); Paripadal 12.84-85 sees the Vaiyai in the morning of the rains red with turbid blood (கலிழ் செங் குருதித்தே) and names it the river of the king whose army kills in war.
teaches: The war poem uses the hill torrent as the image for battle blood and the hymn uses battle blood as the image for the monsoon torrent, so held together they show the comparison running both ways for Tamil poets: the king's killing is a flood and his river's flood is his killing, the river's redness counting as his fame.

note: Both concern the town's gossip about a secret love: Kural 1143's man asks whether gossip the whole town knows is not good for him, since it is like having what he has not yet got; Natrinai 4's friend fears that gossip reaching the mother will end the meetings and asks whether the man will take them to his own town.
teaches: The gossip that the Kural's man welcomes as a foretaste of union is, for the women of Natrinai 4, the danger that ends their meetings, which they can only turn into pressure to marry, so the worth of alar in the secret stage depends on who bears its cost.

note: In Natrinai 386 the girl refuses the hero's offer of a dread oath by the god (அணங்குடை அருஞ் சூள்) because men of his kin do not need it, and he comes with marriage; in Paripadal 8.65-71 the wife refuses her husband's oath by Murugan because the god's spear would devour a false swearer.
teaches: Both women stop a man from swearing by the god, but for opposite reasons, trust in his kin in the courtship poem and certainty of his guilt in the marriage quarrel, which shows that refusing the god-oath was a recognised move whose meaning depended on the stage of love.

note: Kural 1151 says: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 256 is the man telling his grieving wife that he has given up going, through the burnt forest and even through the cool forest of the rains.
teaches: Read together, the Natrinai supplies the one answer the Kural's speaker would accept, a plain 'I am not going', and shows that to be believed it had to renounce the pleasant season as well as the harsh one, since a man who stays only while the road is burnt will go when it rains.

note: Kuruntokai 202 compares the lover to the nerunji, which first gives a sweet flower and then thorns; Kuruntokai 315 makes the man the sun and her shoulders the nerunji that turns to it.
teaches: One weed of poor ground carries two opposite lessons in the same anthology, its turning to the sun as her dependence and its later thorns as his change, so the heroine's image in 315 already holds the pain that 202 states.

note: Kuruntokai 3: the girl says her bond with the hill lord is larger than the earth, higher than the sky, deeper than the sea. Kalittokai 48: the friend tells the hill lord that the girl's grief, weighed, is greater than the hill whose bounds none knows (மலையினும் பெரிதே).
teaches: The same kurinji measure by immensity that the girl uses for her love the friend uses for its cost, so the pair shows that the size of the bond and the size of the grief at his absence are one quantity, and the friend can turn the heroine's boast into a charge against the man.

note: Kuruntokai 217: the friend tells the hill lord that meeting by day is possible while they guard the millet, but she fears his coming by night. Thinaimalai 59: by day the gossip is great, and by night the dangers are as great.
teaches: The Kuruntokai friend still leaves the day open and fears only the night, while the venba's friend closes both, so the pair shows the second step of the convention, where barring day and night together leaves marriage as the only way.

note: Both quote a saying about men's work: 'work is life to men' (வினையே ஆடவர்க்கு உயிரே, Kuruntokai 135) and 'effort, not grace, is men's wealth' (அருள் அன்று ஆக ஆள்வினை ஆடவர் பொருள், Akananuru 75); in both the man does not leave.
teaches: The maxim that a man's life or wealth is his work was common enough to be quoted, yet in both poems it is quoted only to be overruled: the Akananuru hero weighs it against beauty that cannot be given back, and the Kuruntokai friend completes it with its other half, that men are women's life, so the love poets used the work ethic as the premise they argue against.

note: Kural 230: nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach. Kalittokai 43 lines 26-27: the lover is praised as one who, if he could not fill the want of one who told him of poverty, would give up his body (தன் மெய் துறப்பான்).
teaches: The Kural's ranking of giving above life is sung by the girls as a fact about one man to cure a girl's wasting, so the ethical maxim served in akam as the highest praise a lover could receive, and the praise itself works the cure before he comes.

note: Kural 293: do not lie about what your own heart knows, for after the lie your heart burns you; Kalittokai 125 opens with the maxim that those who think no one saw may hide what their heart knows, but no witness is closer than the heart, and then charges the lover.
teaches: The akam friend turns the ethical maxim into a weapon of courtship: the Kural's inner witness, a general law of truthfulness, becomes the ground on which she charges a lover with knowing his own neglect, so the doctrine of conscience was already available to love poetry as rhetoric.

note: Kapilar in Purananuru 123 praises Malaiyan of Mullur for chariots given while sober, more than the raindrops on Mullur's heights; Kapilar in Natrinai 291 measures a girl's ruined beauty by the herd-owners whose cattle the king of Mullur drove off at nightfall on his horse.
teaches: Read together, the same poet's two Mullur poems show the giving king's other face: the wealth praised in puram as countless gifts came partly from night raids on herds, and akam borrows the raid from the side of those who lost everything.

note: Ainkurunuru 78: a woman asks the man to bathe in the dam-breaking flood, likened to Killi's wall-breaking elephant, and take her shoulders as his raft. Akananuru 312: the friend says that if the hill lord means to marry, they will bathe in the flood with his chest as their raft, and the lightning is likened to Vazhuthi's spear.
teaches: The raft of the lover's body runs in both directions: in the kurinji poem the girls take the man's chest as their float as the reward of a promised marriage, while in the marutham poem a woman offers her shoulders as his float to draw him away, and both dress the flood in a king's weapon, so the same intimate game and the same borrowed war image serve the making of a marriage in one land and its straining in the other.

note: Akananuru 23: in the rains the stag embraces his doe (பிணை ... தழீஇ), and the woman asks if this is the time her man meant. Kainnilai 29: kurunthu blooms, the stag embraces his doe and the rain-cloud thunders; the rest is lost.
teaches: The Akananuru poem shows the stag's embrace being weighed as the promised season's clock, which tells a reader of the broken Kainnilai verse what such an embrace was there to measure, even though its own ending is gone.

note: Kural 1230: thinking of the man whose nature is wealth, in this bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை) my life that would not die is dying. Thinaimalai 94: in the bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை), when the moon pours a false day, my life does not stay within but rides away.
teaches: The venba takes the couplet's own phrase for the hour and adds the cause the couplet leaves out, a moon that fakes daylight, so the bewilderment of the evening becomes a trick of the sky rather than only a state of her mind.

note: Kural 1102: other diseases have other cures, but this woman is the cure of the sickness she gives; Kuruntokai 71: if medicine, she is medicine; if treasure, she is treasure.
teaches: The man's claim that she is his medicine is the same in both, but the poem adds treasure (வைப்பு), so under its paalai colophon the cure-paradox of the couplet becomes an argument against leaving to seek wealth.

note: Natrinai 224 sets 'sweet spring has come' (இன்ப வேனிலும் வந்தன்று) beside 'those who assured us we will not part' (பிரியலம் என்று தெளித்தோர்); Ainkurunuru 350 ends with the time of which he assured them (தெளிக்கும் பொழுதே).
teaches: Natrinai uses தெளித்தல் for the man's sworn assurance in the very poem where spring arrives, which supports reading Ainkurunuru 350's தெளிக்கும் as his promise, and shows that spring's coming and the lover's oath were a fixed pair in paalai poetry.

note: Akananuru 229: the girl answers her friend that the man who promised to come at once has not come even in young spring, when the koel calls on the budding branch. Thinaimozhi 13: the flowering season has come and the koel has made all his sworn words false.
teaches: The Akananuru lets the koel mark the date the promise failed, while the venba makes the koel the agent that turns his oath into a lie, so the four-line form compresses the long poem's reasoning into a single accusation aimed at the bird instead of the man.

note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the pale evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 163 she asks the sea who has hurt it, since she hears it crying at midnight.
teaches: Both women treat a natural thing as a fellow sufferer, but the poem shows how the projection is built: she knows the sea grieves because she herself is awake to hear it, so the sympathy is evidence of her sleeplessness rather than a fancy.

note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart where it goes seeking, since the lover lives within it. Kuruntokai 153: her heart, once timid, now goes along the night slope to him without tiring.
teaches: The Kural mocks the heart's going out as needless because he is already within, while the Kuruntokai heroine marvels at the same going as courage, so the pairing shows the couplet's wit resting on an older picture of the heart as a traveller on the lover's road.

note: Both close on the same line, உள்ளேன் தோழி படீஇயர் என் கண்ணே, after a bird-loud shore; Kuruntokai 243 fills the shore with girls playing at sand houses, Ainkurunuru 142 with birds settling to roost.
teaches: The refusal to think of him was a stock closing formula, and each poet earns it with a different shore picture, the girls' play recalling her past in one and the roosting birds setting her sleeplessness against their rest in the other.

note: Ainkurunuru 4: the girls wish that the lover's chest never become a common pond (பழனம்). Kural 1311: the wife refuses her husband's chest because all women feast on it in common with their eyes.
teaches: The fear the Ainkurunuru girls voice before marriage, that his chest may become common property, is the very charge the Kural's wife brings in a sulk after it, so the two show the marutham husband's straying anticipated as a danger and then turned into a reason to refuse him.

note: Akananuru 45, told to bear up, the woman answers with the dangers of his road, the gossip and her own coming madness like Aathi Manthi's; Kuruntokai 290 answers the same counsel ('bear your love') by saying she will waste away like foam on a rock.
teaches: The two poems answer the same counsel to endure in opposite registers, one with public ruin and a famous madness, the other with a silent dissolving, which shows that the heroine's refusal of endurance could be voiced as loud breakdown or as quiet vanishing.

note: Both set a boar with a striped young that has lost its mother beside a man who has left: in 265 the boar rears it after a tiger killed the sow, in 268 it sleeps with it on the peak.
teaches: Taken together the pair fixes the reading of the motherless young in 268 by the tiger-killed sow named in 265, and shows the decade using one creature's care twice, once against a husband and once against a lover.

ullurai.tenor: the love he sowed, which grows of itself without his tending

pairs.situation: he only began the love
it ripens of itself without his care or union
it grows on her, unseen and unwatered by him

ullurai.speaker_fit: the girl uses hill rice of her own hill country, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the young cow comes home at evening keeping close to the bull
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle go home together at dusk while the man stays in the camp away from his wife

ullurai.tenor: the wives the man left, made wary of every bard by one deceiver

pairs.situation: the women once taken in by the man's lying bard
they now fear every bard, even the honest ones

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the heron, fish and lotus of the marutham field in a marutham poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the herons, having fed, come back together at dusk to crowd into their nests
iraicchi.sense: even the birds of the backwater return to a shared home at night, while the man still leaves the girl without one

note: In 332 the beasts fail to tell him that parting is cruel; in 333 the birds fail to tell him that they themselves live paired.
teaches: Read in order, the decade moves from the argument the beasts should have made by precept (parting is cruel) to the one the birds should have made by their own example (we live with our mates), so the wife tries both ways of restraining a man and puts each in a creature's mouth.

note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when giving is out of reach; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the girl, who would find it better to die than live unable to give to suppliants (ஈதல் இரந்தார்க்கு ஒன்று ஆற்றாது வாழ்தலின் சாதலும் கூடுமாம்), would give him whatever he lacks.
teaches: The friend's offer turns the Kural's maxim into a trap for the household: once the lover presents himself as a suppliant for grace rather than wealth, the giving ethic obliges the girl to yield.

note: Purananuru 236 is Kapilar's lament that Pari told him to stay behind and did not take him in death; Patitruppattu 61 has Kapilar, Pari gone to the land from which none returns (வாராச் சேண்புலம் படர்ந்தோன்), arrive at the Chera's camp drawn by a fame for giving without regret.
teaches: Together they show the bard's two answers to his patron's death, the vow to be with Pari in the next birth and the journey to a new patron whose giving is praised in Pari's terms, so the Chera's praise is partly an elegy carried over.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone, her shoulders have lost their old beauty and fullness and her bright bangles slip. Kuruntokai 50: the shoulders he embraced have wasted so that the bright bangles slip past the wrist, adorned with loneliness.
teaches: The couplet names the wasted shoulder and slipping bangle as the sign of separation; the poem shows what the sign was used to say, setting it against his town's ford adorned with flowers, so the body's loss becomes an accusation of a place that still flourishes.

note: In both the woman's heart has followed the man who left (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய்; இறந்தோர் தேஎத்துச் சென்ற நெஞ்சம்); the Kural calls it a fool, Ainkurunuru 317 asks the friend why it is so slow to come back.
teaches: The Kural judges the heart's going as folly, but the Ainkurunuru woman takes the going for granted and worries about the heart's delay, so the same flight of the heart becomes, in the older poem, a second absence that mirrors the man's.

note: Purananuru 189 concludes that the use of wealth is giving, since king and hunter alike eat one measure; Kuruntokai 63's heart argues the same, that there is no giving and enjoying for the penniless, to drive the man to work.
teaches: The puram maxim that wealth exists to be given becomes, in the akam poem, the very reason a man leaves his wife, so the pair shows the giver's ethic carrying a private cost the praise poem never counts.

note: In Puram 385 the lord of Ambar, hearing a bard's drum at another man's door, strips off his earth-eaten rags, dresses him in white and ends his hunger; the guide promises that Karikalan will strip off the bard's stitched rags and give him silk before he asks.
teaches: Puram 385 tells the removal of rags and the gift of cloth as one patron's spontaneous kindness, while the guide poem can predict it as the first step of a known sequence, which suggests the re-dressing of the bard was a recognised rite of reception rather than a single generous act.

note: Kuruntokai 66: the konrai is foolish, blooming on a stray rain before the season he named; 114: the kurundham blooms before the clouds have even shed their drops, and the heroine says it has fixed the season and decreed her grief.
teaches: The premature bloom that the Kuruntokai friend waves away as a plant's mistake is, to the heroine of 114, a verdict, which shows that the consolation of untimely rain only works on someone who does not take the flower as the sign itself.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51: speaking of the man of the good pond town is my grief; get up and go, bard; I have my little son as companion. Kainnilai 41 opens with the same line (பொய்கைநல் லூரன் திறன்கிளப்ப) and ends with the little son as what she owns.
teaches: The two venbas share their first line and their closing son, but where Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51 calls the man's praise her grief (எவ்வம்), Kainnilai 41 says she already knows his doings, so the reworking turns the wife's pain into a cool dismissal while keeping the son as her answer.

note: Both compare a hill girl to the figure carved on Kolli's western face; 89 calls Kolli Porayan's, 100 calls it Ori's.
teaches: The same carved figure serves two poets as the measure of a girl's innocence while the hill is credited to different lords, the Chera Porayan and the archer Ori, so the simile was fixed to the place and outlived the change of its master.

note: The idyll names the courtesans' many deceiving lies and hidden embraces and their draining of rich young men, but lists them among the splendours of the city; the Kural likens the false embrace of women who sell themselves to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room.
teaches: The deceit the Kural turns into horror was already admitted, in the same terms of lying and false embrace, by the court poet, who still counted it as part of the city's wealth, so the moralist's chapter answers a practice that praise poetry had treated as a sign of prosperity.

note: In Akananuru 123 the man in the desert mocks his heart, which can neither cross the hills for wealth nor stay with her without fearing poverty; the Pattinappalai hero tells his heart he will stay with her though the richest city is offered. On the reading that both answer the same choice between wealth and love, the first treats staying as fear of poverty and the second as the right decision.
teaches: Paalai poets argued both sides of the same debate with the heart, and the pair shows that giving up the journey (செலவழுங்குதல்) was a recognised, honourable answer to the very reproach Akananuru 123 makes, not only a failure of nerve.

note: Kural 212 says wealth earned by effort exists to do good to the worthy; in Natrinai 186 the wife says her husband crossed the waste for wealth with a heart that strives for others.
teaches: The wife in the poem defends a painful separation with the Kural's ethic of earning in order to give, so the household rule appears here as the reason that made the paalai journey honourable in her eyes.

note: In Kalittokai 81 the son's prattle is praised as 'நோய் நாம் தணிக்கும் மருந்து', the medicine that eases our illness; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 25 the pain of longing for the man's chest is met by the son's மழலைவாய் கட்டுரை.
teaches: Both make the child's prattle the cure for the wife's love-sickness in a marutham quarrel, and Kalittokai's longer scene shows what the venba compresses: the boy repeats words learned in the street, so his chatter can carry the father back into the house.

note: In Ainkurunuru 224 the heroine says bathing in the falls with them has become hard for him; in Akananuru 38 the friend imagines him finding the pool clear because the girls no longer leap in and bathe there.
teaches: The same lost bathing in the hill pool is blamed on his growing distance by the heroine and traced by the friend to the girls' own absence, so the end of shared play reads as neglect from inside the house and as confinement from the friend's wider view.

note: In Ainkurunuru 103 the friend tells the mother that the shore lord has become fit for the girl and she for him; in Ainkurunuru 280 the friend reminds the hill lord that on hearing he would marry she told her mother.
teaches: The neythal decade stages the friend's disclosure to the mother, and Kapilar's poem shows its price: she spoke only on the strength of the man's word, so her standing at home now hangs on his keeping it.

note: Both are the man at first sight of the girl: Kural 1081 asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, his heart reeling; Natrinai 8 asks whose daughter she is, blesses her father and wishes on her mother the fortune of Thondi.
teaches: Valluvar's man asks what she is and the Natrinai man whose she is, his first words going to her parents, so the Sangam poem shows the couplet's stunned wonder already turning toward the kin and the marriage that will need them.

note: Both use the same formula line (செவ் வேர்ப் பலவின் பயம் கெழு கொல்லி) and the god-made image on Kolli that does not decay: in Natrinai 201 the man says the girl stays in his heart like that image under storm and earthquake; in Akananuru 209 the friend says the absent man cannot forget her beauty, which is like that image.
teaches: The Kolli image lends its one property, that it does not perish, to the lover's memory in one poem and to the woman's beauty in the other, and both times it answers a doubter (the rebuking companion, the weeping girl), so the image worked as a stock guarantee that a bond will last.

note: Kar Narpathu 3: the friend, showing her own distress, says the wind, hail and thundering sky act as if all aimed at one lone woman. Kuruntokai 216: the heroine says the thundering cloud flashes with her life as its aim.
teaches: The complaint that the storm is aimed at her is the heroine's own in the older poem, and in the later venba the friend speaks it for her about 'one woman', so the charge against the rain had become a formula that could be handed from the sufferer to her companion.

note: Both use the simile of a poor man's youth (பொருள் இல்லான் இளமை, 38 line 15; the waste's trees in 10): poem 10 measures a withered landscape by it, poem 38 the girl's face drooping after a night of fear.
teaches: The paalai poet and Kapilar draw on one stock of moral similes, but Kapilar moves it from the land to the woman's body and pairs it with its opposite (the gracious man's wealth), so the girl's face becomes a landscape that his coming can drought or rain on, which is the kali form's way of turning a moral maxim into a lover's argument for marriage.

note: Kalittokai 143's woman asks why the king who guards the world's lives as his own does not guard hers; Purananuru 186 says the world lives by its king and the king must know he is its life.
teaches: The deserted woman takes the puram doctrine that the king is the people's life and finds its edge: a king can guard every life from war and want but not from a lover's leaving, so the akam poem marks a limit of royal protection that the puram counsel does not state.

note: Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what harm to evening; Ainkurunuru 116 has evening come while they weep, having driven before it a morning like itself.
teaches: The Kural keeps a kind morning against a hostile evening, while the older poem, on one reading, lets the evening swallow the morning too, so the couplet's neat split of the day is a later tidying of a grief that had no safe hour.

note: Fragment 1 says enemies cannot escape except by heaping rare jewels with elephants and speaking submissively (யானையொ(டு) அரும்கலம் ... பணிந்துவழி மொழிதல்); Akananuru 124 opens with the same formula (நன்கலம் களிற்றொடு ... வணங்கினர், வழிமொழிந்து) as the condition on which a soldier waiting in camp may go home to his wife.
teaches: The submission the praise poet demands as the enemy's only course is, in the akam poem, the event a homesick soldier waits for, so the formula of tribute served both genres and the end of the king's war was imagined from the camp as the start of a lover's return.

note: Purananuru 56.3-6 sets out the conch-white plough-bearer with the palmyra banner and the gem-dark one with the bird banner as two of four separate gods; Paripadal 1.3-11 gives the same emblems (வால் வளை மேனி, நாஞ்சில், சேவல் அம் கொடி) to one god addressed in the singular.
teaches: Held together, the pair shows that the emblem sets of Balarama and Thirumal were fixed common iconography, but that the Paripadal's Vaishnava singer had already fused the two brothers into one object of worship that the puram poet still counted as two gods.

note: Both open with யாயாகியளே and both have the friend tell how the wife hides her husband's cruelty (கொடுமை) out of shame; in 9 she wilts like an unworn flower, in 10 she comes as leader of the festival yet ashamed.
teaches: Placed together the two poets show the wife's concealment as a set karpu situation with two costs: it wastes her body in private and shames her in public, and in each case it is the friend, not the wife, who breaks the silence.

note: Both open with frogs in every hollow (அவல்தோறு, அவல்தொறும்) and the formula கார்தொடங் கின்றே/கின்றால் காலை; in Akananuru 364 the woman concludes that he in the king's camp does not think of us, in Ainkurunuru 453 that his chariot has set out toward us.
teaches: The same signs of the first rains, in nearly the same words, lead one wife to despair and another to expect the chariot, so the season's onset in mullai poetry is not itself a message: its meaning is decided by what the woman believes of the man.

note: Kural 1150 says the town is raising the very gossip they want, since it will bring the lover round; in Kuruntokai 302 the gossip that calls the pair inseparable is what she fears has kept him away. On this reading the same talk helps in one and harms in the other.
teaches: The pair shows alar cutting both ways in secret love: the talk the Kural's speaker welcomes as a lever toward marriage can, as the poem fears, frighten a lover into staying away altogether.

note: Kural 1 takes the letter அ, first of all letters, as the figure of the First Lord who is first of the world; Paripadal 2.58-59 uses the pointing letters அ, உ and எ (அவ்வும், உவ்வும், எவ்வயினோயும்) to say the god is that, this and whatever place.
teaches: Two early poets built theology from the Tamil alphabet in different ways: the Kural uses the order of the letters to make God the origin, while the hymn uses the pointing letters to make God every possible referent, origin set beside pervasion.

note: Both are spoken to the man about to leave, by the friend on one reading of the Kural: Ainkurunuru 149 asks him not to become able to go after causing her affliction, Kural 1151 tells him to promise a quick return only to those who will survive it.
teaches: The Sangam friend still appeals to the man's character, asking him not to be the kind who can leave, whereas the couplet has given up persuasion and answers his promise with the threat of her death.

note: In Akananuru 388 the girl, in private, mocks the diviner whose god is said to have caused her sickness; in Thinaimalai 12 the friend tells the household to send the velan away, free the kid and recognise the man who saved her from the flood.
teaches: The long poem stops at the girl's private scorn for the rite, and the short one shows the next move, so the pair shows mockery of the velan turning into the friend's disclosure to the family, where dismissing the diviner and naming the rescuer are one act.

note: Both men fear the girl's waist will break: the Kural through the flowers' stems, Thinaimalai 17 if she walks even a little.
teaches: The Kural keeps the snapping waist a joke of praise, a mock funeral drum, while Thinaimalai 17 lets the same fear spill into the man's own body, whose heart sways wherever she sways, so the conceit of her fragility becomes a measure of his surrender.

note: In Kural 1150 the friend tells the girl, the man overhearing, that the town is raising the very gossip they want; in Natrinai 354 the friend tells the man to his face that his friendship has become gossip as loud as the salt traders' din.
teaches: The pair shows the friend aiming the same town gossip toward marriage from two sides: told to the girl in his hearing it is the talk they hoped for, told to the man directly it is a public noise that shames his friendship.

note: Akananuru 4's friend says the flowering land turns its back on loneliness (புலம்புபுறக் கொடுப்ப) as his chariot comes into view; 495's man says the scrub's loneliness has ended (புலம்பு தீர்ந்து) because he came.
teaches: What the friend in Akananuru offers as a sign that he is about to arrive, the man in 495 claims as his own doing, so the land's loneliness was read as the woman's own, ending at the same moment hers does.

note: Paripadal 5.79-81 says what we ask of the god is not wealth, gold or pleasure (பொருளும் பொன்னும் போகமும் அல்ல) but grace, love and aram; Paripadal 21.68-70, after the drinking and dancing of the hill, asks that dwelling at his feet be granted as today (இன்று போல்), with their company.
teaches: The two Murugan songs end in prayers to the same god that pull apart: one refuses pleasure and asks for inner gifts, the other asks that a festival day of liquor, dance and couples simply recur, so the anthology holds both a moral and a festive idea of what worship should obtain.

note: Both are the friend telling the hill lord not to come by night but by day (இரவின் வாரல் ... பகலும் பெறுவை; இரவின் வருதல் எவனோ? பகல்வரின்), and both open on a tusker after a fight with a tiger, wounded in Akananuru 308, dreaming and ashamed in Kalittokai 49.
teaches: Akananuru 308 turns the refusal into a full plan of the day tryst, while Kalittokai 49 builds a triple refrain that calls his love sweet and his coming bitter, so the pair shows the same convention used once as an invitation and once to separate the lover from his risk, with the tiger-fight's aftermath serving each as the danger of the night path.

note: Kural 1268 has the man, held by the king's war, wish that the king win so that he may join his wife and hold the evening feast for guests; Natrinai 374's man, returning from his work, asks travellers about the wife who longs to feast guests yet weeps.
teaches: The couplet gives the feast for guests as the man's own goal after duty, while the Natrinai poem puts the same wish in the wife and shows it unfulfilled in her tears, so the household's guest-feast was the shared picture of reunion that each partner ascribed to the other.

note: 110 tells the three kings that Parambu is hard to take though they join forces; Akananuru 78 recalls Pari, with Kapilar beside him, driving off the tusked kings after years of fighting.
teaches: The akam poem treats as settled history what 110 states as a boast during the siege, so the pair shows the defence of Parambu passing from Kapilar's own war-speech into the shared stock of akam similes.

note: 431 praises those without desire, and 440 tells one how to enjoy desire safely. Parimelazhagar resolves this by making the fault excess in 431, but the verses themselves pull apart.
teaches: Removing and hiding are different programmes.

note: Natrinai 23's friend says the girl's thinness is hidden by her bangles and her loose hair excused by play, but her eyes cannot hide love; Kural 1271 has the man tell her that though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control and have something to say.
teaches: The Natrinai supplies the test behind Valluvar's claim by sorting the signs of love into those an excuse can cover and the eyes, which none can, so the couplet's 'though you hide' turns out to name a practice of concealment the older poem lays out part by part.

note: In 371 the returning hero tells his charioteer that the rain has begun toward where she lives, that she has begun to burn and the herdsmen have begun their flutes; in 364 the heroine herself says the herdsmen's flutes in the rainy evening will take her life.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the man's guess on the road matching what the woman says at home almost sound for sound, so the herdsmen's evening flute was a shared code in mullai by which each partner knew the other's hour, and the hero's haste is grounded in knowing exactly how that evening falls on her.

note: Kural 720 likens speaking before those not of one's circle to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Innaa 10 counts reciting a song where no one grasps its meaning as painful.
teaches: The couplet locates the waste in the hearers' unfitness, and the Innaa, by setting the song beside the poor man's generosity, shows it as a gift wasted on both sides: the giver of words has no receiver, the would-be giver of goods has nothing.

note: Both have the girl hold to the man's goodness while her pallor spreads: in Kural 1184 she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits yet pallor comes; in Ainkurunuru 286 she says he seems to have loved her without blemish yet takes her beauty.
teaches: In both the girl refuses to blame the man and lays the loss elsewhere, on the pallor as a cheat in the Kural and on his love itself in the Sangam poem, so the pair shows a fixed rule of her speech: the waste of her beauty is never his fault in her own mouth.

note: 292 defends a warrior who stopped the king's toddy being mixed and will not wait his turn; 298 has a warrior angry that the king does not tell him 'you go first'.
teaches: Both turn a quarrel over drink into a claim to the front line, which shows the feast's order was read as a promise about the battle, and a warrior who seized one was claiming the other.

iraicchi.act: the young buck leaps and plays together with his doe in the first rains
iraicchi.sense: the creatures keep their mates beside them in this season, so the man who fixed this time will be beside her now

ullurai.tenor: the girl herself, who tasted union and is now bound by longing

pairs.situation: she has tasted the sweetness of union with him
she is now caught in the bond of desire and cannot free herself

ullurai.tenor: the man who took his pleasure of her and went

pairs.situation: the shore lord takes what is not his, her beauty
that beauty was her family's charge, kept for them
she watched against the small thieves and missed the one that mattered

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses her own task on the shore drying-ground, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame; thirattu 9 says Madurai's fame will stand and blossom as long as the king's hill exists (குன்றம் உண்டாகும் அளவு).
teaches: The Kural makes fame the one thing that does not perish, while the Paripadal blessing gives even the city's fame a term measured by a hill, so the poets' praise of undying renown was bounded by the oldest lasting things of the land.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as investigating without favour and acting after judgement toward everyone; in Kuruntokai 276 the lover thinks of taking his case to the just king's court and at once asks what would become of her.
teaches: The lover's question shows where the Kural's impartial justice stops: a harm done without intent by an innocent girl is real but cannot be judged, so the just court is imagined only to be abandoned.

note: In both a man returning from work passes a deer pair: in Akananuru 34 he himself sees the stag feed and guard his doe and urges the charioteer on; in Natrinai 121 the charioteer points to the doe resting with her stag to calm him.
teaches: The same deer pair works as a spur when the hero reads it and as a sedative when the charioteer offers it, so the mullai image carries a promise of home whose force depends on who in the chariot speaks.

note: In Kural 1155 the woman tells her friend to prevent the departure of the one fit for her, since once he goes union is hard; in Kuruntokai 334 she tells her friend that if he leaves, what they lose is only their one life.
teaches: Both speak to the friend before a parting, but the couplet asks for help to stop it while the poem asks for none and names the price, her life, so the pair shows the same plea in two moods, one still bargaining and one already resigned.

note: Both use பொய்யா விளக்கு. In 299 the unfailing lamp of the wise is truthfulness and all other lamps are no lamps. Here the same phrase names money.
teaches: Whether this is a deliberate reversal can't be proved, but the two verses compete for one title.

note: 227 tells Death it has cooked and eaten its seed (வித்துஅட்டு உண்டனை) in taking Valavan; 230 likens Death to a failing farmer who eats his seed (வித்து உண்டாஅங்கு) in taking Ezhini.
teaches: Two poets on different kings make the same argument through the seed image, that a slain warrior was the source of Death's future harvest of enemies, which shows that taunting Death with its own loss was a recognised move in kaiyarunilai and not one poet's conceit.

note: In Akananuru 60 the friend warns the hero not to crush the bangle of a girl fine as Porayan's Tondi; in Kuruntokai 238 the friend tells the lord of the fields to give back a beauty that was like Tondi and go.
teaches: Both friends price the girl's beauty by the Chera port of Tondi, one before harm, as a warning, and one after, as a demand for restitution, so the town's fame served as the standard of a beauty that can be damaged and must be repaid.

note: Kural 578 gives the world to those able to show kannottam without spoiling the task; Patitruppattu 22 lists கழிகண்ணோட்டம், excessive kindly regard, among the obstacles to the wheel of dharma, beside anger and harsh punishment.
teaches: The Chera list names as a fault exactly the excess the Kural's condition guards against, which shows that the Kural's praise of kannottam was already bounded in older court ethics where too much mercy blocked a king's justice.

note: Kural 1224: in the lover's absence evening comes like enemies to a killing field; Kalittokai 120 makes evening a hunter aiming at a deer, a mocker of the beaten, a man pushing a spear into a burn, and Death grinning with the crescent as its tooth.
teaches: The poem unfolds the couplet's single image of evening as executioner into a series of cruelties each aimed at someone already wounded, which shows that the Kural's 'like enemies' means an attack on the defenceless, not just a hostile arrival.

note: Akananuru 226 sets the husband's scandalous bathing with another woman at Matti's Kazhar ford; Ainkurunuru 61 makes Matti's Kazhar the standard for the women he courts.
teaches: For the marutham wife the patron's rich ford had become shorthand for the husband's other women, so a chief's town entered akam as a place of the hero's pleasures, not only of the patron's fame.

note: Kural 443 says that to cherish the great and make them one's own is the rarest of rare things; Patitruppattu 79 says the king honours the great and cherishes the small (பெரியோர்ப் பேணிச் சிறியோரை அளித்தி), between lines on not sparing his life in war and sparing nothing in giving.
teaches: The Kural singles out honouring the great as a ruler's hardest gain, while the Chera poem pairs it with care for the small and sets both beside courage and giving, so the maxim appears as one term of a balanced royal portrait rather than a rarity standing alone.

note: Purananuru 158 names Ori as the one who ruled Kolli (கொல்லி ஆண்ட வல்வில் ஓரியும்) among the seven givers now dead; Natrinai 346 measures the wife's fragrant hair by the kulavi of the great cool Kolli of Porayan.
teaches: Set beside the elegy that names Ori as Kolli's dead lord, the love poem's passing epithet shows the hill in the Chera Porayan's hands, so the pair records that Kolli changed masters after Ori, which neither poem states.

note: The Kural says a trader's true trade is to care for others' goods as his own; the idyll's merchants weigh their own goods and others' alike (தமவும் பிறவு மொப்ப நாடி) and take no more and give no less.
teaches: The idyll's phrase is nearly the Kural's பிறவும் தமபோல், and it adds the working test of fair dealing at the scale, so the maxim appears first as the praised reputation of a real merchant class in a named port before it is stated as a rule for all traders.

note: Naladiyar 125 says the bond (தொடர்பு) with small men wanes (தேயுமே) of itself like the moon while friendship with the great grows; Kuruntokai 42 asks the hill lord whether our bond (எம் தொடர்பும்) will wane (தேயுமோ) even if desire ends.
teaches: The same two words, bond and waning, show the friend putting the lover to the Naladiyar's test of character: a bond that wanes once its first cause, desire, is spent marks the small man, so her question demands that he prove himself one of the great.

note: Akananuru 337: the hero reminds his heart, which presses for another journey, that once it found parting no joy, said 'let wealth stay where it is' and came back alone through the robbers' waste. Kuruntokai 151: the hero refuses the hill path, saying going would end his youth.
teaches: Kuruntokai 151 gives the moment of refusal, and Akananuru 337 shows that such a refusal does not settle anything: the heart that once turned back is urging the road again, so the decision not to leave is a choice that must be remade, not a resolution.

note: Akananuru 86: the husband recalls the wedding held at a bright dawn when the moon stood free of the evil planet on a faultless day. Thinaimalai 54: the friend tells the hero to call the diviners and choose a day.
teaches: The diviners' day that the friend demands in the venba is the day the older poem remembers by the moon's freedom from the planet, so the pair shows the omen-reading as the hinge that turns the secret tryst into the public rite.

note: Kuruntokai 148: if you say this is not the rainy season (காரன்று என்றி), is this a dream? Thinaimalai 103: you say the season has not come (பருவந்தான் பட்டின்றே என்றி); with tears I have cooked my life for it.
teaches: Both women quote the friend's denial of the season with the same என்றி, but the Kuruntokai woman answers with the evidence of the flowers and the Thinaimalai woman with the cost to her life, so the reply moves from disputing the fact to declaring the dispute too late.

note: Both have the friend (for Parimelazhagar in the Kural) speak to the man about to part: Kural 1151 refuses his promise of a quick return, saying tell it to those who will be alive; Ainkurunuru 285 asks how he can part and leave her here with her bangles slipping.
teaches: The Kural states the friend's refusal as a bare threat to the girl's life, while the Sangam poem sets the same refusal in the girl's daily field life and names the visible sign, the slipping bangle, so the Kural's abstract 'those who will be alive' is shown as wasting already begun.

note: Kural 1271 has the man tell the girl that though she hides it, her eyes go beyond her control and speak; in Kuruntokai 312 the man marvels that by dawn she is wholly one of her kin again, face unmoved. On the poem's reading her concealment holds.
teaches: The pair sets two views of the girl's secret side by side: the Kural's man reads it in her eyes, Kapilar's man admires a disguise he cannot see through, so concealment in kalavu is both a failure and an art.

note: Kural 1311: all women feast on you in common with their eyes, philanderer; I will not come near your chest. Thinaimalai 152: the wife refuses her husband's marked chest under cover of the son's drool and her milk.
teaches: The Kural's wife refuses the chest openly and for the least offence, being looked at; the Thinaimalai's wife has proof printed on the chest and still refuses only by indirection, so the couplet's open charge and the quatrain's domestic pretext mark two registers of one refusal, the second keeping the house's peace while making the charge.

note: In Kuruntokai 376 the man says his beloved is cool like Pothiyil sandal in summer and warm like a lotus heart in the cold; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 24 the wife says her shoulders were once sandal paste to him and are now hotter than caustic.
teaches: The lover's praise of a body that tempers every season is answered by the wife's claim that the same body's heat follows his conduct, not the weather, so the courtship image is shown to depend on fidelity.

note: The line ஆசா கெந்தை யாண்டுளன் கொல்லோ closes the friend's memory of how he won the girl in 176 and stands in 325 after the heroine admits she herself told him to go.
teaches: The same cry for the lost support carries blame of the man in the friend's poem and self-reproach in the heroine's, so the pair shows a formula line taking its charge from who speaks it and what precedes it.

note: Kural 1151, the friend (for Parimelazhagar) to the departing man: tell me if you are not going; tell your quick return to those still alive then. Thinaimozhi 12, the friend to the man leaving for wealth: who can know her helplessness better than you?
teaches: Holding them together shows two moves in the friend's attempt to stop the journey: the couplet threatens with the woman's death, while the venba appeals to the man's own knowledge of her, making him the witness who cannot claim ignorance.

note: In 170 a small white gull tears the neythal of the backwater, and the friend is asked why the eyes of one with such a good man grow pale; in 190 reapers cut down the neythal flower while harvesting white paddy, and the man has made her eyes weep.
teaches: Both hide the spoiled eyes in a destroyed neythal, but the destroyers differ: the gull tears it to feed, the reapers fell it only because it stands among the grain they want, so the decade offers two kinds of blame, appetite and indifference, for the same harm.

note: In Natrinai 145 the friend tells the girl that the unjust mother suspects them and still the chariot bell comes softly down their street at midnight; in Ainkurunuru 102 the friend tells the mother herself that the chariot bell rings sweetly to end the girl's grief.
teaches: The chariot bell is the sound of stealth to be hidden from a suspicious mother in one poem and the sound announced to that mother as relief in the other, so the pair shows the disclosure changing the meaning of the lover's signal from danger to remedy.

note: Akananuru 46: the friend refusing the husband entry describes his town's red-eyed buffalo breaking its tether in the night, scattering fish and grazing the lotus. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the red-eyed buffalo breaks its wooden clog, eats the field crop and rests in the shade, and the bard is told to carry this to the flower-like women.
teaches: The same hidden comparison is aimed at different hearers: in Akananuru 46 it shames the husband at the door, in the venba it is sent through the bard to the other women as a warning, which shows the buffalo ullurai was a portable accusation that could be addressed to either party of the triangle.

note: Natrinai 44: the man remembers the girl after she bathed in the falls with her companions, her large eyes reddened by the beating water. Ainthinai Aimpathu 15: the friend says the girl's red-lined eyes reddened because they bathed in the leaping falls after plucking vengai.
teaches: The eyes reddened by the waterfall are a cherished sight for the lover in Natrinai and an explanation offered to others in Ainthinai, so the same bath serves both the love and its concealment, which is why it is safe for the friend to name.

note: The Kural says nothing stands undying in the world but towering fame; the idyll sets beside the patron's choice of fame a crowd of dead rich men past counting whose names went with them.
teaches: The Kural states that fame alone survives without saying what the alternative looks like; the idyll supplies it as a number, the sands of a riverbank, so the couplet's single survivor is measured against a vast forgetting.

note: In Mullaippattu the old women seeking an omen hear a herd girl tell the calves 'இன்னே வருகுவர் தாயர்' and take it as a sign; in Kar Narpathu 2 the lightning speaks his message, 'இன்னே வருவர் நமர்'.
teaches: The same formula of reassurance, 'they will come at once', is an overheard chance word in the idyll's omen rite and the sky's own message in the venba, so the later poem turns the ritual of listening for a sign into the season speaking for the absent man.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; if you mean to come back soon, tell it to those who will still be alive. Aimpathu 34: the friend asks the man whether he will cross many wastes of killing robbers, leaving the woman of sword-bright eyes.
teaches: Both are said to the man at the point of departure to stop him, but the Kural argues from the woman's death and the Aimpathu from the man's own danger among robbers, so the pair shows the two levers the dissuading speaker can pull against the journey, her life and his.

note: Purananuru 2 praises a Chera for feeding the armies without limit while the hundred fought the Five until they fell; the idyll uses the same war to say its king roared at his victory like the Five when all the hundred fell.
teaches: The pair shows two ways Sangam praise borrowed the Bharata war: the Chera poem keeps its king outside the war as the feeder of both sides, while the Tondai idyll puts its king in the victors' place, so the epic could measure a king's giving or his conquest.

note: 134 says the woman's beauty came back by itself with the shore lord; 137 asks whether the women who loved the lord ever get back their former beauty, implying they do not.
teaches: Within one decade the same speaker holds both that beauty returns with the lord and that those who loved him never regain it, so the decade shows the restored beauty of 134 as one turn of a cycle that 137 suspects will not last.

note: Paripadal 8.96-108 shows the crowd at Parankundram carrying flowers, incense and lamps and asking for children, wealth and victory; Thiruppugazh 8, sung at Parangiri, confesses that the poet never worshipped with flowers or walked round the hill and asks only that Murugan come at the hour of death.
teaches: The rites the Sangam festival performs as means to this-world ends become, at the same hill a thousand years later, the list of duties the devotee confesses he failed, and the request moves from children and wealth to rescue at death.

note: In 369 the friend calls the paalai road pleasant, its pods rattling like anklets, and urges the girl to go; in 378 the foster mother, after the girl has gone, can only pray that the same road's sun and bare paths be cooled.
teaches: The one elopement road is a promise to the girl's accomplice and a danger to the woman who raised her, so the pair shows the akam books dividing a single event between voices who cannot both be right about the land.

note: Ainkurunuru 311 has the woman ask whether the man who crossed the forest will stay long (நீடுவர் கொல்); in Akananuru 69 the friend, by its colophon, comforts the woman who fears his delay with the answer that he will not stay long (நீடலர்) though he crossed the Mauryan cut.
teaches: The four-line poem gives only the woman's question and the long poem only the friend's answer, so together they show that the paalai exchange turned on a single verb of delay, asked in one mouth as a fear and returned in the other as a promise.

note: Kural 782: the friendship of the worthy grows like the waxing moon. Thinaimozhi 41: the worthy man's bond has waned since the day she saw him, and his trysts proved false; on a plain reading the heroine's case contradicts the maxim.
teaches: The heroine's question ஐயகொல் ஆன்றார் தொடர்பு tests the Kural's rule against one man and finds it failing, so the akam poem uses the ethical maxim as a weapon: either the rule is wrong or he was never one of the worthy.

note: Kuruntokai 190: at midnight in the storm she hears the cattle stall's one bell ring with every step of the bull; Kural 1168: the night that puts all beings to sleep has her alone for company.
teaches: The Kural's claim that she alone keeps the night company is proved in the Kuruntokai by what she hears: only a wakeful listener counts the bull's every step by its bell, so the single sound measures the sleepless solitude the couplet asserts.

note: In Akananuru 164 the hero in camp says his wife could regain her beauty this season if only the fierce king would release him; in Ainkurunuru 467 the friend says the king is hurrying more than they are.
teaches: The hero's own speech shows the king as what holds him back, while the friend at home claims the king is more eager than the wives, so the friend's comfort is revealed as persuasion built on a report the camp itself contradicts.

note: Kural 1183: the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange; Kuruntokai 236: the friend tells the man that if he means to leave he must first give back the beauty he has consumed.
teaches: The couplet records the exchange as done, and the poem turns the same commercial idea into a demand for repayment that cannot be met, which makes it an argument that he must stay.

note: Kural 882 says to fear the enemy who seems like kin; Thirikadugam counts taking by the hand a man formerly enraged against one as the conduct of one about to die.
teaches: The couplet warns against the hidden foe in general; the verse names the concrete act, taking back a former enemy, and states its outcome as death.

note: Both have the woman speak of her heart that has gone after the man: in Ainkurunuru 295 she wonders whether the heart that went with the hill man will come back or settle there; in Kural 1248 she calls her heart foolish for following the one who left, pining that he will not show grace.
teaches: The Kural judges the following heart a fool because the man has gone and withholds his grace, while the Ainkurunuru girl, with no doubt of him, only wonders whether her heart will return, so the pair shows that the same act of the heart going after the man is not folly in itself and is judged by how the man answers it.

note: Purananuru 152: Ori, met as a hunter in the wilds, gives a strange troupe meat, toddy, gold and gems unasked. Natrinai 52: even wealth equal to the giving of Ori, lord of the Mazhavar, would be slight against his wife's embrace.
teaches: The puram poem shows Ori's giving as so lavish it reached strangers in the wilderness, and the akam poem takes exactly that giving as the upper limit of what a man could hope to gain and still sets it below love, so the pair shows a patron's fame serving akam poets as a fixed measure of wealth.

note: Akananuru 24: in the last days of the cold rains, when the pakanrai opens, the man in the king's camp pictures his wife crossing the cold nights alone; Ainkurunuru 456: in the dewy cold season of pakanrai, the wife asks whether the men who promised to stay do not think of her.
teaches: Her question in 456, does he not think of us, is answered in Akananuru 24, where in the same pakanrai season he does think of her from the camp, so the pair shows that remembering runs both ways while neither lover can know it.

iraicchi.act: the male monkey buries unripe plantains in the ploughed clearing to let them ripen and then rests at ease
iraicchi.sense: the man has laid his pledge by as the monkey lays by its fruit, so she can rest on it until it ripens into marriage

iraicchi.act: the male dove gleans paddy from a ruined village to feed his mate, weak after laying
iraicchi.sense: the man taking her across the waste means to provide for her as the dove provides for his mate

ullurai.tenor: the man, his other women and the household he disturbs
