pairs.situation: he plunges into the company of other women
the household is scattered by his doings

pairs.scene: இருள் புனை மருதின் இன் நிழல் வதியும்
pairs.situation: after his pleasure he would rest at ease in the wife's house

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the buffalo of the marutham pond in a marutham poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the doe and the stag cry out together in the parched track, sharing its hardship instead of parting
iraicchi.sense: even the deer of the waste keep together in distress, while he faces the road alone and she wilts alone at home

iraicchi.act: the tusker embraces his mate and, though starving, does not leave for other lands but suffers the hunger with her
iraicchi.sense: even the beast in drought will not leave his mate for a richer land, so the man who would leave her for wealth falls below it

iraicchi.act: the bull buffalo stays and rests together with his mate in the shaded pool
iraicchi.sense: as the bull keeps beside his mate in her father's fields, the man means to settle with her as husband

iraicchi.act: the hen, thinking of the cock gone to find food, sits on the kalli fork and calls in loneliness
iraicchi.sense: even a bird whose mate is only gone to fetch food cries out, so the man who knows that road knows what his going does to her

note: Naladiyar 2 tells those who gain wealth to share its food with many at once, since wealth turns like a cart wheel; the idyll's bard passes on to others what he received on the road, and the king, weighing the instability of the world, will not dismiss his guest.
teaches: The impermanence that the Naladiyar uses as an argument for giving is already in the idyll a motive at both ends of the gift, the bard redistributing as he goes and the king holding on to the guest, so instability argued for keeping company as well as for releasing wealth before it became a quatrain about wealth alone.

note: Purananuru 55 wishes the Pandya the heat of the sun, the coolness of the moon and the giving of the rain; Kalittokai 100 praises the husband, as king, with the sun's harshness to foes, the moon's coolness to those under his parasol and the rain's giving, then says each praise is ruined by his wife's tears, bangles and pallor.
teaches: The akam friend takes the stock triad of royal praise found in the Purananuru and makes each term hostage to a woman's body, showing that the same encomium could be turned into a reproach by asking whether its subject meets it at home.

note: The Paripadal fragment likens Madurai to the lotus from Mayon's navel, its streets the petals and the lord's palace the pericarp; the idyll has Kanchi's tall-housed town rise like the pericarp of the lotus from the blue god's navel that bore the four-faced one.
teaches: The navel-lotus with the central great house as its pericarp was a shared figure of city praise used for Kanchi as well as Madurai, so it was a convention for a Tamil capital rather than a legend of one city.

note: Kural 319: harm done to others in the forenoon returns of itself in the afternoon; 123: what is done in this life bears fruit in this life, as the women who tormented us have now been burned.
teaches: The Kural's impersonal rule that harm returns soon is here voiced by an injured wife about her rivals, showing how the ethical maxim of quick retribution was taken into akam as a scorned woman's satisfaction rather than a warning to oneself.

note: Purananuru 6 wishes the Pandya Mudukudumi to lean to no side like the beam of a balance (ஞமன்); the idyll gives the same balance (ஞெமன்கோல்) to Madurai's court of justice, which puts away fear, grief, desire, hatred and delight.
teaches: The impartiality that the earlier poem asks of the king in person has, in Nedunjeliyan's Madurai, become the work of an institution, and the idyll spells out the five passions the court must set aside, which the wish to the king left unnamed.

note: Kural 1064 says the dignity that will not beg even when nothing is left is too great for all the world to hold (இடமெல்லாம் கொள்ளா); Paripadal 12.101 ends by telling the Vaiyai that this flower-topped world cannot hold its fame (நின் புகழ் கொள்ளாது, இம் மலர் தலை உலகே).
teaches: The same measure, a greatness the world is too small to hold, is given by the hymn to a river's yearly plenty and by the Kural to a destitute man's refusal to ask, so the pair shows the ethical book taking the praise formula of abundance and fixing it on the one thing that has no abundance at all.

note: Naladiyar 85 says men who forced themselves on other men's wives in a former birth are born eunuchs in this one; 123 says those who think deeds bear fruit in the next birth do not understand, since the fruit comes here.
teaches: The Naladiyar defers the reckoning to a later birth while the quatrain insists on this one, so the pair shows a live disagreement in the didactic age about where retribution is seen, with the love poet choosing the visible, present punishment.

note: 131 makes the friendship good only so long as gossip does not rise; 132 says the town has now made gossip of the lord's very grace.
teaches: Read in sequence the decade's first two poems pass from the condition to its breach: the gossip that 131 named as the bond's limit has arisen in 132, and it has risen not from his neglect but from his kindness.

note: Patitruppattu 17 says the king's great victory drum was made from the kadamba he cut after driving back the sea (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய வலம்படு வியன்பணை); in Akananuru 347 the heroine compares the street's gossip to the drum of Cheralathan who drove back the sea and cut the kadamba (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய பண்ணமை முரசின்).
teaches: The near-identical wording shows an akam poet borrowing the Chera's victory drum, a puram fact, to measure how loud gossip is, so the king's war trophy had become familiar enough to serve as a household simile for noise.

note: Kural 331 calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for lasting. Kuruntokai 143's friend says impermanence alone is permanent, and draws hope from it.
teaches: The Kural uses impermanence to rebuke attachment, but the friend of the love poem applies the same truth to grief, showing that the doctrine was a two-edged tool: what cannot last includes the pallor of longing, so it consoles as readily as it warns.

note: Kalittokai 11: the woman says the man himself told her that in the burning forest the tusker lets his mate drink the little muddy water first, the dove fans its tired mate and the stag shades the doe, so he will return. Kuruntokai 37: the friend gives one tusker stripping the yaa for his mate.
teaches: The later Kalittokai multiplies the single tusker into three caring males and puts the inference in the heroine's own mouth, which shows the comforting iraicchi of porul 5.35 growing from the friend's one proof into a catalogue the heroine argues from.

note: Thinaimozhi 7 uses ஊரறி கௌவை, gossip the town knows, as the harm that a night visit will bring; Kural 1143 has the man welcome the ஊரறிந்த கெளவை as a foretaste of having her. On a plain reading the town's gossip is a threat in one and a gain in the other.
teaches: The same phrase is a warning in the friend's mouth and a prize in the lover's, so the Kural's couplet reads as his reply to exactly the argument the friend uses to keep him away.

note: The Kural says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; in the idyll everyone in the patron's town looks on the arriving bards sweetly and gladly before any gift is given.
teaches: The Kural makes the host's face the guest's first need inside one household; the idyll extends that glad look to a whole town, so the welcoming face becomes a public mark of the patron's realm rather than a private courtesy.

note: The logician's perception grasps name, class, quality and action and sits among ten means; Aravanar's Buddhist logic keeps two means and takes name, class, quality and action out of perception.
teaches: The epic stages the theory of knowledge as a reply across two kaathais: what the Vedic logician packs into seeing, the Buddhist teacher moves into inference, so the dispute is over where conceptual labels enter knowledge.

note: In Kuruntokai 153 the girl's heart, which once took fright when the hill owl hooted, now goes out through the dark night toward him; in Natrinai 83 the friend begs the owl at the town ghat not to sound its fearful cry while they wait awake for him.
teaches: The owl's cry is the standard measure of the night tryst's fear, and the pair shows it split between two roles: love has carried the girl's heart past that fear, while the friend, who manages the meeting, still has to buy the owl's silence with offerings.

note: Paripadal 6.44-51 has the learned brahmins dismayed that the flood is changed by flowers, roots, the food of common people and spilled toddy; thirattu 2.58-63 splits the refusal among பார்ப்பார், அந்தணர் and ஐயர, each for its own stain: toddy, lovers' wedding scents, honey.
teaches: The two songs together show that the priests' refusal to bathe was a set piece of the Vaiyai festival song, and the fragment's three causes make plain what song 6 only lists: every stain that bars the priest is a mark of the festival the town is enjoying, so the scene sets ritual purity against the river's festive use.

note: In Akananuru 279 the man leaves because men who stay at their wife's breast cannot bear to see friends in want and kin in distress; in Kuruntokai 137 the man swears that if he ever leaves his wife, may suppliants stop coming to him.
teaches: The same value, being the one the needy come to, drives the man out of the house in the Akananuru and binds him to it in the Kuruntokai, where losing the suppliants is the curse for leaving, so the puram duty to give could be argued on either side of the akam choice to go or stay.

note: 797 says dropping a fool's friendship is gain. 805 says when an old friend hurts you, consider it folly and go on.
teaches: The same பேதைமை is a reason for leaving in one chapter and an excuse for staying in the next, and the only difference is how old the bond is.

note: Both set the sleeping world against the one woman awake in separation; Kuruntokai 6 leaves her alone awake under the dead night, Kural 1168 makes the night itself her companion, pitied for having no one else.
teaches: The Kural turns the bare Sangam contrast of a sleeping world and one waking woman into a conceit in which the night shares her vigil, so the couplet adds a companion, even a mocked one, to a solitude the older poem leaves complete.

note: Kural 1228 has the waiting woman say the herdsman's flute is the messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills; Natrinai 364's heroine says the herdsmen's kondrai flutes and the cattle bells at evening will take her life if they come with the rain after the named season has passed.
teaches: The couplet's flute that kills is given its setting by the Natrinai poem, cows driven home, bells that never knew thunder and the season he named already gone, which shows why a sweet pastoral sound became deadly: it marks the homecoming hour, and the season promise turns it into proof that he has not come.

note: Ainkurunuru 87: the other woman says the wife sulks at everyone, so why at her. Akananuru 186: the courtesan says the wife quarrels with her (எம்மொடு புலக்கும்), but she is not the enemy; the husband who leaves women pale is.
teaches: The four-line protest that the wife's sulk is aimless becomes in the Akananuru a full defence that redirects the blame to the husband, so the pair shows the courtesan's answer to the wife's anger as a set speech with two steps: she is not singled out, and the fault lives in the wife's own house.

note: In Natrinai 104 the girl asks whether anyone but her thinks of the narrow midnight path he takes while thunder strikes and floods block the way. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 19 the friend, picturing him swimming the falls at midnight, says her heart asks what will become of the girl.
teaches: The girl fears the night path for the man, and the friend fears it for the girl who would not survive his harm, so the pair shows the danger of the night meeting passing through two hearts, with the friend's fear one step removed and therefore usable as an argument for marriage.

note: On the Kural reading where gossip feeds love and keeps it from drooping, Kuruntokai 97 disagrees: the secret turned to talk in the square is one of four things scattered apart, with her beauty lost and the man in his own town.
teaches: The man in the Kural can welcome gossip as fuel for love, while the woman in the Kuruntokai counts it among her losses, so the pair shows that rumour's value in the akam world depends on which lover bears it.

note: In Kuruntokai 201 a bat that has eaten sweet mango gulps sour nelli and hangs from the bamboo, in a poem of good news that the hill lord will come; in Natrinai 87 a bat hanging asleep on a mango only dreams of the sour nelli of a far forest, and her day of longing passes like that dream.
teaches: The same bat, mango and sour nelli carry fulfilment or its absence according to whether the bat eats or only dreams, matching the good news of Kuruntokai 201 and the empty day of Natrinai 87, so the poets varied one fixed image by a single verb to change its sense.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the son has been fed and we are old now (மூத்தேம் இனியாம்); go to the young women's street. Kainnilai 45: we are old now, bard (மூத்தேம் இனிப்பாண), young before, and we did not know he would leave.
teaches: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47 offers age as the reason he goes to younger women, while Kainnilai 45 sets the same words against his old promises, so the pair shows the formula of the ageing wife used once to explain his straying and once to expose a betrayal she could not foresee.

note: Kural 64 makes the gruel stirred by children's small hands sweeter than amrita; Ainkurunuru 309 asks whether wealth gained across the waste is sweeter than an unborn son's smile.
teaches: The couplet's household ranking of children above every delicacy becomes, in the friend's mouth, a direct argument against the wealth journey, showing that the Kural's measure of sweetness was already a tool for weighing a husband's absence against his family.

note: Kural 1265 wishes to see the கொண்கன் with full eyes so that the pallor of her soft shoulders (மென்தோள்) may leave; Ainkurunuru 120 reports that her soft shoulders (மெல் தோளே) have become beautiful because the lord has come.
teaches: The Kural states as a hope that the sight of the shore lord will cure the shoulders, and the Ainkurunuru records the cure as done, so the couplet's optative has an older poem in which the wish was already fulfilled.

note: In Akananuru 38 the friend imagines the hill man, garlanded with vengai and blue lily and carrying a bow, coming to the swing by the asoka and the harvested millet field and finding them deserted; in Natrinai 376 she tells the parrots to tell the man with the garland and bow who appears by the asoka that the mother still guards even the empty field.
teaches: Together they show the harvested millet field as the clock of the kalavu plot: once the crop is cut the daytime meeting place is gone, and the friend's two messages, where our village is in Akananuru 38 and the guard that stays on the empty field in Natrinai 376, both push the man to come openly as a suitor.

note: Kalittokai 136 likens the girl's joy at each meeting to a gambler's winning throw and her grief at his leaving to the loss of a stake; Kural 932 says the gambler gains one and loses a hundred.
teaches: Read with the couplet's arithmetic of the dice, the friend's simile becomes a warning: a secret love that runs on wins and losses must end in ruin on balance, which is why she ends by telling him to take the girl in marriage and stop the game.

note: Kuruntokai 202 sets the nerunji's flower, sweet to the eye, before its thorn as the lover's kindness before his cruelty; Kural 1120 uses only the nerunji fruit, the thorn, to say how soft things feel to her feet.
teaches: Both poets know the nerunji as a plant that pleases first and pricks after; the couplet takes only the prick to praise a woman's delicacy, while the Sangam poem uses the order of flower and thorn to tell the history of a love, so the same plant can measure a body or a story.

note: Kural 1104: the man asks where she got this fire that burns when he moves away and cools when he draws near. Kuruntokai 150: the woman says the pain swells when she thinks of his chest and vanishes when she embraces it.
teaches: The Kural's man finds the paradoxical fire in the woman, but the Kuruntokai heroine finds the same sickness in herself and sets it off by memory, not distance, so the pair shows that the burning-and-cooling belongs to both lovers and that thinking of the absent one is itself the burning.

note: Avvai praises Athiyaman for giving her the nelli fruit without saying what it would do for him; the idyll lists Athikan as the giver of the nectar-yielding fruit to Avvai.
teaches: Avvai's poem makes the hiddenness of the fruit's virtue the point of the gift, whereas the idyll names that virtue openly (அமிழ்துவிளை), so by the time the story joined the list of seven the secret had become its public meaning.

note: Natrinai 52 has the man refuse the 'life of living apart' (பிரிந்து உறை வாழ்க்கை) for his wife's athiral-and-paathiri scented hair; Natrinai 337 has the friend say that wealth-makers by custom live apart (பிரிந்து உறை மரபின) and forgo that same scented hair.
teaches: The shared phrase and the same flowers show the choice put in fixed terms, and the pair tempers the friend's complaint: what she calls a custom set when the world was made, the man of Natrinai 52 does turn down, so it is a choice and not a law.

note: Kural 386 says the land of a king easy to see and not harsh of speech is praised above others; Patitruppattu 86 tells how the report of the king's killing in war made the poet fear him, until he found him the patron of singers who ends the misery of the poor and is gentle as cool river water.
teaches: The couplet treats being easy to approach as a plain royal virtue, while the poem shows what it has to overcome: a king's fame for killing keeps suppliants away, so his accessibility has to be proved against his own reputation.

note: In Akananuru 16 the wife finds a courtesan clasping their son in the chariot street and gently asks if she is his mother too; in Kalittokai 82 the son's visits to the father's women, who adorn and kiss him, make the wife call for a stick.
teaches: The same encounter of the son with his father's women draws grace from one wife and fury from another, showing that marutham poets used it to test the wife's karpu: the Akananuru wife proves her dignity by kindness, the Kalittokai wife her love by jealousy.

note: Kural 1227: the sickness buds at morning and blooms at evening; Kalittokai 130: as the great backwater flowers close at evening, her heart closes in ruin (அழிவொடு கூம்பும்).
teaches: The two invert one flower image: the couplet makes the evening sickness bloom, the poem makes the heart shut with the evening flowers, so love's pain at dusk could be figured as opening or as closing, and the Kural's paradox depends on reversing the shore's ordinary evening closure.

note: Kalittokai 148 calls evening a sickness to the parted and a raft to the joined; in Kural 1226 the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband was still with her.
teaches: The couplet records the discovery and the kali poem the double nature behind it: the same hour is a raft and a suggestive setting (இறைச்சி) for lovers together and a sickness for the parted, which is why she learned its cruelty only after he left.

note: Kural 1235 has the wasted shoulders declare the cruelty of the cruel man (கொடியார் கொடுமை); in Ainkurunuru 117 the woman says it is cruel (கொடிதே) that beauty comes to this in those who do not forget him.
teaches: The friend in the Kural lays the cruelty on the man, while the heroine in the poem lays it on the condition of loving him, so the same lost beauty is a charge against him from outside and a lament without an accused from within.

note: Ainkurunuru 218: throbbing eyes and tightening bangles promise his coming. Kural 1203: a sneeze that starts and dies away makes the woman fear he began to think of her and stopped.
teaches: Both women read the absent man in involuntary signs of their own bodies, but the girl's signs come to completion and promise him while the Kural's sneeze aborts and suggests his forgetting, so the pair shows the same bodily sign-language turned to hope or doubt.

note: Mullaippattu's king lies awake thinking of the maimed tusker, the fallen men and the arrow-struck horses; Nedunalvadai's king goes out at midnight with a lamp-bearer to see his soldiers' wounds (விழுப்புண் காணிய புறம்போந்து) and does not sleep (பள்ளி கொள்ளான்).
teaches: The two idylls give the same scene of a king kept awake in camp by his wounded, as inward thought lying with a hand on the bed in Mullaippattu and as an outward round of inspection in Nedunalvadai, and only Mullaippattu lets the night end in the sweet sleep (இன்துயில்) that the wife at home is denied.

note: Naladiyar 206 says saltless millet gruel among one's own is sweeter than milk rice from strangers' hands; 197 prizes the small chief's greens and varagu rice given with regard over kings' wealth.
teaches: Both value a poor meal for the regard it is given with, but the Naladiyar finds that regard among kin while the Purananuru finds it in a patron who knows a poet's worth, so the pair shows the bard's patron standing where the family stands in the later book.

note: Kuruntokai 290: do those who tell me to bear my love not know what it is, or are they so strong? Thinaimalai 106: who are they who tell the parted to bear it? They are so only for themselves, for the bees already sing in the mullai.
teaches: Kuruntokai answers the counsel to endure by doubting the counsellors' knowledge, while the venba adds the season's evidence against it, the bees already singing in joy, so the refusal to bear up gains in the later poem a reason drawn from the landscape.

note: Purananuru 369 (Paranar, thurai மறக்களவழி) builds the whole battle as a season of rain and tillage, elephants as clouds and arrows as rain on a wet field (ஈரச் செறுவயின்), ending in a request for elephants; Kalavazhi Narpathu 2 gives one farming image, blood running through burst drums like a tank's sluices after the monsoon (கார்ப்பெயல் பெய்தபின்).
teaches: Together they show how the kalavazhi theme changed form: Paranar's single sustained allegory of the farm year, made to earn a gift, becomes in Poigaiyar one quick water-and-field simile per stanza with no request, so the farming root of the genre's name survives only as a store of images.

iraicchi.act: the birds, fed, go back together to their nests at evening
iraicchi.sense: even the birds come home together at nightfall, while he stays away without a thought of her

iraicchi.act: at the tiger's roar the male monkey, called the female's husband, hurries up the slope together with her (உடன்)
iraicchi.sense: even the untaught monkey takes his mate with him out of danger, while the lord went off alone and took only her beauty and her sleep

ullurai.tenor: the girl guarded by her family and the ooran who reached her

pairs.situation: her people have raised and watched over the girl
the man cuts off her young bloom, which turns to pallor

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the sown field, its watchmen and its crab, things of the marutham land (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the bee sucks at the one cluster left on a scorched tree and goes away unsated
iraicchi.sense: the man who left her full love has gone where nothing can satisfy him, so his leaving gains him nothing

ullurai.tenor: the man whose love has stripped the woman's bloom and who goes away

pairs.situation: his love has struck her in her bloom and left her desolate
he slips away down the hill, out of reach

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses the vengai and waterfall of her own hill, things she knows (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the husband who has left home for the other women

pairs.situation: he breaks the restraint of his own household
he feeds on what is not his own, the other women
he settles at ease in their houses

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the buffalo of her own town's fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the husband's new woman

pairs.situation: the other woman, of lesser rank than the wife
she displays herself as if she were the wife
she is new to his favour

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the flowers of her own town's pond, things she knows (porul 7.26)

note: Both use the punnai felled in the war of Anni and Thithiyan as a simile: in Akananuru 145 the foster mother wishes on her own hand the ruin of that tree; in Natrinai 180 the friend fears she will be ruined like it in the quarrel of husband and wife.
teaches: Read together, the felled guardian tree was a stock figure of ruin, and 180 draws from it what 145 does not need, the tree's innocence: it is the bystander destroyed because two powers fought over it, which is the go-between's place in a marriage quarrel.

note: Kural 1147 says love's sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and the mother's words as water; Natrinai 175 shows a mother who has never met the man, believing the hamlet women's petty talk, glaring at the girl's pale body at midnight.
teaches: The poem supplies the order the couplet only implies: the gossip reaches the mother first and her watch follows from it, so she acts on hearsay about a man she does not know, which is why her words feed the sickness instead of curing it.

note: Both have the man say the blue water-lily (குவளை) cannot match the girl's eyes: Ainkurunuru 299 says the lily of her own hill spring can hardly open as her eyes do, and Kural 1114 that the lily, if it could see, would bow its head ashamed.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru states the defeat of the lily as a plain fact of the girl's own hill, and the Kural gives the lily sight and a modest bowed head, so the pair shows the Kural's conceit growing out of the akam habit of measuring the hill girl against her land's flowers, with the lily now made to act out her own modesty.

note: Kural 1102: the man says the jewelled woman (அணியிழை) is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 5: the friend tells the man there is no medicine but him for the bright-jewelled girl (வயங்கிழை).
teaches: The same paradox of the lover as the only cure runs in both directions, the woman for the man in the Kural, the man for the woman here, and the change of speaker turns the Kural's private wonder into the friend's demand that he give the cure.

note: Akananuru 2: a monkey drunk on fallen jackfruit wine sleeps content; the friend says if beasts find unplanned joy so easily, the hill lord's planned joy should not be hard. Natrinai 57: a monkey steals milk from a sleeping wild cow, and the friend ends on the coming harvest that will shut the girl in.
teaches: Both friends press the hill lord to marry with a monkey of his own slopes, but Akananuru 2 draws the moral aloud while Natrinai 57 leaves the monkey's seized moment unexplained beside the girl's closing one, so the pair shows the same urging done once by open comparison and once by hidden comparison.

note: Kural 231: to give and live so that renown arises; there is no other gain for a life. Kar Narpathu 32: bees glad as the hearts of wealthy men who crave undying fame (கெடாஅப் புகழ்வேட்கைச் செல்வர் மனம்போற்).
teaches: The couplet states the craving for renown through giving as the one gain of life, and the venba treats that craving as so familiar that a returning lover can measure a bee's gladness by it, which shows the puram ideal already turned into common stock for akam imagery.

note: In Kuruntokai 66 the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking untimely rain for the season the man named; in Natrinai 248 she calls the thunder false and refuses to be fooled like the young peafowl who dance at it.
teaches: The pair shows a fixed move of the friend's, denying the season by calling some creature of the land deceived, and in Natrinai 248 the move turns inward, since she speaks of herself as the one who will not be fooled, so the device is an argument about belief, not about weather.

note: Paripadal 8.19-21 has the hill's caves (மலை முழை) answer back and forth the cock's crow and the musth elephants' trumpeting that answer the god's elephant and the thunder; Paripadal 19.62-65 has the echoing cave (இசை முழை) take up a lost girl's call and lead her astray.
teaches: In song 8 the cave echo multiplies the god's elephant, his cock and the storm into a sign that the whole hill answers him, while in song 19 the same caves fool a lost girl and the poet calls this the hill's innocent nature, so the pair shows the Parankunram echo used both as a mark of divine presence and as the hill's playful character.

note: Kural 1151: the friend (or the woman) tells the man that his promise of a quick return should be told to those still alive then. Kainnilai 13: told of his going by the long wasteland, her eyes went soft with tears.
teaches: Both answer the man's announcement of departure, but the Kural puts the threat to her life into argued words while the Kainnilai lets the friend report only the eyes giving way on hearing, so the pair shows the same reply could be made as a sharp argument or as a bare bodily fact laid before him.

note: Kuruntokai 66: the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking a stray rain for the season and flowering; Kuruntokai 251: the friend calls the peacocks foolish for dancing to a stray cloud's thunder, and explains the cloud is only emptying its old water.
teaches: Together they show the friend's consolation as an argument about evidence, not a denial of rain: in 66 the flowers misread the rain, in 251 the cloud's thunder is given a cause of its own, so the friend separates rain from season, the very distinction the man's promise rests on.

note: Kural 1229 says that when evening spreads the whole town is bewildered and suffers; Kalittokai 118's refrain says evening torments those parted but cannot dim (கடிகல்லாய்) the beauty, sweet speech and smile of lovers who are together.
teaches: Read beside the poem, the couplet's 'the whole town suffers' shows itself as the lonely woman's projection, since the kali poem insists evening harms only the parted, so the grief belongs to separation and not to the hour.

note: Kural 791: nothing is as ruinous as befriending without inquiry, for once formed a friendship cannot be left; Kuruntokai 247: the friend says she knew then that the man's friendship is flawless, fruitful, righteous and a raft for kin.
teaches: The Kural's test of friendship is meant to come before the bond, but in secret love the bond comes first, so the friend's knowing it to be flawless arrives after the fact and has to argue, in the Kural's own terms of fruit and kin, that the inquiry would have passed.

note: Both are by Kopperunchozhan: in Purananuru 216 he says his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar calls himself 'the foolish Chola's'; in Kuruntokai 20 his heroine says let the leavers be wise and let us be fools.
teaches: The same king, in puram and in akam, gives the name of folly to loyalty that prudence would abandon, his friend's in the one and the waiting woman's in the other, so the akam poem's irony has a model in the king's own creed of friendship.

note: 864 says one who doesn't let go of anger is easy prey for anyone. 899 makes the anger of the exalted able to bring down a king.
teaches: Anger is weakness or supreme power depending on who has it, and 306 warns that it burns the one who has it.

note: Natrinai 306: the millet is being reaped and the hill girl sent home; how will he come now to see her? Ainthinai Aimpathu 18: not even the parrots come to the millet field now; do not forget your bond with her.
teaches: Natrinai states the practical loss at harvest, no place left to meet, and Ainthinai names the risk behind it, that like the parrots he may stop coming once the field is empty, so the pair shows the end of the guarding feared as a test of his memory as well as of access.

note: In Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 10 the girl tells her friend that mother, learning of the union, has barred her from the field; in Thinaimalai 27 the friend tells the man that mother saw him and keeps the girl guarded.
teaches: The same discovery by the mother is grief in the girl's mouth, who wonders whether he will be vexed, and a lever in the friend's, who uses it to tell him to marry now, so the confinement that ends kalavu is also the friend's strongest argument for marriage.

note: The Kural's man says an embrace no breeze can part is sweet to two who love; the Ainkurunuru hero asks if his wife, who held him close against her breasts (மாண்முலை அடைய முயங்கியோயே), is a woman of the sky.
teaches: The Kural names the close embrace as a pleasure common to all lovers, but the Ainkurunuru hero, after absence, finds the same embrace so beyond the human that he takes his own wife for a celestial, so the general sweetness is shown as wonder when it is regained.

note: Kural 1236: with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts the woman is hearing him called cruel; Kuruntokai 77: there is no fault in him, or if any, it is that her soft shoulders proved easy to leave.
teaches: Both women defend the absent man with their wasted shoulders as the evidence, but the poem goes further than the couplet by moving the blame onto those shoulders, while its desert of dead travellers' cairns lets the reproach stand unspoken.

note: Purananuru 2 likens Udhiyan Cheralathan's patience, counsel, strength, wrath and grace to the five great elements; Patitruppattu 14 tells his son, named in the decade's preface as Udhiyan Cheral's son, that he is as beyond measure as earth, water, wind and sky.
teaches: Father and son are both praised through the elements, which shows the element catalogue working as a Chera family formula, and the son's version moves the point from the elements' separate qualities to their shared immeasurability.

note: In Akananuru 98 the girl fears that the mother's velan rite, held for a sickness read as Murugan's seizure, will expose the secret; in the idyll the mother's diviners and offerings to many gods have already failed, and the friend makes that failure the ground for telling her.
teaches: Held together, the two show that the misread sickness and its useless rite are the hinge of the kurinji plot: the short poem stops at the girl's dread of exposure, and Kapilar's idyll starts from the same point and turns the failed cure into the friend's reason to disclose the love and press for marriage.

note: Kural 557 likens the king's lack of grace to the world's lack of rain; Kalittokai 10 likens the drought-dried waste to a world under a crooked-sceptred king whose men rob and kill.
teaches: The comparison runs both ways: the ethics book explains tyranny by drought and the love poet explains drought by tyranny, so the bond between bad rule and failed rain was common enough to be used as vehicle or as tenor.

note: Ainkurunuru 8: the girls wish that the lover's oath sworn here may prove true. Kuruntokai 53: the friend tells the man of the fields that what afflicts them is the oath he swore at the broad ford of their town, holding the girl's forearm.
teaches: The oath the Ainkurunuru girls hope will come true is, in the Kuruntokai, already the cause of their suffering, so the pair shows the kalavu vow of the field country both as the girl's only security and as the wound when it lags.

note: In Purananuru 107 Kapilar says Pari is not the only one who sustains the world: there is also the rain; in Patitruppattu 64 the same poet tells the Chera that he pours greater benefit than the high cloud (மழையினும் பெரும்பயம் பொழிதி).
teaches: Kapilar's measure of a giver is the rain in both poems, but where Pari was granted only the rain as his equal the living Chera is set above it, which shows how the poet's praise scale shifted with the patron and how far the dead friend's standard was raised to honour the new one.

note: Kural 1081: the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman; Thinaimalai 47: she is a beauty that strikes like a goddess (ஏரணங்கு) those who look without thinking.
teaches: The Kural's man hesitates over what she is, while the Thinaimalai speaker has settled it and turns to blame, saying her kin have let such a danger loose unguarded, so the pair shows the first-sight wonder of the couplet hardening into a lover's complaint.

note: Kural 1151 has the woman (or her friend) speak at once: if you are not leaving, tell me; your quick return, tell those who will still be alive. Kuruntokai 43 says neither spoke: she thought he would not go, he thought she would not bear it.
teaches: The couplet is the sentence whose absence Avvaiyar's poem mourns: set beside it, the poem shows a parting that happened because pride on both sides kept that sentence unsaid, so the Kural's bluntness reads as the cure for the silence that undid the Kuruntokai pair.

note: Kural 1085 finds death, an eye and a doe in the young woman's look; Thinaimalai 32 calls the fish-guard's long eyes a weapon (படைநெடுங்கண்) whose guarding falls on the man.
teaches: The couplet lists in the abstract what a first look can be, and the poem supplies the scene that makes 'death' concrete: a girl posted to guard the drying fish whose watch is turned on the man who looks, so the Kural's killing glance is a guard's weapon.

note: In Purananuru 105 Kapilar sends a singing woman to Pari, promising jewels for his gentleness, which is sweeter than the water falling on his hill; in Patitruppattu 67 he sends a bard to the Chera, promising pearls, and fills the road with the king's battlefield of vultures, demons and hacked bodies.
teaches: The same poet's two guide poems show that the guide form takes its content from the patron: a hill chief is reached through his kindness and his streams, a crowned king through the terror of his wars, though both end in the same gift of jewels.

note: Both put the woman in the same bind, nearly in the same words (உள்ளின் உள்ளம் வேமே; உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்): remembering burns her and not remembering is impossible.
teaches: The Kural keeps Avvaiyar's bind and drops her last line, the charge that the man is not noble, so set side by side they show the couplet turning a complaint against him into a pure description of her state.

note: Both call desire for another man's wife பேதைமை; the Kural says it is absent in those who have seen aram and porul.
teaches: The Innaa list explains the shared word by its company: the folly is that of a venture beyond one's strength, like a valourless king in battle, which those the Kural describes would never attempt.

note: In Akananuru 272 the mother sees the night visitor wet from the hill, garlanded with koothalam, and takes him for Murugu, scattering millet in worship; in Ainkurunuru 206 the friend shows the mother a man wet with spray and dew and likens him to a watchman of the rainy hill.
teaches: Where the mother left to herself reads the drenched visitor from the hill as a god, the friend who discloses the love names him as a man like their own field watchmen, so the disclosure works by bringing the stranger down from the sacred to the familiar.

note: Ainkurunuru 377 says the girl left her ball, doll and pebbles to us; Akananuru 369 says the parrot will not drink and the doll gets no offering since she went.
teaches: In Akananuru the left things mourn with the household, while in Ainkurunuru they are a bequest the girl hands back with her childhood, so the same toys can be made grieving witnesses or the plain sign that childhood is over.

note: Paripadal 2 says Maal is younger to those who call him the white one's younger brother and elder to those who call him elder; Paripadal 13 makes the plough-bearer one of Maal's own three forms.
teaches: Held together, the two hymns show Paripadal poets resolving the kinship of Maal and the plough-bearer in two ways: one makes the order of birth depend on who is speaking, the other dissolves the kinship entirely by making the brother a form of the one god.

note: In Akananuru 48 the friend tells the foster mother of a youth with a flower garland and a chariot who stopped by the vengai slope and gazed at the girl; in Ainkurunuru 367 the friend tells the mother of the man who came near with his chariot wearing kongu and vengai flowers, and says the girl's life is joined to his name.
teaches: The same disclosure scene, chariot, flowered youth and vengai included, ends in Akananuru 48 with an inference left to the mother and in 367 with a flat verdict that the girl is already bound to him, which shows the friend's revelation could be pitched as a hint or as a fait accompli.

note: Akananuru 34: the returning man bids his charioteer hurry past a stag that feeds and guards its doe. Natrinai 59: the returning man tells his charioteer of the land where a hunter comes home with his catch and revels at ease.
teaches: Both returning husbands read their own homecoming in a figure of the road, and the figures differ: the stag shows the care he will give, the hunter the ease he will take, so the pair shows the mullai homecoming imagined both as tending and as rest.

note: Both make the cause of love-sickness its cure; in Kural 1102 the man says the girl is the medicine for the sickness she gives, in Ainkurunuru 101 the friend tells the mother the lord's chariot is the medicine for the sickness the girl's eyes caught.
teaches: Valluvar states the paradox as the lover's private wonder, while the Sangam friend uses the same paradox as evidence before the mother, so the idea that only the beloved can cure love began as an argument for marriage before it was a maxim of delight.

note: Kalittokai's brahmins tell the searching mother not to grieve for the girl who followed the man she chose; Ainkurunuru 388's travellers tell the searcher to rest out the noon heat and go on over the little hill to see the couple's road.
teaches: Wayside people meet the pursuer with two different answers, reasons to stop grieving in Kalittokai and directions to go on in Ainkurunuru, so the pursuit was not always treated as something to be talked out of.

note: Kural 1083: the man says he now knows Death, which has a woman's grace and big eyes that make war (பேரமர்க் கட்டு); Kalittokai 108: the man calls the girl the warrior who took up arms against his life, and mocks her trust in her mullai-bud teeth and battle eyes (பேர் அமர் உண் கண்ணும்), while she answers back and at last sets the tryst.
teaches: The couplet's lone confession of being slain by her eyes appears in the herders' poem as a line of banter that the girl hears, throws back and answers with a meeting place, which shows the conceit of the killing eye at work as courtship speech addressed to the woman, not only as the man's inner wonder.

note: Kural 1199: though the one she longs for gives no grace (நல்கார்), even word of him is sweet to her ears. Kuruntokai 60: even if her lover does not grace her (நல்கார்) or desire her, seeing him often is sweet to her heart.
teaches: Both women claim sweetness from a lover who gives none, with the same verb; Paranar's simile of the cripple licking his empty palm beneath the honeycomb shows what the couplet's maxim hides, that this sweetness is tasted only in imagination, a pleasure that is also the measure of what is withheld.

note: Both have the friend speak to the girl while the man overhears about the mother who, not knowing the cause, will bring the velan to hold a veri; in Akananuru 242 the friend says they should go to him before the goat is offered, in Natrinai 273 the poem ends on her trembling heart.
teaches: Together they show the announced veri as a set lever on the overhearing man, the false diagnosis that will expose the secret, and Akananuru 242 states the remedy, his embrace before the sacrifice, that Natrinai 273 leaves him to supply.

note: Both give the man the same words for constancy: Kural 1125 உள்ளுவன் ... மறப்பறியேன், answering the friend who asks whether he remembers; Ainkurunuru 298 உள்ளுபு மறந்தறியேமே, said of a girl who shows him no grace.
teaches: The Kural's joke that he cannot remember what he never forgets answers a doubt about absence, while the Ainkurunuru sets the same claim against her coldness, so together they show the man's never-forgetting was the stock answer to both doubts the friend tests him with: will he stay away, and will he give up if she is unkind.

note: Kuruntokai 183: the great flowering branch of the kaayaa shows like a peacock's neck in the poor forest. Thinaimalai 107: the kodal fears the budding kaayaa as a flock of peacocks.
teaches: The kaayaa-peacock likeness that Kuruntokai offers as the poet's own comparison is in Thinaimalai mistaken by a flower in the scene, so the later poet makes a stock simile into an error committed inside the landscape.

note: In Akananuru 289 the man on his journey imagines her praying 'speak good' each time the lizard chirps; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 42 the lizard chirps at the favourable side, together with a throbbing eye and good dreams.
teaches: The man's imagined picture of her waiting on the lizard and her own report that the lizard has spoken well are the two ends of one practice, which shows that the omen was a shared language the separated lovers each expected the other to be reading.

note: Both open on the neem-bud-eyed crab of the marutham field and its earthen hole (வேப்புநனை யன்ன நெடுங்கள் களவன், வேப்புநனை அன்ன நெடுங்கண் நீர்ஞெண்டு, மண்அளை): in Ainkurunuru 30 it fills its hole with paddy blossom while the girl loses her beauty; in Akananuru 176 it flees the heron into its hole in a poem refusing the husband at the door.
teaches: The neem-bud simile and the crab's earthen hole are a shared marutham formula, and the two poems make it mean opposite things by the act they give it, hoarding in the four-line poem and fearful hiding in the long one, so in this stock image the sense lies in what the crab does, not in how it looks.

iraicchi.act: the peacock dances together with its hen on the high branch in the morning sun
iraicchi.sense: the creatures of his own hill keep company with their mates while he has gone away and left her to pale

iraicchi.act: the elephant, fed, lies down to sleep without fear in the shade of the grove
iraicchi.sense: as the elephant sleeps secure in the grove's shade, the woman joined to this man may rest without fear

ullurai.tenor: the courtesan, used and laid aside by the man

pairs.scene: மூத்து வினை போகிய முரி வாய் அம்பி
pairs.situation: the woman whose service to him is spent
she is no longer honoured or tended
she is kept tied, idle, at the edge of his life

ullurai.speaker_fit: the courtesan is not of the household and may use any thing freely (porul 7.29); the boat is of the shore she names

iraicchi.act: the female monkey takes the ripe fruit from the plant while it is there to be taken
iraicchi.sense: the man should take the girl now, while she is still in the field, before the harvest shuts her away

ullurai.tenor: the lord who has had his joy of the girl and gone off unchanged

pairs.situation: he has leapt away from her once his pleasure was taken
he springs back upright and untouched while she is left with the sickness
he has hooked her beauty and carried it off

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the bamboo and the young monkey of the kurinji slope in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the cloud answers the hill man's shout at once by pouring its rain
iraicchi.sense: in his own land even a cloud answers a call, so the lord who leaves the girl's tears unanswered falls short of his hill's clouds

note: Kuruntokai 3's woman says her love for the hill man is larger than the earth, higher than the sky and deeper than the sea; Ainkurunuru 184's says the friendship with the man whose town the sea adorns is greater than the sea.
teaches: Each heroine measures love against her own lover's world: the hill woman needs the whole cosmos, while the shore woman takes the one thing that crowns his town and sets it below their bond, so the boast of measureless love takes its scale from the land of the man loved.

note: Kar Narpathu 12 says the dark clouds rising every day on the right (வைகலு மேரும் வலம்) are a sign beyond doubt (ஐயந்தீர் காட்சி) that he will come; Mullaippattu opens with a cloud that drinks the sea and rises on the right (வலனேர்பு).
teaches: Read with Kar Narpathu's explicit rule that a cloud rising on the right foretells the lover's return, Mullaippattu's opening simile is already an omen in the sky set before the old women's omen in the street, and the poem closes with the returning army also rising on the right (line 91), so the idyll is framed by the sign and its fulfilment.

note: Kural 261 defines tapas as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Sirupanchamoolam 31 keeps both, adds three more, and says penance so made is sweet, not lowly.
teaches: The couplet defines penance by two ethical acts; the verse keeps them, turns bearing pain into forgetting it, and meets an objection the couplet does not raise, that penance degrades the one who does it.

note: Kural 1088: my might, feared in battle, broke before her bright brow; Kuruntokai 95: her grace like water quenched my strength like fire.
teaches: The Kural reports the man's defeat as a wonder of scale, so great a strength and so small a brow; the Kuruntokai explains it by kind, water putting out fire, so his strength was not outmatched but met by its natural undoing.

note: Same situation and speaker: the woman of the shore says the lord of the ford (துறைவன்) has left her and her bangles slip from her forearm; the Kural keeps the Ainkurunuru's words துறைவன், துற, முன்கை, இறை and வளை.
teaches: The couplet lifts a neythal formula whole, but gives the bangles a new office: in the Ainkurunuru they imitate his desertion, in the Kural they broadcast it like gossip, so the later poet turned the body from mirror of the man into witness to the town.

note: Verse 1 makes a wife chaste as Arundhati a medicine; verse 16 makes the man who won a chaste wife deathless.
teaches: Within the book the chaste wife is given two predicates, cure and deathlessness, so she is valued both for what she does for the husband now and for the name she leaves him.

note: Ainkurunuru 267 opens with the same boar formula as Natrinai 386 (சிறுகண் பன்றிப் பெருஞ்சின ஒருத்தல்); Natrinai's boar sleeps unafraid after raiding the millet, Ainkurunuru's drives off the bowmen to seize the hill rice, beside a man whose words are not to be trusted.
teaches: One formula line for the raiding boar served poets for opposite men, the suitor who swears and weds and the one who flatters without pledge, so the boar's daring is admired or suspected according to what the man goes on to do.

note: Both put the courtesan's report of the wives in the same formula: அழுப என்ப அவன் பெண்டிர் (they say his women weep) in Ainkurunuru 32, கழறுப என்ப அவன் பெண்டிர் (they say his women rail) in Akananuru 76.
teaches: The one formula frames the wives two ways, as melting in tears like wax or as clamouring like a bard's drum, and the courtesan's answer scales with it, from a mocking count of days in the short poem to an open vow to hold him by force in the long one.

note: In Kuruntokai 65 the stag back with its mate in the rains mocks the waiting woman because her man has not come; in 338 the same pairing at evening comes with the chariot that ends her pallor. On the waiting woman's reading in 65 the sign is false; in 338 it is kept.
teaches: The same image of the stag beside its mate is read as a reproach when the man fails the season and as a promise kept when he arrives, so the pair shows that the iraicchi carries no fixed sense apart from whether the man returns.

note: Ainkurunuru 447: may the king's work be released, and then we shall see her bright brow, when the bee opens the red thalavu bud shaped like a kingfisher's beak (சிரல்வாய்ச் செம்முகை). Kar Narpathu 36: the man returning from the work sees the thalavam buds, lovely as kingfishers' beaks (சிரல்வாய் வனப்பின), opened in rows.
teaches: The same thalavu bud is the hour hoped for in the man's prayer while the king's work holds him and the sight on the road once he is released, so read together the bud marks the two ends of a single wait.

note: In Akananuru 162 the man tells his heart that he stood in a midnight storm at a corner of her father's tall house until the strict guards slackened; in Ainkurunuru 60 the friend tells the man that he comes to the tall house while all sleep and asks whether he does not fear her father's spear.
teaches: The danger at the father's tall house that the lover recounts to himself as proof of his devotion is the very thing the friend names to him as a reason to stop coming by night, so the same risk is a boast in his mouth and a demand for marriage in hers.

note: Kural 750 says that whatever excellences a fort has, it is nothing without men excellent in action; Patitruppattu 33 makes the marching army itself a fortress, swords for wall, spears for hedge and arrows for moat.
teaches: The Kural makes the defenders the real worth of a fort, and the Chera poet takes that to its end by removing the walls altogether, so that the fort exists wherever the army camps.

note: Akananuru 28 warns that if the girl does not keep scaring parrots from the millet, mother will set others in her place and his chest will be hard to reach (உறற்கு அரிது); Ainkurunuru 260 says the millet has ripened and the girl is hard to win (பெறற்கரிது).
teaches: Akananuru 28 spells out the custom that the Ainkurunuru poem only implies: the girl's freedom lasts exactly as long as the field needs guarding, so 'the millet has ripened' in four lines carries the whole threat of her being kept at home.

note: Akananuru 86 presents the rite (sand spread under the pandal, தருமணல் ஞெமிரி; the matrons' blessing of chastity; the kin giving the bride, தமர்தர) as the start of the marriage; in Kalittokai 114 the girl, seeing her kin prepare a wedding with sand spread low (தரு மணல் தாழப் பெய்து), says she knows only the one union she made among her play-house companions and that two weddings are against the nature of herd girls. On this reading the rite that makes a marriage in 86 makes none in 114.
teaches: Held together, the two show that akam could place the binding moment of marriage either in the kin's sand-strewn rite or before it in the secret union, so the same ceremony that founds a wife's chastity in Akananuru 86 would, given to another man, be a forbidden second marriage for the herd girl.

note: Fragment 3 has a woman say that another, for all her excellence, is not her equal and knows who her equals are (என்னொடு புரையுநள் அல்லள்); Ainkurunuru 67, a wife's speech in marutham, says the hero's new woman, foolish, sets herself against the wife who is no match for her (தன்னொடு நிகரா என்னொடு நிகரி).
teaches: Ainkurunuru 67 supplies the frame the three-line fragment lacks: claims of who is whose equal are the weapon of the marutham quarrel between wife and new woman, which makes it likely the fragment is such a speech and that its point is standing in the household rather than beauty.

note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 22: the friend asks what will become of the pallor now that the rain says he will come. Kural 1265: the woman says the pallor of her shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading they disagree on whether news of his return can touch the pallor.
teaches: The friend treats the pallor as already beaten by the season's promise, while the couplet's woman refuses any cure short of seeing him, so the couplet sounds like the heroine's unspoken reply to the friend's teasing question.

note: In Naladiyar 390 the wife tells the bard not to lie that the man will be kind, since to him she is the tip of the sugarcane, and to tell it to those who are its middle joints; in Thinaimozhi 37 she tells the bard not to keep pressing, since she never had the gracious regard 'our younger sisters' have.
teaches: The same refusal of the bard, by the same speaker, is filed by the Naladiyar under the chaste wife, so the didactic book reads her sharp tongue to the go-between as a mark of karpu, while the akam venba keeps it as wounded pride with the ironic family word for the rivals.

note: Kuruntokai's friend calls the konrai foolish for taking a stray shower for the kaar rains (வம்ப மாரியைக் காரென); Ainkurunuru calls the forest on his road one that has met the kaar rain (கார்ப்பெயற்கு எதிரிய).
teaches: Holding the two together shows that whether the forest's flowering marks the true kaar was itself what the waiting woman and her friend argued over, Kuruntokai explaining the signs away while Ainkurunuru accepts them.

note: 101 argues at length that Athiyaman's gift never fails however long it is delayed; the akam poem 162 calls Athikan, of the same house, one who never let a suppliant's hope fail (நசைபிழைப்பு அறியா).
teaches: What 101 has to argue as a bard's private reassurance had become, in an akam poet's line, a fixed epithet of the Athiyaman house, so the praise poem shows the experience behind the epithet.

note: In Purananuru 72 Nedunjeliyan stakes his vow on the poverty of not giving to suppliants; the idyll shows his gate never barred, bards, singers and poets called in, and chariots and elephants given.
teaches: Read together, the open-gate scene is the vow's condition kept: what the young king named as the shame he would accept if he failed (not being able to give) is what the poet, in the king's own lifetime, presents as his settled daily practice.

note: Natrinai 327's girl stakes her life on the belief that the noble do not fail in what they owe; Kural 990 says that if the worthy declined in worth the earth could not bear its load.
teaches: The Kural makes the failure of the worthy a cosmic impossibility, while the Natrinai girl turns the same belief into a private wager on one man, so the pair shows what the maxim costs when a single life rests on someone being counted among the worthy.

note: Kural 101: for help given unasked, earth and heaven together are hardly a return. Thinaimalai 62: no one on this sea-girt earth matches the shore lord who once helped in the salt land; seek his equal in heaven.
teaches: The venba takes the Kural's measure of unrequited help, earth and heaven, and applies it to the helper himself: the lover's one service makes him without equal in either world, so the ethical rule of gratitude becomes the friend's argument for the man.

note: Both are a man answering a heart that urges a journey for wealth: in Natrinai 3 he recalls thinking of her at lamp-lighting time on the edge of the wasteland on an earlier journey; in Natrinai 16 he sets out the dilemma that wealth and union cannot both be had and gives up the journey.
teaches: The same refusal is reached once by memory and once by argument: Natrinai 3 calls her sweet as a finished task, putting the journey's goal already at home, and Natrinai 16 states the reason as a rule that wealth leaves no trace, so the decision is held both as felt experience and as reasoned principle.

note: Both refuse the bard who comes with the shore lord's words: Natrinai 167 says his humble words will not remove the pallor of the bangled girl, Ainkurunuru 136 calls him shameless for pouring out words for the lord who made her bangles slip.
teaches: The Natrinai friend grants the bard's skill and denies only its effect, while the Ainkurunuru woman denies him decency itself, so set together they show the refusal of the go-between ranging from courtesy to contempt within the same neythal situation.

note: 449 has the chariot and horses ready on condition the king finishes his work (வேந்துவினை முடினே); Kar Narpathu 20 reports the king's work done (வேந்தன் வினையு முடிந்தன) and the road grown pleasant.
teaches: The pair gives the two moments of the mullai return, the chariot readied in the camp while the king's work hangs, and the fulfilment when the work is done and the rain-cloud itself seems an army going home.

note: Both are the wife in oodal refusing the husband's chest; Ainkurunuru 63 because other women have lain on it, Kural 1311 because all women consume him with their eyes.
teaches: The couplet raises the bar of the older refusal: where the Sangam wife needs the touch of other women to refuse him, Valluvar's wife refuses for their looks alone, so the Kural turns a grievance about deeds into a jealousy of glances.

note: Kuruntokai 375 says it is good if he does not come today because the millet has ripened and the night watchmen beat their drum at midnight; Natrinai 255 says the same, வாரார்ஆயினோ நன்றுமன், because of ghouls, a tiger, a snake and thunder on his path.
teaches: The two give the same wish two different reasons, discovery by the watchmen and death on the path, so the wish that he not come is a set response whose grounds range from the secret to his life, and Natrinai 255 shows the graver one.

note: The Kural rates the worst poverty of the worthy above wealth won under blame; the idyll says the king, offered the treasure Vanan buried in the south, would not say 'let blame come to us', but would rather give treasure away for fame.
teaches: The idyll shows the Kural's maxim as a king's test with a named treasure and adds the alternative the Kural leaves out, giving wealth away for fame, so refusing blamed gain is tied to giving: the ruler's honour lies in both refusing and spending.

note: In Akananuru 34 the returning man sees a stag feed and guard its doe and hurries his chariot home; in Kuruntokai 338 the friend sets a stag resting with its doe at evening beside the news that the victorious chariot has come.
teaches: The stag with its doe is the spur to return in the man's mouth and the sign that the return has happened in the friend's, so the pair shows one iraicchi working at both ends of the journey, as motive and as fulfilment.

note: Both poems use the same line, செய்வினை முடித்த செம்மல் உள்ளம், for the man whose task is done: in 270 he says it of himself, already with her in the rain; in 275 the friend imagines it of him as she listens for a bell at dusk.
teaches: The formula is the hinge of the mullai return seen from both sides of the door: the friend's hopeful projection in 275 is exactly what the man claims in 270, so the waiting and the arrival are framed by one satisfied heart.

note: Thiruppugazh 11 names Murugan's uncle as the one who sleeps on the serpent and who churned the sea of old (பனகம் துயில்கின்ற ... கடல் முன்பு கடைந்த); Paripadal Thirattu 1.68-75 gives the churning to the serpent, who lifted the mountain and was the rope while the discus-bearer (ஆழியான்) only pulled.
teaches: By Arunagirinathar's time the churning is simply Mal's act and the serpent his bed, while the Sangam hymn praises the rope for not breaking, so the pair shows the serpent losing its share of the myth as it became the god's couch.

note: 136 (நாணிலை மன்ற பாண) blames the bard for spilling words for the lord; 138 (பண்பிலை மன்ற பாண) blames him for harsh words in the town and for not bringing the lord.
teaches: The paired rebukes show the bard condemned from both sides, for speaking on the lord's behalf and for failing to deliver the lord, so what the woman rejects is his offering words where only the man's presence would do.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the veri ground the velan prepares (வேலன் தைஇய வெறியயர் களனும்) among the god's dwellings, with village festivals and hill places; the idyll sets mansion women at their windows joining hands to red Murugan and crowding with the veri dancers in Puhar's festival bazaar.
teaches: The veri rite, which the Murugan poem places in the hills and the village grounds, appears in Pattinappalai in a port city's bazaar among the mansions, so the pair shows the possession rite of the hills carried into urban festival life by the time of the idyll.

note: Thirattu 9, 10 and 11 share one frame ('can Madurai decline ... as long as the king's ... exists'); 9 measures it by his hill, 10 by his Vaigai, 11 by his word (வார்த்தை).
teaches: Taken as a set, the fragments move the city's guarantee from a hill and a river to the king's word, so the last stanza rests Madurai's permanence on speech and renown, the poet's own stock, rather than on the land.

note: Both poems close on the same formula for the waiting wife, விருந்து அயர் விருப்பினள் with திருந்துஇழை: in 361 the friend reports it as the wife's state once the chariot is home; in 374 the returning husband imagines it on the road, joined to வருந்தும், her suffering.
teaches: The same line serves as the end of waiting in one poem and as the husband's picture of waiting in the other, so the wish to feast guests was a fixed sign of the wife who keeps the house ready, and whether it is joy or grief depends only on whether the chariot has arrived.

note: 381 makes six assets (army, people, wealth, ministers, friends, fortress) the mark of a lion among kings. Parimelazhagar's 'others' in 661 are exactly army, fort and friendship, which he says don't count as firmness.
teaches: The list of assets is empty without the mind that uses them.

note: The queen gazes at a painted moon with Rohini and sighs; Akananuru 136 sets a wedding at the hour when the moon had joined Sakatam, the Rohini asterism, in a spotless conjunction.
teaches: Since weddings were timed to the moon's union with Rohini, the painting over the queen's bed is also the sign under which she was married, so her long sigh can be read as memory of her own wedding as well as envy of a pair never parted.

note: Kural 572: the world's ways rest on கண்ணோட்டம், and those without it are a burden on the earth. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 54: the husband who resolves to withhold கண்ணோட்டம் while taking the wife's devoted service is told the blame falls on him.
teaches: The Kural states kindly regard as a duty of public life; the venba brings it inside the marriage and makes its withdrawal a husband's blame, which shows the ethical term was already at work in the language of domestic quarrel.

note: Kainnilai 42: the bard may make the man his dancer. Kainnilai 46: the man spoke pleasantly and only seemed ashamed.
teaches: Verse 46 says his shame was a show and verse 42 makes him a dancer, so the decade presents the husband's contrition as performance from both sides, his own acting and the bard's staging.

note: Kuruntokai 263 protests to the girl that the mother's offerings to strange gods are no cure and brand her possessed; Ainkurunuru 243 says to the mother herself that she will believe the ignorant diviner.
teaches: The same protest against the rite is spoken between the girls in Kuruntokai and turned on the mother in Ainkurunuru, so the pair shows the friend's objection to veri moving from private complaint to the first step of telling the household.

note: Both repeat இனிது மன்றஅவர் கிடக்கை; 401 says this world and heaven cannot easily obtain it, 409 says it is worth the whole of this world.
teaches: The same refrain carries two prices, above both worlds and equal to this one, so the foster mother's hyperbole is a varied formula of the decade rather than a fixed claim about the household's worth.

note: In both a bear digs into a snake-haunted termite mound on the path: in 325 on the wasteland road the man would take for wealth, in 336 on the hill path he takes to the night meeting.
teaches: The same bear tearing open the snake's mound marks the danger of the road away from her and of the road to her, so in the anthology the friend's fear attaches to the man's going whichever way he goes.

note: Both men give up a planned journey because of the woman; in 421 her shoulders 'block' the going, in Akananuru 5 her silent grieving and the son at her breast.
teaches: Ainkurunuru keeps only the outcome and one bodily sign of what Akananuru 5 unfolds as a scene of silent pleading, so the short form shows that the persuasion could be left wholly implied once the convention of the abandoned journey was known.

ullurai.tenor: the girl, left to waste if her lover is lost to her

pairs.situation: the loss of the lover, which is what she faces if he does not come to marry her
the girl, kept in the house and unable to go to him
her pallor, a wound the mother's rite cannot reach

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the elephants of the hero's own forest land in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the doe, having fed on the millet ears, rests together with her stag
iraicchi.sense: the pair at rest after feeding promises the hero the same rest beside his wife tonight

iraicchi.act: the tusker, unable to bear his weary mate's pain, fells a tree to feed her and trumpets in grief
iraicchi.sense: even the elephant on that road cannot bear his mate's suffering, yet the man who crossed it has forgotten the one he left weeping

iraicchi.act: the tusker guards from behind his mate and the calf she has just borne
iraicchi.sense: the man will come to wed her and guard her and their household as the tusker guards his own

pairs.situation: the girl, small and defenceless in her own home
the man's coming, which undoes her good name
the clamour of the gossip that follows

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a crab and surf of the neythal shore in a neythal poem (porul 7.27)
