iraicchi.sense: as the elephant keeps its young from the path's danger, the women's love for the man makes them wish him kept from that path at night, so love here means holding back, not coming

ullurai.tenor: the ooran who leaves his own woman and harms others

pairs.situation: he leaves the woman who is his partner
he goes on to hurt other tender women

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the crab and vallai of the marutham field, without leaving the poem's land (porul 7.27)

ullurai.tenor: the man who spoiled her beauty for his pleasure and now sits at ease

pairs.situation: he spoiled her fresh beauty
he took his pleasure of her
he now rests at ease on his shore, unmoved

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses the stork and creeper of her own shore, things she knows (porul 7.26)

note: Kural 1269 says one day is like seven for those who pine with their eyes on the day of return (வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்குபவர்க்கு); Ainkurunuru 350 is spoken on that day, the time he named, and he has not come.
teaches: The couplet measures the waiting before the fixed day as the long part, while the poem shows the fixed day arriving empty, so the Kural's pain has a limit that the Ainkurunuru woman has already passed, when waiting no longer has a date to count toward.

note: In Akananuru 34 the returning man sees a stag feeding and guarding its doe and hurries home; in Kuruntokai 65 the waiting woman sees the stag back with its mate in the rains while her man does not come.
teaches: The same sign of the stag with its mate is read from both ends of the separation: for the man it is a spur to return, for the woman it is evidence against him, so the iraicchi's force depends on who is watching.

note: Ainkurunuru 217: the friend asks why the girl pales even though the man keeps coming. Kural 1187: the woman says pallor came on her thickly the moment she turned a little in his embrace.
teaches: The friend's puzzle, pallor despite his visits, finds its answer in the Kural's hyperbole that the least gap in union breeds pallor, so the pair shows that secret visits, each ending in parting, feed the pallor rather than cure it.

note: In Akananuru 380 the man shows the girls a crab carrying a naaval fruit to its mate and says 'this is a fine way'; in Thinaimalai 40 the girl watches a crab playing with its mate after the man has left.
teaches: The crab with its mate is the shore lover's own emblem of devotion, used by the man in Akananuru 380 to court the girl; Thinaimalai 40 shows the emblem turned against him, watched by the girl alone after he dismissed her ache and went.

note: Kural 1133: the man says he once had shame and sound manliness and now has the palmyra horse. Kalittokai 47: the girl says a man of great strength and restraint has put off his manliness (தன் ஆண்தகை விட்டு) to tell her he cannot live without her.
teaches: The Kural gives the lover's own account of losing his manliness, the threat behind the madal, while Kalittokai gives the girl's hearing of it, weighing whether to believe it and what consenting would cost her name, so the pair shows both sides of the same pressure in secret love.

note: Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man says the mullai buds along the road stand sharp like the teeth of his simple girl (முள்ளெயிறு ஏய்ப்ப). Kainnilai 25: the friend shows the heroine the mullai putting out sharp teeth (கூர்எயிறு ஈன) as proof he will come.
teaches: One bud is read at both ends of the waiting: on the road the man sees her teeth in it, at home the friend offers it to her as his promise kept, so the mullai's teeth tie the two absent lovers to a single sight.

note: Kalittokai 137 says his gentleness burns her worse than fire (தீயினும் கடிது); Kural 1159 says fire burns only when touched, while love's sickness burns when the lover is away.
teaches: The couplet states as a single paradox what the kali poem reaches through three graded steps (word above bow, kindness above enmity, gentleness above fire), so the Kural's compressed contrast between fire and love was the end point of an argued rhetoric the longer form still displays.

note: Naladiyar 222 says those who live by water do not rage when the flood breaks the dam but dam it again, as one bears a valued friend's repeated wrongs; Paripadal 6.83-87 says that even when the breached sluice is closed the spray still wells, as her burning goes on after he returns.
teaches: The two poems use the same breached dam for opposite claims: the Naladiyar makes re-damming the picture of calm forbearance that works, while the Paripadal wife says closing the breach does not stop the leak, so the pair shows that the moralist's patience is exactly what the wronged wife declares impossible.

note: Akananuru 375: the heroine says she would not weep if she knew he passed unharmed the waste where raw youths kill even travellers without ornaments to test their arrows. Thinaimalai 84: the same robbers who shoot travellers with no wealth are the heroine's reason he should not go at all.
teaches: The robbers who kill the penniless serve the Akananuru heroine as a fear for a man already on the road and the venba's heroine as an argument against his setting out, so one road-danger supports both the anxiety after departure and the plea before it.

note: Kural 1122: the man says the bond between him and the girl is that of body and life. Kuruntokai 40: the man says their mothers, fathers and they themselves were strangers, yet their loving hearts have mingled like rain in red earth.
teaches: Both men declare an inseparable bond, but the Kuruntokai first denies any tie of kin, so the union it praises is made between strangers and inseparable only after mingling, which the Kural's body-and-life image, a pair joined from birth, does not show.

note: Kalittokai 144's girl says that when she opens her eyes to seize him he runs and hides in her heart; Kural 1218 says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart.
teaches: The same fancy of the lover fleeing into the heart on waking appears in both, but the kali poem frames it as a madwoman's complaint to the sea, so what the couplet offers as consolation (he never leaves her) is also a sign of her derangement.

note: Kuruntokai 53 names what afflicts them as the oath he swore at their town's ford, holding her forearm before the water goddesses; Ainkurunuru 53 has the friend ask why the ford should be blamed for their sickness when the cause is his oath.
teaches: Read together they show that the ford was both where the oath was sworn and where the household looked for the spirit that seized the girl, so the friend's correction turns the family's diagnosis of possession into a charge of perjury against the man.

note: Both set the wife who has borne a son against the women he prefers: in Ainkurunuru 70 his women are clean and fragrant while she is like a ghoul; in Akananuru 26 she turns to the boy saying 'you suit the good women; I suit this rich one' after the husband shrank from her milk.
teaches: Akananuru 26 shows the scene behind the four-line retort, the husband's flinch from the nursing body, so the Ainkurunuru 'ghoul' reads as the wife's bitter echo of his own recoil.

note: Kural 1265: once she has seen her husband to her eyes' fill the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave; Ainkurunuru 459: she asks whether she can embrace his chest so the pallor of her shoulders goes, while he is away with the king.
teaches: Both name the husband's presence as the cure for pallor, but the couplet makes the cure sight while the Ainkurunuru wife makes it embrace and doubts it is possible at all, because the king's war, not the man, decides when he comes.

note: Kural 1094: when I look she looks down, when I do not she looks and softly smiles. Natrinai 44: after bathing she gave him an unaimed look and a smile and went home, and now, confined, he asks his heart whether she knows.
teaches: The couplet treats the averted look and smile as a sign the man can read with confidence; the poem shows the same sign after the girl has been shut in, when there is no second meeting to confirm it, and the reading collapses into doubt, so the Kural's reading of hints depends on continued access to her.

note: Akananuru 170: since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak, the woman begs the crab to carry her word to the shore lord, at midnight when the sea-crow dreams beside its mate. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 65: she bids the anril, joined with its mate, to tell him 'give back the colour'.
teaches: The long poem shows why a creature is her messenger, since the land itself is mute, while the venba chooses a messenger whose own paired life is the reproach, so together they show the creature-messenger used first for its reach and then for its example.

note: Both rest on the maxim that work is what men are: in Kuruntokai 135 the friend adds that men are the life of the women at home and concludes that he will put off going; in Natrinai 24 the woman adds nothing and praises her friend for consenting to his going. On the plain reading the two conclusions are incompatible.
teaches: The pair shows that the saying about men and work was common ground each speaker could turn either way, toward consenting to the parting or toward stopping it, so the maxim settled nothing and each poem's argument lies in what it adds to it.

note: In 451 the wife argues that endurance in the camp is the king's work, not her husband's; in 460 she admits the king does not weary of the camp and no message comes.
teaches: Read in order, the decade moves from argument to helplessness: the claim in 451 that the king alone should bear the camp turns in 460 into the recognition that the king's appetite for the camp is exactly what holds her husband there.

note: Kural 1205 rebukes the man for barring her from his heart while he keeps coming into hers; in Kuruntokai 302 the man likewise comes only into her heart at midnight, and she asks whether fear of gossip keeps him away.
teaches: Together they give two verdicts on the same phantom visit: the couplet calls it shameless trespass, the poem excuses it as fear of the town, so whether his absence is a fault depends on the reason the heroine allows him.

note: In both the separated woman speaks to the moon about the man who is gone: the Kural asks it not to set so she may see him; Natrinai 196 asks it to show where he hides.
teaches: The Kural compresses into one blessing and plea a scene the Natrinai poem argues at length: the moon sees all worlds, so its silence is a witness's lie and its waning the punishment, which shows how much reasoning lies behind the Kural's single request.

note: Both are the woman saying that his coming will take the pallor from her shoulders: Kural 1265, after she has seen her husband with full eyes; Thinaimozhi 9, if the hill lord comes in this vengai evening.
teaches: The Kural states the cure as a rule in the wife's mouth, while the earlier stage in Thinaimozhi ties it to the flowering vengai, the season sign of weddings, so the coming that cures the pallor is, before marriage, the wedding itself.

note: Both ask what return can be made to the small parrot of the millet field: in Natrinai 194 the friend asks it of the parrot that did not take the millet ears while they played with the hill lord; in Ainkurunuru 288 the man asks it of the parrots that eat the millet while the girl guards it.
teaches: The parrot is thanked in one poem for eating the crop and in the other for sparing it, opposite acts earning the same gratitude, which shows that what the lovers prize is not the bird's deed but whatever keeps the field watch going and hides what they do there.

note: Both by the poet of the paalai (Perunkadungo): the man calls the waste harsh (இன்னா, Kuruntokai 124; கடுமைய காடு, Kalittokai 6) and the woman's side answers him.
teaches: The same poet gives the same plea two answers: in the short poem the friend argues the house alone is as harsh as the forest, a reason for him to stay, while the long poem has the woman draw the next step, that hardship shared on the road is her only joy, so the argument from equal harm leads straight to the demand to go with him.

note: Kuruntokai 30 calls the dream of the lover's embrace a lying dream (பொய்க்கனா) that deceived her and left her wasted; Kalittokai 128 says the dream in which he came kept her life from going, in hope he may come awake. On a plain reading one treats the dream as deceit, the other as ground for hope.
teaches: The same dream of the lover is judged a cruel lie in one poem and the thing that keeps the woman alive in the other, so akam poets held no single view of dreams and used the dream's truth or falseness to mark whether hope survived.

note: Kalittokai 149's friend warns that failing those who helped in want will strike the doer even in his descendants; Kural 110 says one who kills a good done to him has no escape.
teaches: The friend applies the Kural's gravest moral rule to a lover's delay, so the woman who gave herself in secret is counted as a benefactor, and his failure to marry her becomes ingratitude, the one wrong with no escape.

note: Kalittokai 11: the heroine reasons that the man will return because he told her the burning forest holds a tusker that lets its mate drink the little muddy water first, a dove that fans its mate and a stag that shades its doe. Thinaimalai 78: an elephant alone finds no water in the spring and falls.
teaches: The same waterless road gives comfort in Kalittokai 11 and fear in the venba, and the difference is whether the poet gives the elephant a mate: the paired beast turns drought into proof of tenderness, the lone beast only into a measure of danger.

note: The toddy-sellers keep a boar in a pit for many days, fed on rice flour and kept from its sow, to serve its fat to the bards; the couplet says that if no one killed to eat, no one would bring flesh for sale.
teaches: The idyll describes exactly the chain the couplet condemns, an animal fattened in confinement to be served and sold, and offers it as a reward of the road, so the Kural's argument against buying meat cuts against a hospitality the guide poems praise.

note: Ainkurunuru 150's heroine calls the shore lord bitter in union (புணர்வின் இன்னான்) and hard to unite with; in Kural 1152 the woman says union now holds pain for fear of parting.
teaches: Valluvar gives the reason the Sangam poem leaves implicit, that union turns bitter because parting is foreseen, while the poem's pun of the ever-embracing wave (புணரி) shows what that bitterness is measured against.

note: Kural 1060 says the asker must not be angry; 196, after naming the king's fault, blesses his sons and leaves.
teaches: The poet shows how the Kural's demand for an asker without anger can be met without silence: he names the fault plainly and still blesses, so rebuke and the absence of anger are shown to go together.

note: Kural 1224: when the lover is absent, evening comes like enemies to a killing ground. Ainthinai Aimpathu 6: evening, sweet with the bee at the jasmine for those who have company, comes and saws those who have no one.
teaches: Both women make evening a killer, but the venba adds that the same hour is sweet to the companioned, so it locates the couplet's hostility in the absence and not in evening itself, which the couplet's 'when the lover is absent' only implies.

note: Both see the konrai as gold (Kuruntokai: பொன்செய் புனையிழை; Ainkurunuru: சுடுபொன் அன்ன கொன்றை); Kuruntokai's heroine refuses the forest's word that the rains have come, since he does not lie.
teaches: The gold konrai that Kuruntokai's woman must deny, because admitting the season means admitting a broken promise, is here worn by men on his road and praised, so the same flower could be held off as false witness or welcomed as the season's adornment of his way.

note: In 122 the friend warns that the millet will be guarded and the mother frowns on the girl's secret doings; in 134 the mother herself sends the girl to drive parrots from the millet on the hill where the lover set his sign.
teaches: Millet-guarding is both the cover and the clock of the secret love: the same parental order that sends the girl to the field makes the meeting possible, and its ending, which 122 foresees, closes it, so the hill harvest sets the term within which the man must marry.

note: Kural 1164: the sea of love is there but there is no raft of safety to cross it; Kalittokai 134: her grief ends as a man whose ship broke in a shoreless sea is saved by a raft the waves bring, the lovers hastening home. One says no raft exists, the other that the sea itself brings one.
teaches: The two use the same sea and raft with opposite outcomes, which shows that in love the raft is not something the sufferer can find for herself: the couplet's woman has none, and in the poem it arrives only with the beloved's return.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as inquiry, no favour to anyone, holding to the ruler's part and acting after thought; the line says justice done by one who craves wealth is false.
teaches: The couplet's definition is a procedure and says nothing of the judge's appetites; the line adds a condition on the judge himself, so the pair shows that the four steps can be kept in form and still be false if greed sits behind them.

note: Just ten verses apart, this one ends the section on renunciation by promising a nature that can't be shifted, once craving goes. 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which gets there first.
teaches: The Kural moves from the highest claim for human release straight to the strongest claim against human power.

note: Kural 1221 says the hour is not evening but a spear that eats the life of the wedded; in Kuruntokai 319 the rain-evening comes as the stag and the elephant take shelter with their mates, and she asks what will become of her life if he does not come.
teaches: The poem shows why the evening kills: it is the hour when every creature goes to its mate, so the Kural's bare claim that evening eats life gets its cause in the paired beasts the heroine watches.

note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan, called பெருஞ்சோற்று in his colophon name, for giving the great rice without limit while the hundred fought the five; Patitruppattu 30, colophon பெருஞ்சோற்றுநிலை, sung for a son of that line, shows the rite: the drum calls warriors to scatter the great rice, a blood-mixed ball offered to the god and eaten by crows and kites.
teaches: The father's poem only names the great rice as a gift of food, while the son's shows it as a pre-battle offering that binds the warriors and frightens the enemy, so the pair shows the perunjoru as a Chera rite of war that the Purananuru's epithet assumed.

note: In Kural 1259 the woman went to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart joining him; in Kalittokai 87 the wife tells her heart that sulking at a shameless man is pointless and gives up her complaint.
teaches: Both wives abandon the sulk through the heart, but for opposite reasons: in the Kural the heart's desire overrides her, in the Kalittokai the heart concludes that a man without shame cannot be moved by sulking, so ending an oodal can be resignation as well as longing.

note: Kural 610 says a king without sloth (மடியிலா மன்னவன்) gains the whole earth; Fragment 4 praises a king who does not stop for the rains nor slacken for the cold (பனிஎன மடியாய்) and keeps his army in foreign land.
teaches: The Kural states freedom from sloth as a ruler's general virtue, while the fragment shows what it meant in war: refusing the seasonal halt of the rains and the cold that normally ended a campaign, so the king's tirelessness was measured against the calendar of war.

note: In Kural 1157 the woman says her slipping bangles spread the news that the shore lord (துறைவன்) has left her; in Ainkurunuru 140 she asks the bard to tell the lord of the ford (துறைகெழு கொண்கன்) the state of her bangles since he left.
teaches: Valluvar makes the bangles themselves the gossips who publish his departure, while the Sangam woman needs the bard to carry that sign to the man, so the couplet's bangles that speak for themselves compress a scene in which the body's testimony still had to be delivered.

note: Venni Kuyathiyar praises Karikal's victory but says the king he defeated at Venni, who sat facing north to die ashamed of a wound on his back, is better than he; the idyll's catalogue of the peoples Karikalan crushed has no such voice, and praises his men for never turning their backs (ஒருவேமெனப் புறக்கொடாது).
teaches: Both poems turn on the shame of the turned back, but the short puram poem lets a woman poet rank the defeated king's honour above the victor's, while the long praise gives the ethic only to the victor's side, so the pair shows what the conquest catalogue had no room to say.

note: In 251 the speaker begs the millet to ripen late so the girl's days in the field may last; in 259 the millet heads have ripened like the sea drawing back, and the friend asks what they will do.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two poems are the before and after of one threat, making the millet's ripening the clock of the secret love: the harvest that ends the field season also ends the meetings unless the man marries.

note: Verse 9 calls lust for women not one's own what fools love; verse 19 says the man at another's door by night hangs by a thread.
teaches: Within the book the same act is first a fool's desire and then a mortal danger, so the book judges it both by the wanting and by the result.

ullurai.tenor: the man going after wealth and the fresh beauty his going will ruin

pairs.situation: he leaves driven by desire for gain

pairs.scene: நீடு செயல் சிதலைத் தோடு புனைந்து எடுத்த
pairs.situation: the slowly built mound is her fresh beauty, which his going will undo
the ruin is done at one stroke, as her tears spoil her eyes

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a bear met on the forked paths the man must cross, a thing of the poem's own road (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the hill girl feeds the jackfruit to the monkey, treating it as an arriving guest
iraicchi.sense: in this country a guest who comes openly is fed and made welcome, so the man should come as a guest by marriage, not by the fearful night path

iraicchi.act: the tiger joins its female and its distress ends
iraicchi.sense: her sickness, like the tiger's, ends only in union with the man who gave it, not in the diviner's rite

ullurai.tenor: the lovers parted by the town's slander

pairs.situation: the slandering town, which strikes at night
the lovers' bond struck down
the girl left lonely and grieving

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses beasts of the hill in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.sense: even the stork keeps its mate beside it, while the lord leaves her to a sorrow that shows on her body

pairs.situation: low women pull him down to them as ploughmen pull a branch
they bathe in what he gives, while the wife is left with the shame

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a kaanji tree and ploughmen of the marutham town the poem is set in (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the male wild dog, keeping to its mate, lets the doe with her fawn go unharmed
iraicchi.sense: a beast at one with its mate spares another's mother and young, as the man, drawn by his wife, left off his own seizing of wealth and hurried home

ullurai.tenor: the woman whom the town now knows as the man's

pairs.situation: the town's talk, gust after gust
the name of his woman heaped on her until it cannot be brushed off

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the punnai and herons of her own shore, things she knows (porul 7.26)

note: Purananuru 312 assigns each person a கடன்: bearing the son is the mother's, making him worthy the father's, and killing elephants in battle the young man's. Thinaimalai 82 calls going to make wealth the man's கடன், repeating the word three times.
teaches: The venba carries the heroic vocabulary of duty from the battlefield to the trade road: what Purananuru 312 makes the young man's duty in war, the later akam friend makes his duty in wealth-making, and uses it to silence the wife's grief.

note: Both name வல்வில் ஓரி: Purananuru 152 shows the hunter whose single arrow kills an elephant, a tiger, a stag, a boar and an iguana, and who feeds the bard venison; in Natrinai 6 the girl's hair smells of Ori's forest, where the ripe fruit of the kumizh falls as food for young deer.
teaches: The love poet takes from the hunter-patron's fame only his forest's scent and plenty, a place where the very deer his bow kills feed unharmed, so akam borrowed a puram name for the bounty of a land and left its violence behind.

note: Kural 639 says seventy crore enemies are better than a minister at one's side who plots harm; Kalittokai 27 has spring encamp like an enemy army in the land of an unworthy king whose foolish minister let it in.
teaches: The Kural states the danger of a bad counsellor as a maxim, while the kali shows its outcome, the enemy camped inside the land, and uses that sight for spring's assault on a lonely woman, which shows the statecraft maxim already worked as a picture poets could borrow.

note: In Akananuru 122 the girl lists the town, mother, guards, dogs, moon and owl that keep watch, and complains that when all sleep he does not come; in Kuruntokai 375 the friend says it is better he does not come, since the guards beat their drum all night against the tiger.
teaches: The same sleepless watch is used to reproach the lover for missing his chance and to wish him away from it, so the pair shows that the catalogue of obstacles is addressed to the man in both directions, and that its real end is to make the night visit impossible and marriage necessary.

note: Kural 211 asks what the world can give back to the rain, whose obligation seeks no return; in Natrinai 139 the hero blesses the rain cloud as his helper for the night rain that fell while he lay with his wife.
teaches: The Kural's rain serves the world and gets nothing back, while the Natrinai hero answers its private help with a blessing, so the poem shows the one return a person could make to the rain and turns the rain's public good into a favour done to two people.

note: Akananuru 51's man tells his heart that wealth gained by parting is not worth leaving his wife's embrace; Ainkurunuru 337's wife says that for her man wealth is sweeter than the embrace.
teaches: The two poems weigh the same two goods, wealth and the embrace, and reach opposite verdicts according to who speaks: the man at home can still choose the embrace, while the wife whose man has gone can only infer that he chose wealth, so the akam tradition hands each verdict to the one who lives with it.

note: In Paripadal 6.88-92 a husband says a woman bathing in his pool, swept under by a wave, fell on him unbidden, and swears by cool Parankunram; in Paripadal 21.39-45 a wife at a pool on Parankunram loses her float and her husband plunges in and embraces her.
teaches: The Vaiyai song's husband uses a fall in the water as an alibi for touching another woman and swears by Parankunram, while the Parankunram song shows the water embrace on that hill as a husband's rescue of his own wife, so the pair shows one festival accident read either as an excuse for straying or as wedded love.

note: Kural 1168: the night that puts all living things to sleep is pitiable, having no companion but her. Kuruntokai 145: the long night here has only sleepers who will not talk with the sleepless.
teaches: Both women stay awake while everyone sleeps, but the Kural turns her loneliness into a mock pity for the night, while the Kuruntokai blames the sleeping village; together they show that the wakeful heroine's complaint can fall on the night or on the people, and that the couplet's wit grows from the poem's social grievance.

note: Natrinai 12's girl, leaving, pities the companions who will grieve at her ball and anklets; Ainkurunuru 384's girl, on the road, sends those companions word through brahmins that she went so her beauty might flourish.
teaches: The companions are the girl's first thought at both ends of the flight, pitied as she leaves and answered once she is away, and her message turns the pity into a justification that her going completes her mother's care.

note: Both are the man speaking of the madal: Kuruntokai 17 lists as a general rule what men do when love hardens (ride the palm horse, wear erukku, become a street spectacle); Kural 1133 says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal.
teaches: The Kuruntokai poem supplies the public ritual (the erukku garland, the mocking street) that the Kural compresses into a single inventory of loss, and the Kural adds what the older poem leaves unstated: that taking up the madal costs a man his shame and manliness.

note: Kalittokai 81: the boy moves his toy chariot by hand in the yard (கால் வல் தேர் கையின் இயக்க), the father is caught coming from another woman, and the wife ends by going to the boy like a cow to the place where its calf is tied (கன்று யாத்த உழிச் செல்லும் ஆ போல்). Thinaimalai 138: in this boy's father's town the buffalo's milk runs as she thinks of her calf.
teaches: Kalittokai 81 gives the cow's pull to its calf to the mother as an open simile, while Thinaimalai 138 leaves the same yearning beast unglossed in the father's own fields, so the pair shows how the marutham poets could turn one image of parental pull from praise of the mother into a silent reproach of the father.

note: Akananuru 74: the heroine says she could bear the friend's comfort but for the harsh small pipe the unlettered cowherds blow (கல்லாக் கோவலர் ஊதும் வல்வாய் சிறுகுழல்) at evening. Kainnilai 35: the herders who do not know (தெரிவிலர்) blow the sweet pipe (தீங்குழல்).
teaches: Both poets excuse the herders by their ignorance, but one calls the pipe harsh and the other sweet, which shows that the cruelty is not in the sound itself but in the hour and the ear that hears it.

note: Kural 788 says friendship clears distress at once, like the hand of one whose garment slips; the other woman of Natrinai 216 says her lovers do not help her sorrow as the hand helps a hurt eye, yet the town they live in is still sweet.
teaches: The parathai admits her lovers fail the Kural's test of friendship, the hand's unthinking help, and still finds their mere presence in town enough, so the pair shows love surviving a failure that by the Kural's measure would end a friendship.

note: Naladiyar 2: wealth stays level with no one but turns like a cart wheel, so share it the day it comes. Kuruntokai 143 uses the wealth that does not stay with a generous man as the image of pallor that will pass.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues from wealth's instability to giving, and the love poem had already fused the two into one image, the giver whose wealth leaves him, and turned that ethical commonplace into a promise that sorrow too is the kind of thing that leaves.

note: Akananuru 186 has the courtesan say, for the wife's women to overhear, that the wife's real enemy is the husband who leaves women pale and lives in her own house; Paripadal 20.79-82 has the courtesan tell the wife to her face that he is the thief and she is not (அவன் கள்வன்; கள்வி நான் அல்லேன்).
teaches: Together the two show that shifting the blame onto the husband was the courtesan's settled defence in marutham, and that what the Akananuru gives as an overheard boast the festival poem stages as a face-to-face exchange, with the husband's gift on her body as the evidence and a crowd to hear both sides.

note: In 475 the heroine says the bard grieves for her more than his master does; in 480 the bard himself renounces his master over her tears.
teaches: The sympathy the wife reads in the bard's face becomes, by the decade's last poem, a spoken break with the patron, so the decade moves the go-between from the man's party to the woman's.

note: Akananuru 80: the friend says he has come by night across the dark backwater of crocodiles and sharks and asks him to come by day to the grove where they guard drying fish. Thinaimalai 49: no dark at all to cross, since the pearls sweep away the midnight.
teaches: The two friends refuse the same night visit for opposite reasons, the older one because the dark hides beasts and the venba because the shore has no dark to hide him, so the convention needs only the refusal and lets the reason be turned inside out.

note: Purananuru 123 praises Malaiyan for chariots given more freely than the raindrops on the peak of Mullur; Natrinai 170 recalls Malaiyan's single spear routing the many Aryans at Mullur, as the image of wives helpless before one rival.
teaches: Held together they show a chieftain's fame had two faces, giving and lone valour, and the akam poet chose the war face because the household's problem was one woman beating many: akam borrowed from puram exactly the facet its situation needed.

note: Kalittokai 35 line 2 likens humming bees in the boughs to the enjoyment of those who live on a diligent man's wealth; thirattu 8 likens those who live on gifts (பரிசில் வாழ்நர்) to bees eating pollen.
teaches: The bee and the dependent were interchangeable figures that ran in both directions, a season described through patronage in Kalittokai and a society through a flower in the Paripadal, and only the Paripadal says whom the dependents feed on: the households, not the palace.

note: Natrinai 138: the lord of the cool ford where the white heron lays its eggs (வெண் குருகு ஈனும் தண்ணம் துறைவன்) is now known to the old town. Kainnilai 59: the lord of the cool ford where the heron lays its eggs in the thaazhai (குருகுஈனும் தண்ணந் துறைவனை) is now known to the mother, who shuts the door.
teaches: The epithet of the nesting heron frames in both poems the moment the secret becomes known, to the town in one and the mother in the other, which supports reading the breeding heron as a call for the man to set up house now that kalavu is over.

note: In Akananuru 16 the wife finds a courtesan secretly embracing her son in the chariot street; in Natrinai 250 the husband goes to embrace the son in the street and the wife, taking it otherwise, shies away.
teaches: Read together, the small son in the street is where the marriage's suspicions are read from both sides, another woman betraying herself by loving him and the husband being refused because of what his embrace carries, so the child who should join the parents becomes the evidence between them.

note: Akananuru 35's girl leaves the sky-touching walled house desolate (வான்தோய் இஞ்சி நன்னகர் புலம்ப); in Ainkurunuru 386 the mother is bewildered in the tall-walled good house (நெடுஞ்சுவர் நல்லில் மருண்ட).
teaches: The high wall that in Akananuru stands empty after the girl has slipped it becomes in Ainkurunuru the place where the mother is lost, so the house built to guard a daughter is shown to hold only the one left behind.

note: Akananuru 113 praises the Kosar who never swerve from friendship even in bad times, with unswerving plans (திரிபில் சூழ்ச்சி); Kuruntokai 73 holds up the Kosar of the single word, who cut down Nannan's mango, as the model of hard-eyed scheming (வன்கண் சூழ்ச்சி).
teaches: The Kosar's fame was for a kept word carried out by planning, and akam poets drew on it two ways, as loyalty in one poem and as ruthless resolve in the other, so the same people supplied both the virtue and the hard edge of a sworn word.

note: Kural 1227: love-sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and opens in the evening. Kuruntokai 32: if one can tell morning, day, evening, midnight and dawn apart, love is a lie.
teaches: The Kural gives love a daily clock with evening as its worst hour, while the Kuruntokai lover says true love cannot tell the hours apart, so the two set the convention of the evening's pain against the claim that real longing knows no time.

note: Kalittokai 140's rider complains that the town sees his sickness and does not soften (கண்டும் கண்ணோடாது இவ் ஊர்); Kural 576 says those who have eyes and do not turn them kindly are like trees fixed in the soil.
teaches: The madal rider appeals to the civic virtue the Kural names கண்ணோட்டம், so the madal is shown to work through the town's duty of kindly regard, and the town that will not soften is, by the Kural's measure, as insensible as a tree.

note: Kural 1254 says she used to call herself restrained (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன்) but desire breaks out in public; Kalittokai 77 asks whether restraint (நிறை) is easy for one who lives with an enemy, her own heart.
teaches: The Kural blames desire in general for breaking restraint, while the Kalittokai wife places the failure in a precise moment, the sight of the unfaithful husband at her door, so the same loss of நிறை turns from a lover's confession into a wronged wife's helplessness against her own grievance.

note: Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the sceptre that does not bend; Patitruppattu 37 lists the king's victory (வலம்படு வென்றியும்) and his unbending principle (கோடாக் கொள்கையும்) as two separate things he has.
teaches: The Kural makes straight rule the cause of victory, while the Chera poet sets the two side by side as distinct possessions, so the praise poem lacks the causal claim the maxim adds and shows the two were first counted as separate royal goods.

note: Purananuru 5 tells a Chera, lord of a forest land where elephants spread like cattle, to keep away from those who cast off grace and love and to guard the realm as one rears a child; Patitruppattu 71 shows the king burning towns and taking cattle and tribute, then says that had he not weighed the strong and the simple and shown grace (அருளாய் ஆயின்), no one here would live.
teaches: Purananuru 5 asks for grace as the standing temper of a ruler's guard, while Patitruppattu 71 finds it only after conquest, as the sparing of the defeated who pay tribute, so the two Chera poems show grace counselled as a principle of rule and praised as a victor's restraint.

note: 50 sets the hero's stealthy coming, like sleep and without a tryst, against the proper way; 52, with the same shore-army image, names the proper way: choose a day and marry.
teaches: The vague நெறியால் of 50 is spelled out in 52 as நாள் ஆய்ந்து வரைதல், so the sequence moves from forbidding the secret visit to prescribing the rite, with the marshalled shore as the model of order in both.

note: 66 rejects the outward marks of ascetics; 68 rejects four austerities and keeps only restraint of the five senses.
teaches: Together the two verses strip ascetic display in two moves, first the marks on the body and then its austerities, leaving only restraint of the senses.

note: Both speak in the woman's voice after a promise not to part is broken by his leaving: the Kural asks if the believer is at fault; Akananuru 1 asks whether he has forgotten (மறந்தனர் கொல்லோ).
teaches: The Kural turns the broken promise into a question of blame, while the Sangam heroine keeps it a question of memory; the poem shows a woman who will not yet say he broke his word, which the couplet's moral question has already assumed.

note: 780 calls a death that brings tears to one's ruler's eyes worth begging for, in the chapter on martial pride. 723 calls those who die among enemies easy to find.
teaches: The Kural holds both, and each chapter's supreme value is deflated by the other.

note: Kuruntokai 7's onlookers see anklets still on the eloping girl's feet; in Natrinai 12 the friend tells how the girl, hiding herself at dawn, slipped off her pebble-filled anklets and left her striped ball before going.
teaches: Together they show the anklet as the mark of an unmarried girl, read by strangers on the road in one poem and taken off by the girl herself in secret in the other, so the eloping girl performs alone at dawn the change of state that a wedding would have made in public.

note: Akananuru 50: the hidden-tearful girl says the anril on the palmyra by the house cannot sleep at night if parted even once from its mate. Ainthinai Aimpathu 41: the anril cries though its mate has come and rests beside it.
teaches: The anril's wakefulness is a fixed proof of sleepless separation, and the venba reverses its case: the long poem argues from a parted bird by likeness, the four-line poem from a joined bird by greater reason, so the same bird can carry both the analogy and the a fortiori.

note: Both liken the marutham bull buffalo to field warriors (மள்ளர் அன்ன, மள்ளரின்): in Ainkurunuru 94 it rests with its mate in the shaded pool of the girl's father's fields, in Natrinai 260 it leaves the lotus it is tired of and sleeps alone on the sand, in the wife's refusal of the lord.
teaches: The same warrior-like bull stands for the husband to come when it stays beside its mate and for the husband who strays when it wanders off sated, so the image's sense in marutham is fixed by whether the beast keeps to its partner, not by its strength.

note: Akananuru 5: the man tells his heart he gave up the journey when his wife, without a word, showed her grief in her face and her sigh over their son. Aimpathu 39: the man calls his heart foolish, for when they stir to leave for wealth she sobs and sighs; how will she bear it once they are gone?
teaches: Akananuru 5 shows the journey given up on the sight of her mute grief, and Aimpathu 39 shows the man reasoning from her sobs at the setting out to the harder grief to come, so the pair gives the decision against wealth both as what he saw and as what he foresees.

note: In Akananuru 380 the shore lord leaves his chariot far off and asks the girls the name of their town; in Ainkurunuru 198 the tall-shouldered man stands asking about the small ford where girls play.
teaches: The question about a ford or a town is the fixed first move of the shore courtship: Ainkurunuru 198 catches it as it is asked, and Akananuru 380 shows the friend later reading the same pretext as the start of a suit that ends in his shame and her consent.

note: Kural 1320 has the man say that even when he looks at her thinking, she flares up: whom were you thinking of as you looked? In Paripadal 18.8-14 the woman sees him gaze at a peacock and think, says she knows his thought and demands it, and he answers that he was thinking how the peacock had stolen her bearing.
teaches: The couplet ends on the woman's suspicion with no reply, while the hymn supplies the reply that disarms it, that the thought was of her through the bird that took her grace, so the pair shows the silent gaze as a fixed cause of sulking and the lover's answer as part of the same convention.

note: Kar Narpathu 17: on the high rock-ledged hill the thunder crushes snakes and the sky, thick with dark, shows the season; the friend reads it as his return. Kuruntokai 158: the heroine asks the cloud, whose thunder strikes snakes dead on the tall slope, whether it has no pity on lone women.
teaches: The same storm with its snake-killing thunder is a sign of comfort when the friend reads it as the promised season and a terror when the lone heroine faces it at night, so the image carries whatever the speaker's situation gives it rather than a fixed meaning.

note: Both use the moon's spot: the Naladiyar to say the noble cannot bear one stain as the moon does, the Neelakesi to say a work, like the moon, may carry a fault and still be loved.
teaches: The same image yields opposite counsel: for a person's character a single stain is unbearable, but for a poet before an assembly an acknowledged fault is excusable.

note: In 255 the girl fears the midnight path for him and wishes he would not come; in 257 the friend tells the man himself that she knows fierce beasts roam the path and he still comes at midnight, and presses marriage.
teaches: The pair shows one danger serving two speakers: the girl's private fear in 255 becomes in the friend's mouth in 257 a lever on the man, so the convention of the dangerous path is both a feeling and an argument for marriage.

note: In Akananuru 274 the returning man says her town lies in the rainy scrub where a lone herdsman stands in the drizzle with his lambs; in Kuruntokai 221 the waiting woman sees the goatherd with his lambs crowned with mullai buds and says the man has not come.
teaches: The herdsman of the mullai scrub is the season's witness from both sides: on the man's road he marks the way home, at the woman's door he wears the proof that the promised season has come without the man, so one figure serves as sign of return or of broken promise.

note: Kural 1143: the man asks whether the gossip the town knows is not welcome, since it is like having what he has not yet obtained. Kuruntokai 51: the friend says the gossiping town too speaks of the girl with him, and her mother and father favour him.
teaches: The couplet values gossip as a foretaste of a union not yet had; the poem shows the next step, when talk that pairs the lovers joins the parents' consent, so the gossip the Kural's lover enjoys in fancy becomes one of the voices that brings the marriage about.

iraicchi.act: the lizard calls to its mate across the dry forest
iraicchi.sense: the man who passes and hears even the lizard call its mate will think of his own and turn home

iraicchi.act: the bull elephants keep to their herd as they roam the grove
iraicchi.sense: even the elephants on her road stay with their herd, while the girl has left her own band of companions and their wedding for one man

iraicchi.act: the anril keeps with its hen in their nest on the tall branch through the cold midnight and cries
iraicchi.sense: even the birds keep their mates through the cold night, while her lover, who said he would come, stays away

ullurai.tenor: the girl who took the hill man's love

pairs.situation: she took his love without knowing what it would cost
what she took belonged to the dread hill and its man, not freely hers
she now burns and trembles, eyes streaming

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses a peacock and millet of her own hill field, things she knows (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the husband who keeps to other women's houses for fear of his wife's anger

pairs.situation: he dreads the wife's sharp reproach
he hides among the other women

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the heron and fish of the pond of her own marutham town (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the man who lodged for a while with the girl and may leave her

pairs.situation: the man is a passing stranger, not one who stays
he has rested on her and enjoyed her beauty
the girl who bent to him and has nothing to hold him by

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a neythal stork and punnai of the poem's own shore (porul 7.27)

note: Kural 1133: he once had shame and manliness, and now has the palmyra horse that lovers ride. Natrinai 152: love gave him the madal, the erukku gave him gossip, the sun gave loneliness, night gave helplessness.
teaches: The couplet records one exchange, virtues lost for a madal; the poem turns it into a chain of gifts in which each thing hands on the next harm, so the madal is not the end of the loss but the first link of a day-long sequence.

note: Kuruntokai 234 says that for those without a partner every hour is evening; Kuruntokai 240 shows one evening's work, as the north wind blows and his hill sinks from view like a ship.
teaches: Together they show why evening is the worst hour: in 234 it is a state that swallows all hours, in 240 it is the moment the last visible trace of him, his hill, is taken away, so the evening's pain is the loss of sight of him.

note: Patitruppattu 20 says Nedum Cheralathan went against foes on an island in the sea and cut their kadamba; Patitruppattu 45 says his son threw his spear and drove back the sea itself, which no rain or river can change.
teaches: Set side by side, the father's war against islanders in the sea and the son's spear thrown at the sea show the decade's title growing from a naval campaign into a feat against nature, with the human enemy dropped and the sea left as the only adversary worth naming.

note: Ainkurunuru 212: the girl asks why they should be parted from a man of virtue (அறவன்). Kural 1154: the woman asks whether those who trusted the assurances of the one who said 'do not fear' are at fault if he leaves.
teaches: The girl rests her whole security on the man's being virtuous, while the Kural imagines that very assurer leaving and moves the blame onto him, so the pair shows that in secret love the only guarantee was his character and the Kural tests it to the point of failure.

note: Purananuru 93 describes the rite of cutting with a sword the body of a king who died of sickness, so that he goes where battle-slain warriors go; Akananuru 61 opens with the saying behind that rite (blessed are those who die at others' hands, not seized by Death) as the reason a man leaves home.
teaches: Together they show the warrior's creed about a good death working at two scales: as a royal funeral rite in puram, and in akam as a proverb that sends an ordinary man away from his wife to strive.

note: Kalittokai 79: the wife tells the husband not to take up their son, whose hands will pull the pearl chain and garland by which the other women marked him (அணி சிதைப்பான்). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 45: he comes with the son on his chest, the boy's pearl ornaments crushing his frontlet (பட்டஞ் சிதைப்ப).
teaches: Kalittokai spells out what the four-line poem only shows: the son's hands spoiling the father's finery are spoiling the other women's tokens, so the venba's ironic 'he is resourceful' means the child he brings as a shield is also the one who exposes him.

note: Kural 801 defines old friendship as a bond that never curtails the liberties of intimacy (கிழமை); 223 says the king, even as a hero-stone, gives room to friends of old intimacy (கிழமைத் தொன்னட் புடையார்) who come to him.
teaches: The Kural's definition is carried past death in 223: the claim of intimacy that a friend may exercise unasked includes the right to follow the king into death, and the stone honours it by making room, so pazhaimai is tested at its extreme.

note: Kar Narpathu 4's friend points to the bloomed konrai as the season and the cure of pallor; Kuruntokai 66's friend calls the bloomed konrai foolish, fooled by stray rain, and denies that the season has come.
teaches: The friend's comfort can use the konrai either way, as proof the promised season is here or as a false sign to be dismissed, which shows that the consolation lies in the friend's argument and not in the flower itself.

note: In Kalittokai 58 the man threatens madal to the girl herself; in 61 the friend reports the same threat, laughs at it as shameless, and still concludes they must act.
teaches: Read together they show where the madal threat lands: the girl too young to understand it in 58 cannot be moved by it, while the friend in 61 is, so the threat is effectively addressed to the household's guardians.

note: Both have the man, on seeing the girl, take her for an அணங்கு (Kural: அணங்குகொல்; Ainkurunuru: ஆர் அணங்கினளே).
teaches: Valluvar's man hesitates between goddess, peahen and woman, while the Sangam man has settled the question and pins it on her youth (இளையள் ஆயினும்), so the couplet's doubt is a refinement of an older certainty that a hill girl can be a striking power.

note: In both a searching woman asks brahmins on the waste road (அந்தணீர், அந்தணிர்) and they answer that they saw the girl (கண்டனம், கண்டனெம்); Kalittokai adds the sandal, pearl and lute argument and says the way never leaves aram.
teaches: The scene that Ainkurunuru leaves as a bare eyewitness report of the lover's tenderness was later expanded by Kalittokai into an argument that a daughter belongs to the man she follows, so the brahmins' reply grew from testimony into doctrine.

note: Both use the reaped millet stubble of the hill farmer: in Kuruntokai 133 the stubble cropped by parrots puts out leaves again in the rain, as the girl lives on after his first taking of her beauty; in Ainkurunuru 286 the stubble bears pods for his ever-yielding land while her own glow is taken.
teaches: The same stubble is a figure of the girl's own survival in Kuruntokai 133 but of the man's endless plenty in Ainkurunuru 286, set against her fading, so the image of renewal cuts both ways: what revives on his hills need not revive in her.

note: Kural 1285: as the eye does not see the brush that lines it, I do not see his fault when I see him. Thinaimalai 153: my eyes never see the lord, in sulk, in union, or when he leaves in anger.
teaches: The Kural finds one moment when the eye cannot see, nearness blinding it to his fault; the Thinaimalai extends that blindness to every phase of the marutham quarrel and to the man himself, so the couplet's single paradox becomes a whole cycle in which closeness and distance alike keep him out of view.

note: Mullaippattu's king lies sleepless in his tent thinking of elephants wounded by spears and of men who fell repaying their food; Nedunalvadai's king rises and goes out at midnight to see his wounded.
teaches: The two camp kings show one care in two forms, remembered in bed in Mullaippattu and acted out by walking the lines in Nedunalvadai, so the night-time thought for the wounded is a fixed mark of the good war king in these idylls, the more vivid of them putting it into motion.

note: Both argue from an unknown lifespan against putting something off: Naladiyar 19 says do not defer good deeds because the wind may drop the unripe fruit; Natrinai 314 says no one knows the measure of a life, yet he left her for later gain.
teaches: The pairing shows that 'do not defer, life is short' was a shared argument whose object changed with the genre, virtue in the Naladiyar and love in the Natrinai, where wealth-seeking is the deferral blamed.

note: Ainkurunuru 6: may he marry her and our father give her. Ainkurunuru 7: may he take her and go to his own town.
teaches: Read in order, the decade's wishes walk through the rite step by step, the father's giving (6) and then the bride's leaving for the husband's town (7), so the series records the sequence of a Sangam marriage that no single poem states.

note: Kopperunchozhan, the poet of Kuruntokai 53, is the king of Purananuru 216, who tells the doubters that his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar wants no lie that would spoil his fame and will come to share his death. In Kuruntokai 53 his friend-speaker holds a lover to an oath sworn before the hill-goddesses, which he has broken.
teaches: Read together, the king's two voices weigh faith two ways: in puram a friend never met keeps faith with no oath at all, while in his akam poem a lover breaks faith despite an oath sworn before goddesses, so the poet who staked his death on unsworn friendship knew how little a sworn word could hold in love.

note: In Akananuru 297 the man on his way for wealth sees a wildcat's fluffy kitten following its mother like stars round the moon; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 40 the heroine hears that on his road the spotted wildcat watches for prey for its kitten.
teaches: Each lover sees the wildcat with its young on the wealth road from his or her own side, the man as the household he leaves behind and the woman as the provision he goes to win, so the creature gathers both halves of the paalai argument about leaving for wealth.

note: The Kural names customs (உல்கு) as one of the three kinds of the king's wealth; the idyll shows Puhar's customs men levying duty every day without shortfall and stamping the tiger seal on goods for the good king.
teaches: The Kural's single word for customs revenue is in the idyll a working institution with officers, a royal seal and a daily round at the port, so the couplet's category can be seen to name an administration the earlier poets had watched in operation.

note: In Akananuru 56 the wife tells the bard who blundered into her house 'இம்மனை அன்று; அஃது உம்மனை'; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 22 she tells him 'நெறிஅதுகாண் எங்கையர் இற்கு'.
teaches: The same retort appears as a told comic incident in Akananuru and as a direct taunt in the four-line venba, which shows that pointing the bard to the other house was a fixed refusal move the later poet could use bare, without the story.

note: Kural 1233: the shoulders that swelled on the day of union now announce loudly that he has gone. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 14: because he is said to be good, her shoulders have forgotten to waste even if he leaves.
teaches: On a plain reading the two make incompatible claims about the same sign: the Kural takes wasting shoulders as the body's certain witness to separation, while the venba says trust in the man's goodness can stop the body from giving that witness at all.

note: The Kural's man says love is sweeter than toddy because merely thinking of it brings unfailing joy; in Ainkurunuru 325 the man says the scorching waste does not harm him because he has her nature as companion.
teaches: The couplet states that remembered love never fails to give joy, and the Ainkurunuru puts that claim to a hard test, the peopleless summer waste, where the memory works as a travelling companion (துணை), so the maxim gains a situation in which its truth is a matter of survival.

note: Purananuru 369, a kalavazhi for another Chera, maps the battle onto rain and tillage, with elephants as clouds and chariots as ploughs; Patitruppattu 36, also kalavazhi, has the elephants fall with trunks cut like palms in a cleared field.
teaches: Read together, the two show the kalavazhi of the Chera court treating slaughter as farm work, a single cleared-field simile in one poem and a full season of ploughing and harvest in the other, so the thurai's name from the threshing floor shapes its images.

note: In Natrinai 208 the friend says the great rain's voice seems to seek out parted lovers and bring them home; in Natrinai 214 the woman hears the rain's voice as flashing and roaring in mockery of her grief, because he has not come.
teaches: The monsoon thunder is the same sign of the promised season in both, but the friend before the parting reads it as a power that fetches the man and the wife after the deadline reads it as a jeer, so the rain's meaning in paalai depends on whether the promise is still ahead or already broken.

note: Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; Paripadal 13 line 47 says the two deeds are absent where his feet are praised, and gives the god a heart set on a single deed.
teaches: The Paripadal sets the Kural's claim inside a theology: the praisers are free of both deeds because the god himself is beyond the three times and holds to one deed, so the Kural's freedom from karma through praise is grounded in what the praised one is.

note: Purananuru 35.14-21 tells Killivalavan that his sky-touching umbrella is not to keep off the sun but to shelter suffering subjects, under a sceptre like aram itself; Paripadal 3.74-76 says the god, with grace as umbrella and aram as sceptre, made the twenty-one worlds a single shade with no second shade.
teaches: The puram poet has to argue the king into reading his umbrella as protection, a meaning the king may fail, whereas the hymn makes protection the umbrella's very substance in the god and takes over the royal boast of one shade with no rival, so the pair shows divine kingship and the counsel to kings using one ideal to measure each other.

note: Kural 1147: the town's gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water of this sickness. In Natrinai 149 the street women spread the gossip, the mother beats the girl with a cane, and she resolves to leave with the shore lord.
teaches: The couplet says that gossip and the mother's scolding feed the love they mean to kill; the poem shows what that fed love finally does, turning the same two pressures, the street's finger at the nose and the mother's cane, into the reason for elopement.

note: In 1130 she uses 'he lives within me' to refute the town's gossip. In 1249 she uses the same fact against her own heart, to stop it from leaving.
teaches: The argument that once consoled her now traps her.

note: In Kural 1146 the woman says she saw him on one day only and the gossip has spread like the snake seizing the moon; in Ainkurunuru 369 the friend tells the man that his tryst of yesterday (நெருநல்) is already louder in the town's mouth than the seasonal koel.
teaches: Both measure a single meeting against a public noise, the eclipse in the couplet and the koel's cry in 369, and holding them together shows the alar topic's fixed shape: the smaller and more recent the secret, the larger the natural event the gossip is said to outdo.

note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 24: the friend rests her comfort on the man who swore an oath (வஞ்சினம்) and held to it, with the rain as his token. Kural 1154: if he who said 'fear not' leaves, is there any fault in those who trusted his assuring word?
teaches: The friend builds her comfort on his oath, while the couplet asks who is to blame if such an oath fails, so together they show that the whole mullai argument of waiting rests on trusting a man's word, and the Kural names the risk the friend leaves unsaid.

note: Both use the turn 'I do not grieve that she went; I grieve for...' (நோவேன் ... நோவல்): Akananuru 63 for the girl's night in a robbers' hamlet, Ainkurunuru 378 for the friend left behind.
teaches: The 'not this but that' turn of the mother's lament could redirect grief either to the girl's hardships on the road or, as in Ainkurunuru, to the companion at home, so the lament counts the friend's loss as a second wound of the elopement.

note: In Kalittokai 67.6-9 the wife says she will sulk when her husband comes showing the wounds and scars (புண், வடு) that other women's garlands (கோதையால் அலைத்த) left on him, and her heart gives way when she sees him; in Paripadal 12.57-73 the wife herself beats her husband with her garland (கமழ் கோதை கோலாப் புடைத்து), then fears a scar on his chest (வடு அஞ்சி) and her quarrel passes.
teaches: In the Kalittokai the garland-wound is evidence against the husband, written on him by rival women, while in the hymn the wife wields the garland herself and her fear of the scar is what ends her sulk, so the pair shows the garland-blow as a festival game of the Vaiyai town whose meaning, accusation or claim, depends on whose hand struck it.

note: The idyll's king answers both those who seek justice and those who seek their needs, with a clear sight that discerns between them; the couplet says a ruler not easy of access who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself.
teaches: The couplet names access and examined judgment as two duties whose lack ruins a king, while the idyll shows them as one daily audience in which judgment and gifts are granted together and discernment joins them, so justice and giving were seen as a single court function.

note: In Natrinai 300 a suitor sets a great chariot at the gate as the price of the girl's bangles (சிறு வளை விலை); in Thinaimalai 15 the friend says no price, not the sea-girt world, could buy the girl, and she must be given to the elders who come for her.
teaches: Natrinai shows a bride price actually offered, and Thinaimalai answers the practice: by declaring her beyond any price the friend moves the marriage from purchase to gift, so the only claim the household should honour is the formal coming of the suitor's elders.

note: Natrinai 380: the friend refuses the bard, saying they are soiled with ghee and smoke and smell of the new-born son, no match for the decked women of his master's street. Thinaimalai 151: the wife tells the bard her son plays in the dust before this house, not as other women's do, and his master may go and play with 'our younger sisters'.
teaches: Both refuse the bard by setting the soiled household against the decked rivals, but the Natrinai turns the grime on the women of the house as mock unfitness, while the Thinaimalai turns it on the son and calls the rivals 'our younger sisters', so the same refusal could be humble or proud depending on whom the dirt is laid on.

note: In Akananuru 110 a stranger asks the bathing girls if he may eat with them and stay in their noisy fishing hamlet, and they turn him away; in Kuruntokai 345 the friend herself asks the man whether staying with his chariot at their small town by the great water would be a fault.
teaches: The night's stay in the fishing hamlet is the neythal courtship's measure of trust: asked for by the stranger at the start and refused, it is offered by the friend once the love is known, so who proposes the stay marks how far the affair has gone.

note: In 208 the girl's eyes fill with tears whenever his mountain is hidden; in 210 the friend says her sickness may abate if she stands looking at his hill.
teaches: Read together the two poems make the girl's state a function of the hill's visibility, tears when it is hidden and healing when it is seen, which is the argument the friend needs before the mother for letting the girl climb and look.

note: 186 says the world lives by its king; 187 says a land is good wherever its men are good, naming no king.
teaches: Placed side by side in the anthology, the two maxims locate the source of a land's well-being in different hands, the ruler in 186 and the men at large in 187, so the reader sees that Sangam counsel did not rest the realm on the king alone.

note: In Kural 1150 the friend tells the woman the town raises the very gossip they want, since the lover will grant marriage when asked; in Kuruntokai 351 the friend tells the girl to rejoice because their kin have declared the marriage, and asks whether the gossiping town is still the same.
teaches: The couplet hopes the town's gossip will force the marriage, and the poem shows the end of that hope: once the kin declare the marriage, the talk that pressed for it has nothing left to say, so the gossip served its purpose and the friend can mock it.

note: In Kural 1288 the woman says his chest is to her as liquor is to drinkers, though it does shameful harm; Kalittokai 91 ends with the wife saying her heart melts when she sees him whatever wrong he does, so he need not try to please her.
teaches: The Kural states the compulsion as the woman's confession, while the Kalittokai draws its consequence for the man: because she always yields, he has no motive to behave, so the wife's helplessness becomes part of the reason the straying continues.

note: Ainkurunuru 69 has the wife say she has seen the husband's woman crying, eyes reddened, when the cool flood with its flowers swept her sand-play away at the crowded ford; Paripadal 7.25-26 lists among the town's cries the young women weeping that the flood broke the dolls they drew in the sand.
teaches: In the hymn the weeping over sand dolls is one anonymous cry among many on flood day, while the akam wife picks out one such girl to mock as her husband's new woman, so the pair shows the akam poet taking a stock festival scene and turning it into a mark of the rival's childishness.

note: In the Kural the slipping bangles spread the news (தூற்றா) that the lord of the shore has left; in Ainkurunuru 199 the woman names him by the bangles he loosened and asks to climb the high dune to gaze at his land.
teaches: The couplet's woman fears her bangles will publish the loss to the town, while the Ainkurunuru woman makes the loss her name for him and climbs where all can see her looking, so the same token can be suffered as exposure or claimed in the open.

note: Ainkurunuru 159's friend demands that the lord give back her friend's beauty and go, insisting she is not begging; Kuruntokai 349's heroine refuses her friend's proposal to take back their beauty, saying that asking for it back is like demanding the return of what was given to those who begged, and worse than losing life.
teaches: On a defensible reading the two make incompatible claims about the demand 'give back her beauty', a just reclaiming of what was taken or a shameful asking-back of a gift, which shows the formula belonged to the friend's voice and that the heroine could reject it as beneath her.

ullurai.tenor: the man who opens a young woman's love and moves on

pairs.situation: the man takes her first love
she, young and unopened, is the bud
he is of the ford town and goes back to his house

ullurai.speaker_fit: the courtesan, as 'anyone else', may use the pond of the marutham town freely (porul 7.29)

iraicchi.act: the bull stays by its doe in the scorching land and shares the thin shade with her
iraicchi.sense: even the beast of the waste keeps beside its mate in hardship, so the man should not leave his

iraicchi.act: the kid is fed to the full from its mother's udder and plays safe in the shade of the hill
iraicchi.sense: in his land even the young of beasts are nourished and sheltered, yet he leaves her uncared for

ullurai.tenor: the lover who keeps coming unmarried and the watchful village

pairs.situation: he goes about without the partner he has not wed
his stealthy approach to the girl by night
the clamour and watch of the village that make secret visits dangerous

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the hill's elephant and hunters in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the parrot flocks stop coming to the field once there is nothing in it for them
iraicchi.sense: the man, whose meetings in the field are ending too, must not stop coming and forget her as the parrots forget the field

iraicchi.act: the elephant in must, lacking its mate, embraces a rough boulder in her place
iraicchi.sense: even the beast of his land cannot do without its mate, yet the man stays away from the girl

iraicchi.act: the mother beast, thinking of her calf, lets her milk run
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle of his own town yearn toward their young, yet the father of this boy stays away from him

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the girl he has taken up

pairs.situation: he goes about with the new girl
he displays her openly as if she were his wedded wife
he made her bathe with him in the stream

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the swan of her own town's pond, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

note: Paripadal 3.63 says 'you are the fragrance in the flower' (பூவினுள் நாற்றம் நீ) in a run of identities; Tirumanthiram 2639 says the Lord is like the fragrance in the flower, the ghee in milk and the juice in fruit (பூவினுள் நாற்றமும் போலுளன்), mingled everywhere.
teaches: The same image of fragrance in the flower is an identity in the Sangam hymn, where the god is the essence of each thing, and a simile in Tirumular, where the Lord is like that essence and stands mingled in things, so the pair shows the later Saiva poet keeping the image while holding the god at one remove from the world he pervades.

note: The idyll says Nannan brings back treasures from those whose backs he has seen and pours his gifts on poets (சுரக்கும், 71-72) and lays waste the enemy front (முனைபாழ், 59); Akananuru 349, in a heroine's lament, names a Nannan who lays waste the front, breaks forts and pours their wealth unasked (சூழாது சுரக்கும்) on bards who come with their kin.
teaches: An akam heroine can name Nannan's land by a two-line formula that the guide poem unfolds into a whole promise to a troupe, which shows the patron's praise circulated as a fixed epithet that love poets could assume their hearers knew, though the identity of the two Nannans is not certain.

note: Kar Narpathu 20's hero says the king's work is finished and the roads are pleasant; Ainkurunuru 466's friend says the king has released him after the great work and she is sure of his coming.
teaches: The hero announces the release as a fact on the road, while the friend can only infer it at home and stake her certainty on it, so the release from the king's work was the one event both ends of the mullai separation waited on.

note: Kural 1095: the man says she does not look at him directly but smiles with one eye narrowed. Kalittokai 51: the girl says the young man looked at her from the corner of his eye as if to kill and smiled (கடைக் கண்ணால் ... நகை கூட்டம் செய்தான்).
teaches: The Kural reads the sidelong smile as the girl's sign of consent, seen by the man; Kalittokai gives the same sign to the man, seen by the girl after she has lied for him, so the gesture of kurippu is not tied to one sex and seals a secret both have now chosen.

note: Ainkurunuru 218: the girl's eyes throb and her bangles tighten, and she asks if he will come. Akananuru 141: answering the anxious friend, the wife says her dreams are sweet and the house birds give good signs, so may he come for the festival.
teaches: The Akananuru wife reads hope in dreams and household birds while the Ainkurunuru girl reads it in her own eyes and bangles, so the pair shows the omen-reading of akam reaching from the house to the body, and always voiced by the one who waits, against the friend's fear.

note: In Akananuru 151 the woman reports the man's reason that the poor cannot support dependents or laugh among kin, and says his heart has set grace aside; verse 44 gives the same reason, feeding kin's hunger, as one no one could fault.
teaches: The argument for leaving to earn wealth is the same in both, but the akam poem lets the one left behind weigh it against grace, while the fragment's voice treats it as needing no answer.

note: Kuruntokai 15 measures the lovers' fidelity by the good word of the Kosar of Nalur given under the old banyan; Akananuru 113 calls the Kosar many-speared guards who never swerve from friendship even in bad times.
teaches: Akananuru 113 supplies the reputation the Kuruntokai simile depends on: the Kosar were known for keeping faith in adversity, so the foster mother vindicates the eloped girl's bond by the standard of a war band's unbreakable loyalty, not by its feeling.

note: Kuruntokai 213: the friend says he has deep love, since on his road the stag goes hungry and stands as shade for its young. Akananuru 59: the friend says on his road the bull elephant bends a tree so its mate can eat, yet those men do not remember her.
teaches: The same device, a beast caring for its own on the road the man took, is used for opposite ends: in Kuruntokai the friend makes it proof that he will come back, in the Akananuru she makes it the reproach that he does not, so the image does not carry its comfort in itself but takes it from the speaker's verdict.

note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base, like sugarcane, only when crushed; Thinaimozhi 39 has the wife say she has become the crushed cane's refuse.
teaches: The Kural looks at crushed cane from the side of the one who extracts the juice, as a way to get use from the mean, while the akam poem speaks from the cane's side, so the same image shows that what is crushed for its sweetness is left as waste.

note: Kural 1306: without துனி and புலவி, love is like over-ripe and unripe fruit. Thinaimalai 153: in துனி, புலவி and ஊடல், and in the கனி union after, her eyes never see the lord.
teaches: The Kural justifies the graded quarrel as what keeps love ripe, while the Thinaimalai uses the same three words from inside the cycle and finds that none of its stages, quarrel or ripe union, lets her look at him, so the pair sets the doctrine of the quarrel as seasoning against its cost to the one who lives it.

note: Kuruntokai 185: the girl asks what use it is to tell him she has wasted because of him; Kural 1236: with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts her is hearing him called cruel.
teaches: Both heroines decline to blame the man for their wasting body, but for opposite reasons: the Kural's woman defends him, the Kuruntokai's expects no answer from a man as unmoved as the rock under the beaten kaanthal, so the same refusal can be loyalty or despair.

note: Kural 1225: the parted woman asks what enmity she did to evening; 121: she says not one foe but many, the anril, the evening, the rain, the flute, the sea and the dark cloud, have made her their living.
teaches: The Kural names evening as the single enemy of the parted woman, and the quatrain multiplies the enemies across landscapes, showing that the evening of the Kural was the type of a whole hostile world of sights and sounds, each taking its share of her.

note: 471's heroine resents that the bard keeps coming (இன்னும் வருதி); in 477 the man tells the bard to stay a little as her comfort (உயவுத்துணை).
teaches: Read together, the bard's persistence that the wife takes for indifference turns out to be the man's own order, so the decade shows one act judged from both ends of the separation.

note: 139 urges the lord of Nanjil to give now, since he does not fear death for his king and a battle may come any day; Naladiyar 5 says not to hold back a gift thinking it can be given later, since Death drags all away.
teaches: The Naladiyar's general reason for giving now, the certainty of death, appears in 139 as a bard's practical argument tied to the warrior patron's own courage, which shows how the moralist's maxim was already a working plea in the bard's trade.

note: In Kuruntokai 356 the foster mother grieves that the girl who refused milk mixed with puffed rice must now gulp scalding muddy water (கலுழி) by a dried spring; in Ainkurunuru 203 the girl's side says the muddy water (கலிழி) of his land is sweeter than honeyed milk.
teaches: The two poems make opposite claims about the same exchange of home's milk for the forest's muddy water, a pitiable loss to the foster mother and a gain to the girl's side, which shows that the pathos of the elopement poems is the mother's view and not the girl's.

note: Natrinai 9: the eloping man tells the white-toothed girl to go without strain, lingering at every shade, since the road they take (யாம் செல்லும் ஆறே) runs through cool groves where the koel calls. Thinaimozhi 16: he tells the girl with budding teeth that the place they go (நாம் செல்லும் இடம்) is to be desired, as maraa blooms and bees hum.
teaches: Both men answer the girl's fear of the waste by describing its blossoms, which shows a fixed speech of the eloping lover; the venba's own turn is to have the bees hum the paalai melody, turning the name of the dreaded land into the music that leads her across it.

note: Kural 1147: the sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and the mother's words as water; Thinaimalai 41: the heart melts day after day while the talk swells, like a storm cloud pouring.
teaches: The Kural makes the gossip the food of the love-sickness, and Thinaimalai 41 makes the two one weather, the swelling talk and the melting heart pouring together like a cloud, which shows the girl suffering the growth the couplet describes as a cause.

note: Patitruppattu 44 gives the cause of the Mohur war, the king's pledge to the distant Arukai, and the felling of the neem; Patitruppattu 49 gives the kings and Velir who massed at Mohur, the blood-flood and the ruin.
teaches: The two songs divide one campaign between them, the reason and the trophy in one and the coalition and slaughter in the other, so the decade tells a single war across separate praise poems and needs both to be read as history.

note: Natrinai 2's onlookers see the elopement road as a wasteland where a tiger cub with blood on its mouth eyes deer at evening, and call the youth's heart crueler than thunder; in Natrinai 9 the eloping man describes the road as cool groves of koels and mango buds where she may linger in the shade and make sand dolls.
teaches: Read together, the two poems give the same udanpokku road two natures by speaker, a tiger's evening for the bystanders and a spring garden for the lover, so the danger of paalai is a judgment the voices make and not only a fact of the land.
