note: Ainkurunuru 44 says the tortoise's young grow by looking at the mother's face; Siddhar 176 says the sea tortoise's eggs take form as the mother thinks of them, and asks when the poet will so reach God.
teaches: The same belief, that the tortoise nurtures without touch, serves the Sangam friend to argue that a wife needs only her husband's presence and the later siddhar to describe grace given by attention alone, so a piece of animal lore carried a model of care at a distance from household love into devotion.

note: 146: the friend asks whether 'those who unite the parted' (பிரிந்தோர்ப் புணர்ப்போர்) have come, staffs in hand. 156: the hero asks the Brahmin with his staff whether his learning holds a medicine 'that unites the parted' (பிரிந்தோர்ப் புணர்க்கும்).
teaches: The same phrase names the go-between's office from both sides of kalavu: in the friend's mouth the uniters arrive as joyful elders of a marriage embassy, while the hero doubts that a Brahmin's book can unite anyone, so the phrase shows that union was expected from social go-betweens, not from learning.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Thinaimalai 86: told that he will surely go, the heroine says to name anyone who could bear it.
teaches: Both meet the news of his going by sending the message elsewhere, to whoever can survive it, and the venba supplies the starving elephant's waste that the couplet leaves out, so the Kural's bare retort is shown to be the stock reply of the paalai heroine to the announcement of departure.

note: Both carry the same thurai, the friend showing the season to reassure the heroine, with the konrai in bloom; Akananuru 4 ends with his chariot in sight, Kar Narpathu 4 with the season as medicine for her pallor.
teaches: Set together they give two endings to one speech: the long poem can produce the man himself on the horizon, while the four-line venba has to stop at the season and so makes the season itself the cure.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one was there but the thief, only a heron watching for aaral fish on the day he took her. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: does the heron of the grove not know his cruelty, though it saw him go and turn graceless?
teaches: Kuruntokai's heron proves that the secret union had no witness worth the name, and the venba goes one step on, upbraiding that same silent witness for not knowing what it saw, so the heron of kalavu moves from absent proof to complicit bystander.

note: Both state the same sign of separation on the same body part: the broad shoulders (பணைத்தோள்; பணைநீங்கி) waste and the bangles slip once the partner is gone.
teaches: The Kural gives the slipping bangle as a plain effect of the partner's absence, while the Ainkurunuru woman names the departed men as those who killed her longing, so the poem shows the bodily sign being used as an accusation, which the couplet's general statement leaves out.

note: Kural 261 defines தவம் as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Ainkurunuru 111's woman says she is no performer of hard penance and so could not live apart from him.
teaches: The heroine's disclaimer assumes exactly the Kural's definition of penance as the bearing of suffering, so the pair shows that the endurance of separation was already counted as an ascetic feat, and that the lover's refusal of it is a refusal of tapas.

note: Purananuru 151 refuses the young Vicchi lord the poet's embrace because of a door shut against singers; Kuruntokai 328 measures gossip by the uproar of Kurumbur when bards saw the Vicchiyar chief stand like a tiger against the kings.
teaches: The Vicchi house is remembered by singers in two ways at once, its war-cry loud enough to be an akam poet's yardstick for noise and its door shut against bards in puram, so the pair shows that a chief's fame for valour could circulate apart from, and despite, his name for giving.

note: Kural 1124: she is to him as life when present and as death when she goes; Kuruntokai 280: for one day's union he would not want half a day of life after.
teaches: The couplet equates her presence with life, the poem goes further and trades the rest of life for one day of her, so the man's praise of love moves from equation to sacrifice.

note: Vaanan's Sirukudi, its fields and groves, is the vehicle for the wife in both: her hair smells like its groves in Akananuru 204, her bangles are as precious as the town in Natrinai 340.
teaches: Held together, the two show one patron's fertile town used as the standard of a wife's worth from both sides of a marriage: the faithful husband hurries home to a beauty like Sirukudi, and the wronged wife names the same town to measure what her husband has taken.

note: Both set a wife's or beloved's shoulders against heaven. 906 says that fearing those shoulders leaves no worth even in a godlike life, and 1103 asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on them.
teaches: Fear and love differ, but the books value the same intimacy in opposite ways.

note: Both close on 'each time I see the sky' and the eye: Aimpathu 5 says drops mingle and fall from the eye (துளிகலந்து வீழ்தருங் கண்); Ezhupathu 15 says the eye tosses with water as the sky tosses with clouds (நீரோ(டு) அலமரும் கண்).
teaches: The shared closing formula could match eye and sky in two different ways, by substance in Aimpathu (tears are the rain's drops) and by motion in Ezhupathu (the eye tosses as the sky tosses), so the formula fixed the pairing but left the basis of the likeness to the poet.

note: Kural 1286: when she sees him she sees no fault, when she does not see him she sees only faults; Kuruntokai 252: urged by her friend to reproach him, she says the worthy cannot speak blame to a face.
teaches: The couplet presents her silence before him as a blindness of love; the poem's woman sees the fault plainly and calls him crooked, yet keeps silent by a rule of the noble, so the same silence can be read as love's blindness or as chosen restraint.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 229: so go, finish the work, but do not linger, for the north wind has come.
teaches: Faced with the same announcement of departure, the Kural's speaker refuses any promise of a quick return as useless to the dying, while the Natrinai friend bargains for exactly that promise and binds it to a season already arrived, so two stances to a leaving husband stand side by side: refusal by death, and consent with a deadline.

note: The bereaved mother in Natrinai 293 wishes that the young man's mother may suffer great anguish like hers (எம்போல் பெரு விதுப்புறுகமாதோ); the mourner of Purananuru 291 wishes the same on the king (என்போற் பெருவிதுப்பு உறுக) whose garland sent the man to his death.
teaches: The shared curse formula shows that akam treated a daughter's elopement as a bereavement in the full puram sense: the mother speaks in the words a mourner uses over a warrior's body, aimed at the one who caused the loss.

note: Both set the home feast against the king's war: the couplet says let the king fight and win and let us feast at evening; 442 says if the king's war subsides she will receive guests in plenty.
teaches: The poem names whose feast the couplet's விருந்து is, the wife as hostess of guests and mother of a son, so the couplet's private wish is shown to be the restoration of a whole household that the king's war holds in suspense.

note: In Kuruntokai 2 the man asks the bee, knower of flowers, whether any is more fragrant than her hair; in Natrinai 277 the woman curses the bee for sucking the yellow peeram but not her yellow pallor, because it has no scent, and asks it to carry word to her man.
teaches: Akam's bee is a judge of scent, and the pair shows the limit of that office: it can testify to a beloved's beauty in union but cannot be made to carry the scentless pallor of separation, which is why the girl's appeal to it fails.

note: Both say the woman is the cure of the love sickness: Kural 1102 says every other illness has a different cure but hers is cured by herself; Ainkurunuru 99 says the broad-shouldered girl has become the medicine for his sickness.
teaches: The couplet's paradox that the cause is the cure is put by the Sangam poem as something that has already happened (ஆகிய), placing the claim after the first meeting, which is where the Kural sets it too, under the joy of union.

note: Patitruppattu 31.1-10 shows crowds from the four quarters who go unfed (உண்ணாப் பைஞ்ஞிலம்), bathe at the cold ghat and praise the red feet of the tulasi-garlanded lord before going home glad; Paripadal Thirattu 1.43-46 shows the crowd at the god's town bearing food offerings, umbrellas, incense and flowers, in a town like a heaven of enjoyment.
teaches: Read together the two give two modes of early Mal worship, a fasting and bathing crowd in the Chera poem and a feasting, paired and pleasure-seeking crowd in the Koodal hymn, so devotion to the same god was already practised as abstinence in one place and as festival in another.

note: Kar Narpathu 14: the cool cloud laughs softly as the mullai shows its teeth, and the friend is sure he will come; 122: the sky seems to laugh with its lightning and the heroine's shameless life breaks.
teaches: The laughing sky is a good omen in the friend's mouth and mockery in the heroine's, which shows that the same rain-cloud laughter could be heard as welcome or as scorn and that the stock image carried no fixed meaning apart from the speaker.

note: Kuruntokai 240: the waiting woman sees mullai buds like a wild cat's teeth (வெருக்குப்பல் லுருவின் முல்லை) crowding the bush as the north wind comes and his hill sinks at evening. Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man sees the mullai buds pointed like the teeth of his girl.
teaches: The same bud-and-teeth simile becomes a predator's teeth for the waiting woman and the beloved's teeth for the returning man, so the mullai bud's meaning in these poems is set by which side of the separation is looking, not by the flower.

note: Purananuru 35 tells Killivalavan that his tall umbrella is not for shade from the sun but to shelter suffering subjects, and that rain comes in the land of the just sceptre; Kalittokai 99 asks the husband, addressed as king, whether his wife fell outside the shade of the parasol he calls virtue's shade and the working of his sceptre.
teaches: The friend in the Kalittokai uses the same counsel a puram poet gave a king, that the parasol exists to shade those who suffer, and turns it on the household, showing that the akam poets could hold a husband to the standard of kingship and find him failing his nearest subject.

note: Kural 1311's woman refuses the philanderer's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Natrinai 360 the friend, or on the colophon's second reading the wife in oodal, refuses him at the door and pictures yesterday's women left like a doll after the festival.
teaches: Both refuse the straying husband, but the couplet objects that he is shared, while the Natrinai shows how he uses and discards each courtesan, so the wife's scorn reaches past her own wrong to the rivals he abandons.

note: Both set the hill tiger with its mate beside the velan's rite: in Natrinai 322 the tiger lurks to ease its hungry female, in Ainkurunuru 246 it ends its distress by joining her.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the kurinji tiger used as the counter-image to the veri rite: what relieves a creature of the hill, by hunting for its mate or by joining her, is the partner and never the offering.

iraicchi.act: the elephant, finding the pool dry, holds close to its mate on the hillside
iraicchi.sense: even in drought and danger the beast keeps to its mate, so the man who sees it will turn back to her

iraicchi.act: the herons, having fed, settle together on the punnai for the night
iraicchi.sense: even the birds come home to roost at dusk, so the man too should stay and make this town his home, that is, marry

iraicchi.act: the stag, judging the pool's little water too scant for both, pretends to drink so that the doe may drink her fill
iraicchi.sense: the man whose heart has gone that way will see such care and his heart will turn back to the wife he left

iraicchi.act: the hunter comes home with his catch and, forgetting his trade, takes his ease in his own house
iraicchi.sense: the hero, his task done, is going home to the rest and the wife that wait for him

note: Both are spoken by the woman about the pallor that the man's presence will remove: Kural 1265 wishes to see him and says the pallor will then leave; Ainkurunuru 263 says he has come and her beauty has come back.
teaches: The Sangam poem gives as an accomplished fact, in two verbs set side by side, what the couplet can only promise, showing the restored beauty as the very event of his arrival rather than its later result.

note: In Akananuru 283 the friend, arranging the elopement, wishes rain to fall on the forest and cool it so the road is sweet; in Kuruntokai 378 the foster mother, after the girl has gone, prays the sun not burn and cool clouds hang over the waste.
teaches: The same wish for a cooled desert passes from the accomplice who sends the girl to the woman who has lost her, so the pair shows the foster mother's grief taking the form of blessing, joining in the elopement she did not choose.

note: Kuruntokai 196: the husband who once called neem sweet now calls the cool spring water of Pari's Parambu hot and brackish; Purananuru 176: the poet regrets the days lost like people who scorned the clear spring of Parambu because it was in their own town.
teaches: Read with the Purananuru, the friend's choice of Parambu's water carries its proverbial lesson: the sweetest thing is scorned when it is near, so she diagnoses the husband's turning as contempt bred by having the wife at home.

note: Kural 447: who can ruin those who keep companions that rebuke them? Kuruntokai 58: the man tells his rebuking companions (இடிக்குங் கேளிர்) that it would be well if they could hold back his sickness, but it has spread past bearing.
teaches: The Kural makes the rebuking companion a ruler's best protection; the lover grants the rebuke its good intent and shows where it stops, since love has spread like butter on hot rock before any word could check it, so the ethic of correction meets its limit at kaamam.

note: Akananuru 376: the courtesan asks the lord to give back her beauty, which was like Kuttuvan's Maranthai. Kuruntokai 34: the friend calls the wife's bright brow lovely as Kuttuvan's Maranthai.
teaches: The same Chera port is the standard of beauty for a wedded girl and for a courtesan, so the akam poets used Maranthai's fame as a neutral measure of a woman's nalam whatever her standing.

note: The seventh preface says Selvakkadungo, after his sacrifice, gave Ogandur and 'confounded the purohita' (புரோசு மயக்கி); the ninth preface uses the same phrase of Ilanjeral Irumporai (புரைஅறு கேள்விப் புரோசு மயக்கி), beside mantra worship, the installing of the spirits of the crossroads and the shanti rite.
teaches: The repeated phrase shows that the preface-writers had a fixed slot for a king's dealings with his purohita, and the ninth preface fills it with a larger ritual programme than the seventh, so the prefaces record the growing weight given to priestly rites in the picture of Chera kingship.

note: In Purananuru 98 the foes who see Anji's war elephants with blunted tusks bar their fort gates; Patitruppattu 53 warns the Chera to take another road home, since his elephant, seeing any gate, will charge it.
teaches: Read together they show the praise of the war elephant pushed one step further: in Avvai's poem the gates close in fear, while the Chera poet makes the elephant's habit so fixed that the king's own ancestral city is in danger, so the boast works by turning the threat inward.

note: In Akananuru 80 the friend tells the shore lord that they spend the day scaring birds from the fish their father brought, and bids him come by day; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 47 the hero sees the girl scaring birds from the fish her brothers brought and finds her a tormenting goddess.
teaches: Guarding the drying catch is the neythal girl's appointed work and so the one place she is seen by day: the friend can offer it as a meeting place, while the hero's first sight of her there already places her among the kinsmen whose catch she guards, which is why the sight brings fear.

note: In both the stag (இரலை) with his young doe is shown to the reader in the rains: in 242 he stands searching for her when the herd scatters, and the returning man hurries; in 256 he rests holding her in the shade, and the man gives up going.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the iraicchi's sense fixed while the man's act changes: the stag keeping to his doe stands for the man's duty to his wife both when he hurries home and when he declines to leave.

note: Both are the friend's speech to a man about to leave: Kural 1151 says tell me only if you are not going, and tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 71 grants the woman may let him go and asks whether he can stroke her eyes and leave.
teaches: The couplet argues from the woman's death, the Natrinai friend from the man's own tenderness at the moment of leave-taking, so the two show the dissuasion speech had two separate levers, her survival and his ability to bear the parting.

note: 395: the chief shows his wife to the bard and tells her to care for him as for himself; Kural 81: the whole of keeping house and guarding goods is for tending guests.
teaches: The couplet says the household exists for the guest; the poem shows the moment that claim is enacted, when the master hands the guest over to the mistress of the house, so the guest is taken into the household rather than merely fed by it.

note: In Kural 1155 the woman asks her friend, if she would guard her, to stop the man's departure; in Natrinai 124 the friend does exactly that, telling the man not to go and pointing to the season.
teaches: The Kural gives only the request, while the Natrinai shows the friend carrying it out, adding the rainy-season argument and the anril image, so the couplet's appeal is revealed as the opening move of a known scene in which the friend speaks for the woman to the man.

note: Kural 791 warns that nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, since for the faithful there is no leaving once the friendship is made; Kuruntokai 313 says the friendship with the shore lord is tied and settled, hard to untie.
teaches: The heroine states as her settled joy the very fact the Kural gives as the reason for caution, so the pair shows that love's bond is the friendship the ethics book warns about, entered without the inquiry it prescribes.

note: In Kural 1082 the man is struck by her answering look as by a goddess with an army; in Natrinai 82 the man says he cannot bear to look at her form, which strikes his eyes like Valli joined with Murugan.
teaches: The Kural puts the wound in her returned glance, the Natrinai in his own looking at her beauty, and only the Natrinai can name the goddess as the hill's own Valli, so the divine attack of the Kural's abstract couplet is, in the older poem, a local deity of the land where the love happens.

note: Both are the friend's warning, heard by the man, that the millet field is ending and the girl will be confined: in 313 the crop has just reached reaping time; in 306 the reaping is done and the field is bare stubble.
teaches: Read together they show the harvest working as a clock for the secret love, with the friend's message moving from 'soon' to 'now' as the millet goes from ripe ear to stubble.

note: In Kalittokai 16 virtue itself runs to block the man's venture for wealth; in Kalittokai 150 the friend says he left 'giving up virtue' (அறம் துறந்து) and still assures the woman that he will not prove false.
teaches: In 16 virtue is the force that keeps him home, while in 150 the friend grants that he broke virtue by going and yet trusts his word, so the two poems split the man's duty into staying (அறம்) and keeping faith (not being பொய்), which can come apart.

note: In Akananuru 296 the friend refuses the man who bathed in the great Vaigai with a dark girl and comes home with his chest still wet; in Kalittokai 98 the man claims he only bathed in the Vaigai's new flood and the wife turns the flood itself into the courtesan.
teaches: The Akananuru records water play in the Vaigai as the plain occasion of an affair and its gossip, while the Kalittokai husband offers that same occasion as an innocent excuse and the wife answers by making the river a figure for the woman, so a known scene of straying becomes the material for the wife's metaphor.

note: Ainkurunuru 15 has the wife say that the man whose town's reed is a float to the bathing women is no husband of hers; in Akananuru 186 the courtesan says their bond was only as far as bathing together on a float of reed (வேழத்துப் புணைதுணை யாகப் புனல்ஆடு கேண்மை).
teaches: The same reed float is the wife's proof that he belongs to other women and the courtesan's plea that the affair was mere water-play, so the pair shows the marutham reed raft as a contested sign whose meaning depends on which woman speaks.

note: In Natrinai 246 the friend sees the golden konrai and the rumbling sky and says this is the season he named, so he will come; in 109 the heroine sees the same konrai under the sea-fed clouds and says he will not appear.
teaches: The same golden konrai is read as proof of return by the friend and as proof of desertion by the heroine, which shows that the flower settles nothing by itself: it only fixes the day by which his failure becomes certain.

note: Both close on எழுகமோ, shall we rise; 235 sets it against holding him and saying 'we will not part', 236 gives the destination, நும்மூர்ச் செல்கம், we will go to your town.
teaches: Read alone, 235's 'shall we rise' could mean only leaving the tryst; the next poem fixes it as setting out for his town and names what forced the choice, the mother's knowing and the gossip, so the decade moves from weighing elopement to proposing it.

note: Both returning men order the goad (Ainkurunuru: முள் இட்டு ஊர்மதி; Natrinai: தீண்டா வை முள் தீண்டி), and Natrinai's order opens with the same half-line ஏமதி வலவ தேரே that Ainkurunuru 485 uses.
teaches: Natrinai adds that this goad has never before touched these horses, which shows what Ainkurunuru's bare order assumes: the goad's sting was the convention for an urgency greater than any the charioteer had known.

note: Kural 1231: thinking of him who went far, her eyes are ashamed before fragrant flowers; Ainkurunuru 458: the rain-beaten kondrai flowers have come to resemble her eyes, which lost their beauty when he left.
teaches: The couplet's eyes lose a contest with flowers they once outshone; the Ainkurunuru poem reverses the direction, bringing the flowers down to the state of the eyes, so the wasted eyes become the measure the season is read by.

note: Puram 7 praises Karikalan for delighting in plunder by the light of burning enemy towns, so that the good things are gone from others' rich lands of fields and fish; the idyll shows his own land as one umbrella under which all five landscapes mingle in plenty.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the same Chola fertility, fields where water and fish abound, as what Karikalan destroys in other kings' lands and what he guarantees in his own, so the guide poem's harmony of the five lands is the domestic face of a conquest the puram poet praises openly.

note: In Akananuru 66 the husband, on his way to a new wedding, lifts the crying son to his chest and gives up the wedding; in Kalittokai 79 the wife forbids him to take up the son, since the boy would wash off the other women's marks, and sends him back to them.
teaches: The husband's embrace of the son is the turning point of return in the Akananuru but is refused as a ruse in the Kalittokai, so the same gesture can end the husband's straying or be read by the wife as one more performance.

note: Akananuru 236 likens the heroine to Aathimanthi, who wept from land to land and town to town asking 'have you not seen Aattan Atthi?', the dancer the flood took. Kuruntokai 31, by Aathimanthiyaar, has a woman of the dancing ground search festival and dance for the chief who is a man of the dancing ground.
teaches: Read with Paranar's simile, the unnamed 'man of the dancing ground' in Kuruntokai 31 is the lost dancer of the legend, and the poem gives in the first person the search the Akananuru turns into a stock comparison for a woman maddened by loss.

note: Kalittokai 81: the wife asks the toddling son to repeat the words the 'mothers' of the big street taught him, and the husband blames the bard. Kainnilai 41: she knows his doings, having the sweet babbling son as her own.
teaches: Kalittokai 81 shows a son's prattle betraying where his father has taken him, which supports reading Kainnilai 41's 'we know' as knowledge gained from the boy's babble rather than only as a mother's comfort.

note: Kural 1104's man asks where she found a fire that burns when he moves away and cools when he draws near; Kuruntokai 376's man says she is cool in summer and warm in the cold season.
teaches: Both men praise her as a reversal of temperature, but the couplet makes it depend on his distance and the poem on the season, so together they show the convention of the beloved as a climate of her own, which the Kural turns inward into the lover's desire.

note: Ainkurunuru 236's friend says the north wind leaves the good house's tall mansion desolate (நன்மனை நெடுநகர் புலம்புகொள) as a reason to leave; Akananuru 35's mother says the girl left the high-walled good house desolate (நன்னகர் புலம்ப) by going.
teaches: The same desolation of the great house is the cause of the girl's going in the friend's plea and its effect in the mother's lament, so the two speakers each blame the empty house on the other side and the elopement is seen whole only from both.

note: Kural 660: making wealth by deceit and feeling safe is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. Kuruntokai 29: the heart, passing over good counsel, is like a fresh unfired pot set out in the rain, plunged into a flood it cannot hold.
teaches: In both the unfired pot is ruined by what it is made to hold, so the image locates the fault in the vessel rather than the water: wealth got by fraud undoes its keeper as desire taken in against counsel undoes the heart.

note: 183 says that it is better to die than to live by backbiting, because it is a false kind of life. In 1141 backbiting is what keeps someone else alive.
teaches: The same act has a very different moral look from the side of its target.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kuruntokai 207: he left without telling her, thinking that if he spoke, going would become hard, and she heard of it from others.
teaches: The couplet's demand to be told assumes the parting is spoken; the Kuruntokai man knows the power of that speech so well that he avoids it, so the heroine is denied even the chance to answer him that the Kural's speaker uses.

note: Akananuru 18 has the same thurai, the night-comer told to come by day: the friend tells the hill lord the night ford is deadly and he may meet the girl by day in the kaanthal grove. Kuruntokai 141 gives the refusal to the heroine, who only reports her mother's errand to the millet field.
teaches: Held together they show the one message in two voices: the friend may name the day meeting outright, while the heroine can offer it only by passing on her mother's errand, so the day tryst comes through indirection exactly where the speaker's freedom is narrowest.

note: Kural 43 makes the chief duty the care of five: ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself; Patitruppattu 70 says the king, with his kin around him, fed the gods with sacrifice, pleased the sages with learning, put elders before his sons, and so paid the ancient debts (தொல்கடன்).
teaches: Read together, they show two accounts of what a man owes: the Kural spreads the duty over five equal claims including guests and himself, while the Chera poem counts it as an inherited debt to gods, sages and elders paid off by sacrifice and learning, so the king's virtue is framed as settlement rather than care.

note: Kural 1122: the man says the bond between him and the girl is that of body and life; in Kuruntokai 222 the man says she takes the head of the raft when he does, the tail when he does, and would follow him into the current.
teaches: The couplet names the inseparability as a metaphor, and the poem shows how a lover knows it: she mirrors his every movement in play and would follow him into danger, so the body-and-life bond is proved by action before it is stated.

note: Kural 913 makes the embrace of women who love for wealth a falsehood, like holding a stranger's corpse in the dark; in Paripadal 20.79-82 the paid woman herself argues that the payment was fair (விலை தந்தான்) and that the falsehood is the man's.
teaches: The Kural judges the bought embrace from the client's side, so the deceit is hers; the Paripadal lets the woman answer from inside the bargain, and on that reading the two cannot both stand, since one places the lie in her love and the other in his gift of what was not his to give.

note: In both a cry of 'tiger' on the vengai slope brings men running: in 48 the girls' cry brings the young hunter who becomes the lover, in 52 a hill girl's cry for flowers brings the hill men with bows.
teaches: Together they show the vengai-plucking cry as a known custom of the hill, and 48 turns that public alarm into the private occasion of a first meeting that 52's heroine now wants kept secret.

note: Kural 1014 says shame is the ornament of the worthy and without it a proud walk is a disease; verse 11 says the worth of a shameless man is laughable.
teaches: Both deny worth without shame, but the verse makes the failure social ridicule where the couplet makes it a sickness of the man himself.

note: In Ainkurunuru 131 the woman says the lord's friendship is good only while no gossip rises in the town; in Kural 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is the manure on which her love-sickness grows.
teaches: Valluvar's woman turns the gossip into nourishment for her love, while the Sangam woman, speaking to the man's bard, treats the same gossip as the limit the bond cannot outlive, so the couplet's paradox rewrites a fear the older poem left plain.

note: Both are the man arguing with his heart over leaving his wife for wealth; in Akananuru 199 he refuses even riches like the land Narmudi Cheral won back, in Natrinai 262 he ends on the unbearable shame of poverty, which on the plain reading tips him toward going.
teaches: Read together they show that the debate with the heart had no fixed outcome in the tradition: the same scene of the wife's shoulders could close either way, and what decides each poem is the argument the poet places last.

note: Both put a doe with her frisking fawn on the rainy mullai road (Ainkurunuru: மறியுடை மான்பிணை; Akananuru: மறிஆடு மருங்கின் மடப்பிணை); in Akananuru the stag feeds and guards her and the returning man hurries his chariot home.
teaches: The image the waiting woman sets on his road without comment is, in Akananuru, the very sight that turns the man homeward, so the doe and fawn worked as a shared sign that the rains call the traveller back to wife and child.

note: Both are virali-guide poems that open with the same words, செல்லா மோதில் சில்வளை விறலி, and send the dancing woman to a king on the battlefield; Purananuru 64 says they will see Kudumi and leave behind their watery gruel, Patitruppattu 57 says they will see the king who fears suppliants' distress more than women's sulking eyes.
teaches: The shared formula shows that the virali guide poem had a fixed opening used across Pandya and Chera praise, and the difference in what follows shifts the motive from the bard's hunger in the Purananuru to the patron's own anxiety in the Patitruppattu.

note: Kural 1218: in sleep he is on her shoulder, and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart. Kuruntokai 30: on waking from the dream she finds only the empty bed and calls herself alone and pitiable.
teaches: The Kural consoles the dreamer that waking only moves the lover inward, while the Kuruntokai woman finds no such refuge and is left alone, so the two disagree on whether the waking after a love dream is a loss or a passage into the heart.

note: Kuruntokai 17: when love hardens, men ride the palm stem as a horse, wear erukku buds as flowers and are jeered in the street. Natrinai 146 addresses such a rider in his erukku chaplet and promises that kind people will gather and offer him shade like a just king's umbrella.
teaches: The street that mocks the madal rider in Kuruntokai 17 is also the street that pities him in Natrinai 146; set side by side they show that the ride works by public feeling, ridicule and compassion together, which is what presses the girl's people to yield.

iraicchi.act: the birds go together to their nests in the grove at evening
iraicchi.sense: even the birds come home together at dusk, while he does not come or think of her

ullurai.tenor: the lord of the ford and the woman caught in his bond

pairs.situation: his sweet approach hid the line that holds her
caught, she cannot survive being parted from him

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the angling of her own shore, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant guards its herd and tramples a path through the burning bamboo so that they go out together
iraicchi.sense: even the beast in the fire takes its own out with it, while the man would cross that land leaving his wife behind

iraicchi.act: the craving female calls out at midnight from the nest she shares with her mate
iraicchi.sense: the bird that has its mate beside it still calls for him, while the heroine, whose lover does not come, can only lie awake listening

ullurai.tenor: the husband who has eaten up his wife's beauty

pairs.situation: the wife's beauty when it was full
he bites into it and spoils it
in the pond of his own town, his own house

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the fish and lily of the pond of her own town, things she knows (porul 7.26)

note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; in Natrinai 218 the girl, past the promised season, lists the evening's creatures, the bats going home, the cock calling his mate, the owl, and asks if she must hear the andril alone.
teaches: The Kural woman makes evening a fellow sufferer, while the Natrinai girl finds every creature of the evening paired or going home, so the same projection onto nightfall can give companionship or prove isolation, and the unmarried girl gets only the second.

note: Both hold that wealth does not stay: Kural 332 says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance and goes as it disperses; Natrinai 16 says wealth vanishes like the trail of a fish in a pond.
teaches: The Kural uses wealth's impermanence to counsel detachment, while the Natrinai man uses it to choose his wife's gaze over a journey, so the same doctrine served an argument for staying at home in love as well as one for letting go.

note: Kural 83 says the life of one who tends guests daily does not fall into ruin; the verse says a family gains glory by the food it gives.
teaches: The couplet answers the fear that giving food ruins a house; the verse claims more, that it is the source of the family's distinction, so feeding is shown as both safe and the very thing that ranks a house.

note: Kural 1284: she went to sulk, but her heart forgot it and went to unite; Ainkurunuru 118: she went meaning to rage at the unjust man and hold him back, but thought again, relented and came away.
teaches: Both women set out angry and lose the anger on the way, but the Kural's anger turns into union while the Sangam heroine's turns into retreat, so a failed quarrel need not end in an embrace: it can end in pity and silence.

note: Purananuru 39: because justice stands firm and unfailing in the Chola court at Uranthai, justice is not this king's own fame. Natrinai 400: like justice that never fails in the Uranthai court of the warlike Cholas, he knows no failing in her heart.
teaches: The puram poet says Uranthai's justice is too settled to count as any one king's merit, and the courtesan borrows exactly that settledness for her lover's place in her heart, so an inherited institution, not a person's virtue, was the akam poet's measure of a love that cannot change.

note: 409 uses high and low birth as a working scale, even to overturn it. 972 denies the scale at the root: birth is the same for all beings, and only deeds differ.
teaches: The two arguments against birth rank are different in kind.

note: Ainkurunuru 8: the mother wishes that the king rule justly and there be no theft (and in poem 10, that the rains come). Kural 545: rain and harvest gather in the land of a king who rules by the sceptre's nature.
teaches: The mother's prayers for just rule and for timely rain stand as separate wishes in the decade, while the Kural makes the second follow from the first, so a household's prayer list shows the belief that the Kural later states as a law of kingship.

note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the idyll opens on a world where the rain does its work, one seed yields a thousand and men are free of disease, and credits it to the rule of the patron's ancestors among truthful men.
teaches: The idyll gives the Kural's cause-and-effect rule a cosmic setting and a past: the plenty is the order of the world itself and belongs to the ancestors' rule, so a king inherits a moral weather he must keep up rather than earning it afresh, which is what the counsel later in the poem asks of him.

note: Both say the man's chest belongs to many women: Ainkurunuru 25's friend says the ooran's chest (மார்புபலர்க்கு) brings grief to many; Kural 1311's wife refuses his chest (மார்பு) because all women feast on it with their eyes.
teaches: The friend counts the cost to the many women his chest has harmed, while the Kural wife refuses that chest because it is shared even by looks, so held together they show the same charge of a common chest used first as report to the mother and then as the wife's own ground for refusal.

note: Kural 657 says the worthy prefer utter poverty to wealth gained under blame; the friend in Akananuru 112 says the worthy, however deep in love, do not want a pleasure that comes with blame (சான்றோர் பழியொடு வரூஉம் இன்பம் வெஃகார்), and so the hero should marry.
teaches: The same rule of the worthy, refusing any gain that brings blame, governs wealth in the Kural and love in the Akananuru, and the friend turns it from a counsel of going without into an argument for marriage, which removes the blame without removing the pleasure.

note: In both the wife, parted from her man, speaks of the evening: the Kural asks the evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Ainkurunuru 339 asks whether evening exists in the land he went to.
teaches: The couplet gives evening a hard partner of its own, and the Sangam wife supposes his land has no evening at all, so the pair shows the same assumption from two sides: evening is the hour that should force lovers together, and only an absent or hard-hearted partner escapes it.

note: Kural 1227 (the woman) calls love a sickness that buds in the morning, opens through the day and blooms at evening; Kuruntokai 136 (the man) says love is neither a spirit nor a disease and does not swell and subside, but has its season like an elephant's musth when it finds one to look on.
teaches: The two agree that love keeps time but disagree on what kind of thing it is: the Kural's woman makes it a disease with a daily clock inside her, the Kuruntokai's man denies it is a sickness at all and makes it a latent season set off from outside by sight, so whether love is illness depends on whether one is waiting or seeing.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my home and keep the evening feast. Natrinai 221: the work done, the man bids the charioteer hurry to the wife who loves to host guests and the son who now calls him.
teaches: The Kural states the soldier's wish to trade the king's war for the evening feast at home in two lines; the Natrinai scene fills that home with a hospitable wife and a child just learning to walk and call him father, so the 'feast' of the couplet is shown to be a whole household's welcome, not only the wife's.

note: Kural 580 says that those who want a refinement worth loving will drink poison they see poured; Natrinai 355's friend says the very refined (நனி நாகரிகர்) drink even poison if old friends give it, and asks the man to be kind to the girl by கண் ஓடி.
teaches: Valluvar files the poison saying under கண்ணோட்டம; the Natrinai quotes it and then asks for exactly that kindly regard, so the pairing shows the courtesy ideal of the chapter on statecraft working in love poetry as the friend's lever to bind a man to a girl who has no one else.

note: Kural 1188: people say she has grown pale, and no one says he left her; Kuruntokai 245: worse than her lost beauty would be his unkindness becoming known to many.
teaches: On the plain reading the two women want opposite things from the town: the couplet's woman resents that the blame falls on her body and not on him, the poem's woman dreads exactly that blame reaching him, so the lover can either demand that the fault be named or shield it at her own cost.

note: Akananuru 49: the foster mother remembers seeing that the girl who loved her parrot, ball and play-seeds (கிளியும், பந்தும், கழங்கும்) was not as before, without guessing why. Aimpathu 33: the girl no longer thinks of doll, ball, parrot and playmates, and the mother asks whether she will go after her lover.
teaches: In both the neglected playthings are the sign that the girl has passed out of childhood into love, but Akananuru 49 reads the sign too late and dwells on the mother's missed chance, while the venba reads it and turns at once to the burning road, so the pair shows the same evidence serving regret or foreboding.

note: In Natrinai 359 the friend says the hill lord gave them a leaf skirt (உடுக்கும் தழை) that they dare not wear for fear of the mother nor return for fear of hurting him; in Ainkurunuru 201 the leaves have become their skirts (எமக்கும் தழையாயின) and the friend asks the mother what tree on his slope they come from.
teaches: The leaf skirt that in Natrinai is a gift too dangerous to wear before the mother becomes in the Ainkurunuru the very thing the friend shows her, so the pair traces one courtship token from the secret it endangers to the disclosure it carries.

note: In Kar Narpathu 1 the friend says that with the sky roaring and pouring, the man who said 'we will come' can hardly fail to come now; in Natrinai 248 the friend says the same roar is false thunder and not the promised season. On the plain reading the two friends make incompatible claims about what the rain shows.
teaches: Set side by side, the same evidence serves the friend either way: when the season must mean his return she affirms it, and when his absence would make him a liar she denies it, so the season's sign was something the friend argued about rather than read off.

note: Kural 1265: the pallor of her shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with her eyes. Kainnilai 19: the friend says the brightness returning to her forehead shows he is coming, before he has come.
teaches: On the Kural's reading the body recovers only from the sight of him and news cannot cure it, while the Kainnilai friend reads a recovery already begun as a sign of his return, so the two disagree on whether the body answers his presence or foreknows it.

note: Paripadal 1.32-33 says Thirumal's coming is hard to know even for sages free of confusion; Tirumanthiram 13 puts Vishnu who measured the earth among the gods who, measuring by thought, still cannot conceive the Lord. On the plain reading the two give the unknowable highest place to different gods, and one puts the other's god among the baffled seekers.
teaches: The same argument from unknowability served two rival theologies, and the Saiva poet reuses it by moving Thirumal from the place of the unknown into the place of the seeker, so ineffability became a way to rank gods.

note: Ainkurunuru 213: the girl says she can live only if he comes. Kural 1263: the wife says she still lives on the longing for her husband's return from war.
teaches: For the wife the longing for return is already enough to keep her alive, while the unmarried girl says life itself waits on his coming, so the pair grades the same dependence: hope sustains in marriage, only presence sustains in secret love.

note: 123 praises Malayan of unfading fame (தொலையா நல்லிசை) at Mullur; Akananuru 209 names the Mullur king Kari whose fame does not pass (செல்லா நல்லிசை), who killed Ori and gave the Kolli hills to the Cheras.
teaches: The akam friend uses Kari's lasting fame as a fixed point to measure the heroine's beauty, which shows that the bards' praise of Kari had become a shared reference that akam poets could cite to measure something else entirely.

note: Both hang the woman between love and shame: the Kural has the two hung from a carrying pole that is her life, Kuruntokai 112 names the town's talk as the fear and pictures her as a branch an elephant has snapped that still hangs by its fibre.
teaches: Kuruntokai 112 gives the Kural's evenly balanced pole a cause and a breaking point: the weight on shame's side is the town's gossip, and the balance is already a break held only by a strand, which the couplet's still image does not show.

note: Kural 1168 has the sleepless woman say the night, which puts all creatures to sleep, has only her for company; Natrinai 132 begins with the great town asleep but fills the house with the cold wind, a trembling dog, guards by the bed and watchmen ringing the bell.
teaches: The couplet's solitude of the one waker is qualified by a poem in which others do wake, but only to keep her in, so the sleepless night of the guarded girl is not loneliness but confinement.

note: Naladiyar 390 has the wife call herself the tasteless tip of the sugarcane to the lord of the town; Thinaimozhi 39 has her say she has become the chewed pith of the cane after he ate her beauty.
teaches: The marutham wife reaches for sugarcane in both books, but the Naladiyar places her at the less sweet end of a cane still whole, a matter of rank among his women, while the Thinaimozhi has the cane already chewed and spat out, so the same image measures either neglect or use and discard.

note: Both are neythal poems about a man who will not marry: in 263 an old lame stork brings sea fish to his pregnant hen in the field, in 272 a red-beaked sea crow searches the backwater for fish for his hen heavy with young on the sand.
teaches: Two poets put the same act, a male shore bird feeding its pregnant mate, beside the same complaint, so the provider bird was a conventional reproach that let the women shame an unmarried lover without naming his fault.

note: Akananuru 165: onlookers see the mother after the elopement rest under the nochchi the girl touched and embrace her doll. Natrinai 143: the mother herself weeps at the playmates and the nochchi and confesses she noticed the scent of the girl's hair and said nothing.
teaches: Held together, the two give the mother's grief from outside and from inside: what onlookers see as pure loss, her own words show to include guilt, since she read the signs in the girl's hair, heard the gossip, and chose silence.

note: Kural 265 says tapas is striven for here because whatever is wanted is gained as it is wanted; Patitruppattu 74 says the king told his grey-haired elder that generosity, dignity, wealth, offspring, the divine and everything belong to those who have tapas (தவம்உடை யோர்க்கென), and let him go to the wide forest.
teaches: The Kural states the promise of tapas as a reason to strive, while the Chera poem shows a king applying it to another, releasing his aged counsellor from court to the forest, so tapas appears as the last stage of a life of royal service and its grant as a king's virtue.

note: Paripadal 2.5-12 tells the ages of the world in the order sky (as sound), wind, fire, water, earth; Thiruppugazh 21 names Mayon as the one who became sky, wind, fire, water and earth in the same order, and the seven worlds, yet touches none of them.
teaches: The five-element order credited to Thirumal survives a thousand years into Arunagirinathar, but what the Sangam singer told as successive ages of the world's making the later poet states as the god's present pervasion of all things.

note: Akananuru 315's mother saw the girl's hair curl and breasts swell and blames herself for not guarding her; Ainkurunuru 374's mother says the girl's hair was not yet long enough to be knotted.
teaches: On one reading the two mothers read the same hair in opposite ways, as a sign of womanhood missed in Akananuru and as proof of childhood in Ainkurunuru, so the lament can either confess overlooked signs or deny that there were any.

note: Kuruntokai 163 asks the sea who has afflicted it (யாரணங் குற்றனை) since she hears it even at midnight; Thinaimalai 38 asks the sleepless sea who did this to it, 'like me'.
teaches: Kuruntokai leaves the girl's own state unsaid behind her question to the sea, while Thinaimalai 38 names it, the breast of the shore lord and a sleeplessness 'like mine', so the pair shows the later poet making explicit the projection the older poem left to the hearer.

note: In both the wife's bangles slip from her wrist because of the man; in Ainkurunuru 20 they loosen as she thinks of him, in Kural 1157 they broadcast that he has left.
teaches: The Sangam poem treats the slipping bangle as the private effect of memory, while Valluvar makes the same bangle a gossip that announces his desertion to everyone, so the couplet turns an inner sign into public scandal.

note: In 367 the friend tells the heroine that the young men have come wearing a garland of mullai and blue lily and that her man will surely come today; in 361 the friend reports that he himself and his young men are wearing mullai as his chariot reaches the house.
teaches: Read in sequence the two poems show that the mullai garland was the badge of the returning party, worn first by the retinue as a herald and then by the master on arrival, so the friend could promise the return from the young men's flowers before any chariot was seen.

note: Kural 804: the wise welcome the unasked acts of old friends; Kuruntokai 265 likens the kaanthal bud opening to the bee to duty-knowing men opening to the worthy they have long known, then shows the man ashamed and ready to act once told.
teaches: The Kural's ethic of intimacy is used in the poem as a simile for nature and then as a forecast of the lover's conduct, so the old-friendship rule becomes the friend's evidence that he will marry without being pressed.

note: Both show an elephant that has escaped the curve-striped tiger; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 16 it lies hurt on the hero's night path, in Thinaimalai 25 it is the likeness of the trembling girl.
teaches: Ainthinai Aimpathu 16 puts the escaped elephant on the man's path as a danger the sleepless girl imagines, and Thinaimalai 25 makes the escaped elephant the girl herself, still shaking after the danger, so one stock scene can stand either for the night road or for the fear it leaves in her.

note: In the Kural the woman pities the evening as a fellow sufferer and asks if its mate is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 118 the evening is loveless (நாரில்) and the birds and beasts that settle in loneliness are company she gets no comfort from.
teaches: Read together they show two answers to the same hour: the Kural's woman finds a companion in the grieving evening, while the Sangam woman finds the whole world, beasts and gatekeepers included, going home around her, so the evening isolates rather than consoles.

note: Both paalai poems use Udhiyan Cheral's great occasions as similes: Akananuru 233 compares the crowded hills of the man's road to the ghouls gathered at Udhiyan's great feast; Natrinai 113 compares the left wife's sob to the pipe blown after Udhiyan's battle.
teaches: Held together they show akam poets dividing one king's famous scenes between the two halves of separation, his feast for the harsh road the man crosses and his battlefield's lament for the woman he leaves.

note: Kalladanar shows Nedunjeliyan's work in enemy country: fouled fords, plundered fields, felled guarded trees, burned houses, an empty waste; the idyll shows tuskers, horses and herds brought by the light of burning towns flowing into Madurai like the Ganges into the sea.
teaches: The two poems are the two ends of one process under the same king: the ruin praised in the Purananuru is the source of the abundance praised in Maduraikkanchi, so the city's splendour is the enemy land's emptiness moved to the capital.

note: Akananuru 308: a tusker worn from fighting a tiger, its long wound unwashed, marks the hill of a man who comes by night; the friend asks him to come by day. Ainthinai Aimpathu 16: an elephant that escaped the tiger shrinks at every footfall on the path, and the girl cannot sleep remembering that path.
teaches: In Akananuru the tiger-wounded elephant only marks the hill while the friend argues for day visits, whereas Ainthinai carries the beast's after-fear onto the path itself and into the girl's sleepless eyes, showing how the same hill emblem can move from scenery to the measure of a lover's dread.

note: Kural 1224: when the lover is away, evening comes like enemies coming to a killing ground. Thinaimalai 97: the sun sets like the discus Maayavan hurled at his foes' elephant, and she cannot bear the evening.
teaches: Both make evening a killing, but the couplet gives the killers no face while the venba names them through the land's own god, so the waiting woman of the mullai sees her evening through the war myth of the god of her own landscape.

note: Akananuru 242: the mother, not knowing of the man who chased parrots from the millet with them, calls the ignorant velan, and before the kid's life is given he should come and embrace the girl. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 12: parrots raid the millet, the girl has embraced him fully, and the velan has resolved to cut the kid.
teaches: Both set the embrace against the kid's sacrifice, but the older poem makes the embrace the remedy that must come before the rite, while the venba gives both as done, which leaves the velan preparing a useless sacrifice for a cure already taken.

note: Kuruntokai 188: evening has come, aiming at her beauty, when the mullai has budded and he has not come; Kural 1221: she tells evening it is not evening but a time that eats the lives of wives.
teaches: The Kuruntokai shows why the evening attacks: it arrives with the season he promised to return by, so its hostility is the broken promise made visible, which the Kural's address to the evening leaves unstated.

note: Both end on the same conditional of the camp: the king's elephants with tusk-rings split on enemy forts, and 'if the fierce king releases us' (வினைவிடப் பெறினே / முன்னுதல் பெறினே).
teaches: Akananuru 164 sets the fort-blunted tusks after a whole season scene and her regained beauty, while 444 keeps only the tusks and the sight of her, which shows the worn elephant is the paasarai situation's own sign of a war too long, not a seasonal ornament.

iraicchi.act: the cock scratches up the wet sand for the day's food and, having caught it, stands looking to its hen
iraicchi.sense: the man's own errand of provision is done and, like the fowl, he turns to the wife he provides for

iraicchi.act: the twisted-horned stag leaps about together with the young doe in the rain-fed millet
iraicchi.sense: the beasts of the season are already together, as the husband and wife will be when the chariot that passes them arrives

iraicchi.act: the wise little sparrow labours to build its nest and keeps to it while the north wind shakes it on the bamboo
iraicchi.sense: even a small bird holds to the home it built when the cold wind blows, so a man who leaves his wife's bed in that wind is a fool

ullurai.tenor: the man's going and the girl's tears

pairs.situation: he drops away from her to his own country
her store of sweetness is broken and her eyes run

ullurai.speaker_fit: the girl uses the jackfruit and honeycomb of her own hill slope, things she knows (porul 7.26)

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman; Kalittokai 109: the man watching the buttermilk girl reports that the town's wives, judging her fit to be an anangu to everyone (யார்க்கும் அணங்கு ஆதல் சான்றாள்), keep their husbands in and shut their doors when she comes.
teaches: Beside the couplet, the herders' poem shows that the word அணங்கு named a real danger, a beauty that strikes whoever sees it: what is one man's private bewilderment in the Kural becomes in Kalittokai a judgment the whole town shares and acts on by guarding its men.

note: Both answer a husband who denies the other woman with the same verb, கண்டிகும் (we saw): Natrinai 20's heroine describes a woman leaving his bed with crushed garland and loosened hair, Ainkurunuru 121's friend a girl leaping into the sea with her garland soaked.
teaches: The one retort to a denial can be built two opposite ways, by showing the rival as a spent lover whose body carries his marks or as a child at play, so the 'we saw her' formula's sting lies in how the witness chooses to portray the woman, not in the seeing.

note: Kuruntokai 283 reports the man's maxim that the life of those who have nothing is more shameful even than begging, and he leaves for wealth; Kural 1064 says the worth that will not beg even when nothing is left is too great for the world to hold. On the reading that 283 ranks poverty below begging, the two rank the same states in opposite order.
teaches: The Kural makes the destitute man who refuses to beg the height of dignity, while the akam hero's maxim makes destitution itself the deepest shame, so the poems show that the urge to go for wealth rested on a ranking of poverty and begging the Kural explicitly reverses.

note: Kar Narpathu 11: the kodal puts out clusters like the raised heads of snakes, and the scrub announces his quick return. Thinaimalai 107: the kodal, fearing the kaayaa as peacocks, shrinks, and the cloud like a five-headed snake falls on my head.
teaches: Kar Narpathu uses the snake-headed kodal as a happy sign of his return, and Thinaimalai keeps the snake likeness but lets it run on into the logic of snake and peacock, so the same image that comforted the waiting woman becomes a fable of fear.

note: Kural 620 says those who toil on without flagging see fate's back; in Natrinai 88 the friend tells the girl not to be stricken as though by their own old deeds but to rise, go and speak to the man.
teaches: The Kural states for the man of affairs that effort overturns fate, and the Natrinai shows the same refusal of fate in a girl's friend inside a secret love, where the effort is speech to the man, so the rule had a domestic use, and the friend's action is an answer to the household's fatalism.

note: Thiruppugazh 18 names Murugan of south Parankunram as the one who took the girl the hill people gave (குன்றவர்கள் தந்தபெண்); Paripadal 9.67-69 has Valli's kin, the kurinji hill-men (குறிஞ்சிக் குன்றவர் ... வள்ளி தமர்), turn the wives' quarrel into a thumbai battle on that hill.
teaches: In the hymn the hill people appear only as givers of the bride, while in the Paripadal they stay her partisans after the marriage and fight for her against the sky-born wife, so the pair shows Valli's marriage remembered as an alliance with her kin that carried on into the god's household.

note: Natrinai 289's woman says her lover would not shift from his word even if the earth shifted, though the promised rains have come without him; Kural 1154's woman asks whether any fault lies with those who believed the assuring words of one who then left.
teaches: On the plain reading the two women answer the same broken promise in incompatible ways, one keeping her faith in his word intact and blaming only her unpitied state, the other turning the promise into a charge against him, which marks out the range a waiting woman's speech could take.

note: Kalladanar tells the same king that he has seen the ruin of the enemy's land, ending on a doe with her fawn, her stag killed by a tiger, nibbling velai flowers in a manless waste; the idyll lists, line by line, each human use of the enemy's land replaced by a wild one, with the owl and its mate in the fallen mansions and the boar and its sow in the ploughed fields.
teaches: Both poets of this king measure conquest by animal couples moving into places emptied of human families, so the ravaged-land description had a fixed device; the idyll turns Kalladanar's single pathetic image into a systematic inversion of the land's uses, which is the material its kaanchi counsel will later weigh.

note: 258 says the household will give the girl if the lord of the hill weds her; 254 says the wealthy ones have taken her to their hill country.
teaches: Read against 258's conditional promise, 254 is its fulfilment, so within one decade the hill man's daughter passes from being offered to being carried off to the man's country.

note: In Akananuru 272 the mother, seeing the garlanded lover at night, takes him for Murugu and worships; in Ainkurunuru 182 the friend points to a garlanded chest and says he is no god of power.
teaches: Read together, the two poems show the misreading the friend's disclosure has to undo: the household's habit of turning a garlanded young man into a god, which in Akananuru 272 leads to worship and in Ainkurunuru 182 is corrected by naming the garland as a shore man's hand-woven wreath.

note: In Akananuru 254 the waiting wife watches the house dove fly with its mate while the man drives home; in 425 the man on the road hears the forest dove croon for its mate.
teaches: Together the poems place the paired dove at both ends of the return journey, in the wife's courtyard and on the husband's road, so the same creature serves as the sign by which each partner reads the other's longing.

note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather together in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; the idyll grants that in Karikalan's land, under a sceptre it has just called just, the rain can fail in great drought, and gives the harvest to the Kaveri instead.
teaches: On the idyll's reading the just king's land is not spared drought, which the Kural's couplet implies it should be, so the poet keeps the king's righteousness and the land's plenty together by moving the source of harvest from the sky, which answers to the sceptre, to the river, which does not need to.

note: Kural 1262: if she forgets him today her beauty will leave and her bangles slip. Kainnilai 58: if she sits thinking of him, her bangles will not hold. On a plain reading forgetting ruins her in one and remembering in the other.
teaches: The couplet makes memory the thing that keeps her body whole and the venba makes memory the thing that wastes it, so together they show the bangle as a sign the two traditions could hang on either side of remembering the absent man.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of keeping a household is for caring for guests; Natrinai 41's friend says men suffer far off in the waste because they want the household where the wife cooks for a night guest.
teaches: The couplet's rule becomes, in the friend's mouth, a reason for the separation itself: if the house exists for the guest, then the husband's absence earning for it is the rule at work, so the Kural's praise of hospitality is shown to carry the cost the wife bears in paalai.

note: Both are the woman speaking of her heart against the man in oodal: the couplet says the heart's anger is false because it yields at the sight of him; Ainkurunuru 151 grants that the heart has already melted and refuses all the same.
teaches: The couplet treats a heart that yields as proof the quarrel was never real, while the poem keeps the refusal standing after the heart has gone over, so the Sangam woman's oodal is a decision of will against her own feeling rather than a mood that the man's presence dissolves.

note: Kural 1207's woman says she does not know forgetting and that even remembering burns; Natrinai 357's woman says the remembered day of play with the man has scarred her heart and will not fade, and on that she says she can bear the delay.
teaches: In both, memory cannot be shed, but the couplet makes it a burn and a danger, while the Natrinai makes one remembered day the scar on which the woman rests her claim to endure, so the same unfading memory is wound in one and support in the other.

note: In Akananuru 34 the man, his work done, bids the charioteer drive fast so that his wife may regain her beauty; in Kuruntokai 400 the man thanks the charioteer who cut a new way across the gravel and brought the chariot home to the wife in pain.
teaches: The two poems are the command and the thanks of one homeward drive: Akananuru 34 asks for speed, Kuruntokai 400 credits the charioteer with the resolve and the shortcut, so the driver is shown sharing the husband's care for the wife and earns praise for it.

note: Kuruntokai 158: the woman asks the storm cloud, whose thunder strikes snakes on the slopes and can shake the Himalaya, whether it has no pity for women without a companion. Natrinai 238: the woman tells the season's cloud that its coming is not like the noble, and its thunder that dulls the snakes' hoods is not sweet even to a hard heart.
teaches: Both women rebuke the thundering cloud of the season, but the Kuruntokai shames it by its might, while the Natrinai holds it to the conduct of the noble (சான்றோர்), so the reproach to the absent man is voiced in one through power misused and in the other through manners breached.

note: Kural 1097 says small words without real anger and hostile looks are the signs of those who are close while seeming distant; 100 says the one who wants love does not give up hinted speech.
teaches: The line says the lover speaks by hint and the couplet shows how hints are read, even harsh ones turned inside out, so the pair gives both the speaker's practice and the hearer's skill.

note: In Akananuru 117 the foster mother asks whether the hair she once combed and the girl would not let her wash now falls loose, dressed with her lover's flowers; in Natrinai 143 the mother recalls telling the girl her hair smelled fragrant.
teaches: Both mothers read the daughter's love in her hair, one before the flight and one after: the fragrance the mother let pass in Natrinai 143 is the lover's flowers that Akananuru 117 imagines on the road, so the hair is the household's evidence of a bond it could see but not stop.

note: In Kural 1313 the man complains that whatever garland he wears she says he wore it for another woman; in Paripadal 6.91-92 the wife asks who pressed into his garland and what touched it, and he blames the river.
teaches: The Kural states the suspicious garland as a pure case of love's jealousy, with no cause given, while the Paripadal gives the garland a real crushing and a real crowd in the water, so the pair shows the couplet's general complaint distilled from a festival in which the evidence truly could point either way.

note: Both poems are on the death after Venni: 65 mourns the king who sat north ashamed of a back wound, and 66, addressed to the victor Karikal, says that king is better than him; both use the phrase புறப்புண் நாணி.
teaches: Read together they show the honour code reversing a battle's result: the loser's chosen death, mourned in 65 as the stopping of a whole country's life, is used in 66 to rank him above the victor, said to the victor's face.

note: Kural 1146 says she saw him on only one day yet the gossip spread like the eclipse; Natrinai 138 says that their meeting at the ford was once known only to their eyes and asks whether the whole festive town does not know it today.
teaches: The Kural compresses into an eclipse the leap from one private sight to public talk that the Natrinai spreads over a remembered garland and a dancing town, and the Natrinai's overhearing hero shows the complaint was spoken to push him toward marriage.

note: Kural 1222 asks the pale evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Kuruntokai 92 at sunset watches birds hurry home with food for their young.
teaches: The Kural guesses that the evening suffers from a cruel partner like hers; the Kuruntokai's dusk answers that every creature in it is hurrying home to its own, so the hard-heartedness is her man's alone and not the hour's.

note: Ainkurunuru 185's man is taken by the Korkai girl's teeth bright as pearls; in Akananuru 27 the friend says the girl's red mouth with teeth like Korkai pearls may not hold the man who means to leave for wealth.
teaches: The pearl-toothed mouth of Korkai is what draws the man at first sight in Ainkurunuru 185 and what the friend in Akananuru 27 fears is not enough to keep him, so the same harbour formula marks both the start of the beauty's power and its limit against the call of wealth.

note: The same question, யாரையோ, is asked in both: in 245 the shore lord, struck at first sight, asks the girl 'who are you?'; in 250 the wife, estranged, asks her husband 'who are you?' as he comes to embrace their son.
teaches: Holding the two together traces the question across the whole course of akam love, from the wonder of a stranger at first meeting to a wife's pretended non-recognition in sulking, so the same words that began the bond are later used to deny it.

note: Purananuru 19 has the cut-trunked elephants rolling on the ground like ploughs (நாஞ்சில் ஒப்ப நிலமிசைப் புரள) in a field where old mothers weep for their sons; Kalavazhi 40 has all the elephants fall as if the god of the silver plough (வெள்ளிவெண் ணாஞ்சிலான்) were ploughing the world.
teaches: The Purananuru simile sits beside the mothers' grief, while the Kalavazhi lifts the same plough image to a god's tillage and drops the mourners, showing how the battlefield-as-ploughing figure grew into a frame of pure praise once the kalavazhi became a genre of its own.

note: Both have the friend bid the hill lord not come at midnight for fear of beasts: Ainkurunuru 296 in four lines, fearing a fierce beast; Akananuru 92 with a tiger striking an elephant, and then the offer that tomorrow she and the girl will be guarding the millet, where he may meet her by day (பகற்குறி, the colophon says, to press marriage).
teaches: Akananuru 92 spells out the day tryst at the millet field, which shows that the opening of Ainkurunuru 296, the millet the hill girl guards, is not idle scenery but the same unspoken offer, so the short poem's refusal of the night already points to where and when he may come.

note: Kural 1103: the man asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world is sweeter than sleep on the beloved's soft arms; Kuruntokai 288: the woman asks whether the world of the gods is sweeter even than the hurt that comes from kin because of her lover.
teaches: The couplet weighs heaven against the joy of love, the poem weighs it against love's pain, so the woman's claim is the stronger: not only the embrace but even the suffering it brings outweighs the gods' world.

note: Both are about a mother whose daughter has eloped: Akananuru 165, seen by onlookers, has a calf drinking at the buffalo in the old town, the playmates mourning and the mother crying 'let my life end'; Natrinai 271, in the mother's own voice, has a buffalo calf asleep on the dung of the house, the playmates going home at evening and her curse on Death for not taking her.
teaches: The two poems share an inventory for the house a daughter has left (the buffalo calf beside its mother, the girl's playmates, the mother's wish to die), which shows these were the fixed signs of that grief and lets the calf safe beside its dam be read as the daughter who did not stay.

note: Kural 1192 says a lover's grace to those who love is like rain to those who live by it; Kuruntokai 327's man has learned to withhold grace from those who live only if he is gracious (நல்கின் வாழும்), and water reaches her as a flood from his hill.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's rain of grace is shown in reverse: the one who lives by it is denied it, and the water that does come down from the lover's hill is muddy and destroys, so dependence on grace is seen from the side of its failure.

note: Kural 744 says a fort is that which destroys the besieging enemy's spirit (உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்ப தரண்); Fragment 2 lists a fort with tall wall, battlements, guard forest and deep moat and says that it is the defending kings who lose heart (நெஞ்சுபுகல் அழிந்து) at the Chera march.
teaches: On the plain reading the two make opposite claims about the same contest of nerve: the Kural gives the fort the power to break the attacker's spirit, while the praise poem says a perfect fort could not keep its own kings' spirit from breaking, so the war of morale the Kural assigns to walls the poet assigns to the king's army.

note: On the plain reading the claims are incompatible: in 170 the woman holds up her pallid eyes as evidence against the friend's word that he is good, while in Kural 1190 she would rather be called pallid than have the friend blame his unkindness.
teaches: Read together, the two show the heroine taking the side opposite to whoever speaks to her, so her pallor is not a fixed verdict on the man but an argument she turns against his praise or for his defence as the friend's stance requires.

note: Natrinai 86 blesses the men as அறவர் for coming back before the season they named; Ainkurunuru 472 says the season has come and its makers feel no shame at their false word.
teaches: The named season works as a vow with a moral verdict either way: kept early it earns the title of righteous men, broken it is charged as shamelessness, so the return date was judged as truthfulness rather than as mere timing.

note: For Parimelazhagar, the schools conflict on everything in 242 and yet converge on அருள். On 353, he says that their conflict leaves doubt only experience can settle.
teaches: Together they give his view of religious pluralism: agreement in ethics, and no resolution by argument in metaphysics.

note: Akananuru 282: the father agrees to give the girl to the hill lord whose hunters bring ivory, gold, gems and pearls together, and the household prays for the wedding day. Thinaimozhi 50: the heroine asks whether the sea lord will come to the front yard where coral, pearls and crystal are heaped as if in praise.
teaches: Akananuru 282 makes the suitor's treasure of the land the very thing that wins the father's consent, so beside it the shore's coral, pearls and crystal piled at the heroine's door read as the bride-wealth her question 'will he come?' is waiting for.

note: Both have the parrots take the girl's sound for their own call: in Kuruntokai 291 the man says the parrots take her clapper's sweet call for one of their own and will not rise, so she weeps; in Ainkurunuru 289 the friend says the parrots, taking her voice for a parrot's, come to the millet, so the elders may stop her guarding.
teaches: Kuruntokai 291 makes the image a lover's praise and a small vexation, while Ainkurunuru 289 follows it to its consequence in the household, the loss of the guard duty and so of the trysts, which turns the man's compliment into the friend's argument for marriage.

note: Kural 414 offers listening as the help left to one who has not studied; Pazhamozhi 11 names study and listening as the two routes and condemns the man who has taken neither.
teaches: Together they show listening as the fallback the Kural concedes and Pazhamozhi makes the minimum, so the man without even that has only luck left.

note: In Akananuru 16 the wife meets a courtesan cuddling her son in the chariot street and asks 'are you his mother too?'; in Kalittokai 84 the husband's women, the boy's 'mothers' (தாயர்), stop him in the street and load him with gifts, and the wife reads the shark ring as a message.
teaches: The two poems show that the son in the street was a fixed channel between wife and courtesan: the Akananuru wife disarms the rival by granting her a mother's place, while the Kalittokai wife finds that the same motherly gesture is used to send her a sign, so the courtesy of Akananuru 16 had a hostile counterpart.

note: Both say the rain-season flowers have opened like eyes (கண்ணெனக் கருவிளை மலர; கண்மலர்போற் பூத்தன) as the friend's season sign.
teaches: In Kar Narpathu the eye-like flowers speak and announce the man's return, in Ainkurunuru they only mark a season he cannot forget, so the same flower simile let the friend present the hedge either as a messenger or as a calendar.

note: Kural 1215 says what was seen awake was sweet then, and the dream too is sweet while it is seen; Kalittokai 68 says the husband's embrace is like wealth won in a dream, different on waking.
teaches: The Kural's lover levels waking and dream, both sweet while they last, but the Kalittokai wife uses the dream to name a possession that vanishes, so the dream simile can console a parted lover or indict an unfaithful husband depending on whether the absence is chosen.

note: In Akananuru 84 the man in the king's war camp sees the drum-voiced rain-clouds and thinks of his wife in her small village; in Kuruntokai 380 the waiting women hear the cloud roar like the drums kings beat in victory while the lover stays far away.
teaches: Read together, the simile in the women's mouth names the cause the man's poem shows from inside, the king's campaign, so the rains are the same drum to both and the season of war and the season of waiting are one.

note: Both use the same pair of similes for the rain flowers: konrai like gold (பொன் என), kaayaa like sapphire (மணி என); Natrinai's returning hero urges his charioteer on, Ainkurunuru's promises to bring his wife to see the scrub.
teaches: The same jewelled konrai and kaayaa that make the returning man in Natrinai hurry home become, once he is home, a sight he promises to return to with his wife, so the formula's force changes from summons to leisure with the man's place in the journey.

ullurai.tenor: the man who comes by day close to the girl's house

pairs.situation: he is no longer content with meetings in the grove by day
his coming near the village sets the household and the town in alarm

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the elephant herd of the kurinji hill in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the waterfall bears sandalwood down to the burnt clearing and makes it fragrant
iraicchi.sense: the hill's own stream heals the scorched field as the hero ought to come and soothe the girl he has left burning, so his absence is the deceit

iraicchi.act: the male bird calls to its mate again and again so that they may delight together
iraicchi.sense: at this season even birds call their mates, yet he does not come to her
