ullurai.tenor: the man and the woman whose eyes he has made weep

pairs.situation: her opened, flower-like eyes, named in line 4 by the flower's own word பல்லிதழ்
he harms her in passing, while about his own gain, not aiming at her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the neythal and the reapers of the fields beside her own shore town, things she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the tusker carries the little water of a muddy rock pool in his trunk and pours it on the head of his heat-worn mate
iraicchi.sense: the man who passes such care on his road will be moved to the same care for the wife he left

iraicchi.act: the heron searches the sea together with its mate and drops the fish it catches into the mouths of its young in the nest
iraicchi.sense: the man who now comes openly will keep a house as the heron does, seeking with his wife and feeding their own

note: Ainthinai Aimpathu 45: will the herons of the grove let his oath go unpunished? Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: the heron of the grove saw his cruelty and does not know it. On a plain reading one makes the herons guarantors of his oath and the other finds the heron a useless witness.
teaches: Held together, the two shore venbas show the heroine's trust in the grove's herons as witnesses of a secret oath collapsing once he has gone: the birds she counted on to hold him are the birds she then reproaches for seeing nothing.

note: Two claims about the sharpest edge (எஃகு). In 759 wealth is the sharpest steel for cutting an enemy's pride. In 773 the edge of valour is helping that enemy when he falls.
teaches: Cutting and sparing are both called sharpness.

note: Kar Narpathu 12: his coming is certain; every day the dark clouds, like elephants anointed with oil, rise on the right. Natrinai 237: look, the clouds rise like the elephants Andiran gathered.
teaches: Both friends point a pining woman to clouds that rise like elephants as proof of the season's return, but Kar Narpathu's anointed elephants and the rising on the right make the cloud an omen, while Natrinai's patron's elephants make it a gift laid up for those who wait, so the same image could reassure by augury or by the ethic of giving.

note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue more than asking, even water for a cow; Paripadal 10.87-88 has bathers who, seeing what they lack, do good works in hope before they speak the shame of asking (இளிவரவு கூறாமுன்).
teaches: The festival bathers apply the Kural's horror of asking even to what they want from the river, choosing an offering over a spoken request, so the ethic against begging shaped how people framed a petition in worship.

note: Kural 812 asks what it matters whether one gains or loses the friendship of those who are friends while there is profit and leave when there is none; Thinaimozhi 33 calls the husband's conduct exactly such a friendship.
teaches: The Kural can shrug at the self-serving friend because a friend can be dropped, but the wife cannot treat a husband with that indifference, since what he consumed was her youth, so the akam poem shows where the maxim's calm stops working.

note: Both set a newly calved buffalo cow beside her calf in the marutham town: in Ainkurunuru 92 the suitor names it as he promises to come for the girl, in Kuruntokai 181 the wife names the same cow, grazing near the calf the ploughman tied, as she speaks of matrons worn by the great house's duties.
teaches: The suitor's emblem of the home he offers becomes, in the wife's mouth, the emblem of the home that has used her up, so the one buffalo image measures how courtship's promise of motherhood reads after years of karpu.

note: Kural 1251 has desire's axe break the door of restraint (நிறை); Paripadal 6.22-23 has the flood break its dam as lovers of one desire break the restraint that fills the heart (உளம் நிறை உடைத்தென).
teaches: The Kural's woman speaks of restraint broken as her private defeat, while the Paripadal makes the same breaking of நிறை the measure of a flood the whole town celebrates with drums, so the pair shows the Kural's image of a lost guard was also, in the festival, a public and welcome release.

note: Kural 333: wealth does not stay, so when you get it do at once what stays. Natrinai 46 calls the wealth the man leaves for மன்னாப் பொருள், wealth that does not last.
teaches: Both call wealth impermanent, but the Kural still tells a man to get it and convert it into lasting good, while the friend uses its impermanence to argue against going after it at all, which shows the couplet's maxim leaving room for the very journey the akam poem condemns.

note: In Akananuru 317 the man's quoted promise names the spring signs, the koel in the mango and the kongu and kuravam dropping flowers, and he arrives on time; in Ainkurunuru 350 the time of his assurance comes and he does not.
teaches: Akananuru 317 shows that the catalogue of spring flowers and birds was itself the wording of the man's promise, so the Ainkurunuru decade's list of the same signs is the promise read back to an absent man, and 317's ending is the one the decade is denied.

note: In Natrinai 86 the friend reads the flowers of the late dew and early summer as true signs that the man came before his season; in Natrinai 99 she calls the rainy-season flowers foolish, blooming for a rain that is not the season, because he has not come.
teaches: Read together they show that the friend's reading of the season's signs follows the man's conduct, not the signs themselves: when he keeps time the flowers are witnesses, when he does not they are fools, so the season in akam is an argument made for the woman's sake.

note: Kural 1085 finds death, the eye and the doe all in the young woman's look; Ainkurunuru 361 grants the eyes are fierce, then ranks her breasts fiercer and her shoulders fiercer still.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on the first sight puts all the deadliness in the look, and the Ainkurunuru poet answers that the eyes are only the first and mildest weapon, which shows the old akam poets could treat the same stricken lover as half joking where the couplet keeps him grave.

note: Kural 1103 asks whether heaven is sweeter than sleeping on the beloved's soft arms; in Kuruntokai 323 the man calls every other day chaff and counts as lived only the days spent sleeping on her shoulders.
teaches: The couplet ranks the embrace above heaven's pleasure; the poem turns the same ranking on time itself, so the pair shows the claim growing from a comparison of joys into a measure of which days of a life count as lived.

note: In Natrinai 386 the friend recalls the hill-lord coming humbly with the word வதுவை so that the village shone; in Ainkurunuru 230 the friend announces the wedding for the hill-lord who once guarded millet with them and wasted the heroine's beauty.
teaches: Both friends mark the wedding as the end of kalavu, but one remembers the suitor's humility and the other his damage, so the go-between's announcement of marriage could be told as the lover's submission or as payment of what he owed.

note: Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety is hard to remove except for those who reach the feet of the one who has no comparison; Patitruppattu 73 calls the Chera one to whom others are no comparison (நினக்குப் பிறர்உவமம் ஆகா) and ends with the poet grieving (வருந்துவல் யானே) that people will not believe his praise.
teaches: The Kural makes the incomparable one the end of anxiety for those who come to him, but the Chera poet shows the same attribute, given to a king, bringing anxiety to the one who praises, since what has no comparison cannot be made credible to hearers.

note: Both liken the girl to Kuttuvan's Thondi: in Ainkurunuru 178 the courting man calls her like Thondi of Kuttuvan of the just sceptre, while in Akananuru 290 the heroine says her eyes, once like the neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour, have lost that likeness and turned pale while he delays marriage.
teaches: The Thondi likeness is the lover's praise in courtship and becomes the heroine's own measure of loss when marriage is delayed, so the beauty the man praises to win her is the very thing his delay spends, and the friend of 179 and 180 is right to press him.

note: Both liken a woman's beauty to Kuttuvan's harbour town Maranthai: in Akananuru 376 the deserted courtesan asks the man to give back her Maranthai-like beauty before he goes; in Natrinai 35 the friend, the day after the wedding, asks whether the wife's Maranthai-like beauty has slackened though he has not left her side.
teaches: The same city-simile measures a beauty the man must answer for in both, but the pair shows it waning for opposite reasons, the courtesan's because he left and the new wife's while he stays, so the Natrinai places the loss in love itself rather than in absence.

note: Both open on a buffalo that breaks its tether (கயிறுபரிந்து; நோன் தளை பரிந்து) and grazes the town's crops; Akananuru 46 anchors the image in a second marriage over sixteen lines, Ainkurunuru 95 only in 'he gave us a hard sickness even by day'.
teaches: That a four-line poem can rest the whole charge on the rope-breaking buffalo, with no wedding named, shows the image was already a fixed sign of the straying lord, which the longer Akananuru poem spells out rather than invents.

note: The idyll says Thiraiyan is of the line the waves brought (திரைதரு மரபு); Akananuru 340, a shore poem, likens the girl to his Pavaththiri of many flowering seaside groves.
teaches: Read together, the two place Thiraiyan as a ruler of the coast: the praise poem's sea-born lineage and the love poem's choice of his seaside town as the measure of a neythal girl's beauty rest on the same identity, so the akam simile draws on the fame the guide poem states.

note: Kuruntokai 25: no one was there but the thief and a heron watching for aaral fish on the day he took her, so what can she do if he lies. Kainnilai 50: she will tell neither him nor the anril, only the stork of the grove that saw his hard oath.
teaches: The heron that in Kuruntokai only proves how alone the heroine was becomes, in the venba, the one hearer she trusts with the broken oath, so the bird witness of kalavu moves from a sign of her helplessness to the only court left to her.

note: Both honour the feet of one who walked on the flower: மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் in the Kural, தண்டாமரைமேல் நடந்தான் in the Neelakesi.
teaches: An avowedly Jain poet uses the flower-walking epithet for his god, so the Kural's disputed epithet was current in Jain praise and not only open to other readings.

note: Akananuru 34: the returning man sees a stag feed its doe and guard her sleep and bids his charioteer hurry home. Kuruntokai 213: the friend says that on his road, they say, the stag starves to shelter its young, so he has deep love.
teaches: The friend's comfort in Kuruntokai is a prediction that the man will see the beasts' care and be moved; Akananuru 34 shows that very sight working on the man himself, so the two poems give the two ends of one iraicchi, the promise at home and its fulfilment on the road.

note: Both are the deserted woman facing the town's gossip: in Kural 1149 she asks how she can be ashamed of gossip when the man who told her not to fear has left her; in Natrinai 116 the bond has burst like a fallen jackfruit yet the women still keep up their talk of her.
teaches: In the Kural his leaving cancels the shame of the gossip, while in Natrinai the gossip outlives the bond it was about, so the pair shows two answers to the same abandonment: indifference to talk or bearing talk about a love that is already gone.

note: Both men are going home with the task done; in 161 he wonders whether the omen birds have already told her, in 169 he speaks to the house lizard and asks it to chirp for her.
teaches: Together they show the returning husband imagining the omen from her side and then trying to work it from his own, so the signs she watches for become signs he wishes he could send.

note: In Akananuru 242 the friend calls the velan ignorant (அறியா வேலன்) for finding Murugan's seizure in the girl; in Natrinai 34 the friend addresses Murugan himself, who knows the sickness is not his yet comes to the veri at the velan's call, and calls the god a fool.
teaches: Together they show the friend's scorn for the veri rite moving up from the priest to the god: where one poem blames only the diviner's ignorance, the other makes the god complicit, since he knows the truth and comes anyway.

note: Kar Narpathu 14: the friend says they are sure he will come quickly, since the rain cloud laughs softly as the mullai shows its bright teeth. Kuruntokai 220: the jasmine buds open like a wild cat smiling, the evening is here, and he has not come.
teaches: Both poems read the opening jasmine as a smile with teeth, but in the friend's venba it is the season laughing in welcome and in the heroine's Kuruntokai poem it is a wild cat's grin, so the one image turns from promise to mockery once the day of return has passed.

note: The idyll counts the noise of the garlanded crowd playing together on cool Parankunram among the sounds of the marutham countryside; Paripadal 17 describes the crowds revelling between song-rich Koodal and Parankunram, garlanded men and women dancing so that the bees cannot reach the flowers.
teaches: In the Maduraikkanchi the Parankunram festival is one sound among the reaping drum and the herons, part of the king's agrarian land, while the Paripadal makes the same crowd its subject and the hill's beauty, so the festival a court poet counted as rural plenty became, in the devotional songs, the sign of the god's hill.

note: Kural 774 praises the warrior who sends his spear off in an elephant and laughs as he plucks another from his own body; in Kalavazhi 23 the strong men (வயவர்) hurl and split the elephants' foreheads, and the field is Chempiyan's.
teaches: The Kural keeps the spear-thrower's own pride and wound in view, while the battle-song shows the same feat only through the speared elephants and credits it to the king, so the pair shows the warrior's deed moving from his ethic into his lord's fame.

note: Kural 552 calls the sceptre-holder's demand a robber's demand at spear-point; 184 likens the greedy king to an elephant loose in a field.
teaches: The Kural condemns excess levy from the subject's side as robbery, while Pisirandhaiyar argues from the king's side that grabbing wastes more than it yields and leaves the king himself unfed, so the same rule is given both a moral and a prudential ground.

note: Akananuru 80 forbids the night swim and offers a day meeting in the punnai grove; Thinaimalai 35 forbids the night and warns that a day visit brings gossip.
teaches: Set beside Akananuru 80, where the day meeting is the friend's remedy for the night's danger, Thinaimalai 35 shows a later stage in which the day too is closed by gossip, so that the only road left is marriage.

note: In Akananuru 48 the foster mother asks why the girl will not drink milk and has paled, and the friend tells her of the young hunter; in Kuruntokai 396 the foster mother, after the girl has gone with her man, recalls that she would not drink her milk or take up her ball.
teaches: The same symptom, refused milk, stands at two points of one story: in Akananuru 48 it is a question the friend answers in time to open the way to marriage, in Kuruntokai 396 a clue the foster mother reads only after the elopement, so the akam poets used it as the sign that decides whether disclosure or udanpokku follows.

note: Avvaiyar's Purananuru 97 warns Anji's enemies that his worn swords, spears and elephants prove resistance is hopeless; her Kuruntokai 91 makes the night terror of a frontier town fearing Anji the measure of a wife's sleepless marriage.
teaches: The same poet supplies both sides of Anji's war: the puram poem speaks for the conqueror's threat, the akam poem borrows the sleeplessness of the threatened town, showing that the fear puram praise produces was available to akam as an image of domestic misery.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world stands because there are men who would give their lives for fame; Natrinai 115 says the absent lover, of great love, would not stay away even for endless fame.
teaches: On one defensible reading the two rank the same goods in opposite order, puram putting fame above life and akam putting love above fame, so the friend's comfort works only by overturning the heroic scale the puram poem praises.

note: In Ainkurunuru 66 the wife asks who the woman is who stole his homecoming to his toddling son; in Akananuru 16 the wife tells how a young courtesan found that son alone in the chariot street and hugged him as her own.
teaches: The son is the wife's claim on the husband, and the pair shows the rival reaching for it from both ends: diverting the father on his way to the child, and taking the child into her own arms.

note: Both are courtesans answering, within hearing of the wife's side, the wife's talk against them: in Akananuru 76 she vows to hold him as the Kaveri took Atti; in Kuruntokai 364 she points to the coming thunangai festival where eyes clash.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the concubine's convention of answering slander not with denial but with a public contest announced in advance, a river's seizure or a festival's rivalry, so the household quarrel is moved out into the town's open spaces.

note: Kural 113 says to give up at once gain made by leaving fairness, even if it brings good; Kalittokai 14 says wealth made by leaving the straight way is an enemy in this life and the next.
teaches: The Kural allows that unfair gain may bring good and asks for sacrifice anyway, while the love poem denies it brings good in either world, so the woman's argument is stronger than the ethics book's rule.

note: Mullaippattu 85 lights the wife's room with பாவை விளக்கிற் பரூஉச்சுட ரழல; Nedunalvadai 175 lights the king's midnight round of the wounded with பாண்டில் விளக்கிற் பரூஉச்சுட ரழல.
teaches: The same half-line of a lamp's thick flame burning lights the sleepless wife at home in Mullaippattu and the sleepless king in camp in Nedunalvadai, so the formula belongs to the night vigil itself and the two idylls assign that vigil in opposite directions.

note: 371 says the girl went having judged this the path of right (அறநெறி); 376 calls the fate that joined and sent her without right (அறனில் பால்).
teaches: One decade by one poet lets the mother both concede that her daughter chose rightly and curse the joining as wrong, so the dispute over whether elopement is அறம் is staged inside a single lament rather than between mother and girl.

note: Kuruntokai 212 has the friend say the shore lord's chariot comes, bells ringing, only to be seen and goes back leaving shame; in Kuruntokai 311 the chariot that would not stop was seen by the whole troop of flower-gathering girls, and the heroine asks how the gossip can end.
teaches: Read together, the chariot that the friend in 212 calls mere display is in 311 the very evidence the gossip rests on, so the lover's conspicuous visits are both his courtship and the cause of the alar.

note: Kural 1209: her life is ending as she thinks of the unkindness of one who said they were not separate. Kuruntokai 218: he, like life to her life, who could not bear a parting even a blink long, can now forget her and stay away, and she will still think of him.
teaches: The couplet names the wound as the broken claim of oneness; the Kuruntokai poem gives the claim its measure, not a blink apart, and adds what the woman does with the wound, vows, omens and thought, so the poem shows the couplet's dying as a life kept busy with ritual.

note: Kalittokai 67.3-5 says the Vaiyai beating against the wall (மதில் பொரூஉம்) is the only enemy the walled town has known; Paripadal 12.9 has the town hear that the Vaiyai has come beating against Madurai's wall (மதுரை மதில் பொரூஉம்) and rush out in finery to meet it.
teaches: The akam poem turns the river's assault on the wall into a boast that no army ever reached Madurai, and the hymn shows what that only siege was like inside the walls, a summons that sends the whole town to dress and ride out, so together they show the flood as the city's one welcomed attack, the festival standing where war stands for other towns.

note: Thinaimalai 1 gives the man's question to the girls about a wounded beast (ஏமரை); Thinaimozhi 8 gives the friend's answer that no wounded tusker came this way.
teaches: Put together the two short books make one exchange, and the question's lavish praise of the girls' faces next to the friend's flat denial shows each side treating the wounded animal as a cover: he courts through it, and she refuses through it.

note: Ainkurunuru 47 has the woman tell the man that her companions know he tells many lies, just like his bard; Paripadal 18.16-22 shows her making the bard see the nail marks, the embrace and the ornaments on the man and calling his song a bloom of lies (பொய் வளம் பூத்தன).
teaches: The Ainkurunuru gives the charge that the bard lies as his master does, and the hymn gives the proof shown to the bard's face, the marks the hill's women left, so together they show the god's festival hill as one of the places where marutham's straying was caught, with the bard's song refuted by the body.

note: Akananuru 85: the friend says the cool rains, when the elephant feeds his young mate and calf with bamboo shoots, are the season he promised, so do not weep. Kar Narpathu 38: the bull elephant plays with his mate in the cool season, yet he has not come, and the colophon says the friend tells her he lied.
teaches: The elephant pair in the rains is the friend's proof of his promise in one poem and her proof of his breach in the other, so the creatures' act carries the same sense in both while the verdict on the man turns on whether he has come.

iraicchi.act: the male wild dog, gone on a hunt, grieves remembering his mate who lies starving
iraicchi.sense: the man who has left on his own hunt for wealth is bound to grieve for his wife in the same way, so the heart should turn back

ullurai.tenor: the husband who leaves the wife and returns at his convenience

pairs.situation: he quarrels with the household and goes off
he seeks other women
he comes back when the trouble at home has passed

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the bee of her own town's lotus fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the girl and the hill lord meeting secretly by night

pairs.situation: the lovers' secret union
the fear that her kin and the town will learn of it
the girl must hide the traces of the meeting before she is seen

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a monkey of the kurinji slopes in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

note: Kural 49 says that what is called virtue is household life; in Natrinai 166 a husband says that seeing his wife he is like those settled in virtue, and gives that and his son's first play as reasons he will not leave.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's claim used as an argument against the paalai journey: a husband offers the household's settled virtue as his answer to the pull of wealth abroad, which makes the maxim a reason to stay.

note: Kural 214 says one who knows what is fitting (ஒப்புரவு) lives and others are counted among the dead; in Natrinai 220 the lover says the townspeople, if they knew ஒப்புரவு, would side with him and tell him not to be a stranger to the girl.
teaches: The lover appeals to the Kural's civic duty of fellow-feeling to claim the town's support for a love match it is condemning, so the pair shows ஒப்புரவு invoked against the town's own idea of propriety.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman. Natrinai 155: at their second meeting he asks her aloud whether she is the goddess of the sea or of the backwater, and she answers with a smile and tears.
teaches: The couplet leaves the man's doubt as a question in his head; the poem puts the same question to the girl and lets her answer it, since a smile and tears are a woman's reply, not a goddess's, so the doubt is settled by her response.

note: Kural 580 praises those who, wanting a refinement worth loving, see poison poured and drink it; Kalittokai 74 calls the women who trust the husband's words though they see his graceless ways deluded, like those who eat poison knowing it kills.
teaches: Knowingly swallowing poison is a mark of courtesy in the Kural and a mark of delusion in the Kalittokai, so the same act is judged by whom it is done for: forbearance toward a friend is refinement, forbearance toward a faithless lover is folly.

note: In Kural 1247 the woman in separation tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both; in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 34 she foresees her heart throwing off shame and going with her life after him.
teaches: The couplet poses the choice between desire and shame as a demand on the heart, and the venba shows the heart's answer and its cost, since choosing desire there means the life leaving the body with it.

note: Kural 86 says the one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next becomes a good guest of those in the sky; Patitruppattu 21 calls the king's kitchen-fat an ஆவுதி (oblation) beside the sacrificial one and says the two smells together please the gods who abide in the sky.
teaches: The Chera poem shows the mechanism the Kural only asserts: feeding guests reaches the gods because the kitchen smoke is itself counted as an oblation, so hospitality was understood as a second sacrifice rather than merely compared to one.

note: Both describe the reaped millet field as a broken stalk-head stubble in nearly the same words (பொறை இறுத்த கோல் தலை இருவி; குலவுப்பொறை யிறுத்த கோல்தலை மருவி), and both picture the man finding it empty and sad (பைதல்; பைதலன்).
teaches: The shared formula shows that the reaped field was a fixed sign of the closed meeting-place: Natrinai's friend uses it as a threat to make him ask for the girl, while Akananuru's friend imagines him already standing there grieving.

note: Kural 1102: medicine for a disease is something other than it, but for the sickness this woman gives, she herself is the cure. Natrinai 53: the mother prescribes the stream water from the lover's hill as medicine for the girl's shivering.
teaches: The couplet states as a paradox that the cause of love-sickness is its only cure; the poem shows the mother unknowingly obeying it, sending the girl to water that comes from the lover's own hill, and the friend reports it so that the man listening learns he is the medicine and must come to marry.

note: In Ainkurunuru 31 the other woman holds the lord to an oath he swore her at the bathing ford; in Akananuru 166 the same kind of lord swears to his wife by the god of Velur that he never bathed with the other woman, and the courtesan asks who then held the float with her yesterday.
teaches: Held together, the two show the marutham lord's oaths cancelling each other: the bathing he swore by to the courtesan is the bathing he forswears to his wife, so one of the two oaths must be false and each woman is left holding an oath the other's makes worthless.

note: Kural 1265 says the pallor of her shoulders will leave once she has seen her husband her eyes' fill; in Ainkurunuru 229 the friend sees the brow's golden beauty returned and asks whether he came in the night.
teaches: The couplet makes the lover's presence the cure for pallor, and the poem turns that rule into a means of detection, so the cure that the heroine longs for is also what betrays her secret meeting to the friend.

note: Purananuru 67 asks the swan, flying from the ford of Kumari to the northern mountain, to stop at the Chola king's palace with the poet's name; Natrinai 356 likens the man's toiling heart to the swan that grazes the southern sea and carries food to its chicks on the Himalaya.
teaches: Both send the swan between the southern sea and the northern mountain, but puram makes it a messenger to a king while akam makes its tireless feeding flight the lover's own heart, so the long-flight swan served as a go-between in one genre and as the self in the other.

note: Both are by Kapilar: in Purananuru 109 the kings besieging Paari's Parambu, with its jackfruit and its springs, cannot take it by force, but bards who come singing will be given it; in Natrinai 253 the girl, grown beautiful and hard to reach, is like Paari's jackfruit hill closed in by rain.
teaches: Read with the puram poem, the akam simile carries its argument: Parambu yields not to siege but to those who come asking, so the friend's comparison tells the man that the girl will not be had by stealth but only by asking for her in marriage.

note: Kural 392 calls numbers and letters the two eyes of living beings; Thirikadugam makes learning the letters first the opening step on the path of excellence.
teaches: The couplet values letters as sight; the verse gives them a place in time, first, before the parents and inherited conduct, so literacy becomes the start of a moral sequence.

note: Both have the man in love rank a small favour of the beloved above the highest good: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed god is sweeter than sleep in her soft arms; Ainkurunuru 290 says parrots merely looked at and shooed by the hill girl are more fortunate than a just king.
teaches: The Kural sets union against heaven, while the Sangam poem sets far less, a glance and a shooing given to birds, against a righteous kingdom, so the pair shows the measure working at both ends: even the least share of her notice outweighs the highest worldly good.

note: Ainkurunuru 89: the other woman tells the bard the wife is greatly graced, only because she wants the name of wife. Naladiyar 390: the wife tells the bard not to lie that he will be kind; she is the dry end of the cane and the others its sweet middle. On a plain reading each woman says the other has his favour.
teaches: Each woman tells the same messenger that the other is the favoured one, so the bard meets the identical complaint at both doors and the triangle has no one who admits to being loved; the Naladiyar files that voice under the chaste wife, the Ainkurunuru gives it to the rival.

note: Natrinai 210 says grand speech and harsh riding are not wealth, only the fruit of deeds, and the wealth of the worthy is a gentle-eyed nature; Kural 241 says the wealth of grace is the wealth of wealths, since the base also hold goods.
teaches: The friend aims the Kural's general ranking of wealths at a particular rich husband who has hurt his wife, and narrows grace to fear of the dependant's distress, so the maxim is shown at work as a rebuke inside a marriage.

note: Natrinai 378: the bond began when the shore lord came and broke up their little striped sand-house and spoke soft words. Ainthinai Aimpathu 44: the weeping girl tells her mother that the sea came and wrecked her sand-house.
teaches: Natrinai 378 shows that the wrecked sand-house is the very scene where the secret love began, which turns the girl's excuse in Ainthinai Aimpathu 44 into a coded confession: the 'sea' that broke her play is the man of the sea.

note: 376 is the mother's curse on the fate without right (அறனில் பால்) that sent the girl; 393 describes her from outside as one who quarrelled with right and blamed it (அறம்புலந்து பழிக்கும்).
teaches: The curse the mother speaks in her own voice in decade 38 is named in decade 40 as a quarrel with அறம் that the daughter's return is meant to heal, so the poet frames the lament as a dispute with the moral order that the homecoming settles.

note: In Akananuru 48 the foster mother asks why her daughter will not drink milk (பாலும் உண்ணாள்) and has paled; in 168 the friend tells the man that the girl will drink milk again if he shows grace.
teaches: Refusing milk is a fixed sign of secret love that the friend can turn two ways: toward the household, as the symptom she explains in disclosing the affair, and toward the lover, as the cure only he can give, so one sign drives both halves of the push toward marriage.

note: Kural 1226: she did not know, while her husband had not yet gone, that evening brings sickness. Ezhupathu 21: before he returns, the evening comes with the rains to torment her, and no one lives in such folly as she.
teaches: The Kural names the woman's ignorance at the time of parting as the cause of her suffering, while the Ezhupathu's மடம் is a folly she still lives in now, knowing the evening, so the pairing separates ignorance that excuses from folly that the speaker mocks in herself.

note: Akananuru 82.1-10 makes the hill country a stage: wind in bamboo the flute, the waterfall the drum, bees the lute, monkeys the audience and the peacock a dancer; Paripadal 21.30-38 has the peacock dance, the thumbi as flute, bees as lute and the waterfall as drum on the god's hill.
teaches: In the Akananuru the hill's orchestra is a love poem's setting, praising the hill man's country and ending in the woman's lonely night, while the Paripadal keeps the same instruments, drops the monkey audience and the lovers, and gives the scene to the god with the drum, so the pair shows a figure from akam landscape reused as worship of the hill's own god.

note: Akananuru 395: the woman says the man crossed a forest where a fork-horned stag, chasing the mirage, strays off the path and calls for its grazing doe in a failing voice. Aimpathu 36: an elephant pair takes the white mirage for water, runs to it together and falls with tangled legs.
teaches: The two poems take the same chase after a mirage to opposite ends: in Akananuru it parts the stag from its mate and gives the abandoned woman her own cry, in the Aimpathu the pair are fooled and fall together, so the image can either mirror her loneliness or shame the man who leaves when even deceived beasts do not part.

note: Kalittokai 142's girl, once laughing with hidden teeth, now laughs aloud and weeps so all hear and sings her love to the worthies; Kural 1138 says love does not stop to weigh restraint but breaks secrecy and comes into the open.
teaches: The couplet states as a law what the kali poem stages as a scene with an audience and a song, and shows the price: once love breaks into the open, the woman faces two pains, love and gossip (காமமும் கௌவையும்), where the couplet names only the first.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win; let us join the house and keep the evening feast. Kar Narpathu 20: the king's work is finished, so the roads home are sweet.
teaches: The couplet is the wish spoken while the war goes on and the venba is the same man once it is granted, so read together they give the before and after of one situation, the hero held by the king's war until it ends.

note: Both are the friend comforting the wife with the same formula, that the man has very great love (பெரும்பேர் அன்பினர், மிகப் பேர் அன்பினர்) and would not stay even if he gained something: Kuttuvan's land in Akananuru 91, endless fame in Natrinai 115.
teaches: The comfort is a fixed frame whose slot each poet fills with the highest prize of the puram world, land in one and fame in the other, so the formula is a measure of love against the goods of war.

note: Kalittokai 85 says the father uses the lying bard as a fishhook to bind the hearts of the women he wants. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50 tells the bard to go on without pause to the street of the gold-like women.
teaches: Kalittokai names the bard as the husband's lure for other women, which explains the venba's order to keep going to that street: the wife is sending the go-between back to his real work, so refusing the bard and accusing him are one act.

note: Purananuru 72 has Neduncheliyan vow to rout the kings who mocked him and seize them together with their drums (முரசமொடு); Natrinai 39 names Cheliyan as the one who took the drums and crossed the foes' guarded walls (முரசு கொண்டு ஓம்பு அரண் கடந்த) and likens the girl's shoulders to his Koodal. The Natrinai does not say which Cheliyan; the drum-taking matches.
teaches: The pair shows a king's battle vow hardened into a stock epithet inside a love simile and turned on the lover: the city of the king who took walled forts becomes the measure of shoulders that overpower the man, so puram conquest lends akam its language of love's assault.

note: The Kural says the base, like sugarcane, yield only when crushed; the idyll's cane presses roar day and night and the bard is told to drink the juice as he likes.
teaches: The Kural's image of giving extracted by force uses the same press that the idyll presents as the very sound of open plenty, so the simile's sting depends on the contrast: what the base give only under crushing, the cane in a good land gives to any passing guest.

note: Natrinai 80 names in one line a girl who bathes in the cold pond of the month of Thai with her jewelled companions (தைஇத் திங்கள் தண் கயம் படியும்); Paripadal 11.74-92 sets out the rite itself: Aathirai, the brahmins, the elder women of the ford, the dawn bath and the fire.
teaches: The akam poem's passing mention of a Thai bath points to a guarded public rite with priests, elder women and mothers, so the girl a lover sees there is seen at a sanctioned gathering of maidens, which is why such a meeting could happen and why shyness must restrain her.

note: Kural 1192 likens a lover's grace to the rain that sustains those who live by it; Kalittokai 71 likens the husband's once-a-year visit to a drizzle that cannot satisfy paddy withering for want of rain.
teaches: The Kural's rain stands for grace given in its season, and the Kalittokai shows the same image under neglect: a token visit is not rain but drizzle, so the wife measures grace by its sufficiency, a test the Kural's simile assumes but does not state.

note: In both the wife's shoulders waste and she will not call him cruel; in Ainkurunuru 11 she says he is good while her own shoulders say he is not, in Kural 1236 she is pained that others call him cruel because her shoulders and bangles slacken.
teaches: The Sangam poem sets the accusation inside her own body, against her own words, while Valluvar moves it to other people reading her body, so the couplet's defence of him against outsiders presupposes the older poem's private split between what she says and what her shoulders show.

note: In Kuruntokai 63 the man's heart argues that work for wealth must be pressed because the penniless can neither give nor enjoy; in 331 the friend says he goes for wealth he rates above them (நம்மினுஞ் சிறந்த).
teaches: The same journey for wealth is a duty in the man's reckoning and a ranking of the women below gold in the friend's, so the pair shows that the paalai departure is argued from both houses and that neither side's account mentions the other's.

note: In Akananuru 194 the heroine hears the peacock cry in the very rains her lover named for his return and he has not come; in Paripadal 14 the peacock's cry on the god's rainy hill is like the words calling the departed lover 'do not delay, come'.
teaches: The Paripadal's simile only works for a hearer who knows the mullai convention the Akananuru poem dramatises, the rains as the deadline of return, so the devotional poet borrows the heroine's grief as an ornament of the god's hill and makes the peacock say the summons she can only feel.

note: In 257 the father worshipped the god and begged for the daughter; in 259 the daughter herself worships the clan god of the hill.
teaches: Read together the two poems pass the rite from father to daughter: the god who gave her in answer to the father's begging now receives her own offering, made when she has a love of her own to pray for.

note: Ainkurunuru 188's man compares his love's eyes to the neythal blooming at dawn at Korkai's great ford; in Natrinai 23 the friend says the girl's eyes have faded like the small-leaved neythal of Korkai's harbour.
teaches: The same Korkai neythal serves for the eyes in bloom when the lover praises them and for the eyes faded when the friend presses for marriage, so the flower's daily opening and closing lets one image carry both the courtship's first wonder and its later cost.

note: Both invoke Vishnu's realm as the highest measure. 610 offers it to the sleepless ruler, and 605 has just listed sleep as a boat to ruin. 1103 asks whether that realm is even as sweet as sleep on a beloved's arms.
teaches: The Porul and Kamam books rank sleep and sovereignty oppositely.

note: Kural 1188 says people call her pale but no one says he left her; Ainkurunuru 225 asks whether the lover himself does not perceive the paling of her brow.
teaches: Held together they show the pallor seen by the whole town yet unread by the one man it concerns, so the symptom that exposes her to gossip fails at the only task she wants of it, reaching him.

note: Kuruntokai 2 has the man ask the bee whether any flower it knows is more fragrant than the girl's hair; Ainkurunuru 93 shows bees, already fed full in many groves, coming to hum at her flowered crown.
teaches: What Kuruntokai 2 leaves as a question to the bee, Ainkurunuru 93 answers from the bee's own conduct, since a bee sated on every grove that still seeks her hair has given the verdict the lover asked for.

note: Purananuru 42: the Chola's army roars like the sea. Thinaimalai 52: the sea, with waves for mahouts and boats for elephants, is like a king's force rising.
teaches: The puram simile is run backwards in the neythal venba: where the war poem makes an army sound like the sea, the love poem makes the sea a mustered army, so that the shore lord is held to a king's measured conduct and the wedding becomes his orderly campaign.

note: Both guide poems describe the bard's lute part by part, and both lay its leather cover like the line of soft hair on a woman's belly (மயிர் ஒழுகிய); Porunaratruppadai's woman is newly pregnant, Malaipadukadam's a bride whose hair still smells of the wedding.
teaches: The hair-line simile for the lute's cover recurs, with the same verb, in two idylls by different poets, so it was a fixed part of the bards' description of their own instrument, and each poet varied only the stage of the woman's life.

note: Verse 7 defines the four kinds of எச்சில்; verse 8 says what they bar and what keeping them yields.
teaches: The pair shows the book's method: a definition followed by its prohibitions and a reward in learning, so purity rules are presented as a discipline of the scholar.

note: Kural 1102: the jewelled woman is herself the cure of the sickness she causes; Natrinai 294: at the wedding, the friend says the man's chest has become both the sickness and the joy, as the sky bore both fire and wind.
teaches: The couplet states the paradox as the lover's private discovery in secret union, while Natrinai 294 has the friend confirm it at the wedding, so the pair shows the same claim moving from a lover's wonder to a public fact once marriage makes the cause of the sickness its lawful cure.

note: Akananuru 80: the friend says they spend the day driving birds from their father's drying fish and bids him come by day to the punnai grove; Thinaimalai 44 names the grove where the girl went to drive birds from the drying fish (புட்கடிவான் புக்க).
teaches: The long poem spells out the trade behind the short one: naming the grove where the girl chases birds from the fish is the friend's way of replacing the dangerous night swim with a day meeting, which Thinaimalai 44 implies but never states.

iraicchi.act: the stag eats only what is left and stands as shade over its young in the sun
iraicchi.sense: the man who sees such care on his road will remember his own and come back to shelter her

note: Patitruppattu 56 says the king is not skilled at dancing before the drums of the festival ground (ஆடல் வல்லான் அல்லன்); 52, in the same decade, shows him leading the thunangai dance by lamplight, giving his lead hand, until the queen grows angry.
teaches: On a literal reading the two poems disagree about whether he dances at festivals, and holding them together shows that 56's denial is a joke the decade's hearers would see through, a mock dispraise that only works because his festival dancing was known.

note: The preface praises Perunjeral Irumporai for defeating Adhiyaman and razing Tagadur (தகடூர் எறிந்து), sung by Arisil Kizhar; Purananuru 230, by the same Arisil Kizhar, whose colophon names its subject as Ezhini the Adhiyaman who fell fighting at Tagadur, says Death lost more than the grieving, hungry world when it took him. On the reading that both refer to that war, one counts Tagadur's fall a glory and the other a loss to the whole world.
teaches: Read together, they show one court poet singing both sides of one war, the victor's fame and the fallen chief's elegy, so praise and lament were offices a poet filled by occasion, and the Tagadur campaign survives as triumph and as ruin in the same voice.

note: Kural 1227 says the sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and blooms at evening; in Ainkurunuru 183 evening arrives early in the harsh day while the neythal of the backwater closes.
teaches: The Kural's flower metaphor for evening pain gains a real flower in the Sangam poem, and the two move in opposite directions: as the shore's neythal closes at evening, the sickness opens, so the landscape's hour of rest is the lover's hour of full bloom of pain.

note: Natrinai 81's man pictures his wife eager to prepare a feast for his coming (விருந்து அயர் விருப்பொடு); Ainkurunuru 482's man calls himself the great feast she will have (பெருவிருந்து).
teaches: Read together they show the word virundhu turning in the return poems from the meal the wife prepares to the husband himself as the guest she receives, so his homecoming is framed as the household's rite of hospitality.

note: Kuruntokai 42's friend asks the hero whether their bond will wane even if desire ends; Kainnilai 4's friend asks the girl whether he is one to join and then forget.
teaches: The one doubt about the man's constancy is put by the friend as a challenge to him in Kuruntokai and as a comfort to the girl in Kainnilai, so the pair shows the friend's double office of pressing the hero and calming the heroine with the same question.

note: The fourth preface tells Narmudi Cheral's own deed: he cut off Nannan's head and felled his gold-bearing vaakai at the root (பொன்படு வாகை முழுமுதல் தடிந்து); 88 lists the wearing down of Nannan of the bright-flowered vaakai (சுடர்வீ வாகை நன்னன் தேய்த்து) among the deeds of the ancestors (பெரியோர் மருக) of the ninth ten's king.
teaches: A victory that the fourth decade gives to one named king appears in the ninth as one item in a list of ancestral deeds, beside the kadamba and the spear thrown into the sea, so the decades show single kings' wars becoming the common record of the Chera line.

note: Kuruntokai 135: the friend tells the heroine not to cry: the man himself said work is life to men and men are life to women of the house, so he will put off his going. Thinaimalai 82: the friend says a man's duty makes him go for wealth, so she should not grieve. On the plain reading the two friends draw opposite conclusions from the same premise.
teaches: Both friends begin from the maxim that work belongs to men, but the Kuruntokai adds that men are women's life and concludes he will stay, while the venba stops at the man's duty and concludes he will go, so the outcome turns entirely on whether the maxim's second half is said.

note: In Natrinai 68 the friend wishes someone would bow and tell the mother that shutting young girls in the house is neither right nor good for it; in 351 she tells the mother herself that the confinement has made the girl paler, that worshipping gods will not help, and that guarding the millet field would restore her.
teaches: Together they show the friend's case against the girl's confinement in two stages: a wished-for argument from what is proper, then her own direct plea that adds the evidence of pallor the mother has misread and a cure that quietly returns the girl to her lover's field.

note: In both idylls the waiting wife is told இன்னே வருகுவர் and still weeps; in Mullaippattu the words are an omen overheard from a herd girl to her calves, in Nedunalvadai they are the foster mothers' practised comfort.
teaches: Mullaippattu's promise is a sign that its poem fulfils with the returning chariot, while Nedunalvadai's is only kind speech that its poem never fulfils, so the same words separate a poem of waiting rewarded from one that can end only in the poet's wish.

note: Akananuru 246's friend says the gossip about the hero was louder than the uproar at Venni when Karikal broke the strength of kings and eleven Velir and their drums were left on the field.
teaches: The akam poet remembers Venni for the noise of Karikal's victory over many kings, while 66 remembers it for the defeated king's honourable death, so one battle served akam as a measure of loudness and puram as a lesson in honour.

note: Akananuru 195's mother asks the diviner whether the youth will bring the girl first to her house or to his own (எம்மனை முந்துறத் தருமோ? தன்மனை உய்க்குமோ?); Ainkurunuru 399 proposes the answer: the anklet-removal in his house, the wedding in ours.
teaches: The question Akananuru leaves to the diviner Ainkurunuru settles by dividing the rites between the two houses, which shows that which house received the couple was a matter of standing that families negotiated, not only a mother's anxiety.

note: Akananuru 371: a twist-horned stag whose mate was shot will not drink the little water of the pool (சில்நீர் உண்ணாது) and lies stricken; the man crossing alone sees it and thinks of his love's eyes. Aimpathu 38: the stag feigns drinking the pool's little water so the doe may drink.
teaches: Held together, the two stags at a pool of scant water show the paalai poets making the stag's not drinking the sign of love both while the mate lives and after she dies, and Akananuru 371 bears out the friend's hope in 38, since there the traveller does see such a stag and his thoughts turn home.

note: Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and strength but the palmyra horse; in Thinaimalai 16 the man stands on the madal in the street and will not leave until she grants him her breast.
teaches: The couplet names the madal as the lover's only strength in general terms, and the quatrain shows what that strength is in use: a public siege in the street with a single stated condition and no second way, so the 'safeguard' is pressure on her household, not comfort for him.

note: 2 tells of the man who dressed the girl's hair with flowers and drove off the musth elephant from the platform; 14 tells of the elephant driven off and concludes that no one but him shall touch her shoulders.
teaches: Read in order, 2 lays out the evidence (the flowers in her hair, the rescue) and 14 draws the verdict, so the disclosure to the household is built like a case: first the facts, then the right those facts give him.

note: Kural 1234: with the partner gone, the shoulders lose their old beauty (தொல்கவின்) and the bangles slip; Ainkurunuru 455: the shoulders, their bangles loosened, have lost their old beauty (தொன்னலம்) just as the rains begin that stop the kings' war.
teaches: The couplet states the wasting of the shoulders as the general mark of separation; the Ainkurunuru poem times it to the rains that end the campaign, so the slipping bangle becomes evidence that he is overdue, not only that he is away.

note: Natrinai 8 places in Poraiyan's Thondi neythal flowers that look like eyes; in Akananuru 290 the heroine says her eyes, once like the cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour, have lost that beauty.
teaches: The Thondi neythal and a woman's eyes were a fixed pair that ran both ways, the flower measured by eyes in a man's first praise and the eyes by the flower in a woman's grief at separation, so one token marked beauty found and beauty lost at two stages of love.

note: In Akananuru 167 the man tells his heart, which is pressing him to leave for wealth, that after a sweet night with his wife in the tall house he would lie sleepless in a ruined village hall, and gives up the journey; in Natrinai 366 he tells his heart that whoever leaves her washed, flower-tied hair and soft bed in the north wind that shakes the sparrow's nest is a fool.
teaches: The two give the same refusal two arguments: Akananuru 167 sets the home against the terror of the road, while Natrinai 366 never reaches the road and argues from the season alone, a cold wind that even a bird's home must withstand, so the stay-at-home decision could rest either on fear or on a general law of the world (உலகியல்).

note: Parimelazhagar uses Indra to illustrate both verses: 25 for the failure that shows the ascetic's power, and 144 for greatness lost through another's wife.
teaches: This is one story serving two chapters in the commentary, though neither verse tells it.

note: In Akananuru 19 the man reproaches a heart that neither stayed with her nor crosses the hills with him; in Ainkurunuru 329 he says the heart was taken by her and wonders whether it will come back with him.
teaches: Read together they show two accounts of the traveller's divided heart: the Akananuru man blames it for wavering between her and the road, while the Ainkurunuru man concedes it never left her, so the reproach of Akananuru 19 becomes in the short poem a plain admission that he travels heartless.

note: Both are Paranar's and both use Nannan's cruelty to a woman as a measure: Kuruntokai 292 curses the mother to go to hell like Nannan who killed a girl for eating a fruit; Natrinai 270 tells the husband his cruelty is worse than Nannan's to a woman's hair.
teaches: Holding them together shows that Paranar made one king's notorious offence against a woman into a standing scale for cruelty in love, turned in one poem on a guarding mother and in the other on a straying husband.

note: In 14 the woman says his past praise of her shoulders, eyes, teeth, brow, hair and breasts has turned to estrangement; in 22 she asks whether he has praised the same teeth, hair and breasts as they will be when old.
teaches: The two poems run the same catalogue of praise through time: 14 looks back at praise already withdrawn, 22 looks ahead to the aged body, so together they make the lover's blazon a promise that covers the whole life of the body, which leaving for wealth would break.

note: Kalittokai 139's rider swims the sea of love with the madal as his raft (மடல் புணையா நீந்துவேன்); Kural 1134 says the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness.
teaches: Where the couplet's flood sweeps away the raft of shame, the kali lover takes the shameful act itself as his raft, so the two together show the madal as what is left when shame has failed: a raft made of the loss of one.

note: Kural 316 says one must not do to another what one knows to be painful; in Kalittokai 62 the girl states that rule and the man answers that sweetness lies in the one who needs, and that seizing moon-faced women is virtue.
teaches: The Kalittokai lets the lover contest the Kural's rule with an argument from pleasure rather than ignore it, showing that the love poets knew the non-harm maxim and staged its failure under desire.

note: Both are the friend speaking to the woman while the man overhears, about the town's gossip; in Kural 1150 the gossip is welcome because it will push him to marry, in Natrinai 72 his anxiety about gossip is read as a sign his love is drying up.
teaches: In the same speech situation the friend can treat gossip as an ally or as a threat depending on how the man reacts to it, so the pair shows that alar works on the lover's resolve, not on the woman's name.

note: In Akananuru 38 the friend imagines the hill man finding the swing, the pool and the reaped field empty, and regrets that she forgot to tell him 'the high hill crowned with that white waterfall is our village'. Ainthinai Aimpathu 12 is that telling: the guarding is over, and this village by the clean waterfall is our place.
teaches: The longer poem shows the cost of not telling him where the house is when the field closes, and the quatrain makes the telling itself, so the pair shows pointing out the village by its waterfall as the friend's expected move at harvest, the step that turns field meetings toward the house.

note: Naladiyar 45 scorns men who praise teeth as jasmine buds, having seen fallen teeth in the burning ground; in Kalittokai 22 the woman asks the man who praised her teeth like jasmine buds whether he praised them falling out.
teaches: Both deflate the same compliment with the same decay, but to opposite ends: the ascetic uses the fallen teeth to free a man from desire, the wife uses them to bind him to her for life, so the image of the body's ruin cut both for and against staying with a woman.

note: Natrinai 167: the friend refuses the bard who came with the shore lord's message (துறைவன் தூதொடும் வந்த ... பணி மொழி). Kainnilai 51 uses the same words for a bird (தூதொடு வந்த பணிமொழிப் புள்ளே) and tells it to fly off.
teaches: The formula that names the bard refused at the door is given in the venba to a bird, showing the short form compressing the social scene of வாயில் மறுத்தல் into a creature of the shore while keeping the old wording.

note: Both are Kayamanar's poems of the mothers left after an elopement: in 189 the foster mother wanders the house and says the town has lost its treasure; in 195 the birth mother claims her years of care and asks the diviner which house the pair will reach first.
teaches: Read together the two mothers' griefs differ in kind: the foster mother mourns a public loss, while the birth mother, conceding she has no claim on the youth, turns grief into a practical question about the return, which shows the elopement already moving toward an accepted marriage.

note: Kural 1261: my eyes have lost their lustre (வாளற்று) and my fingers are worn from counting the days since he left. Thinaimalai 99: like my lustre, my eyes have lost their light (வாள் இழந்த), my shoulders their beauty, my soft fingers worn with counting the days.
teaches: The venba keeps the couplet's two proofs of waiting, dim eyes and worn fingers, but sets them as a retort to a friend who called the grief idle (வாளா), so the Kural's private lament is turned into evidence in an argument.

note: In Natrinai 155 the hero on the neythal shore asks the girl whether she is a goddess of the sea; in Ainkurunuru 182 the friend says the one who struck the girl at the great ford is no god.
teaches: The belief that a beloved seen at the shore must be a divine power runs both ways, the man thinking her a sea goddess and the household thinking her stricken by a god, and in both the cure of the error is the same: the striker turns out to be a human lover who must be named.

note: Both have the wife's side refuse the husband who has been with other women: the Kural's woman will not touch the chest other women's eyes have fed on, the friend of 46 refuses him the door and says 'go, who stops you'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into one refusal what the Sangam poem makes a situation with a hidden buffalo image, a report of a new marriage and a mocking release, so the couplet is the end point of a whole marutham scene.

note: Both answer a lover's departure by saying she will not live until he returns: Kural 1151 says to tell his quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 19's friend says go, knowing well she will not live the few days till you come.
teaches: The couplet's bitter refusal of comfort appears in Natrinai 19 inside a friend's demand for marriage in the secret stage, so the claim that she will die before he returns worked in kalavu as pressure to marry and not only as grief.

note: Akananuru 20: the friend, with the man listening unseen, says that on the town women's talk of a chariot on the dunes the mother has forbidden their shore play (அன்னை கடிகொண்டனளே). Kainnilai 52: the mother has kept the girl in (அன்னையும் இல்கடிந்தாள்), and the speaker asks whether to tell the man of the blame.
teaches: The long poem lets the man overhear the mother's ban, while the venba weighs telling him outright, so the pair shows the ban as the friend's lever for marriage, worked by indirection in one and nearly by open message in the other.

note: Purananuru 185, by Thondaiman Ilanthiraiyan himself, says the realm is a cart that runs well only if its driver is skilled and otherwise sinks in the mire of enmity; the idyll shows the same king's court running smoothly, justice and gifts granted to all.
teaches: Read beside the patron's own conditional maxim, the bard's portrait answers the king's worry with a finished picture: what Ilanthiraiyan states as a risk depending on the driver, the guide poem states as already achieved, which shows the work praise did for a king who wrote about failure.

note: Akananuru 266's wife says her husband played in the evening flood with young women and lost his shame (நாண்இழந்து), and the talk is loud as a feast; Paripadal 10.63-68 shows lovers in the flood hiding their joy for fear of gossip (அலர் அஞ்சி).
teaches: The Paripadal shows that the flood-play crowd expected lovers to hide, so the wife's charge that he 'lost his shame' accuses him of breaking a restraint the festival itself kept, not of joining the play.

note: Akananuru 82 makes the hill a stage with bamboo flute, waterfall drum, bee lute and peacock dancer, ending in the heroine alone with tear-filled eyes; 111 rebuilds the stage in the rain-forest with the glory lily's hands, the sky's call and the bee lute.
teaches: Moved from the kurinji hill to the mullai forest, the nature-theatre keeps its function of tormenting the lone woman but changes its occasion, from the lover seen by many in secret love to the season of a husband's promised return.

note: In Kural 1183 the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; in Thinaimozhi 36 the friend tells the man that he both gave the beauty and took it back.
teaches: The Kural's exchange is a loss suffered in separation, but the friend makes the same giving and taking an argument against the husband: since he alone gave and took, there is no one else to blame and nothing anyone can do to him, which turns the woman's lament into an accusation.

note: Kural 1203: a sneeze that seems to come and then dies away makes her think he seems about to think of her and does not. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 41: sneezes come one after another, so he is thinking of her. On the plain reading the same sign gives opposite verdicts.
teaches: Both women read the sneeze by the same folk belief, but the Kural uses its failure for a wry doubt while the venba piles it up as proof, which shows the belief was firm enough to support either despair or hope depending on what the body did.

note: Both see the thonri open like a lamp in the rains: in Akananuru 235 (சுடர்கொள் அகலின்) the heroine asks whether he has forgotten them; in Kar Narpathu 26 (கார்த்திகை ... விளக்கிற்) the friend says the rain has come with his message.
teaches: The lamp-like thonri is evidence that he has forgotten for the heroine and evidence that he has sent word for the friend, so the one sign of the promised season can be read against him or for him depending on who speaks.

note: Ainkurunuru 355: he turned back from the wealth journey without blessing it; Akananuru 337: the heart once said 'let wealth stay there' (அவணதாகப் பொருள்) and came back alone, and now presses for a second journey.
teaches: Akananuru 337 supplies the sequel the Ainkurunuru decade leaves out: the return for love that 355 presents as final is, a season later, reopened by the same heart, so the turning back is one move in a recurring quarrel between wealth and the wife.

note: 52: the shore is like a king who rises without haste, so fix a day. 53: the shore is like a king who has risen and will not settle, so come before our kin move.
teaches: One image of the shore as a royal army is given opposite tempos, unhurried and restless, to argue first for deliberation and then for urgency, which shows the poet using the image to set the pace of the plea rather than to carry a fixed sense.

note: The same gesture, the husband holding his wife's small back (சிறுபுறம் கவையினன்) while she attends to their son: in Akananuru 26 after he had held off for fear of spilling her milk, in Ainkurunuru 404 while she nurses.
teaches: Akananuru 26 shows the back embrace as the husband's answer to a wife who has turned to the child after his coolness, so when the foster mother in 404 calls the same gesture good she approves the father's inclusion of himself in the mother and son, the very move that ended a sulk elsewhere.

note: Kural 1227: the sickness buds in the morning, opens through the day and blooms at evening; Kuruntokai 234: for those without a partner the dawn and the day are evening too.
teaches: The couplet keeps evening as the climax of a daily growth, while the poem refuses any such gradation and makes every hour evening, so on one reading the parted woman has no easier morning at all, which the Kural's flower image allows.

ullurai.tenor: the husband who goes to other women

pairs.situation: he takes a fresh woman as his daily fare
his chest carries the smell of the women he has lain with

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses a creature of the pond of her own town, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the solitary heron sleeps at ease in the flowering grove
iraicchi.sense: on his shore even a bird alone can sleep, while she, alone because of him, loses her colour

ullurai.tenor: the man who has already won the girl and the household that now guards her too late

pairs.situation: the man has already touched the girl in secret
the household was careless while the secret love began
now the household guards her closely, so meetings are barred

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses things of the hill, the land of this kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

note: Akananuru 167: the man asks his heart whether, after tonight with his wife in the tall mansion, they will lie tomorrow sleepless in the ruined hall of a deserted village. Aimpathu 40: after tonight on the shoulders of her of the cool garland, where will they lie tomorrow, alone beyond the hill paths?
teaches: Akananuru 167 answers its own question with a ruined lodging described in full, while Aimpathu 40 leaves the place unnamed (என்கொலே சேக்கும் இடம்), so the pair shows the same tonight-and-tomorrow argument against the journey working either by the horror of a described shelter or by the bare want of any.

note: Kural 1251: the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted by shame (the woman speaks). Kuruntokai 149: her modesty struggled long, held as long as it could and now gives way.
teaches: The Kural states the collapse of restraint as a single blow of an axe, while the Kuruntokai gives it duration and fellowship, a modesty that 'suffered with us' long before giving way, which shows the couplet compressing a process the older poem tells as a struggle.

note: 76 opens: killing and being killed is not new (புதுவது அன்று), it is the way of the world; 192 says dying is not new (சாதலும் புதுவது அன்றே).
teaches: The same commonplace serves opposite ends: in 192 the oldness of death leads to calm toward great and small alike, while in 76 it is granted only so that one king's feat can stand out as the thing never heard of before.

note: Kural 567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's power; Patitruppattu 22 puts தெறல் கடுமை, severity of punishment, in one list with too much kindness and too much love as obstacles to dharma's wheel.
teaches: Read together, the Kural treats harshness on its own while the Chera poem sets it beside its opposite excesses, so the older list frames royal justice as a mean between cruelty and indulgence rather than as the avoidance of cruelty alone.

note: Kuruntokai 40 marvels that two whose mothers, fathers and selves were strangers have hearts mixed like rain in red earth; Kuruntokai 229 marvels that two who fought as children under their nurses' eyes have been joined in marriage, and credits fate (பால்).
teaches: The anthology explains a match both between strangers and between childhood neighbours, and in each case puts the cause outside the families: loving hearts mixing on their own in 40, fate's apportioning in 229, so union by kin arrangement is the case neither poem celebrates.

note: Both are the man's speech under paalai about leaving for wealth: 63 asks his heart whether she can come along on the work; 71 calls her both medicine and laid-up treasure.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two give the man's full answer to the case for earning: 63 asks how wealth helps if it takes him from her, and 71 says she is already the treasure, so the journey has no object.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of keeping a house is for tending guests; in Natrinai 280 the wife, urged not to sulk at her philandering husband, says she cannot even sulk because her house, like the Velir's Kunrur, is never free of feasting guests.
teaches: The Natrinai shows the Kural's household duty turned into a weapon in love: hospitality is a reason no one can fault, so the wife uses it to refuse both the sulk and the husband, and the virtue becomes the frame of her pride.

note: Both wives turn away the bard over the husband's வாய்மொழி: Akananuru 146 pities the woman who will trust that deceiver's word as she once did; Ainthinai Aimpathu 21 says the bard who asks her to trust it is hawking needles in the smiths' street.
teaches: Akananuru 146 shows the wife as a past victim of the man's word, and 21 shows why that history makes the bard's pleading absurd: she is the one market where his word cannot be sold.

note: Ainkurunuru 65: the wife tells the husband not to embrace her body that bore their son, since it would spoil his chest. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 56: with the son trampling him, he praises her slackened breast, though he presses the budding breasts of a girl elsewhere.
teaches: In both the body that bore the son is the ground of the wife's sulking: in Ainkurunuru she withholds it as unfit for his groomed chest, in the venba she sees his praise of it as a cover for his taste for younger bodies, so the mother's body is what she bars him from and what he flatters to come back.

note: Kalittokai 145's woman begs the sun not to set and speaks of bearing evening's enmity (மாலைப் பகை); Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what enmity (பகை) to evening.
teaches: The couplet's riddle about why evening is hostile is answered in the kali poem by an action: she asks the sun to stay and hopes the man will come at dawn over the sea, so the hours are enemies or friends according to when the parted can expect his return.

note: The Kural counts every day without a glorious wound (விழுப்புண்) as wasted; the idyll's king walks the camp at midnight in the rain to see the glorious wounds (விழுப்புண்) of the warriors who felled elephants.
teaches: The Kural makes the wound a soldier's private reckoning of his days, and the idyll shows its public side, the king coming out at night to look at each wound, so the honour the soldier counts by was conferred in person by his king's seeing it.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute, herald of the burning evening, kills like a weapon; 112: at sunset the sweet flute turns hot, and the friend answers that he will not fail and they must stand ready to receive him.
teaches: The Kural stops at the killing flute, while the quatrain gives the friend's reply to that very hour, turning the evening's heat into the household's readiness for a guest, so the flute is shown to be a test of trust as well as a pain.

note: The Paripadal hymn makes the god lying in waking sleep on the many-hooded serpent in the milk sea one of his three cosmic forms; the idyll places the one on the serpent bed at a grove shrine on the road where bards stop to praise him and play a little.
teaches: Together they show the serpent-bed form both as cosmic theology and as the god of a particular shrine on the road to Kanchi, so in the Sangam period the same image was already tied to local worship that a passing bard could visit.

note: 483's man drives so the woman may get back her beauty (தன்னலம் பெறவே); in 200 the friend sees the bangles tighten and the brow grow lovely now that the lord of the golden chariot has come.
teaches: The same anthology gives the restoring of beauty first as the returning man's purpose and then as a fact the friend watches on the woman's body, so nalam regained is the agreed proof, in mullai and neythal alike, that a separation is over.

note: Kar Narpathu 1: the friend says the man who promised to come when the rain hung low can hardly fail to come now that the clouds roar and pour. Kuruntokai 216: the heroine says the great cloud pours, thunders and flashes with no pity, aimed at her life.
teaches: The rain of the promised season is the same sign in both, but the friend reads it as his oath falling due and the heroine as the deadline passing on her; set side by side, the poems show the rainy season carries both senses at once, and the speaker decides which is heard.

note: Natrinai 250: the man, come home with his son, tells the bard how his wife, seeing him approach, shrank away like a startled doe asking 'who are you?'. Thinaimalai 145: amid songs, tunes and horns he came carrying his son to our place like Indra.
teaches: The Thinaimalai gives the son-bearing return from outside, as a procession fit for Indra, and the Natrinai gives it from the man's side, where the same entry ends in his wife's recoil, so together they show that the son as passport was a public spectacle whose private outcome the poets left open.

note: Kural 322 makes sharing food the chief of all precepts; Thirikadugam counts living beside those who do not share their food as something that yields no good.
teaches: The couplet praises the sharer; the verse shows the cost of the non-sharer falling on his neighbours, so sharing is a public good of a settlement, not only a private virtue.

note: In Akananuru 91 the friend comforts the waiting woman with the elephant who in the drought shrinks together with his hungry mate; in Natrinai 137 the hero shames his own heart with the tusker who breaks an omai tree to feed his young mate.
teaches: The drought elephant that keeps faith with its mate is used by the friend to assure the woman that the man still loves her and by the man to accuse himself of leaving, so the image's single sense, even beasts do not desert their mates, could be turned to comfort or to reproach.

note: The Kural says many will live by a king who looks at people not alike but by rank (வரிசை); the idyll's king crowns warriors with the gold thumbai 'not asking who they are' but weighing their order (முறைகருதுபு), after listing the deeds that rank them.
teaches: The idyll shows a ceremony in which the king's ranking goes by deeds rather than by birth, which supports reading the Kural's வரிசை as an order of merit and shows what the couplet's 'many will live looking to it' meant in practice for a warrior following.

note: Both bid the charioteer drive fast at the evening of the rains, when swarms of bees hum at the fragrant mullai; Akananuru 204 frames it with the Pandya's victory camp and ends on the woman's shoulders.
teaches: Ainkurunuru gives the bee-and-mullai evening with only the girl's sorrowing heart for a goal, Akananuru wraps the same scene in a Pandya campaign, so the pair shows the king's war as an optional frame around a fixed core of season, hour and hurried drive.

note: Kural 1303 says that not embracing the one who sulks is like adding pain to those already in distress; Ainkurunuru 50 tells the husband who gives no refuge that the household and they suffer, and his wife weeps too.
teaches: The Kural states the cost of withheld grace for one sulking woman, while the Ainkurunuru friend counts it across the whole household, its wealth and its people, so the older poem makes the husband's refusal a failure of the house and not only of love.

note: Patitruppattu 11 says Nedum Cheralathan cut down the enemy's kadamba at the root and made of it his roaring war drum; Patitruppattu 44 says his son cut the Mohur king's neem at the root to make a drum and dragged it off with elephants.
teaches: Read together, the father's kadamba and the son's neem show the guardian tree turned into the victor's drum as a rite of the Chera line, repeated across generations, so that each king's voice in war is literally made from a defeated enemy's sacred tree.

note: Patitruppattu 44 says the king cut the Mohur neem at the root and dragged it with elephants for a drum; the preface names it as the neem guarded by Pazhaiyan and says the elephant cart was tied with ropes of his widowed wives' hair.
teaches: The preface supplies the detail the song withholds, the rope of the defeated king's widows' hair, so the felling of the tree is shown to be a humiliation of the enemy's household as well as the taking of his sacred tree.

note: Akananuru 53: past the lettered hero-stone of men felled by the archers' fine arrows, the heroine says his love is for wealth more than for her (பொருளே காதலர் காதல்). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 32 keeps the lettered stones, the archers' fine arrows and the claim that his love's longing has become hard-won wealth.
teaches: The venba compresses Akananuru 53's scene and accusation into four lines but drops the friend's defence that he goes from a giving heart, putting his 'fitting labour' in its place, so the later poem shows which part of the older argument had become formula and which part it chose to change.

note: Verse 4 lets the books go where six kindly acts are seen; verse 14 puts the books outside one who keeps six abstentions.
teaches: The repeated close shows the chapter treating conduct over books as a refrain, and the two lists divide that conduct into acts of kindness (4) and acts of refusal (14).

note: Natrinai 12's girl, leaving by stealth, pities her companions (அளியரோ அளியர் என் ஆயத்தோர்) who will grieve at the ball and anklets she left; Ainkurunuru 397's speaker sends word ahead to her companions (என் ஆயத்தோர்க்கே) that she is coming.
teaches: The companions whose grief the girl foresaw as she slipped away are the first she sends a message to on the way back, so the playmates frame the elopement at both ends, its first cost and its first news.

note: Both use fire for the belly. 947's fire is a measure to observe, and 227's is the disease of hunger that won't touch one who shares food.
teaches: One is the eater's problem and the other's cure is ethical, which widens what 'not falling ill' means.

note: Kural 1308: what use is suffering when there is no lover who knows we suffer? Ainthinai Aimpathu 29: she would refuse his embrace, but he has no thought of her refusal, so she will serve him.
teaches: Both say a protest needs a lover who registers it, and the venba draws the practical end the couplet stops short of: with no such lover, the wife abandons oodal and goes back to service.

note: Ainkurunuru 37 has நயந்தோர் உண்கண் பசந்துபனி மல்க, the eyes of those who loved him pale and brimming; Kural 1232 has நயந்தவர் ... பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண், pale eyes streaming that seem to tell of the beloved's unkindness.
