teaches: Valluvar keeps the Ainkurunuru's very words for the pale, wet eyes but changes their office: in the Sangam poem they are evidence the wronged woman cites against his lying oath, in the couplet they become speakers that publish his unkindness to others, so the image moves from accusation to involuntary gossip.

note: In both the returning man drives through the rain-season scrub where deer run startled; Natrinai 242 follows one stag that will not leave but searches for its scattered doe.
teaches: Ainkurunuru leaves the startled beasts as the land the chariot breaks through, while Natrinai singles out one stag seeking its mate, so the pair shows how the same stock scene becomes a mirror of the man's search for his wife only when one creature is given a lover's act.

note: In Kuruntokai 236 the friend tells the lord of the shore to give back the beauty he consumed before he leaves; in Kuruntokai 349 the woman answers such a proposal by saying that demanding back what was given is worse than losing one's life.
teaches: The demand to return her beauty, which the friend can make as a just claim, the woman herself refuses because it treats her love as a loan, so the same claim is fair in a friend's mouth and shameful in the giver's, by the code that a gift is not taken back.

note: Kural 820 warns against the bond of those who are friendly at home and slander in the assembly; Kalittokai 25 compares her eyes, which shine while he is near and weep when he goes, to the bond of mean men who praise to the face and slander behind.
teaches: The friend turns the moralist's type of false friend into a figure for the woman's own body, whose eyes, bangles and brow publish her state once he leaves, so the danger the Kural sees in other people becomes, in love, the betrayal of the self by its own signs.

note: Kuruntokai 21: though the forest's konrai says it is the rainy season, the heroine will not believe it, for he does not lie. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 26: the friend says the thundering rain is the time he named, fitting his word.
teaches: Both trust the man's word, but they draw opposite conclusions from it: the friend reads the rain as his promise kept, the Kuruntokai woman reads his absence as proof the rain is not yet the true season, so the same faith can either confirm the season or deny it.

note: Kalittokai 15 ends a long plea with the argument that wealth can be made any day, but asks whether it can bring back youth once it has passed (வளமையோ வைகலும் செயல் ஆகும் ... இளமையும் தருவதோ). Thinaimalai 85 builds its whole verse on the same contrast of வளமை and இளமை.
teaches: The venba condenses into four lines the closing move of a long Kalittokai paalai, keeping even the rhyme of வளமை and இளமை, which shows that the retort had become a fixed argument of the separation poem that needed no road scene to carry it.

note: Natrinai 362's eloping man tells the girl to play gathering velvet mites while he leans on a vengai on guard; Ainkurunuru 383 shows from outside the youth holding the maraam branch while she picks flowers for her doll.
teaches: Natrinai gives the man's own promise of guardianship and Ainkurunuru the onlooker's view of his delight in her child's play, so together they fix the eloping hero as an indulgent guardian of a girl still at play rather than a seducer.

note: Both are Paranar's, both the man speaking to his heart after meeting the girl: in Akananuru 152 her shoulders are like the plumage of the joyous peacock on the Ezhil hill of Nannan, lord of Paaram; in Natrinai 265 her hair is like the plumage of the joyous peacock (கலி மயில் கலாவத்து) on Ori's Kolli, and Paaram, guarded by Minjili, is another of her measures.
teaches: The pair shows Paranar keeping one formula, a chief's hill peacock, for the girl and changing only the chief, and Akananuru 152 supplies the Paaram-Nannan link that makes sense of the elliptic 265: her beauty is ranked among the guarded possessions of the hill chiefs.

note: Purananuru 188 says a rich man's days are fruitless without toddling children (குறுகுறு நடந்து); Ainkurunuru 403 shows a toddler (தளர்நடை) pulling a toy chariot and named after his grandfather.
teaches: Purananuru gives as general counsel that toddling children are what make a life worth having, and Ainkurunuru adds, through the grandfather's name the boy bears, that the toddler is valued also as the next link of a famous line.

note: Natrinai 13 likens the girl's red-lined eyes to the arrows millet-watchers pull out of a felled beast; Thinaimalai 22 has her eyes as two arrows that have felled the man.
teaches: The friend of Natrinai 13 gives the eyes the hunters' bloodied arrows, and the man of Thinaimalai 22 draws the consequence that he is the beast they brought down, so the two poems together show the eye-as-arrow belonging to a hunting household's daily kill.

note: Kural 1264: thinking of the return of the man who left the love they shared, her heart climbs up as on branches. Thinaimozhi 14: though he left for wealth even after seeing the koel's season, her heart watches for his coming.
teaches: The couplet's heart rising in hope of his return gains in the venba a bitter premise, that he chose to leave in the very season of love, so the longing is shown to persist against her knowledge of his choice, not out of ignorance of it.

note: Purananuru 312 assigns bearing the son to the mother and making him worthy (சான்றோன் ஆக்குதல்) to the father; in Kalittokai 86 the mother herself teaches the son which of his father's qualities to copy and which to refuse.
teaches: Read together, they show the puram division of duties failing inside the house: when the father is the bad example, the mother takes over his task of forming the son, sorting his public virtues from his private fault, which the puram poem's neat allocation never anticipates.

note: In both the mother acts out of not knowing (அறியாமையின் / அறிந்தனள் அல்லள்) and calls the rite; Akananuru 98 fears that if the rite fails the secret will become gossip, Ainkurunuru 242 says it is cruel to leave the mother in her grief.
teaches: Akananuru 98 counts the cost of the rite to the girl, the secret turning into gossip, and Ainkurunuru 242 its cost to the mother, a grief spent on a wrong cause, so the case for disclosure in the veri situation rests on two separate harms.

note: In 1 the man asks after the arrow-struck deer; in 9 he tells his companion that the asking after a beast was a ruse (வஞ்சமே) and that he was the one taken.
teaches: The book places the pretext and the confession apart, so 9 tells the reader how to read 1: the hunter's question was never about game, and the hunter who set out to deceive came back captured.

note: Kuruntokai 80 has the other woman announce she will bathe with lilies in her hair at the flooded ford and dare the wife to guard her husband; Ainkurunuru 64 has the wife report that many saw him bathing there with his beloved.
teaches: Read together, the public bathing that the wife cites as proof of his fault is the very display the rival intends as her victory, so the same act counts as scandal in one voice and as triumph in the other.

iraicchi.act: the newly calved buffalo cow gives her flowing udder to the calf she loves
iraicchi.sense: the nursing mother in her father's town is the household of wife and child the man promises if he wins her in marriage

iraicchi.act: the storks move off together in a line and feed side by side
iraicchi.sense: even the storks of the shore feed in company, so a town, however good, is misery to the one left to live there alone

iraicchi.act: the male monkey shakes down ripe fruit for the mother monkey and her young, who eat it below
iraicchi.sense: even the monkey on the mountain he crossed provides for its mate and young, while he who passed it does not think of her

iraicchi.act: the sparrow cock gathers cane flowers to build a nest for his hen as her laying nears
iraicchi.sense: even a village sparrow provides for his mate in her time, while the husband's care for his wife exists only in the bard's words

ullurai.tenor: the girl marked by the man's gift, and her mother

pairs.situation: the girl who wears the leaves from his hill is marked by them
the mother would find her daughter changed and grow alarmed

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a cow, its calf and the kaandal of the hill slope in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

note: Both are by Maruthan Ilanaganar on the same occasion (the man, his work done, speaks to his charioteer): in Akananuru 34 a stag feeds and guards his doe, in Natrinai 21 a forest cock scratches out its morning food and looks to its hen, and both close the image on the same word, பெருந்தகை / பெருந்தகு.
teaches: Holding the two together shows one poet keeping a fixed frame for this thurai, a male creature's noble care for its mate seen from the speeding chariot, and changing only the creature, so the iraicchi of the homecoming was a reusable device rather than a chance sight.

note: Kalittokai 146's woman says that if she told her pain to the night that puts many to sleep (பலர்த் துயிற்றும் யாமம்), it would not sleep; Kural 1168 says the night that puts all beings to sleep has no companion but her.
teaches: Both make the night, the one who puts all to sleep, the only wakeful companion of the deserted woman; the kali poem goes further and threatens to keep the night itself awake with her song, turning the couplet's pity for the night into her power over it.

note: Kuruntokai 17 says men whose love hardens ride a palm stem as a horse, wear erukku buds as a garland and become a spectacle in the street; in Natrinai 220 small boys with erukku garlands and a horse that does not eat roam the street with the man.
teaches: Kuruntokai 17 states the madal as a lover's desperate public act, and Natrinai 220 shows children copying its very costume as a street game, so the madal was familiar enough to be play, and the lover uses the children's ease against the adults' censure.

note: In Kural 1102 the man says every disease has a cure other than itself, but this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes; in Natrinai 140 the refused man tells his heart there is no other medicine for the sickness he has.
teaches: The Kural states the paradox from the side of a man already united with her, the Natrinai from the side of a man refused, so the same claim that she alone is the cure is a joke in fulfilment and a sentence of endless pursuit in refusal.

note: Akananuru 28 warns that the millet ears are bowing and stalks are showing, so the girl may soon be replaced at the field; Thinaimozhi 2 says the guarding of the fields has ended.
teaches: Read in order the two poems give the harvest as the clock of the secret love, a warning while the ears ripen and the closed field once they are cut, so the end of the field-watch is the end of their meetings.

note: Akananuru 369: after the daughter's elopement her parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play and her doll gets no offering. Aimpathu 33: the girl herself has stopped thinking of doll, ball, parrot and playmates.
teaches: Aimpathu 33 says the girl has forgotten her toys and companions, and Akananuru 369 says those toys and companions still mourn her, so together they show the mother's grief as a forgetting that runs one way: the house keeps faith with a child who has already left it in mind.

note: Kuruntokai 65: the stag that drank the clear water among the hard pebbles frisks with its sweet mate, as if mocking the woman who waits; Kuruntokai 250: the stag that drank the water of the pebbled hollow frisks with its mate as the man hurries home.
teaches: The anthology uses one sight from both ends of the separation: to the waiting woman the frisking pair is a taunt, to the returning man it is a spur, so the same iraicchi accuses the absence on one side and hastens its end on the other.

note: Purananuru 6 ends by wishing Mudukudumi to last on earth like the cool moon and the burning sun; the idyll uses the same pair to show Nedunjeliyan shining among his kin, then closes on the good time he has been given within a bound.
teaches: The kaanchi poet takes the dynasty's formula of sun and moon but uses it for brightness among kin, not for duration, and pointedly ends on the limit of the span, so the closing withholds exactly the wish for lastingness that the praise poem gave.

note: Both compare the girl's beauty to Arkkadu of Azhisi, father of Chendan: Natrinai 190 at its height, which the lover's heart rejoiced in; Kuruntokai 258 as it wastes under gossip.
teaches: Held together, the two poems use Azhisi's rich town as a fixed standard of the girl's beauty and show both ends of it, the lover's delight and the friend's report of its ruin, so that one patron's town served the poets as a measure of beauty gained and lost.

note: Both poems end on the same demand, வண்ணம் தா ... தொடுத்து: in 63 the heroine and her friend would accost the shore lord themselves; in 65 she sends the paired anril to say it.
teaches: Two poems of one sequence ending on the same words show the demand for her colour passing from a plan to face him to a message given to a bird, which tells us how far her confidence in meeting him has fallen.

note: Kural 1248 has the woman call her heart a fool for running after the man who left; in Kuruntokai 11 the woman herself bids her heart rise and follow him even past the land of the Vadugar, since staying here cannot be survived.
teaches: The heart that the Kural woman scolds for following is the one the Sangam woman sends out on purpose, so the same impulse is folly in the Kural's chapter and the only means of survival in Maamulanar's poem.

note: Akananuru 266 has the wife tell her husband that his bathing yesterday in the new flood with young women, gazing again and again at one woman's rain-cool eyes, is now loud gossip; Paripadal 7.65-76 shows the scene itself: a bard praises a bather's eyes, the lover who looked at the bathers is pulled into the mud and his head trodden on by the woman in her sulk.
teaches: The Akananuru gives only the aftermath, the wife's reproach once talk has spread, whereas the Paripadal shows the gazing at the eyes and the quarrel breaking out at once in the river, so together they show the river bathing as the very occasion of the marutham sulk, with its offence and its punishment both public.

note: Kalittokai 101 says the herd girl's shoulders go to the one who seizes a bull that does not fear even a rutting tusker (கடாஅக் களிற்றினும் கண்ணஞ்சா ஏற்றை); Purananuru 342 says the chieftain's daughter's beauty is for fighters alone (பொருநர்க்கு அல்லது பிறர்க்கு ஆகாதே), her brothers threshing the battlefield with elephants for oxen.
teaches: Both give the girl only to proven courage, but the chieftain's family proves it in a war that uses elephants as threshing oxen, while the herders stage the proof on their own working animal inside a fenced pen, so the mullai contest is the puram bride-test turned from a siege that ruins the town into a bounded festival.

note: In Natrinai 334 the monkeys frolic with their male in the falls and the friend fears for the girl's life if the lover comes through the stormy night; in Ainkurunuru 279 the female monkey frolics with her mate and the friend warns that his coming will set the village gossiping.
teaches: Under the same image of monkeys at play with their mates, the friend has two separate reasons to keep the lover away, the night path's danger in Natrinai and the village tongue in Ainkurunuru, so the pair shows that the creatures' open play stands for exactly the freedom secret love lacks on both counts.

note: Kural 1216: if there were no waking, the lover in the dream would not leave. Kuruntokai 30: a lying dream of his embrace deceived her, and she rose and felt over the bed, alone.
teaches: The Kural blames waking in the abstract, while the Kuruntokai poem shows the very moment, the hand on the empty bed, so the couplet's complaint gains a scene and the scene gains a name for its cause.

note: In Akananuru 388 the old velan says 'my lord's seizure brought this sickness; I know the cure', and the girl mocks him. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 20 the velan, not knowing that the hill man took her nature, says a spirit has seized her and sheds the kid's blood.
teaches: Akananuru lets the velan claim knowledge of the cure and Ainthinai calls him plainly the one who does not know, so together they show the veri rite built around the diviner's ignorance, with the girl's secret as the one thing his craft cannot read.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: peacocks like dancing women, the konrai in bloom and humming bees make this season the medicine for her pallor, says the friend; 111: the forest as a stage, the bees as lute and the peacock dancing make the heroine ask how to survive.
teaches: Set side by side, the two show that the rainy-season pageant had two fixed readings, the friend's cure and the heroine's ordeal, and that the dancing peacock and humming bees are the same evidence in both: what differs is whether one trusts the promise.

note: Natrinai 300 has the water-lily bend to the lotus in the wind as attendants bow to an angry princess; Ainkurunuru 68 has the lily open at dawn like the lotus, while the wife complains that the other woman will not hold herself in.
teaches: The pairing shows that lily and lotus were a shared code of rank in marutham: in Natrinai the lesser flower bows and order holds, in Ainkurunuru it apes the greater flower, which is exactly the other woman's offence.

note: In Akananuru 75 the man quotes the saying that effort, not grace, is a man's wealth and declines to follow it; in Kuruntokai 174 the woman, whose man did follow it, concludes that wealth alone is wealth and grace belongs to no one.
teaches: Together they show the wealth-over-grace maxim as a live argument of the paalai poems argued from both ends: the man can refuse it out of love, and the woman, when he does not, turns it from a rule of conduct into a bitter verdict on the whole world.

note: Purananuru 34 states that there is no expiation for killing a benefit and binds the poet to praise the king who fed the bards; Kuruntokai 225 makes a king who forgets, once enthroned, the help he had in ruin the type of ingratitude the lover must not imitate.
teaches: The puram poem casts the king as the benefactor to whom gratitude is owed, while the akam friend can cite the king who forgets his helpers as a familiar figure, so the same norm of gratitude was also turned against kings, and borrowed to bind a lover to marriage.

note: In Akananuru 72 the girl says the man who came through the midnight rain with only a spear for company (எஃகு துணையாக) is not cruel and the fault is hers; in Natrinai 168 the friend asks the man who comes at midnight with his spear for company (எஃகு துணை ஆக) whether that can be called good conduct. The same act is blameless in one and a failure of conduct in the other.
teaches: The same lone midnight journey is innocent to the girl and faulty to the friend, which shows the night tryst was judged by who spoke: the girl takes the blame on herself, while the friend's charge is her lever toward marriage.

note: Verse 23 makes guarding the gate of a wall-less old town painful; 24 makes living in an old town without protection painful.
teaches: The second verse moves the pain from the guard's futile labour to the townsman's daily exposure, so one weakness is felt by both its defenders and its dwellers.

note: Kural 612 warns against letting a task die half done; in Natrinai 284 the man's own reason says the same, that leaving work unfinished brings ignorance and disgrace, while his heart urges him home.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's maxim on unfinished work already living inside an akam man as the voice of his reason, and the Natrinai adds what the maxim leaves out: obeying it costs a body torn like a rope between two tuskers.

note: Kural 1226: she did not know evening brings sickness while he who wed her had not left. Natrinai 54: the small dull evening is deeply lonely, she tells a heron going home to its kin, and begs it to carry her plight to him.
teaches: The couplet says evening hurts only when he is gone; the poem shows why, through the heron that at evening flies home to its flock, so the hour that sends every creature to its kin is the hour that marks her lack, and her plea that the bird delay its homing for her is the couplet's sickness acted out.

note: Kural 81 says that all of keeping a home and guarding its goods is for caring for guests and doing good; Natrinai 84 says the man leaves his wife for the waste because he cannot live a home life that fails to relieve those who come begging.
teaches: The Natrinai shows the cost of the Kural's rule: if a household exists to give, a household without wealth fails its purpose, so the very ideal that defines home life is what sends the husband away from home and leaves the wife to grieve.

note: Paripadal 5 refuses wealth, gold and pleasure and asks the god for grace, love and aram; Paripadal 13 asks for nothing but more of the worship, which it calls the fruit of past penance and names its kaamam.
teaches: Read in sequence the two closes show a step in the hymns' idea of what to ask: from the god's virtues instead of wealth to worship as its own reward, so that by Paripadal 13 the act of praising is both the fruit of tapas and the whole of desire.

note: 1018 sees shame as the condition of virtue, with virtue itself ashamed to approach the shameless. 1075 is a kind of counter-case: the base still have conduct, with fear and desire in place of shame.
teaches: Their conduct looks alike and differs in its source.

note: Both are the man's words to the girl at the end of the road as his own place comes into view (எம் சிறு நல் ஊரே; நம் மலைகெழு நாட்டே); Natrinai urges her on (ஏகுதி) because the day is ending, Ainkurunuru tells her to go slowly (மென்மெல ஏகுமதி) because the wasteland is behind them.
teaches: The same command to walk on means hurry in Natrinai and go slowly in Ainkurunuru, so the man's care at the journey's end is shaped by what threatens, the coming night or the danger just passed.

note: In Natrinai 30 the friend tells the denying husband கண்டனென் ... கண்டு எவன்செய்கோ, I saw, and what can I do having seen; in Ainkurunuru 122 the friend's having seen becomes a mocking portrait of a girl asking a heron for her jewel.
teaches: Natrinai 30 admits that the friend's witness gives her no power over the husband, and the Ainkurunuru decade shows what she does with that powerless witness instead: she turns it into ridicule, the one weapon left to a go-between who cannot compel.

note: Both turn on the man's possible lie: in Kuruntokai 25 the girl says that if he denies his word she can do nothing, since only a heron watched; in Ainkurunuru 283 the friend says that even if he makes great promises and leaves, many women are caught in his net of lies.
teaches: The girl of Kuruntokai 25 treats his lie as her private helplessness with no witness, while the friend of Ainkurunuru 283 recasts it as his habit, a net that has caught many, so the friend's voice turns the heroine's fear into a public charge that can be used to press him.

note: In Akananuru 17 the foster mother remembers her girl tiring at a little ball play and lying in her arms, and asks whether those feet can walk the waste; in Natrinai 179 the nurse recalls the girl sobbing and refusing milk over a creeper the cow ate, and hears she has crossed the waste smiling.
teaches: Both measure the elopement by remembered childish frailty, but 179 ends on the girl's smile, so the pair shows the nurse's lament with two endings: fear for a frail child in 17, and in 179 bewilderment that a child who wept at a small loss left without grief.

note: Kural 227 says the evil disease of hunger hardly touches one accustomed to பாத்தூண், sharing before eating; the line says பாத்தூண் comes easily to those who willingly bear a burden.
teaches: The couplet gives what the habit of shared eating protects against, the line gives what makes the habit easy, so together they show shared food as both the fruit of shouldering a charge and the guard against the hunger the miser fears.

note: In Kural 1236 the woman, bangles slipping, is hurt when her friend calls the man cruel; in Natrinai 133, with the same slipping bangles, the friend says he will not cause them suffering, and the word gives the woman a little relief.
teaches: Held together they show the friend's two possible speeches and the woman's response to each, blame wounds her and defence of him comforts her, yet the Natrinai measures that comfort as a smith's sprinkle on a furnace, small and passing.

note: The Kural likens those fallen from their station to hair fallen from the head; the friend says broken jewels can be rejoined but lost worth and fame cannot be washed clean even by sages.
teaches: The friend uses the Kural's idea that a fall in standing is beyond repair as an argument for speaking at once, not for keeping quiet: because a girl's good name cannot be restored once it is lost, the secret has to come out before gossip costs her it, so the maxim on honour drives the plot of disclosure.

note: In Akananuru 97 the kuravam blooms (குரவுமலர்ந்து) in a spring when the man has not come and the woman cannot stop her tears; in Ainkurunuru 357 the kuravam's flowering is what makes the man give up his journey.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the spring flowers acting on both lovers at once: the same blossoming that tortures the waiting woman in Akananuru 97 is, in 357, what turns the man back, so the season's sign has power over him and fails only when he ignores it.

note: Kural 17 says even the wide sea would lose its nature if the cloud that drew from it gave nothing back; Paripadal 7.1-10 begins with clouds that have drawn the dark sea fully (பௌவம் செவ்விதா அற முகந்து) and ends the sentence with the land's good and beauty swelling as the Vaiyai comes.
teaches: The couplet states the exchange between sea and cloud as a warning about withholding, while the song follows the same water through rain, falls and river into the Pandya fields, so together they show that the Kural's abstract cycle was the felt shape of the flood festival, praised in the hymn as the return the couplet only demands.

note: Both have a woman awake at midnight with a love too great to get past: the Kural's flood with no shore and only herself awake, Natrinai 335's great love with no one to clear it while moon, surf, wind, anril and lute keep the night going.
teaches: The couplet's 'only I am here at midnight' is filled in by the older poem with a crowd of sounds and scents that will not stop, showing that the woman's solitude is not silence but a shore night that keeps working on her.

note: Akananuru 369: the foster mother grieves that since the girl left, the parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play and the doll gets no offering. Thinaimalai 73: the mother says the girl has given up her playmates' parrot and the pond's blue lily.
teaches: Read together they give both sides of the break: in the Akananuru the home's things go without the girl, in the venba the girl has already let go of the things her beauty was measured by, so the mother's grief covers both what the house lost and what the daughter chose.

note: Kalittokai 139 calls the horse she gave a shelter (ஏமம்) against the army of love; Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard (ஏமம்) and no strength but the madal.
teaches: Both use the same word ஏமம் for an act of humiliation, and the kali poem shows how the safeguard works: it is spoken to the worthies whose duty is to treat another's pain as their own, so the madal protects by putting the assembly under obligation.

note: Patitruppattu 27 describes the enemy's watered land, ruined by the king's angry look, as knowing no uproar but the carters' shouting; 28 says the king's own land knows no heat but the uproar of the river's red flood.
teaches: The poet uses the same 'no uproar but a harmless one' figure for the land the king destroys and the land he guards, which shows that the two were equally blessed and that only the king's anger made the difference.

note: Both use the Kazhar legend of Aathi Manthi and Attan Atthi; 222 names Maruthi, who restored the lover and entered the sea, 236 has Manthi searching town after town.
teaches: One legend served two speakers: the friend holds up Maruthi's fatal deed as a fame to win, the wife holds up Manthi's lament as her own shame, so the story was a shared stock the poets bent to opposite purposes.

note: Kural 773 says fierceness is great manhood, but help given when misfortune befalls the foe is its cutting edge; Kalavazhi 35 ends with the enemy king falling with his royal elephant, struck like a lion on a thunder-struck mountain, and goes no further.
teaches: The Kural locates the height of valour in the moment after the foe falls, and the kalavazhi, built to stop at the field of killing, has no place for that moment, so the couplet names exactly what the battle-song leaves out.

note: In Purananuru 23 the poet says he has come having seen Nedunchezhiyan's work in enemy land, which ends as a waste where a doe whose stag a tiger killed nibbles velai with her fawn; in Patitruppattu 23 the bards say they came and saw (கண்டனம்) the lands of the Chera's foes turned to forest where the wild cow lives happily with her bull.
teaches: The two bards' reports end on a female beast in the ruined land, but Kalladanar's widowed doe carries the human loss into the forest while Gauthamanar's paired wild cow celebrates the wilderness's return, so the same reporting convention could either mourn or exult over conquest.

iraicchi.act: the heron feeds what it takes for its chick and shades it from the sun with its wings
iraicchi.sense: even a bird keeps steady, self-forgetting care for what it holds as its own, so the hero should stop coming and going and marry her

iraicchi.act: the koel, together with its mate, calls back eagerly in the flowering season
iraicchi.sense: in the season when even the koel is with its mate, the man who left has failed to come, so she reads it as his forgetting

ullurai.tenor: the girl and the shore lord who enjoyed her love and now stays away

pairs.situation: her beauty was taken in the secret union
she cannot eat for longing
she is now kept apart at home and lives alone

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a heron of the neythal backwater in a neythal poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the hen kite, alone on the bare fork, calls out for its mate
iraicchi.sense: the lonely call on his road is the call of the woman he has left behind, which is why her nature does not leave him however far he goes

ullurai.tenor: the lover who stays away and the girl who waits for him

pairs.situation: the lover turns away and does not come
the girl stays on, waiting in longing

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses wild sheep of the kurinji hill in a kurinji poem, without leaving the land (porul 7.27)

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the women he goes to

pairs.situation: he has had his fill of one woman
he tires of another

pairs.scene: அயலது குன்று சேர் வெண் மணல் துஞ்சும்
pairs.situation: he sleeps away from home, not in his wife's house

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the buffalo of her own field town, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the women he goes to

pairs.situation: he leaves the house for the women of the town
he spends his nights with women who receive him

pairs.scene: பண்டு தாம் மரீஇய பூம் பொய்கை மறந்து
pairs.situation: he forgets the wife he once lived with

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the bee of her own town's fields and pond, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the tusker goes about together with his mate beside their calf
iraicchi.sense: the hill lord should keep the girl as the tusker keeps his mate and young, in a household, now that the field meetings have ended

note: Kural 338: the bond of body and life is like a bird that flies off leaving its nest alone. Natrinai 153: her heart has gone after him and her body, left behind, lives on by eating, like the lone man guarding a ruined town.
teaches: The poem shows the couplet's departure without the death: the heart flies off as the life does in the Kural, yet the body stays, sustained only to keep watch over its own emptiness, so separation in love is a death the body is made to outlive.

note: Purananuru 55.1-2 (மலைப் பெருவில் பாம்புஞாண் ... ஒரு கணை ... மூவெயில்) and Paripadal 5.24-25 (நாகம் நாணா, மலை வில்லாக, மூவகை ஆர் எயில் ஓர் அழல்-அம்பின்) give the three-forts deed in the same parts: mountain bow, serpent string, one arrow; both also turn on Siva's forehead eye.
teaches: The same tripura formula serves a puram poet as the vehicle of counsel to a Pandya king and a devotional poet as the prelude to Murugan's birth, showing that Siva's deed was common stock usable for statecraft and worship alike in the Sangam period.

note: Thiruppugazh 12, a Parankunram song, has Indra's daughter and the hunter girl both embrace Murugan's twelve shoulders; Paripadal 9 sets the same two wives at the same hill in a quarrel with blows of garlands.
teaches: The later hymn keeps the two consorts side by side in a single embrace, while the Sangam song lets them fight over him at the same shrine, which shows the co-wives' rivalry was once part of the hill's sacred lore and was smoothed away as the pair became fixed icons of devotion.

note: Kural 1276: the woman tells her friend that his great comfort and eager lovemaking hold the hardship to come and the thought of his lack of love; in Natrinai 177 the girl tells her friend she reads his going in his being more tender than before, along with his spear wiped and his shield decked.
teaches: The couplet names one sign, excess tenderness; the poem shows it read together with the readied weapons, so the Kural's inference is the abstract of a scene in which caress and war gear together give the man away.

note: Ainkurunuru 66: the wife asks who the woman is who snatched away his coming home to his rich house when he was thinking of his toddling son with his little chariot (தேரொடு தளர்நடைப் புதல்வனை). Thinaimalai 124: before the boy appears drawing his toy chariot this way, the man has already bathed and embraced her 'sisters'.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 66 grants that the toddler with his chariot did pull the father toward home and blames a rival for stopping him, while the venba times the man's straying 'before the boy appears' and so denies the child ever had that pull, which shows the toy-chariot son working as the conventional test of a straying father's heart, passed in one poem and failed in the other.

note: Purananuru 2 says the Chera has forbearance, breadth of counsel, strength, fierceness and grace like the nature of the five elements, without saying which goes with which; Patitruppattu 90 likens the king to water for his kindness, to the sky for being beyond measure and to the sea for not lessening however much is taken, naming each ground.
teaches: The ninth ten does explicitly what the Purananuru catalogue leaves implicit, joining each natural power to one royal virtue by a stated reason, so the pair shows the elemental praise of Chera kings being turned from a list into reasoned comparison.

note: Both set the absent man's wellbeing above the woman's pallor: the friend's blessing நோய்இலராக, the Kural's 'let my body pale, if he is well'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into the woman's own mouth a blessing that the Akananuru gives to the friend, showing how the anthology's go-between voice was absorbed into the single speaker of the later couplets.

note: Kural 1156: if he is hard enough to speak of leaving, the hope of his grace is vain; Natrinai 296: told he will go, the woman asks what will become of her, since he leaves with a heart set on work even in the season when the kondrai blooms and the parted grieve.
teaches: Kural 1156 finds the man's hardness in the announcement itself, and Natrinai 296 adds a second measure the couplet does not give, the timing: to leave in the very season made for grieving apart shows a heart given wholly to work.

note: Paripadal 5.79-81 says we ask not wealth, gold or pleasure but grace, love and aram; at Parankundram in Paripadal 8.103-108 the festival crowd asks for a dream lover made real, a child in the womb, success in making wealth (செய் பொருள் வாய்க்க) and victory in war.
teaches: The same collection holds a poet's refusal of worldly boons and a festival crowd's petitions for exactly those boons, so the Paripadal's devotion is not one ethic: the singer's ideal prayer and the people's practical vows stand side by side in it.

note: Kural 1233: the shoulders that swelled on the day of union now seem to announce the parting; Kuruntokai 299: the woman's shoulders gain beauty when he joins her and waste when he leaves, after the tryst on the shore.
teaches: The couplet gives the swelling and the wasting as public evidence that others read, while the poem gives them as the woman's own bewildered discovery, tied to the day her eyes saw him and her ears heard him, so the same bodily sign is both the town's proof and her private record.

note: Kalittokai 133 defines அறிவு as bearing the words of fools (பேதையார் சொல் நோன்றல்) and பொறை as bearing with those who do not cherish you; Kural 153 calls bearing with fools the strength of strengths.
teaches: The same act is filed under different virtues: the kali friend calls forbearance toward fools wisdom and keeps patience for those who neglect you, while the Kural calls it strength, so this forbearance had no fixed place yet in the lists of virtues, standing under wisdom in one and strength in the other.

note: Akananuru 369's girl refused the rich wedding her kin were preparing (தமர்மணன் அயரவும் ஒல்லாள்); Ainkurunuru 379's mother asks whether going with him is sweeter than a good wedding among her companions.
teaches: Akananuru states the refusal of the home wedding as a grievance, and Ainkurunuru asks the question that refusal implies, whether the road was sweeter to the girl, so the mother's lament moves from blaming the choice to trying to imagine the girl's own preference.

note: In 477 the man tells the bard to stay with his grieving wife (துனி மலி துயரமொடு) and promises his chariot; in Akananuru 314 the wife has asked the bard what will become of her, and the man arrives to end her துனிகொள் பருவரல்.
teaches: The man's instruction and promise in Ainkurunuru and the friend's welcome in Akananuru are two ends of one convention: the bard is posted with the wife to field her question, and the chariot's coming is what answers it.

note: In Akananuru 317 the man had promised to come back in the spring when the kongu and kuravam flower and the koel calls, and his arrival ends a pallor the mother had noticed; in Ainkurunuru 366 the friend tells the mother the girl's pallor is because the kongu has flowered.
teaches: Read through 317, the friend's excuse in 366 is no excuse at all: the kongu's flowering is the season a man promises to return by, so pointing the mother to the tree points her to an absent lover, and the pair shows a seasonal sign doing the work of a confession.

note: Both poems call on the potter of the town: Purananuru 228 to make the burial urn for a dead Chola king; Natrinai 200 as the crier who proclaims festivals, asked to proclaim the bard a liar.
teaches: Taken together, the potter appears as the town's public servant for both its funerals and its festivals, and the friend's commission parodies the solemn address to him by making the crier's voice carry a domestic quarrel.

note: Kural 211 measures giving without return by the rain, to which the world gives nothing back; Paripadal 10.125-127 measures the Vaigai's flood over the fields by the Vazhuthi who pours gold into poets' hands.
teaches: The Kural makes nature the model for the giver, while the Paripadal makes the king the model for nature, so the pair shows the comparison between rain and royal giving could run in both directions, with the Pandya's gift treated as the surer standard.

note: In 322 thinking of her turns a hot road cool; in 328 a road cooled by rain and flowers is hot because he has left her.
teaches: The two poems of one decade run the same switch in both directions, so the poet shows that paalai heat is set by her presence or absence in the man's mind and can override real rain as easily as real sun.

note: Purananuru 3 counsels the Pandya Vazhuthi that suppliants have crossed deadly roads and his strength is to read their need and end their poverty; Paripadal 10.125-126 names the Vazhuthi who pours gold into the hands of poets in want (இலம்படு புலவர்).
teaches: What the puram poet urges on a Vazhuthi as a duty to be kept, the devotional poet takes as so settled a fact of the Pandya house that it can serve as the vehicle for praising the river itself.

note: Both have the waiting woman put a question to or about evening: the Kural asks evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Ainkurunuru asks whether his land has this loveless evening at all.
teaches: The Kural explains the man's calm by a hard heart that evening shares, the Ainkurunuru by a land the evening may not reach, so the two give the waiting woman two answers to why he does not suffer the hour she suffers.

note: Here giving and austerity cannot last without rain. In 34, virtue is simply a spotless mind and everything else is noise.
teaches: If virtue is only inward, the drought in 19 shouldn't threaten it.

note: Both say the fragrant cool rain-season laughs with mullai buds for bright teeth (முல்லை ... இலங்கெயிறு ... நறுந்தண் கார் ... நகும்); in Kar Narpathu 14 the friend reads the laugh as proof he will come quickly, in Kuruntokai 126 the woman hears it mocking her: where are they?
teaches: The later poet took the older line almost word for word and reversed what it means: the same laughing season is a sign of his return to the friend who comforts and a jeer at the deserted woman, which shows that the image itself carries no fixed mood and the speaker's place in the situation decides it.

note: Ainkurunuru 4: the girls wish that the lover's chest never become a common field-pond (பழனம்). Ainkurunuru 84: the other woman says his chest is a pond where many bathe.
teaches: The decade of wishes prays against exactly the outcome this decade reports, his chest as a pond for all, so the anthology's own order sets the bride's fear and the courtesan's taunt in one image eight decades apart.

note: Kural 1167: the woman swims the fierce flood of desire and sees no shore, and at midnight only she is awake; in 387 she swims across the evening to reach the night as its bank, and finds the night's flood larger than the sea.
teaches: The couplet's shoreless flood gets its hours in the poem: the evening is the first water and the night a second, larger one, so the shore the Kural's woman cannot see is the bank of evening that only opens onto the night.

note: Kural 1251 has the woman say love's axe breaks the door of restraint (நிறை) barred with shame; Natrinai 369's heroine, left unmarried while he seeks wealth, says she cannot swim across a love that breaks her restraint (நிறை அடு காமம்) like the Ganga in flood breaking dams.
teaches: Both name the same loss, restraint broken by love, but the Kural's image is a single blow to a closed door while the Natrinai's is a flood from the Himalaya that keeps coming each evening, so the poem adds what the couplet lacks: that the breaking recurs at a fixed hour and the woman's question is endurance, how to swim, not resistance.

note: Akananuru 315: the mother who saw the girl grow and suspected, yet did not shut her in (செறியேன்), mourns her elopement. Kainnilai 59: the mother, seeing the young man come through the gap, at once blocks it and shuts the door.
teaches: The confinement one mother blames herself for omitting is done at first sight by the other, and the friend reports it as the pressure that forces marriage, so the pair shows the mother's guard as the hinge between the two endings of kalavu, marriage and flight.

note: Naladiyar 6 starts from the appointed span of days and concludes: give your wealth away, for tomorrow the funeral drum may sound; the idyll starts from the good time given within a bound and concludes: rejoice and live sweetly every day.
teaches: Both counsels rest on the same premise of a fixed span, but the idyll, after showing the king's giving, lets pleasure stand beside it as a right answer, while the ethics book allows only giving, so the later text narrows a kaanchi argument that once had room for enjoyment.

note: Kural 1084: the eyes of this artless girl devour the life of those who see them; Kuruntokai 72: the eyes of the girl scaring sparrows from the millet have, like arrows, made him sick for all to see.
teaches: The poem places the couplet's paradox, the simple girl with killing eyes, in her actual work of chasing small birds off the hill millet, and adds what the couplet lacks: the wound is public, known to everyone.

note: In Natrinai 61 the mother asks the sleepless girl 'don't you sleep, my little one?' and the girl keeps the reason in her heart; in Ainkurunuru 107 the friend tells the mother that the girl does not sleep whenever she hears the waves.
teaches: The question the girl will not answer in the Natrinai is answered for her by the friend in the Ainkurunuru, so the pair shows the friend speaking the very secret the girl's modesty withholds from the mother.

note: Thinaimalai 131: the wife tells the graceless bard he need not fashion words to begin a reconciliation; she turned the day she heard the man's lies. Kainnilai 46: the man spoke many pleasant things and seemed ashamed; useless bard, say nothing false and go.
teaches: Thinaimalai 131 dates her refusal to the lies she heard, while Kainnilai 46 adds that the man had already acted out his shame, so the pair shows the bard's plea coming after the husband's own performance has failed.

note: In Kural 1222 the parted woman pities the dim evening as a sufferer like herself; in 110 the hills weep in pity for her while the wild jasmine laughs.
teaches: The Kural lets the woman lend her grief to one hour of the day, while the quatrain divides the whole landscape into those who mock her and those who mourn with her, so the pathetic projection becomes a judgment on which things are great.

note: Kural 211 asks what the world gives back to the rain, to show that obligation seeks no return; Patitruppattu 55 wishes the giving king's days to pass like white clouds that pour rain, protect the land and go up to rest on the hill.
teaches: Both use the rain cloud for the giver, but the Kural stops at the absence of return, while the Chera poem imagines what the cloud has after giving, rest on the hill, and makes that the blessing on the king's lifespan.

note: In Akananuru 9 the returning husband pictures his wife at the evening when calves come home, standing at a corner of the house and praying at every chirp of the lizard; in Mullaippattu the old women seek the omen at evening, a calf supplies it, and the wife will not accept it.
teaches: The husband's picture of a wife eagerly reading every omen is his own fancy on the road; Mullaippattu, told from the house, gives the omen-seeking to the old women and shows the wife refusing its comfort, which qualifies the hopeful, praying wife of the man's imagination.

note: In both the man decks the eloping girl's hair with forest flowers, maraa in Akananuru 257 on the summer road, vengai in Ainkurunuru 396 at the edge of his town.
teaches: Akananuru's adorning happens on the march and admires how she walks, while Ainkurunuru's is a pause that lets her rest before she enters his town as a guest, so the flowers in her hair move from a token of the road to a preparation for her reception.

note: Kural 1288 tells the thief that his chest is to her as toddy is to drinkers, though it does them shameful harm; Kuruntokai 309 says the women are like the neythal that blooms again in the field it was weeded from, though he does them many unkind things.
teaches: Both say she cannot leave him though he harms her, but the Kural calls the bond an addiction while the poem calls it rootedness in his own field, so the pair shows the same dependence judged as weakness and as loyalty.

note: Natrinai 45: the friend tells the rich man's son that they are fishermen's daughters who drive birds from drying shark and smell of fish (புலவு நாறுதும்), so their life is no match for his. Thinaimalai 51: we watch and sell the fish on the sand that reeks of it.
teaches: The venba keeps only the smell and the trade and drops the explicit 'go away, we are not your equals' of the Natrinai, which shows how far the later poet could rely on the reader supplying the refusal from the fish-smell alone.

note: Mullaippattu 1-6 likens the rain-cloud rising from the sea to Mal, who grew to measure the world; Kar Narpathu 1 likens the rainbow to the garland on the chest of Mal, coloured like the warring sea.
teaches: Both mullai poems open their rains with Mal, the god of the mullai land, so the land's god is the first image of its season; the later venba moves him from the rising cloud to the rainbow, making the sky his adorned chest rather than his growing body.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai describes the twice-born at Eragam in full, never failing in the six duties, keeping the three fires and chanting at the proper hour; Paripadal 14 compresses them to a riddle of counts, இரு பிறப்பு, இரு பெயர், ஒரு பெயர், and says the god delights in their aram.
teaches: The idyll's full portrait supplies what the Paripadal's terse count assumes, so its இரு பிறப்பு is the same இருபிறப்பாளர் the idyll names, and the brahmins' ritual life is shown to be, for both poems, one of the things Murugan is praised for enjoying.

note: Kural 51 defines the wife as one who lives within the means of the man who took her; Natrinai 110 shows a spoilt girl who once refused honeyed milk now eating only at alternate meals in her husband's poor house, refusing her rich father's food.
teaches: The poem shows what the couplet's rule costs and how strange it looks to her own family, who ask where she learned it, so living within his means appears as a change of person rather than a skill.

note: The Kural likens the wealth of a man of நயன் to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town; the guide says he went to Karikalan like a bird that thinks of a fruiting tree, through a gate that bars no one in need.
teaches: The Kural states the tree from the giver's side and makes its public place the point, while the idyll shows the same tree from the hungry bird's side and supplies the condition the couplet compresses into உள்ளூர், an open gate, so the maxim's promise turns out to depend on access as much as on fruit.

note: Kuruntokai 121: the heroine grants her friend that for the hill man's failure to keep the tryst (தான்குறி வாயாத் தப்பற்கு) her own shoulders have turned pale, as the branch goes down with the langur that missed its leap. Thinaimozhi 41: for the same failure she questions his nobility.
teaches: The same failed tryst draws two answers from the heroine: in the Kuruntokai she takes the fault into her own body, while the later venba turns it outward into a charge against his worth, which shows accusation as a second, sharper register of the same situation.

note: Purananuru 343: the father refuses even wealth like Kuttuvan's Musiri humbly offered, and suitors' armies crowd the town; Kalittokai 103: the herd girls say they want no price (விலை வேண்டார்), only a man who will fall between the killer bull's horns as between their breasts.
teaches: Read together they show who sets the bride's terms: in the puram town the father refuses wealth and the girl becomes the cause of a war, while in the herders' song the girls voice the refusal themselves and name the one price they accept, so the mullai poem gives the woman the choice the puram poem leaves to her father and the kings.

note: Kural 1161: she would hide this pain, but it wells up like spring water when drawn. Natrinai 382: at evening she must hide her grief even if her life goes.
teaches: The couplet gives the woman's wish to hide her pain without a reason and says it fails; the Natrinai woman supplies the reason, that the slander of his enemies would shame him, so concealment in separation is shown to be a duty to his name and not only her modesty.

note: Both list the flowers of the first rains (Ainkurunuru: தோன்றி, தளவம்; Natrinai: பிடவம், தளவம், கொன்றை, காயா); in Natrinai the returning man sees them and tells his charioteer the kaar has begun.
teaches: What the woman praises as the beauty of his road Natrinai shows from the other end, the man reading those same flowers as his deadline and driving hard, so her praise rests on a hope the hero's poem shows being kept.

iraicchi.act: the waves come up to the doorstep of his hamlet and go back again
iraicchi.sense: even the sea of his own country comes and returns, so his going is not the end of his coming

ullurai.tenor: the hero who has hurt her and the woman who still softens toward him

pairs.situation: the flower opens at the very tread that crushes it, as she softens at his wrong
its scent will not stop, as her love goes on unasked
the treader is a simple, blundering bird, as the hero's wrong is careless rather than meant

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses a flower and a bird of her own shore, things she knows (porul 7.26)

iraicchi.act: the tusker stays beside his loving she-elephant after fighting off a rival
iraicchi.sense: even the beast on his hill keeps by its mate, while the hero has taken the girl and left her

iraicchi.act: the boar keeps the motherless young with it while it sleeps
iraicchi.sense: even the boar does not leave the young that has lost its mother, so the man's leaving her can bring nothing good

ullurai.tenor: the husband, who after his wife has borne a son grazes on what other flowers remain

pairs.situation: the wife who has newly borne his son

pairs.scene: தின்ற மிச்சில் ஓய்நடை முது பகடு ஆரும்
pairs.situation: the ageing husband feeding on leftovers, the women beyond his house
the new young women he takes up

ullurai.speaker_fit: the courtesan, not bound to the heroine's world, may use any thing, and the bull at the field is of her own marutham town (porul 7.29)

ullurai.tenor: the lover who enjoys the girl and rests at ease

pairs.situation: he takes his pleasure of the girl in secret love
he then rests content and does not hasten to marry her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a creature of the backwater in a neythal poem without leaving its land (porul 7.27)

ullurai.tenor: the secret love and its traces, erased by the public declaration of marriage

pairs.situation: the marks of the lovers' secret meetings that set the town talking
the kin's loud public declaration of the marriage
the trail of gossip is wiped out

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the crab and the surf of the shore, the land of this neythal poem (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the conch rises on the wave joined with its mate (துணை புணர்ந்து)
iraicchi.sense: even the conch of his own sea keeps to its partner, so a lord of this shore who leaves the woman he joined falls below the creatures of his shore

note: Kural 1146: gossip about one day's meeting has spread like the serpent seizing the moon; in 395 the woman says no one frees her as the people here free the moon the snake swallows, nor even tells her not to fear.
teaches: The eclipse served both as a spectacle everyone sees and as a rite in which everyone rushes to help: the Kural takes the first sense for gossip, the poem the second for rescue, and the woman's complaint is that her eclipse draws the town's eyes but none of its help.

note: Akananuru 17: the foster mother remembers how the girl, tired after ball and jacks, would lie in her arms, and wonders how her small feet will manage the waste. Kuruntokai 144: the foster mother remembers the girl's play in the backwater and the waves and sees her gone over the gravel to the far mountains.
teaches: Both foster mothers measure the elopement by the girl's play, but the Akananuru measures it on the body (tired feet, sweat), while the Kuruntokai measures it on the map, from sea shore through waste to mountain, so the pair shows the sevili's lament working through both the body and the landscapes the girl crosses.

note: Natrinai 66 is the mother at home picturing her eloped daughter on the hot track; Natrinai 324 is the man or onlookers on the track picturing the mother at home.
teaches: Each poem imagines the other end of the elopement: the mother sees only her daughter's eyes red with suffering, while those beside the girl see her running as at play and give their pity to the mother, so each grief misjudges what the other side sees.

note: Both are a wife's sulk at the husband's straying, fixed on his chest: Kural 1311 refuses his chest because all women feast on it with their eyes; Natrinai 20 describes the girl who slept on the lord's chest and walked off at dawn with crushed earring and withered garland.
teaches: The Kural states the wife's charge in general terms, and Natrinai 20 shows the single scene behind such a charge, the rival's disordered body read as proof and blessed in irony, so the couplet's reproach rests on a convention of reading the other woman's appearance as evidence.

note: Kural 43 makes the chief duty of the householder the care of ancestors, gods, guests, kin and self; Paripadal 17.42-46 says the god's festival and the fine feasting of guests pass in turn between the hill, the Vaiyai and Koodal, and the song closes with a prayer made with kin (யாமும் எம் சுற்றமும்).
teaches: The Kural lays the duties to god, guest and kin on one household, while the hymn shows the same duties carried by a whole region in turn, hill, river and city, so the pair shows the couplet's private order also lived as the civic round of Madurai's festivals.

note: Kuruntokai 156: the lovesick hero asks the Brahmin whether his unwritten learning holds a medicine to unite the parted. Kural 1102: the man says other illnesses have other cures, but this woman is herself the cure for her sickness.
teaches: The couplet reads as the answer to the Kuruntokai hero's question: no learned remedy exists, because only the woman herself cures the sickness she causes, so the pair turns the hero's doubt of the Brahmin's lore into the Kural's general rule of love's medicine.

note: Kural 222 says taking is bad even if called a good path, and giving good even without a higher world; Patitruppattu 52 says the king's hand bends down to give to suppliants and does not know how to open upward to take (இரப்போர்க்குக் கவிதல் அல்லதை இரைஇய மலர்பு அறியா).
teaches: The poem turns the couplet's two verbs into two postures of one hand, palm down to give and palm up to receive, so the rule against taking becomes a bodily habit the king cannot break.

note: Both are the girl's fear for the man on the hill path at midnight in rain: Akananuru 72 lists the path's dangers (a tiger that killed an elephant, a snake's gem, crocodiles) and ends by blaming herself; Natrinai 255 lists ghouls, a tiger that fought a tusker, the snake searching for its gem and thunder, and ends by wishing he would not come.
teaches: Read together, the same catalogue of night dangers leads to two different conclusions, self-blame for drawing him out and the wish that he stay away, so the poets used the fixed list as a premise and placed the girl's character in what she concludes from it.

note: Ainkurunuru 43: the woman tells the man of the rich town that his bard is a greater liar than he and swears many oaths (பாணன் பொய்யன் பல்சூ ளினனே). Thinaimalai 131: she tells the bard, whose lute is bent like a prawn, not to fashion words of reconciliation, since she has heard the man's lies (ஊரன்பொய்).
teaches: Ainkurunuru 43 ranks the bard's lying above the man's in a single comparison, while Thinaimalai 131 dates her refusal from the day she heard the man's own lie and so sets the bard's words aside as useless rather than worse, which shows the go-between's credit in marutham falling with his master's and not on its own.

note: Akananuru 82 makes the hill a stage where the waterfall is the drum, the bamboo wind the flute and the bees the lute, with a peacock dancing; Thinaimozhi 7 compresses it to one line, the cascade sounding as lute, flute and drum.
teaches: In both the orchestra of the hill sets up an audience: in Akananuru 82 many saw him at the field, and in Thinaimozhi 7 the night visit will be known to the whole town, so the stage image carries the danger of the love being seen and heard.

note: Both turn on assurance (தெளிப்பவும், தெளித்தசொல்): in Ainkurunuru 21 the friend sets the man's assurances against the girl's paling eyes; in Kural 1154 the woman asks whether those who trusted the assuring word are at fault if he leaves.
teaches: The Kural asks who bears the blame once a trusted promise fails, while the Ainkurunuru shows the body already failing while the promise is still being spoken, so the couplet's moral question comes after a doubt that the older poem places in the girl's eyes before any leaving.

note: The Kural argues that if no one killed to eat, no one would sell meat; the idyll praises a city where killing is banned and beasts crowd safely at the meat-sellers' huts, yet the same city fries fish and flesh in its toddy-shop yards (lines 176-177) and its fishermen eat prawns and tortoise (lines 63-64).
teaches: Held together they show the ban on killing in the older poem as the virtue of particular classes in a city that still ate meat, whereas the Kural's demand-side argument makes every buyer answerable, so the later ethic is stricter than the ideal the idyll praised.

note: In Natrinai 287 the girl says he came unafraid of the dread crocodile of the backwater; in Thinaimalai 46 the friend bars him from the night when the striking shark circles.
teaches: The night beast of the backwater counts for the girl in Natrinai 287 as the proof of his love and for the friend in Thinaimalai 46 as the reason to stop him and ask for marriage, so the same danger is read by each speaker to serve her own aim.

note: Natrinai 380: the friend refuses the bard, saying our breasts ooze milk, we smell of new birth and are no match for the man of the jewelled women's street. Kainnilai 48: the man does not embrace the sandal-cool breasts; we have grown old with sagging breasts; come for no answer.
teaches: Natrinai 380 makes motherhood the wife's disqualification and Kainnilai 48 makes age, so the pair shows the wife's body at two stages of marriage offered in the same mocking way as the reason the man has gone elsewhere.

note: Kural 1288 addresses the lover as thief whose chest is like toddy that harms; Kuruntokai 318 calls the man thief too, but also the one bound by his oath and the raft who must carry her across.
teaches: The Kural's 'thief' names only the sweet harm, while the poem turns the same title into a claim: whoever stole is bound to restore, so the word becomes the ground of her demand for marriage.

note: Kural 1302, spoken by the friend, says sulking is like salt and a little too much spoils it; Paripadal 6.98-99 has those around the wife say that if the sulk festers much love is spoiled (துனி நனி கன்றிடின் காமம் கெடூஉம்).
teaches: The same counsel to a sulking wife appears in both, but the Paripadal shows it said aloud at the festival and then acted on by skilled pleaders until the sulk is understood, so the Kural's measure of salt turns out to belong to a social practice of reconciliation, not only to one friend's private advice.

note: Purananuru 3 tells the Pandya his word will not move even if the earth moves (நிலம் பெயரினும், நின்சொற் பெயரல்) and is husband of a lady of faultless chastity; Patitruppattu 63 tells the Chera that even when the earth changes its nature his spoken word does not fail.
teaches: The same hyperbole for a Pandya and a Chera shows that the unmoving royal word was shared praise across dynasties, and the Purananuru poet turns it into a lever (so read the suppliant's need) where Kapilar leaves it as one of four bounded traits.

note: Ainkurunuru 43: the woman tells the man his bard is a bigger liar than he is and swears many oaths. Kainnilai 37: the wife tells the bard to stop pouring out lies before her.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 43 ranks the bard's lying above the man's, and Kainnilai 37 lets her silence the bard directly while the man is only named, so together they show the wife's anger moving onto the go-between as the safer target.

note: In 426 the man has given up the king's hard task to stay with his wife; in Akananuru 214 the man in the camp says the war is their own duty (அமரும் நம்வயினதுவே) while imagining her lonely rainy evening.
teaches: Held together, the poems show that the mullai husband's bond to the king's war was not fixed: one binds himself to it despite her loneliness, the other renounces it for her brow, so akam staged a real choice between royal service and the wife.

note: Pannan of Sirukudi is praised in Purananuru 173 as the healer of hunger whose house feeds crowds; in Akananuru 54 his village's gooseberry gives the simile and he is called one who lives not for himself but for others.
teaches: An akam poet could fold a puram patron's reputation into one epithet inside a love poem, which shows how well-known Pannan's generosity was.

note: Kapilar praises Malaiyan in Purananuru 123 as giving more chariots than the raindrops on the heights of Mullur; in Kuruntokai 312, also Kapilar's, the girl comes at midnight filling Malaiyan's Mullur forest with her fragrance.
teaches: The same poet uses his patron's hill both as the measure of a king's countless gifts and as the secret ground of a tryst, which shows a court poet setting his love scenes inside the land he praised in puram.

note: Kural 1134: the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness (the man speaks). Kuruntokai 149: her modesty is a small sand dam that holds as long as it can and gives way when the sweet flood presses (the woman speaks).
teaches: Both picture desire as a flood against shame, but for the man shame is a raft that is swept away with him on it, and for the woman it is a dam that holds the water back, so the shared image is divided by gender: his shame rides the flood, hers resists it.

note: 151: on the hill path a hen whose mate fell to a hawk keeps calling, and the hero decides leaving her would be the end of youth. 154: in the waste a hen whose cock has gone to find food calls in loneliness, and the heroine asks how men learn to part.
teaches: The same carrier, a hen calling for an absent mate on the road, works from both sides of the separation: in the hero's mouth it is the reason he stays, in the heroine's it is the reproach to a man who went anyway, so one native image can hold both the decision and its blame.

note: Both make the woman's pain open with the evening: the Kural's sickness buds at dawn and blooms at evening, and in Kuruntokai 108 the jasmine opens red in the sunset as the cows go home and she says she will not survive.
teaches: The Kural's flower metaphor for the sickness rests on a real mullai sight that Kuruntokai 108 shows, the jasmine opening at red dusk as the herds return, so the couplet's conceit is that scene folded into the body of the woman who watches it.

note: Both turn on the same word. In 594 wealth seeks out அசைவிலா energy. In 371 அசைவின்மை is itself produced by a fate of gain.
teaches: The causal arrow reverses, so the question becomes whether steadfastness is one's own at all.

note: Kural 1268 has the man wish that the king fight and win so that he may join his wife and hold the evening feast; in Natrinai 121 the charioteer reports that the king has let them go and drives him home to the wife preparing the evening feast for guests.
teaches: The couplet is a wish spoken while the war still holds him, the Natrinai poem the same wish granted and on the road, so together they show the full arc of the mullai return, and that the king's release and the evening guest-feast were the fixed terms of it.

note: Kural 1234: with the partner gone, the shoulders lose their old beauty and fullness and the bright bangles slip. Thinaimozhi 47: the heroine asks her friend whether he has abandoned her, as pallor spreads and the bangles of her soft shoulders slip.
teaches: The couplet states the sign as a fact of separation, while the venba makes the heroine read it as a question, has he left me?, so the slipping bangle becomes the evidence by which she learns his desertion rather than its mere effect.

note: Kalittokai 9: the mother asks travelling brahmins whether they saw her daughter and the youth; they say they did, and argue that as sandal, pearl and music serve others than their source, so the daughter belongs to the man she followed. Thinaimalai 89: travellers say they saw the man like the sun and the girl like the moon.
teaches: The venba keeps Kalittokai 9's frame of the mother questioning travellers and their 'we saw them' but drops the brahmins' argument that a daughter belongs to her husband, so the consolation shrinks to an image of a well-matched pair, and the mother is left with a report rather than a reason.

note: Akananuru 47: if we have finished the work here, rise quickly, heart (வினைஇவண் முடித்தனம் ஆயின்). Kar Narpathu 24: rise, heart, leaving all the work lying (எல்லா வினையுங் கிடப்ப). On a plain reading they disagree on whether the task must be done before he turns home.
teaches: The older poem holds the man's return behind the finishing of his task, while the venba's man drops the task once the rain and the memory of her hair reach him, so the same address to the heart sets duty and love in two different orders.

note: In both a king in a rain-soaked camp will not sleep (கண்படை இலனே; பள்ளி கொள்ளான்); in Akananuru the soldier cites it to tell his heart the war is his duty while she hears the evening alone, in Nedunalvadai the poet sets it beside the queen's grief and prays for the war's end.
teaches: The king's sleepless diligence is the soldier's reason for staying away in the Akananuru and the poet's ground for hoping the war ends soon in the idyll, so one camp image can either lengthen the separation or promise its end, depending on whose grief frames it.

note: In Akananuru 66 the husband, dressed for a new wedding, stops his chariot when his son runs to him and gives the wedding up; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 26, as the drums of his new wedding sound, the little one who goes after his chariot comes to grief. On the reading of இவன் as the son, the appeal that succeeds in one fails in the other.
teaches: Akananuru 66 presents the son as the force that turns a husband back from another marriage, and 26 shows the same scene with the opposite outcome, so the son's claim emerges as a hope the wives hold rather than a rule the poems guarantee.

note: Both use the same half-line, திண்டேர்ப் பொறையன் தொண்டி: Akananuru 60 makes the girl's bangle as fine as Poraiyan's Thondi; Kuruntokai 128 makes the girl the ayirai fish of Thondi's harbour, longed for by a wingless heron on the eastern sea.
teaches: Poraiyan's Thondi served the love poets as a stock measure of the desirable, but they could aim it two ways: as a measure of the girl's worth that the man must win by marriage, or, set against the eastern sea, as a measure of how far out of reach she is.

note: Kural 788: friendship clears distress at once, as the hand of a man whose garment slips; Kalittokai 34: the lover has come on the promised day as a hand clears what troubles the eye.
teaches: Both use the hand that moves to the body without thought as the figure of help that needs no asking; the Kural gives it to friendship, the kali to a husband returning on the counted day, so the reflex image measures the ideal of timely help in both public and private bonds.

note: Kural 1222 asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Kalittokai 129 asks the sea, the anril on the palmyra and the little flute in turn whether, like her, they have someone who loved and left them.
teaches: The poem shows the couplet's question as one move in a round of addresses to sea, bird and music, so the Kural's single address to evening reads as a compressed survival of a sung form in which each sound of nightfall is asked whether it too was abandoned.

note: The friend argues that wealth moves from one to another by former deeds (பழ வினை), so leaving to earn it is pointless; Kural 619 holds that even when fate denies, effort pays the wage of the body's labour.
teaches: The friend uses the doctrine of former deeds to keep the man home, while the Kural grants that doctrine only to deny that it excuses idleness, so the same belief about fate served the akam poets as an argument against striving and the moralist as one to be overruled.

note: In Purananuru 343 a father refuses suitors even if they bow and offer wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) like Muziri's, where ships bring gold for pepper; in Akananuru 149 the man refuses precious wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) even if easily won, beside Muziri where Yavana ships bring gold and take pepper.
teaches: Muziri's sea trade was the stock measure of the wealth a woman outweighs, used by the war poem for a father keeping his daughter and by the love poem for a husband keeping his wife.

note: Akananuru 45: the lover crossed a summer forest where the dried pods of the uzhunjil rattle like the drums of a dancing ground. Kuruntokai 39: they say his road is the hard waste where the wind makes the dried uzhinjil pods rattle.
teaches: The rattling uzhinjil pods are a fixed sign by which a waiting woman pictures the man's road; the Akananuru makes the sound a dance drum, while Kuruntokai 39 keeps it as hearsay ('they say'), showing that the woman's knowledge of the waste is report, not sight.

note: Kural 1330 says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is the embrace that follows; Paripadal 20.109-112 says it is the Vaiyai's nature to join lovers so that quarrel, friendship, parting, love and toddy are praised together.
teaches: The Kural's rule that the sulk sweetens union is a statement about two lovers, and the Paripadal extends it to a whole town's festival, closing a poem whose centre was a bitter public quarrel by counting that quarrel among the river's pleasures, so the couplet's private economy of oodal is shown working at civic scale.

note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and those of the six duties forget their books; Patitruppattu 24 names the six duties (ஓதல் வேட்டல் அவைபிறர்ச் செய்தல் ஈதல் ஏற்றல்) and says the king walks by the word of those who keep them, so that the world walks by his.
teaches: The Kural makes the Brahmins' learning depend on the king's protection, while the Chera poem makes the king's conduct depend on the Brahmins' word, so the pair shows the relation running both ways: guarded by the king, they in turn guide him.

note: In both the friend tells the lover that the girl will go with him: in Akananuru 107 because she cannot bear his repeated departures, in Ainkurunuru 236 because the mother knows, gossip has spread and the house is desolate.
teaches: The friend's offer of elopement is made from two opposite pressures, the grief of his going in the Akananuru and exposure at home in the Ainkurunuru, so udanpokku appears in the anthologies as the answer both to separation and to discovery.

note: 60 likens Valavan to the strong ox that drags the salt cart's sunken wheel out of the rut on the road from the backwaters to the hill country; Akananuru 140 likens the speaker's suffering to that of the ox yoked to the father's salt cart sunk in deep mire.
teaches: The salt cart in the mire is a shared image of the coastal trade road, and the two books use opposite ends of it: the puram poet praises the king as the ox that frees the wheel, the akam speaker feels like the ox straining under it, so one working scene serves for strength in one and for heartache in the other.

note: Both have the man say that the woman herself is the only cure for the sickness she causes; the Kural states it as a paradox of medicine, Natrinai 80 says it to his own heart so that the friend who keeps him off will hear.
teaches: The couplet's general paradox becomes in the older poem a lever in a negotiation: by declaring the girl his only medicine where her guardian can overhear, the rejected man turns a private conceit into a claim on the friend's pity.

note: Both are poems in which the hero stops his heart from leaving; 126 argues that youth is worth more than wealth, 137 sets before the heart the tusker who breaks a tree to feed his mate in the drought.
teaches: The same thurai (செலவு அழுங்குதல்) is won once by reasoning and once by an animal example from the very road to be travelled, so the anthology shows two ways a hero could argue himself out of leaving: a calculation of value, or the shame of being harder than a beast.

iraicchi.act: the troop of female monkeys bathes in the falls, swings on the bamboo and frolics together with their male by day
iraicchi.sense: the lovers of this hill should have their joy together openly, as the monkeys do, not by a lone night journey through rain and lightning

iraicchi.act: the tusker, holding his young mate close, brings her down into the hill hamlet by the common ground
iraicchi.sense: as the tusker brings his mate openly into the settlement, the man should take her openly into the village by marriage

ullurai.tenor: desire and the bond that should outlast it

pairs.situation: desire, which comes down in one burst and is spent
the bond, which should go on sounding after the desire has passed

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the rain and waterfall of the hero's own hill in a kurinji poem, without leaving its land (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the anril cries out in the night even while its mate rests close beside it
iraicchi.sense: if a joined bird laments, the heroine parted from her man cannot be asked to sleep

note: Kural 1157: do not the bangles slipping from my wrist spread the news that the shore lord has left me? Ainthinai Ezhupathu 66: will the thief-hearted shore lord walk off by another path while her good bangles slip?
teaches: The couplet makes the slipping bangle a herald announcing his departure, while the venba places it at the moment of his going and calls his heart a thief's, so the pair qualifies the Kural's sign: the bangle that tells the town of his leaving also convicts him of planned deceit.

note: Purananuru 105 sends a bright-browed virali to Pari, saying she will get jewels (சேயிழை பெறுகுவை) and likening his gentleness to water coming down his hill; Patitruppattu 87 sends a singing woman to Poraiyan, saying she will get fine jewels (நன்கலம் பெறுகுவை) and setting his kindness against the cane carried by a flood that bears sandal to the sea.
teaches: Perunkunrur Kizhar splits Kapilar's single guide poem into two of his own, the water likeness in 86 and the sending of the singer with the promise of jewels in 87, which shows how a short Purananuru guide poem served the Patitruppattu poets as a pattern they could take apart.
