note: Akananuru 122 lists the hindrances that keep the lover away (the sleepless town, the mother, guards who hurry, the dog, the moon); the idyll lists nearly the same (guards hurrying, the fierce dog, the mother waking, the moon) as what turns him back every night.
teaches: In Akananuru 122 the girl uses the catalogue of hindrances to complain about their secret love, whereas the friend in the idyll gives it to the mother as proof of the man's constancy, since he goes back each time without anger, so the same list can work as a lament or as a testimonial depending on who is listening.

note: Kural 773 calls generous help to a fallen foe (ஊராண்மை) the cutting edge of valour. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 52: the friend mocks the husband for treating his going to the other street as ஊராண்மை, manliness before the town.
teaches: The Kural makes ஊராண்மை a virtue of restraint toward the weak, while the friend uses the same word for the husband's public swagger in neglecting his wife, so on a plain reading the two give the word opposite contents, and the venba's sarcasm depends on the higher sense the Kural fixes.

note: The same deep-voiced drum (தழங்குகுரல் முரசம்) sounds in both camps; in Akananuru 24 it keeps the sword-bearing army awake at night, in 448 the man meets sleeplessness thinking of her.
teaches: Read together, the drum that keeps the soldiers sleepless for the king's war is the same drum under which the man lies sleepless for his wife, so the camp's wakefulness is shown to be both duty and longing at once.

note: In Natrinai 80 the man says there is no medicine but the girl for his sickness; in Natrinai 64 the deserted woman says that even if he comes he is no medicine for her sickness.
teaches: Read together, the two poems show the anthology using one figure, the beloved as the only cure, at both ends of secret love: the pursuing man asserts it and the abandoned woman revokes it, so the claim holds only while hope does.

note: Kural 428: not to fear what should be feared is folly, and to fear it is the work of the wise. Kalittokai 42 line 26: the friend checks her own reproach, saying he is not a lawless man who fears nothing that should be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சா அறன் இலி அல்லன்).
teaches: The Kural's prudence about danger is turned by the friend into a moral standard for a lover, where what should be feared is breaking a girl's heart, and failing it makes a man அறன் இலி; the pair shows the maxim already working as a test of character in love, not only in counsel.

note: Paripadal 5.48-49 narrates the birth on a lotus bed in the green pool of the Himalaya; Paripadal 8.11-16 says Parankundram equals the Himalaya because its pool equals that pool of the lotus that bore him.
teaches: Read together, the birth story of song 5 becomes the title deed of song 8: the poet claims the Himalaya's sanctity for a Pandya hill by matching its pool to the birth pool, so the myth is used to found a local shrine.

note: In Kural 1151 the friend tells the departing man to promise a quick return only to those who will still be alive; in Ainkurunuru 368 the friend invites him to stay and enjoy the cool summer with them if the girl is not to be ruined.
teaches: Both hold the girl's life against the journey, but the couplet does it by refusing his comfort and 368 by tempting him with the season's pleasure, so together they show the two strategies of the friend who would stop a departure, the bitter and the sweet, around the same threat.

note: Kural 1150 says the town raises the very talk we want and the lover will grant (நல்குவர்) if he wishes; Ainkurunuru 181 says if the shore lord grants (நல்கின்), this clamouring town will be sweet to live in.
teaches: The Kural names the town's clamour as a lever that can push the lover to grant marriage, and the Ainkurunuru poem shows the far side of that lever: once he grants, the same noise becomes the festive kuravai of a town she can live in happily, so gossip and celebration are one sound judged before and after his word.

note: Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet (இறைவன் அடிசேரா தார்) cross the sea of births; Paripadal 21.16 asks only that dwelling at the foot of the god's hill (குன்றத்து அடி உறை) be granted, and line 68 repeats it as dwelling at the god's feet (நின் அடி உறை).
teaches: The Kural's feet are a way out of rebirth, while the Paripadal makes the same feet a place on the ground, the foot of one hill where worshippers ask to go on living, so the pair shows the god's feet as a refuge of release in the ethical book and as a home on earth in the older festival hymn.

note: Both count the girl's posting to the millet field as luck for the secret love: in Natrinai 134 the friend tells the girl that the mother herself sent her with the clapper to the field near the meeting place; in Ainkurunuru 281 the man blesses the parrots whose raids set her to guard.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show that the field watch which makes the day trysts possible is set up by agents who do not know what they serve, the mother by her order and the parrots by their raids, so the kalavu depends on the household's own ignorance.

note: In Akananuru 26 the wife turns to their son and the husband, saying he too loves the child, embraces her back and weeps; in Kuruntokai 359 the friend tells the bard that the man embraced his son and the son's mother embraced the man's back.
teaches: In both reconciliations the son carries the embrace between husband and wife, and with the roles reversed (in one the husband clasps the wife's back, in the other the wife the husband's), so the akam poets made the child the agreed route back into a marriage after estrangement.

note: Kural 1226: the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband had not left; Kuruntokai 352: the woman says she knew the reality of the small dull evening only when she could not see him.
teaches: The couplet states the late discovery of evening's pain as a bare fact, and the poem gives the sign through which she learned it, the creature that leaves its day-tree lonely at dusk, so the knowledge the Kural reports is shown arising from a scene in which the hour itself repeats the parting.

note: Both open with the ripe sweet mango that falls of itself into the water below; in Kuruntokai 8 the courtesan has the vaalai fish snatch it, in Ainkurunuru 61 it drops into the deep pond of Kazhar, the town the wife uses to measure his new women.
teaches: Held together, the formula shows the falling fruit as the man who drops to whoever waits below, used by the courtesan to boast she caught him and by the wife to say he keeps falling into new marriages.

note: Kural 159 says those who bear the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers; the verse ranks those who bear above those who rise up and revile.
teaches: The couplet measures the forbearer upward against the renouncer and the verse measures him against the reviler beside him, so forbearance is placed both by its reward and by the act it refuses.

note: In Akananuru 197 the friend comforts the woman with the image of a tusker embracing his pregnant mate on the man's road; in Ainkurunuru 323 the man himself crosses a road where a red dog hunts for his craving pregnant mate.
teaches: The friend's reassurance rests on an assumption that the man will see such creatures and remember, and Ainkurunuru 323 shows it from his side: he does see the male caring for its mate and finds the girl's nature has come with him, so the comfort offered at home is confirmed by the road.

note: Akananuru 351: the returning man imagines the lizard that chirps whenever she thinks of him sounding at her ear as medicine for her aching shoulders. Kainnilai 18: the friend tells her the truthful lizard has chirped, seeing the traveller come.
teaches: The man in the Akananuru counts on the lizard to announce him and the friend in the Kainnilai reports that it has, so the pair gives both halves of one belief, that the traveller's approach reaches home through the lizard before he does.

note: Akananuru 185: her bright bangles slip as the man crosses summer hills where seed-bearing bamboo bursts with the twang of warriors' bows. Thinaimozhi 18: on the road where sun-split bamboo sheds pearls, her bangles seem ready to fall.
teaches: In the Akananuru the bursting bamboo is a sound of violence on his road, while the venba makes the same bursting shed pearls, a treasure dropped in the land where he seeks wealth, set against her bangles falling for nothing, so the image of the split bamboo is turned from danger to the waste of what is precious.

note: 214 reasons that even if there is no joy beyond, good deeds may end rebirth or leave fame; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there is no higher world.
teaches: Both test good conduct on the supposition that there is no heaven, but the Kural rests there while the king reaches for a further reward, release or fame, so the pair shows two ways of answering doubt about the next world.

note: Kural 1249's woman asks her heart whom it goes seeking when he is within it; Kainnilai 6's girl lets her heart go unspoken to his jewelled chest.
teaches: The heart's going out to the lover is chided as foolish in the Kural's separation chapter but is a silent secret gift in Kainnilai's secret stage, so the same movement of the heart is judged by whether he is still near.

note: Ainkurunuru 71: the wife says people report he bathed yesterday with his beloved (நெருநை ... ஆடினை என்ப), and the gossip can no more be hidden than sunlight. Akananuru 266: the wife opens with the same report (ஆடினை என்ப மகிழ்ந, நெருநை), compares the uproar to a victory feast, then says the gossip is no grief to her beside his broken oath.
teaches: The same reported charge, that he bathed with her yesterday, is the whole case in the Ainkurunuru but only the preface in the Akananuru, whose wife sets the gossip aside for the oath he broke, so the pair shows the bathing formula as a fixed opening of marutham complaint that a longer poem could push past to a deeper wrong.

note: In Kural 1209 the woman's life fails as she dwells on the lack of grace of one who said they were not apart; in Ainkurunuru 109 the friend asks what the many days of his grace were worth now that he has left.
teaches: Valluvar turns the memory of past grace into a slow inward death, while the Sangam friend turns it into a reproach spoken to the mother, so the same memory serves as private lament in the couplet and as public evidence in the decade.

note: Kural 780: a death that fills the eyes of those who maintained one with tears is worth begging for; Mullaippattu's king remembers those who fell having made good the rice they ate (சோறுவாய்த் தொழிந்தோர் உள்ளியும்).
teaches: The Kural measures the warrior's best death by the tears of the one who fed him, and the idyll shows that patron from inside, lying awake over the men who repaid his rice with their lives, so the maxim gains a scene where the debt of food and the king's grief are both seen.

note: 283 line 6 names the assembly hall of the Kosar (கோசர் அவைக்களத்தானும்); Akananuru 262 names the town-elder Kosar (ஊர்முது கோசர்) who blinded Anni Mignili's father.
teaches: Both poets know the Kosar as a body that sits in judgment, an institution in the puram fragment and the source of a borrowed story in the akam poem, so the Kosar's council was famous enough for an akam speaker to cite it as a known wrong.

note: Kar Narpathu 12: the dark clouds, like oiled elephants, rise on the right every day (ஏரும் வலம்), a sign beyond doubt. Ainthinai Aimpathu 1 ends on the same omen, வலனேருங் கார், after giving the cloud the colour of Mal, the spear of Murugan and the garland of Shiva.
teaches: The rightward rise is a fixed reassurance in the mullai venba, and holding the two together shows the Ainthinai poet strengthening a plain omen by assembling three gods' emblems around it, where Kar Narpathu leans on its daily regularity.

note: In Kural 1133 the turned-away man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal that lovers ride; in Natrinai 377 the turned-away man, speaking for the friend to hear, asks whether riding the madal and praising the girl through lands and towns will not kill him like a disease.
teaches: The Kural states what the madal costs the man, his shame, while the Natrinai shows what it would do, carry her beauty's praise through every town, so the threat works on the friend because his loss of shame would become the girl's public exposure.

note: Natrinai 198 gives the foster mother's own words to those she meets in the waste, describing her daughter and blessing them; Ainkurunuru 390 gives the onlookers' reply to a woman who folds her hands to every good person and asks again and again.
teaches: Natrinai lets the searcher speak and Ainkurunuru shows how she looked to those she asked, wandering and worshipping strangers, so the two halves of the wayside exchange make up one recognised scene in which the onlookers' certainty answers her supplication.

note: Kural 1222's woman asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Natrinai 343's woman asks whether there is no such evening in the land where her lover went.
teaches: Both turn the woman's grief into a question about where evening reaches, but the Natrinai grounds it in a village dusk of cows, offerings and a crow going home to its kin, so the couplet's bare question gains the scene that makes the absent man's freedom from evening seem unnatural.

note: The Kural says only those who live by their own ploughing truly live and all others bow to eat and follow behind; the idyll's bard, who lives by praise, is fed millet and beans at the farmers' village.
teaches: The idyll shows the arrangement the Kural ranks: the bard is exactly one who eats from another's plough, yet the guide poem treats being fed by farmers as the patron's honour and the bard's due, not as a lesser life, so the Kural's verdict is a moral claim against the old patronage order.

note: The Kural's man says the fire she gives burns when he moves away from her (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம்); Ainkurunuru 322's man, far from her on the summer road, says the thought of her makes the burning path cool (தண்ணிய).
teaches: Held together they give opposite laws for distance: in the couplet absence from her is the source of heat, while in the desert poem absence is already given and her remembered presence is the only coolness, so whether she burns or cools depends on whether the man is measuring his desire or the land.

note: The idyll makes the battle of Venni, where two great kings fell on one field, the crown of Karikalan's praise; Puram 66, addressed to Karikalan himself, says the king who was wounded in the back at Venni and starved himself facing north is the better man.
teaches: The same victory at Venni is in one poem the proof of Karikalan's greatness and in the other the occasion for saying the loser surpassed him, which shows that praise addressed to a victor could, in this poetry, rank the defeated king's honour above the win itself.

note: In Akananuru 164 the man in the war camp says she would regain her old beauty in this season if only the king released him from his work (வேந்தன் வினைவிடப் பெறினே); 498 reports that the king left off his war (வேந்துதொழில் விட்டென) and her shoulders, bangles and eyes recovered.
teaches: Read together, the two poems give the conditional and its fulfilment of one plot, and show that in these mullai returns the woman's beauty hung on the king's campaign, not on the husband's will alone.

note: Kural 555: the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction wear away the wealth of the king who causes it; Kalittokai 34: her eyes stream like the subjects under a king whose justice has failed.
teaches: Read with the Kural, the woman's tears carry the threat the moralist gives to the subjects' tears, that they wear down the ruler who causes them, so her weeping is an accusation against the absent husband as well as a sign of grief.

note: Kural 1185: look there, my lover is going; look here, the pallor is spreading on my body. Kuruntokai 205 asks how the pallor on her forehead knew so soon, when the shore lord has only now driven away.
teaches: The couplet's two pointing words make his going and her paling one instant; the Kuruntokai poem has the same instant but turns it into a question to the pallor itself, and supplies the scene the couplet leaves out, the white chariot rising like swans and the sea spray on its wheels.

note: Kural 1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe; Kuruntokai 272 likens her eyes to the bloody arrow her brothers drew from a stag near a doe parted from its herd.
teaches: The poem stages the couplet's three-way question as one hunt: doe, killing shaft and eye stand together, and because the shaft belongs to her brothers, the deadliness of her look is also the threat of her kin to the suitor.

note: Both have the man set the gods' world against lying in the beloved's arms: the Kural asks whether Vishnu's world is sweeter, Kuruntokai 101 puts earth and heaven together on one pan of a balance against a single day of embrace.
teaches: The Kural's open question about heaven has an older Sangam answer: the poet had already weighed both worlds together against one day and found them light, so the couplet's question reads as an allusion to that verdict rather than a doubt.

note: Both have the thunder (ஏறு) make the gem-bearing serpent cower (மணி நாகம் அனுங்க) as the rain-cloud goes. Kar Narpathu 20: the returning man tells his charioteer the king's work is done. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 28: the friend tells the heroine the beauty spots will spread on her breasts.
teaches: A near-identical half-line serves at both ends of the journey, in the returning man's mouth and in the waiting woman's friend's, which shows the serpent cowering at the thunder as a shared formula of the mullai rains rather than one poet's image.

note: Kural 616: effort produces prosperity and its lack ushers in poverty. Natrinai 52: the heart set on ஆள்வினை is loveless, and wealth made by toil is a slight thing.
teaches: The Kural makes effort the source of fortune and the duty of a man; the husband of Natrinai 52 calls the heart that obeys that duty loveless and declares its fruit slight, so read together they show that the ethics of ஆள்வினை and the akam of the home make incompatible claims on the same man.

note: Natrinai 71 opens by calling wealth impermanent (மன்னாப் பொருள்) to keep the man at home; Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so whoever gets it should do at once what lasts.
teaches: The same premise, that wealth does not last, yields opposite advice: the Kural tells a man to seek and spend it on what endures, the friend uses it to argue he should not seek it at all, which shows nilaiyaamai served the akam poets as a rhetorical weapon before it was a doctrine.

note: Akananuru 66: the husband, dressed to wed another, is drawn home by the little son who runs to his chariot, and the wife says the old saying about sons has proved true. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51: the wife sends the bard away, saying her little son with gold bangles is her companion.
teaches: The son works on both sides of the marutham quarrel: in Akananuru 66 he pulls the straying father back into the house, in the venba the wife holds him up as companion enough to refuse the father's go-between, so the child is at once the husband's way in and the wife's reason to keep him out.

note: 1066 says nothing shames the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow. 780 says this death is worth begging for, with the same root (இர-).
teaches: Only something beyond the Kural's worst disgrace could justify the word.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 71-77 places the hill west of Koodal, with bees humming over pool flowers that open like eyes; Paripadal 8.17-28 makes the same bees, pools and flowers the god's procession, the coming from your hill to Koodal (குன்றத்தான் கூடல் வரவு).
teaches: The guide poem fixes Parankundram by its position beside the city, while the Paripadal turns the road between them into a seasonal procession of sound and bloom, so together they show the shrine defined by its tie to Madurai rather than as a lone mountain retreat.

ullurai.tenor: the ooran who takes the girl's beauty and keeps to his own house

pairs.situation: he takes the ripe bloom of the girl
he withdraws with it into his own home and does not come back

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the crab and paddy of the marutham field, without leaving the poem's land (porul 7.27)

iraicchi.act: the hen, her mate struck down by a hawk as he rose, cannot find him and keeps calling
iraicchi.sense: a woman left behind would call so for a man lost on such roads, so the hero who hears it will not leave his beloved

iraicchi.act: the gull lays its eggs and makes its home in a boat at the ford
iraicchi.sense: even the gull settles its household at his landing, so he too should take her home and make a household with her

iraicchi.act: the sparrows come back at evening to the nest in the eaves and stay there with their young
iraicchi.sense: even the house sparrow is home with its young at nightfall, while he stays away in another land

iraicchi.act: the stags come in together with their herd at evening and leap for joy
iraicchi.sense: the beasts come home in company at dusk, which the man who left has not done, and so both of them suffer apart

iraicchi.act: in the drought the tusker scoops water from the rock spring and runs with it to his mate
iraicchi.sense: even on that road a male's first care is his mate, so the man crossing it holds his wife in mind and works for her

note: In Akananuru 292 the girl dreads the stranger velan's rite and the kid's killing because she would be ashamed; in Kuruntokai 263 the friend protests that the same rite praises strange gods that cure nothing and brands the girl as possessed.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the veri rite wounding the secret love from both sides: to the girl it threatens exposure, and to the friend it threatens a false name, possession, for a love she insists is blameless.

note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart whom it goes out looking for, since the beloved is already within it. Kainnilai 21: the woman says her heart has gone after the man, swimming the long way through the scorched forest.
teaches: Both women speak of a heart that leaves to follow the man, but the Kural calls that going needless because he lives inside her, while the Kainnilai takes the heart's long swim as real, so the pair sets an inward answer to absence against the older picture of the heart travelling the road.

note: Both open with உள்ளார் கொல்லோ தோழி, the friend asking whether the men who crossed the waste will not think of them; Kuruntokai 16 answers with a lizard calling to its mate, Natrinai 92 with a tusker winning water for its mate and calf.
teaches: The formula comes with its answer, a male creature caring for its mate on the road the man has taken, and the pair shows that answer sharpened: a lizard's call only reminds, while a tusker that provides and then moves on mirrors the man who left to provide, so the friend's comfort lies in the likeness.

note: Paripadal 11.106-110 tells literally of a youth whom the Vaigai's current carries off while a girl takes his heart (கடும் புனல் கை வாங்க, நெஞ்சம் அவள் வாங்க); in Kalittokai 98 a husband swears he was delayed bathing in the Vaigai's new flood, and his wife answers that people saw the new flood drag him off, a flood that was a woman.
teaches: The wife's figure of the woman as a flood that carried him off is the Paripadal's festival event turned into an accusation, so the river festival was both the occasion of a man being swept away by a look and the stock excuse for it, and the Kalittokai's irony depends on the audience knowing the Paripadal scene.

note: Kar Narpathu's friend sees flowers bloom like the woman's eyes and hears them announce his return; in 492 the man sees peacock, mullai and deer as likenesses of her and comes home.
teaches: The same likening of the season's things to the woman works from both ends of the separation: for her the flowers that resemble her eyes are messengers of his return, while for him the creatures that resemble her are what sent him home, so the comparison is the bond that carries the promise across.

note: Ainkurunuru 41 says the lord turns gold-pale the bodies of those who trusted his word; Akananuru 146 has the wife foresee that the next woman who believes the deceiver's word (வாய்மொழி நம்பி) will weep and go pale as she did.
teaches: Held together, the two show that pallor from a trusted word was a fixed charge against the marutham husband: the Ainkurunuru states it as a habit of his town in four lines, and the Akananuru turns the same charge into a forecast for the rival, so the wronged wife becomes the proof of what awaits the other woman.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai has a flesh-eating demoness dance the thunangai after the god kills Sur; here the bard's praise is likened to the finger-snapping before the goddess of the thunangai, mother of the one who killed Sur in the sea.
teaches: Both guide poems use the Sur victory and its thunangai dance, but the god's guide poem uses it to praise the god while the king's guide poem makes it the model for praising a man, so the form of Murugan's praise was lent to the praise of a patron.

note: Kural 222 says taking is bad even if called the good path to heaven, and giving good even if there were no higher world; thirattu 12 praises a city that rejoices to see receivers (ஏற்பாரைப் பார்த்து உவக்கும்) and ranks its life above heaven. On the reading that ஏற்பார் are those who take gifts, the fragment honours the very taking the Kural calls bad.
teaches: Both cut the value of giving loose from heaven, but the Kural does it by condemning the receiver while the Paripadal makes the receiver's presence a joy of the city, so the two hold opposite views of whether asking belongs to the good life.

note: Both turn on the leaf-garment and the pun on வேங்கை (kino tree and tiger); in 20 the tigers are the girl's brothers and mother and the gift is refused, in 31 the tiger is the man himself and his gift is praised.
teaches: Read together, the friend moves the tiger from the girl's family to her lover as she moves from turning the leaf-garment away to pressing the girl toward him, so the same pun marks which side of the courtship holds the danger at each stage.

note: Paripadal 8.10-11 says that because of the god Parankunram equals the Himalaya (பரங்குன்று இமயக் குன்றம் நிகர்க்கும்); Paripadal 18.5-6 says this hill takes up the contest to stand level with the hill that bears the god's glory (ஏறுமாறு ஏற்கும் இக் குன்று).
teaches: Song 8 states the equality as a settled fact granted by the god's presence, and song 18 turns it into a challenge the hill still accepts, so read together they show the Paripadal poets making Parankunram's rank against the northern mountain a standing claim each hymn renews.

note: Salt in both, and both about intimacy that hurts a little.
teaches: In 802 the worthy are salt to friendship's liberties, and in 1302 lovers' sulking is salt that spoils when overdone. 1302 supplies the measure 802 leaves out.

note: Verse 3 gives the chaste wife public praise and power over rain; verse 4 says any garlanded woman's heart turns to a new man even if she has the love god.
teaches: The surviving fragments hold both the highest claim for a wife's chastity and a denial that any woman's heart stays put, so either the lost story set them in different mouths or it made chastity a rare exception; the conflict depends on reading verse 4 as about all women.

note: Kural 1090 says brewed toddy (அடுநறா) delights only those who drink it, unlike love, which delights those who see it; Paripadal 21.20 has a dancer held by the joy of brewed toddy (அடு நறா மகிழ்) sulking at her husband, and the poet says such scenes, when recalled, are a painting's beauty.
teaches: The Kural separates the drinker's private pleasure from the beholder's pleasure in love, while the Paripadal mixes them in one woman, drunk and sulking at her husband, and makes her a picture for onlookers on the hill, so held together they show that at the shrine festival even the drinker's mood became something seen and enjoyed by others.

note: Akananuru 91 says the man would not stay away even if he gained Kuttuvan's rich Kudanadu; in Natrinai 105 the man's heart, midway on the road, turns back to her hair, fragrant as the kuvalai of Kuttuvan's western hill.
teaches: What the friend in Akananuru 91 asserts from outside, that Kuttuvan's whole land would not hold him, Natrinai 105 shows from inside his heart, where Kuttuvan's country survives only as a measure of her fragrance.

note: Kural 559 says that if the ruler bends justice the sky withholds rain; Kalittokai 99 praises the king for rains that come by his rightness and then asks whether his wife alone lies outside that rightness.
teaches: The Kural ties rain to the king's public justice only, while the Kalittokai grants the rain and still finds injustice at home, so the friend shows that the doctrine's measure of a ruler can be met in full while a wife is wronged.

note: Kar Narpathu 33: the man says he set as his sign the time when the cloud that drew up the sea (கடனீர் முகந்த) would gather on the western hill. Kainnilai 34: as the cloud that scooped the sea pours (கடல்முகந்து கார்பொழிய), the lover has come.
teaches: Held together, the two verses close the loop of the mullai promise: one poet's hero names the sea-drinking cloud as his appointed sign, and the other poet has the lover arrive exactly as that cloud breaks.

note: In Akananuru 242 the mother calls the diviner not knowing that the man who chased parrots from the millet with them came to the girl in love; in Natrinai 288 the friend fears the diviner will say the girl went to scare small parrots from the millet and Vel seized her.
teaches: Natrinai 288 puts in the diviner's own verdict the very scene Akananuru 242 says the mother does not know, so the pair shows the veri's error lying not in the facts but in the agent: it finds the right place, the millet field, and names the god instead of the man.

note: In Akananuru 74 the friend comforts the heroine that the man, seeing the rain-washed scrub, will think of her and say 'drive, charioteer of the strong chariot'; Ainkurunuru 488 is a returning man saying just that as the rains begin.
teaches: Akananuru 74 shows the waiting wife doubting the comfort that he will remember her at the rains, and Ainkurunuru 488 gives the very order the friend predicted, so the decade supplies the man's side of a promise that the akam comforting formula only foretells.

note: Kainnilai 45: we are old now and did not know he would leave. Kainnilai 48: grown old with sagging breasts, we want no answer from him.
teaches: In 45 her age is the vantage from which she sees his promises were false, and in 48 it becomes the ground of her refusal, so the decade moves age from grief to a reason for closing the door.

note: The Kural's worthy man is like the balance that first levels itself and then weighs; the idyll's court is straight like the balance once it has put away fear, grief, desire, hatred and delight.
teaches: The idyll's list says what the Kural's 'first making itself level' consists of, the clearing of five named passions before judgment, so the couplet's compressed image can be unpacked from a description of a working court.

note: Purananuru 105 says Pari's gentleness is sweeter than the water that comes down every peak of his hill (நீரினும் இனிய சாயல்); Patitruppattu 86 says Poraiyan is sweeter and cooler of gentleness than the water of the Vaani (வானி நீரினும் தீந்தண் சாயலன்), after the poet admits he had feared him for his slaughter in war.
teaches: The formula of a patron gentler than running water passes from Kapilar's hill chief to a Chera king, but the later poet sets it against the king's reputation for bloodshed, so the same praise is used to answer a suppliant's fear of a warrior king.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone her shoulders lose their old beauty and fullness and the bangles slip. Thinaimozhi 19: the woman, picturing him halting in the stony waste where the doe cries with the stag, says her shoulders slip with her bangles.
teaches: The couplet gives the wasting shoulders as the plain sign of absence, and the venba supplies what she is thinking of while they waste: his fear on the road and the paired deer that keep together, so the symptom is tied to an imagined scene rather than to absence alone.

note: Both open on striped frogs croaking and close the scene with the formula கார்தொடங் கின்றே காலை.
teaches: The identical formula leads in Akananuru to an evening the heroine cannot swim through and in Ainkurunuru to a chariot arriving today, showing that the first-rain formula was a neutral hinge onto which either the dread of evening or the promise of return could be fastened.

note: Both picture a public hall (பொதியில்) fallen to ruin, its pillar abandoned by its god; in Purananuru 52 it is the fate of lands the Pandya conquers, in Akananuru 307 a dove clings to it with its mate.
teaches: A ruined hall abandoned by its god was a stock picture of a conquered land, and the akam poet turns it round: even in that ruin a pair of birds keeps faith, which makes the hero's leaving harsher.

note: Kuruntokai 8 has the courtesan boast that the husband talks big at her house but dances like a mirror puppet to his son's mother; Ainkurunuru 67 has the wife call the new woman naive for matching herself against her, since the women who have drawn him off outnumber bees. On one reading each woman claims the other holds no power over him.
teaches: Each side belittles the other through the man's nature, the courtesan by making him the wife's puppet and the wife by making him a bee of countless flowers, so neither woman's speech can be taken as the truth of the household.

note: In Kural 1168 the woman says the night that lulls every creature to sleep has only her for company; in Kuruntokai 86 she asks at midnight whether anyone else hears the cow's bell.
teaches: The Kural asserts that she alone is awake; the Kuruntokai poem tests the claim with a question and finds one other wakeful thing, a lonely cow whose bell rings with her, so the solitude the Kural states is shown as a search for a companion.

note: Both idylls have women reassure the waiting wife with the words இன்னே வருகுவர் (they will come soon), and both have her refuse it in tears: காட்டவுங் காட்டவுங் காணாள் கலுழ்சிறந்து here, உகத்தவை மொழியவும் ஒல்லாள் மிகக்கலுழ்ந்து in Nedunalvadai.
teaches: The promise of a quick return and the wife's weeping refusal form one fixed sequence in both idylls, but Mullaippattu takes the promise from a herd-girl's words to a calf, read as an omen, while Nedunalvadai puts it in the grey-haired nurses' mouths as plain comfort, so the convention let the same words come from chance speech or from household authority, and in both the comfort must fail.

note: 376 calls the joining that sent the girl away a fate without right; 394 says the loveless right has after all shown grace (அன்பில் அறனும் அருளிற்று).
teaches: The same poet lets the verdict on அறம் turn with events, loveless when the girl left and gracious when she returns, so in these decades the moral order is judged by its outcome for the household rather than held fixed.

note: Both open with the friend's formula to the mother, அன்னாய் வாழி வேண்டு அன்னை, answering her question why the girl has grown pale (பசந்தனள்); in Akananuru 48 the friend tells the whole story of the hunter who came asking after a tiger, in 366 she answers only that the kongu has flowered.
teaches: The shared formula shows these are two answers to one stock question: Akananuru 48 discloses the love by a full story and leaves the wise to infer the rest, while 366 compresses the same disclosure into one seasonal sign, so the reader learns how far the friend's hint could be shortened and still be understood.

note: Both name the same five, taste, light or sight, touch, sound and smell; the Kural, in its chapter on renunciants, puts the world in the grasp of the one who discerns them, while Paripadal 13 says the five and the faculties that take them are the god.
teaches: The Kural's five, which the renunciant must master, are in the Paripadal the god himself, so the same old list of five could ground either a discipline of withdrawal from the senses or a worship through them.

note: Kural 1168: the night, which puts all living beings to sleep, is to be pitied, for it has no companion but her. Kuruntokai 28: she wants to strike, butt or cry out at the town that sleeps unaware of her pain.
teaches: Both set one sleepless woman against a sleeping world, but the Kural turns the loneliness into pity for the night, while the Sangam poem turns it into rage at the town, which shows that the same isolation could be voiced as tender complaint or as a wish to wake everyone.

note: Both are men arguing with hearts set on wealth, and both make the desert's killers the argument: in 327 the archers pity no victim and grieve only when they miss; in 337 the Mazhavar kill a starving messenger in case he has gold and leave scorning his rags.
teaches: Side by side they show the road weighing a man's life only by what he might carry, which is the very reckoning the heart is making when it trades her company for wealth.

note: Akananuru 1's woman asks whether he has forgotten his word that they would never part (பிரியலம் என்ற சொல்) now that he has gone for gold; Ainkurunuru 336 says he embraced her as if he would never part (பிரியலர் போலப் புணர்ந்தோர்) and went for wealth.
teaches: Akananuru 1 rests the betrayal on a spoken vow, while the Ainkurunuru wife rests it on the embrace alone, so together they show that in paalai the embrace itself was read as a promise that the pursuit of wealth broke, with or without words.

note: The same line, the otter getting a vaalai fish as its daily food, addresses the husband in both; in Kuruntokai 364 it is spoken by the household concubine answering the wife's slander, in Ainkurunuru 63 by the wife refusing him.
teaches: Because rival women use the identical otter line, the image belongs to the husband, a daily hunter in his own pond, and each woman fits it to her side of the quarrel.

note: Kural 1157 says the bangles slipping past the wrist spread the news that the lord of the shore has left; in Natrinai 136 the father fits the girl with golden bangles that cannot slip, which hide the blame of her shoulders.
teaches: If, as the Kural says, slipping bangles are the body's gossip, the Natrinai shows that gossip could be silenced by a tight bangle, so the sign of separation was something a household could conceal, though only the lover could cure what it signified.

note: Akananuru 135 likens the heroine's shaken heart to Kazhuvul's Kamur when fourteen Velir attacked it together; Patitruppattu 71 has Kazhuvul, chief of those who live by cattle, bow his head (கழுவுள் தலைமடங்க) when the Chera's archers drove off the herds.
teaches: Kazhuvul is besieged by a coalition of Velir in one poem and humbled by the Chera in the other, which shows his herders' stronghold as a repeated prey of greater powers and explains why an akam poet could use it as a byword for a heart under assault.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend shows the bloomed konrai and the dancing peacocks and calls the season medicine for the pallor. Kuruntokai 148: the friend denies that the konrai and kurundham mean the rains, and the heroine asks if she is dreaming.
teaches: The friend's proof from the season only works before the season is spent; once the konrai has bloomed and he has not come, the same flower proves his breach, so the comforter must deny the season and the heroine turns the argument against her.

note: In both the bard who came for the shore lord is told to report what he has seen of the woman: Natrinai 291 கண்டாங்கு உரையாய், Ainkurunuru 140 காண்மதி பாண நீ உரைத்தற்கு உரியை.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 140 names the message only as the state of her slipped bangles, while Natrinai 291 fills the same eyewitness report with a puram image of cattle raided at night, so the pair shows the three-line convention of the bard as witness expanded by borrowing from war poetry.

note: Tirumanthiram 10 says he himself is the earth, the sky, the fire, the sun, the moon, the rain and the sea (தானே opening each line); Paripadal 4.25-34 says only that two of the god's qualities are in each of the sun, moon, rain, earth, flower, water, sky and wind, and that these came about by parting from him (நிற் பிரிந்து).
teaches: The two lists cover nearly the same things, but the Sangam hymn keeps the god outside them, each element holding a pair of his qualities as a share that left him, while Tirumular erases the gap and makes him the things themselves, so the pair shows identity with the elements was a later and stronger claim than participation.

note: Both use the formula of the world that cannot do without water (நீர் இன்று அமையா உலகம், நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு): Kural 20 as the first step of an argument that all conduct depends on rain, Natrinai 1 as the measure of how she cannot live without him.
teaches: The same clause is a step in Valluvar's proof about rain and a simile of a woman's dependence in Kapilar, which shows it was a common saying both drew on, apt to the akam poet for a lover's need as it was to the moralist for the world's.

note: Both are Perumpathumanar's onlookers on an eloping pair: in Kuruntokai 7 they ask who these good, pitiable people are, the bowman and the girl with anklets still on, heading into the bamboo wilds; in Natrinai 2 they say the youth's heart is crueler than mountain-shaking thunder.
teaches: The same poet lets the onlookers pity both runaways in one poem and in the other lay the whole blame on the man who leads her into the tiger's country, so the kandor voice was a place to judge the hero, not only to witness the pair.

note: Both name the seven givers (Pari, Ori, Kaari or Malaiyan, Athikan or Ezhini, Pekan, Aay, Nalli), with the shared formula for Pekan's hill guarded by a fearsome god (அருந்திறல் அணங்கின் / அருந்திறல் கடவுள்) and the same closing என ஆங்கு எழுவர.
teaches: The seven were a fixed list with stock epithets that a poet could set before a living patron, and the two poems use it differently: Perunchithiranar says the seven are dead so Kumanan must take their place, while the idyll says Nalliyakkodan already bears alone the yoke the seven bore together.

note: Kural 1309: sulking, like water in the shade, is sweet only with those who love. Ainthinai Aimpathu 27: the faded wife asks whether she is still one the man would sulk at.
teaches: The Kural's rule that a quarrel belongs inside love lets the wife read the man's absence of pulavi as the absence of love, so the venba shows the rule used as evidence by someone on the losing side.

iraicchi.act: the stag clasps its doe and takes shelter with her as the rain-evening comes
iraicchi.sense: even the beasts seek their mates for shelter at the evening of the rains, while the man who should be with her has not come

iraicchi.act: the male sea crow, having caught a red prawn, searches the backwater and calls the mate it loves to share it
iraicchi.sense: even the shore bird provides for and calls its mate, while the man has not yet married the girl

iraicchi.act: the boar rears and protects the striped young whose mother the tiger killed
iraicchi.sense: even the boar guards its motherless young, yet the man has forgotten and left his wife and son

iraicchi.act: the crab plays with its mate
iraicchi.sense: even the crab keeps its partner at play beside it, while the man who should have stayed has gone

iraicchi.act: the stag returns to frisk with its sweet mate when the rains come
iraicchi.sense: even the stag keeps the season and comes back to its mate, yet the man who promised has not

iraicchi.act: the crows hang on the dripping branch through the rainy night, sustained only by thinking of the feast to come
iraicchi.sense: she too lies awake through the cold night living on the thought of what she longs for, and he who knows it is not with her

iraicchi.act: the birds pair and stay together on the branch, calling
iraicchi.sense: even the birds keep with their mates in this season, while he has gone off like a stranger

note: Kuruntokai 320: on the dune of drying fish and prawns she has not even one day's laughter with the shore lord to be blamed for, yet the town gossips. Kainnilai 54: on the same drying-ground he lied to her and enjoyed her beauty. On a plain reading one heroine denies what the other confesses.
teaches: The prawn-drying ground serves one heroine as the scene of an innocence the town will not credit and another as the scene of her seduction, so the stock place of neythal kalavu could carry either a defence before the town or an accusation of the lover.

note: Ainkurunuru 9: the girls wish that their bond with the lover not become town gossip (அம்பல்). Kural 1143: the man welcomes the gossip the whole town knows, since it feels like having her already.
teaches: The same talk of the town that the women pray to escape is a pleasure the man savours, so read together the two show that in secret love gossip threatened the woman's standing while it flattered the man's hopes.

note: Natrinai 335: the sea's sound never stops and the tide comes and goes, and with the anril and the lute the night cannot be survived. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 60: the sea, like her, does not sleep as the tide shifts, because the shore lord took her beauty and left.
teaches: In the Natrinai the restless sea is one of the things that keep the heroine awake, while the venba makes the same tide sleepless for her own reason, so the pair shows the neythal sea turning from a cause of sleeplessness into a fellow sufferer.

note: Kural 616 says effort brings prosperity and its absence brings want; Natrinai 252 states the same as the man's resolve (no rare wealth for those who stay) and then shows the planned work blocked by the woman's beauty.
teaches: The pair shows the maxim of effort accepted in full by the lover and yet not acted on, so the Natrinai marks the limit of the Kural's rule: it decides nothing while something dearer than prosperity stands in the way.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is the messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). Kainnilai 35: the herders, heedless, blow the sweet pipe at that hour.
teaches: The couplet makes the flute a weapon; the Kainnilai adds that those who wield it do not know they are wounding anyone, so the evening's weapon kills without a killer who intends it.

note: Akananuru 374: campaign over, the man bids the chariot go through the morning rains so the slender wife may receive him as a guest. Natrinai 221: the man bids the charioteer go so he may hear his small son's first call to him.
teaches: Both homecoming speeches to the charioteer turn on விருந்து, but the Akananuru makes the returning husband the guest his wife receives, while the Natrinai makes the wife the one who loves receiving guests and adds the son, so the convention could place the hero either as guest or as master of a hospitable house.

note: In Akananuru 122 the house cock and the owl that eats house rats are among the night's watchers that keep the secret lover away; in Kuruntokai 107 the wife curses the cock for ending her sleep beside her husband and wishes it prey to the wildcat that hunts house rats.
teaches: Held together they show that marriage did not free the lovers' night from its old enemy: the cock that guarded the house against the secret lover still cuts short the wedded night, and the wife's curse sends it to the very rat-hunters of the courtship poem.

note: Kuruntokai 73 (Paranar) tells of the Kosar who cut down Nannan's fragrant mango and drove him from his land; Kuruntokai 292 (Paranar) tells of Nannan killing a girl who ate a green fruit the stream carried down, refusing eighty-one elephants and her weight in gold.
teaches: Read together, Paranar's two poems hold both halves of one tale, the cruelty over a fruit and the tree's later felling, and each friend uses a different half: one as a model of hard scheming, the other as the type of cruelty to curse a watchful mother with.

note: Both pair the town's gossip with the mother's word: Kural 1147 says gossip is manure and mother's words water to this sickness; in Ainkurunuru 113 the town names her the lord's woman, mother calls her, and she says it is only a fever (வெம்மை).
teaches: The Kural calls the love a sickness that gossip and the mother feed, and the poem shows the girl turning that very likeness into her alibi, naming the fever and hiding its cause, so the couplet's metaphor began as the lover's cover story.

note: Both mark the loss in the shoulders and the slipping bangle: Ainkurunuru 28 has the bright bangle loosening as the soft shoulders pale (ஒண்டொடி நெகிழ, மென் தோள் பசப்பது); Kural 1234 has the bangle slipping from shoulders that have lost their old beauty.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru friend uses the paled shoulders to tell the mother that a man, not the ford goddess, is the cause, while the Kural keeps only the signs, so the couplet's portrait of wasting shoulders was in the older poem a piece of evidence in a disclosure.

note: 141: the heroine asks the friend to tell the lover not to come in the deep night, when the tiger lies in wait on the slope. 153: her heart, once afraid of an owl or a monkey in the yard, now goes along the slope to him in the dense dark night.
teaches: The dangers of the night slope are the argument she uses to keep him away, yet her own heart travels that road without fear, so the pairing shows the night-danger plea as care for him rather than prudence she lives by.

note: In Akananuru 170 the woman begs the crab to carry her word to the shore lord, since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 42 she begs the crab not to trample his chariot's tracks.
teaches: Taken together they show why the crab is the neythal heroine's confidant: it alone moves where the lover moved, so she can ask it either to carry her word to him or to spare the one trace of him she still has.

note: The Kural man cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the Ainkurunuru man knows she is a shore girl and says she is harder to win than the mountain nymphs (வரையர மகளிரின் அரியள்).
teaches: The likeness to a goddess can carry two different fears: in the couplet it is bewilderment at what she is, in the shore poem it is despair of reaching her, so the divine comparison in akam measures distance as often as beauty.

note: Akananuru 364's heroine says the rains have begun and her lover in the fierce king's great camp, set on victory, does not think of them (நம்மும் உள்ளார்); Ainkurunuru 461's friend says the men of the victorious king's camp will not rest content having left her.
teaches: The same facts, the rains begun and the man held in a victorious king's camp, support despair in the heroine's mouth and assurance in the friend's, so the mullai situation was fixed and only the speaker decided its meaning.

note: In Kuruntokai 2 the man asks the pollen-seeking bee whether any flower is more fragrant than his woman's hair; in Ainkurunuru 240 the friend says bee swarms crowd his chest because it smells of the fragrant girl's hair.
teaches: The scent of her hair that the lover praises in private to the bee is the very thing that betrays the secret union to the friend, so the bees that witness his boast in one poem become the witnesses against him in the other.

note: In Kural 1130 the woman says he lives in her heart while this town (இவ் வூர்) says he is loveless and far; in Ainkurunuru 110 the friend says we call him ours while this town (இவ்வூர்) says otherwise, and asks fate to make it so.
teaches: Both set the lovers' word against the town's, but Valluvar's woman rests in her inner certainty while the Sangam friend turns to fate to make the bond public, so the couplet's private comfort appears in the older poem as a demand for marriage.

note: Kural 1269: for those who wait for the day of return, one day passes like seven; Kuruntokai 271: one day of union has turned into very many days of sickness.
teaches: The couplet stretches the waiting days, the poem multiplies the one day of joy into a long illness, so the woman's suffering is measured not only by slow time but by a debt that a single meeting keeps collecting.

note: Perunkoppendu in Purananuru 246 refuses a widow's life and chooses the pyre; the female monkey in Kuruntokai 69, unable to bear widowhood (கைம்மை உய்யா), leaves her young with kin and leaps to her death.
teaches: The akam friend borrows the puram queen's refusal of widowhood and gives it to a creature of the hill, making the girl's not outliving her lover a law of nature for the night-visitor to weigh, not a royal vow.

note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the wife tells the bard to carry to the other women the man's description as lord of the town where the red-eyed buffalo breaks its clog, sinks into the pond and gorges on the crop. Kainnilai 37: the rutting buffalo plunges into the pond before the wife tells the bard to stop lying.
teaches: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49 tells the bard to deliver the buffalo as the man's own portrait, which shows that in Kainnilai 37 the same plunging buffalo set before the bard is a character sketch of the husband and not just the setting of his town.

note: Mangudi Kizhar ends Purananuru 24 by saying that the only ones who truly lived are those who, born in the wide world, did not pass with the many but stayed in fame; in the idyll he says the kings who ruled the wide world with their fame spreading are more than the sand on the shore, and are gone.
teaches: The same poet who told this king that fame alone outlasts death here counts the famous kings by the grains of sand, so fame does not exempt anyone from passing and is itself common; the counsel of the idyll is harder than the short poem's consolation, and the pair shows the kaanchi argument being sharpened by its own author.

note: Both say the lute is outdone by one's child: Kural 66 that only those who have not heard their children's prattle call the lute sweet; Ainkurunuru 410 that the bard's lute did not match the hour when the son rode on his father's chest.
teaches: The Kural's maxim has a scene behind it in which the lute is actually playing in the courtyard while the child plays, so the comparison was first a judgment between two pleasures heard together, and the child's worth lay in the whole family hour, not in speech alone.

note: Kar Narpathu 4's friend calls the season of humming bees and a forest in bloom the medicine for the heroine's pallor (பசலை மருந்து); in Ainkurunuru 342 the bees revel on the flowering nunavam and he has not come.
teaches: The friend can call the flowering season a cure only because it guarantees his return; Ainkurunuru 342 shows the same flowering turning into the sickness once the season arrives without him, so the convention's comfort is only as good as the man's timekeeping.

note: Fragment 1 states as the poet's rhetorical question that enemies have no way but to submit (பணிந்துவழி மொழிதல் அல்லது); Purananuru 17 gives the enemy kings' own words as they decide to submit to the Chera Irumporai for fear of losing their walls and forts.
teaches: Held together, the two show that the Chera praise poets treated submission not only as the king's due but as a reasoned choice the enemy makes on seeing his anger, so the boast of the fragment rests on a scene of calculation that Purananuru 17 spells out.

note: Kalittokai 11: the woman recalls that the man, calling the forest cruel, told her the tusker there lets his mate drink the little muddy water first and the stag gives its own shade to the doe. Aimpathu 38: the stag, judging the pool's little water too scant, feigns drinking so the doe drinks.
teaches: Kalittokai puts the beasts' care in the man's own report, so the woman reasons that one who saw and told it will not let her wither; Aimpathu 38 adds the stag's pretence, a deceit in the service of love, and sets it on the road his heart has already taken, so the same proof is offered from the friend's side and made finer.

note: Verse 64 makes tending guests the duty by which a chaste wife is a friend; verse 63 counts a bangled wife who dreads guests among things that yield no good.
teaches: The two adjacent verses give the same rule from both sides: hospitality is the wife's first duty, and failing it alone makes her a loss to the house.

note: In 66 the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking the untimely rain for the season; in 382 the friend says the rain itself is untimely, since if it were the season the man would have come.
teaches: The friend's comfort moves from blaming the tree to denying the season: in 66 nature is fooled by false rain, in 382 the man's promise is made the test of what the rain is, so his word outranks the calendar of flowers.

note: Paripadal 9.70-85 says that on the god's hill dancers outdo dancers and bards outdo those practised in song, the skilled the skilled; Paripadal 17.9-21 matches each human performer not with another performer but with a thing of the hill doing the same act.
teaches: Song 9 makes the festival a rivalry of like with like among people, and song 17 widens the rival to the bee, the falls and the peacock, so the pair shows that for these poets the god's hill was praised by contest itself, and the strongest praise was to have nature enter the contest.

note: Akananuru 388 would ask the velan whether his god goes hunting with blood-smeared arrows; Ainkurunuru 250 tells the beads that Vel, lord of the valli forest, is not the afflicter.
teaches: Akananuru separates god from lover by asking about the lover's hunt, Ainkurunuru by naming the god's own peacock and valli, so together they show the girls answering the rite by setting the two lords side by side in each other's emblems.

note: Kural 599, in the chapter on energy (ஊக்கமுடைமை), says the elephant, for all its bulk and sharp tusks, fears a tiger's attack; Kalavazhi Narpathu 16 shows horses, urged on (ஊக்கி) by picked warriors, leaping onto the elephants' brows like tigers springing up a hill.
teaches: The battle verse turns the Kural's animal fable into tactics: the tiger's assault on the elephant is what cavalry does to war elephants, so the couplet's claim that drive overcomes size had a familiar picture on the field, and Poigaiyar's simile names the driving force with the Kural's own word.

note: Fragment 4 has the bard come to see the king (வந்தனென் பெரும கண்டனென்) in his camp with the army camped in foreign land (வேறுபுலத்(து) இறுத்த ... தானையொடு), where elephants full of strength (மைந்துமலி) tear up their posts; Purananuru 22 ends with the poet come to see the Chera Irumporai (வந்து இனிது காண்டிசின்) with his army camping in foreign land (வேறுபுலத்து இறுக்கும் தானையோடு) and opens with strong elephants (மைந்து மலிந்த மழ களிறு) standing at their posts.
teaches: The shared phrases show that the bard's visit to a Chera king in his foreign war camp was a set scene with its own diction, and the one change, elephants standing quiet at the post in Purananuru 22 against elephants tearing the post up in the fragment, turns the same scene from settled order to war still pending.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 167 gives the attending gods as a sum (நால்வேறு இயற்கைப் பதினொரு மூவரொடு); Paripadal 8.4-7 names the same thirty-three group by group: twelve, two who speak of medicine, eight, and eleven from the lord of Aathirai.
teaches: The guide poem's 'eleven times three of four kinds' is spelled out in the Paripadal as four counted groups, showing that the Vedic thirty-three were known in Tamil by their divisions and that both poets made Murugan the one they attend.

note: In both the fallen vengai flowers look like a tiger: in Akananuru 228 a she-elephant bolts from them on the man's moonlit way home, in Thinaimalai 26 the girl will not survive his night visit.
teaches: Akananuru 228 shows the vengai's false tiger frightening a beast on the path, and Thinaimalai 26 transfers that fright to the waiting girl, which shows that the friend's case against the night visit rests on fear of a likeness rather than on any real tiger.

note: Kural 1061 says not asking even from those who give gladly is worth ten million times more; 159 treats asking a glad giver as honourable and refuses only the grudging gift.
teaches: The bard's code and the Kural's draw the line of dignity in different places: for the bard the giver's gladness makes asking clean, for the Kural even the gladdest giver does not, so the Kural's chapter on the dread of asking rejects the very compromise the parisil poems lived by.

note: 784 says friendship isn't for laughter (நகுதல்). 860 makes நகல் the very source of good ways, which Parimelazhagar glosses as friendship.
teaches: The same root gets very different valuations in the chapter on what friendship is for and the chapter on hostility.

note: Kuruntokai 200: surely he has forgotten, but we do not forget; Kural 1207: what would become of her if she forgot, when she knows no forgetting and remembering burns.
teaches: The Kural keeps forgetting inside the woman, as a danger she cannot afford, while Avvaiyar turns it outward as a charge against the man, proven by the rains that came on time, so the same refusal to forget can be self-torment or an accusation.

note: Both use the reign of a weak ruler (மெல்லியான் பருவம்) for nightfall: in 129 the confused dark comes like the weak reign after a just king; in 120 the cruel evening vanishes as the enemy of a weak reign is driven off when a good king appears, the lover's return.
teaches: The same poet places one political figure at both ends of the night, darkness arriving as misrule after a just king and lifting when a rightful king returns, so in these poems the absent lover stands in the place of the king and his coming restores order, not only pleasure.

note: Purananuru 109 is Kapilar's boast during the siege of Paari's Parambu that the three kings cannot take it by force; Akananuru 78 recalls Paari with Kapilar beside him, holding out for years and driving away the kings with elephants.
teaches: The akam poem treats as settled fame what the puram poem speaks in the middle of the siege, so Paari's resistance with Kapilar had become a reference point another poet could use to praise a girl's fragrance.

note: Kuruntokai 140: the woman asks how the gossiping town came to know the grief she bore in silence; Kural 1180: the woman says it is not hard for the town to learn the secret of those whose eyes beat it out like a drum.
teaches: The Kural answers the Kuruntokai woman's question: she kept silent, but her eyes told the town, so the gossip she resents is her own grief made public by her body, not betrayal by anyone else.

note: Ainkurunuru 219: the friend asks why the girl's forehead pales since the hill man went away. Kural 1188: the woman complains that people say she has grown pale, and no one says that he left her.
teaches: The friend's question names the man's leaving together with the pallor, which is exactly the acknowledgement the Kural's woman says the world withholds, so the pair shows the friend as the one voice that ties the girl's pallor to the man who caused it.

note: Naladiyar 370 makes the fresh flood (புதுப்புனல்) a type of what does not last: it ends when the rain ends; Paripadal 7.84-86 prays to the Vaiyai's flood that the bathing in it may never be left (நின் படிந்து நீங்காமை).
teaches: The same new flood that the ethical quatrain uses to prove that pleasures and loves dry up is, in the festival hymn, the object of a prayer for permanence, so the pair shows the didactic poet reversing the devotional value of the river by fixing on its ending rather than its yearly return.

note: Kural 1189: the woman says let her body turn pale as it will, if the man who persuaded her is well. Kuruntokai 27: her beauty, of use neither to her nor to him, is left for pallor to eat, like milk spilt on the ground.
teaches: The Kural lets the woman accept pallor as a price paid for his welfare, while the Kuruntokai poet counts it pure waste, a yield that reaches no one, so the same pallor in absence is read as sacrifice in one and as loss with no gain in the other.

note: Both are by Peri Saathanar and both name the man as the one who chased parrots from the millet with them (கிளி கடிந்து ... நம்மொடு; கிள்ளை நம்மொடு கடிந்தோன்): in Natrinai 25 he leaves without finding a chance to speak, and in Akananuru 242 the mother, not knowing this same man came in love, calls the velan.
teaches: Read together, the poet's one formula marks two stages of a single courtship, the silent visitor at the millet field whose plea the friend carries and the unseen cause of the sickness the mother misreads, so the parrot-chasing stranger is what separates the friend's knowledge from the mother's ignorance.

note: Kuruntokai 315: the heroine says the hill man is like the sun (ஞாயிறு அனையன்) and her shoulders like the nerunji flower. Thinaimalai 89: the man is like the hot sun and the girl like the cool moon.
teaches: In the Kuruntokai the man as sun makes the woman a nerunji that turns after him, while in the venba she is the moon, a second light of her own, so the same sun-image yields dependence in one poem and parity in the other.

iraicchi.act: the reed of his town serves as float and partner to the women bathing in the flood
iraicchi.sense: as his town's reed partners the bathing women, so the man partners them and not his wife

iraicchi.act: the old lame stork goes hunting and brings sea fish to his pregnant hen, who cannot reach the shore
iraicchi.sense: even a crippled old bird provides for the mate who carries his young; the man, whole and young, has not even married the girl he has made to suffer

iraicchi.act: the anril feeds and roosts on the palmyra always joined with its mate
iraicchi.sense: the bird that never parts from its mate is the fitting voice to shame the man who parted from her

iraicchi.act: the hunter brings his kill home to his own hut and household in open delight
iraicchi.sense: the man should likewise take what he has won home openly, instead of coming to her by night and by day
